Take a rubber band and pull it by both ends. It gets longer, and we can see it. Now take a steel bar and pull it with the same force. It looks as if nothing has happened. Yet the steel bar has also become longer, only by so little that our eyes cannot notice it. This is true of every object: when a force acts on it, it changes its shape. When we step onto a bridge, the bridge bends a little. When we sit on a chair, the legs of the chair get a little shorter. When a motor drives a shaft, the shaft twists a little, one end more than the other.

The band, the bar, the bridge, the chair and the shaft have something in common. They are all made of material, and under a force they all change their shape. So mechanics calls them by one name.

Definition 1.1 Body (telo)

A body (telo) is an object made of material whose motion and change of shape we study. We imagine the material distributed continuously, without gaps, so that every point of the space the body occupies is a point of the material. So a body is made of points. This picture of matter is called a continuum (kontinuum).

Source: CM §3.2.1 (PDF p. 111), CM §1.1 (PDF p. 30).

In reality matter is made of molecules with empty space between them. But molecules are so small that for a bridge, a shaft or a bar only pieces containing an enormous number of molecules matter. So we may treat matter as if it filled space without gaps (CM §3.1, PDF p. 110). When we speak of a point of a body, we mean a point of this continuous material.

From history

Until the end of 1820 nobody had tried to derive general equations of rest and vibration for bodies that return to their original shape after unloading. Only separate theories were known, for bending and twisting and for the vibration of bars and plates, and even these were incomplete (LOVE, PDF p. 23). From the eighteenth century the picture of Isaac Newton prevailed, that bodies are made of small particles that act on one another with forces (LOVE, PDF p. 23). Navier was the first to try to derive general equations from it. He read his memoir to the Paris Academy in May 1821 (LOVE, PDF p. 23). He took the molecules as points, and the force between two of them as one that changes when their distance changes slightly (figure 1.1, LOVE, PDF p. 23). In his view the response of a body to a change of shape arose from these changes of the forces (LOVE, PDF p. 23). To obtain the equation for one molecule he had to add up the forces of all the other molecules on it. This is a triple sum, which he replaced by continuous summation over the volume, that is, by matter without gaps (LOVE, PDF p. 24). We take the same step: there are enormously many molecules in a small piece and they are small, so we replace the sum over them by summation over continuous matter. Navier's contemporaries, however, did not grant him this without objection. The validity of the procedure was disputed and his derivations were not generally accepted (LOVE, PDF p. 24). Siméon Denis Poisson and Augustin-Louis Cauchy followed Navier's example, and according to Augustus Edward Hough Love their molecular theories differ greatly from today's picture of molecules (LOVE, PDF p. 24).

Changes of shape of bodies under a force are mostly small, but they decide whether a structure holds. A structure (konstrukcija) is anything built to carry forces, such as a bridge, the frame of a building or a machine part. It holds if under the forces it does not break and does not bend or stretch so much that it can no longer do its job. A bridge that bends a few centimetres under a truck is fine. A bridge that bends a metre is not. So we begin the book with the question of how to describe a change of shape with numbers. We will build the answer step by step, starting from the simplest case. Where we need new mathematics, we will stop and develop it completely, and then return to mechanics.

1.1 A bar that stretches

The simplest case is a straight bar (palica), a body that is much longer than it is thick. If we cut the bar perpendicular to its length, we get a face called a cross section (prečni prerez). The axis of the bar is the straight line along the bar through the centres of its cross sections. We pull the bar at both ends along its axis. The forces that act on a body are called its loading (obremenitev), so we speak of the bar before loading and after it. Before loading it has length \(L\). When we pull it, it has length \(L + \Delta L\). The number \(\Delta L\) is the elongation (raztezek) of the bar, that is, the change of its length. In this book the Greek letter \(\Delta\) (delta) always means a change: we read \(\Delta L\) as "the change of the length \(L\)". If we compress the bar, it gets shorter, and the elongation is negative.

Is the elongation a good measure of how strongly the material of the bar is stretched? Take two bars of the same steel with the same cross section, one 1 m long and the other 2 m, and pull them with the same force. The longer one stretches twice as much. This is no surprise. We can think of the longer bar as two shorter ones placed end to end (figure 1.4). The force that pulls the longer bar pulls each of the two halves, so each half stretches as much as the short bar, and together they stretch twice as much. But the material in the two bars is loaded the same: every centimetre of the longer bar stretches exactly as much as every centimetre of the shorter one. So the elongation does not tell us how hard the material is loaded. Mostly it tells us how long the bar is.

What matters for the material is the stretch of every centimetre, of every metre, that is, the elongation per unit length. We get it by dividing the elongation by the length.

Definition 1.2 Strain of a bar (deformacija palice)

A bar with initial length \(L\) that stretches by \(\Delta L\) has the strain (deformacija)

\[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L} . \tag{1.1}\]

Source: BARBER §1.2.1 (PDF p. 32), EP Example 2.3.1(d) (p. 60), SADD §2.2 (PDF p. 42).

In everyday language "deformation" means a change of shape. In mechanics the number that measures this change is called the strain. Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit: the metres cancel. For the 1 m bar and the 2 m bar of our example we get the same strain, which is what we wanted. Other books also call this number the relative elongation or the engineering strain, and often write it \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), where \(x\) is the direction of the axis of the bar. Why two indices when there is only one direction? For a bar one would indeed be enough. In a body that is not a thin bar, however, we will describe the strain of the material around a point by several numbers, and each of them will be fixed by two directions. When the two directions are the same, as in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the number measures how strongly the material is stretched in that direction. When they differ, as in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the number describes how the right angle between the directions \(x\) and \(y\) changes. A deck of cards pushed sideways at the top leans over: the cards keep their length, but the right angles in the side face of the deck become slanted (figure 1.5). So the index \(xx\) says that the number measures a change of length in the direction \(x\) and not a change of angle. We will meet these numbers properly when we describe strain in space (SADD §2.2, PDF pp. 41-46).

From history

Dividing the elongation by the original length seems obvious today, but it was not always so. In 1826, in the first printed edition of his book on strength of materials, Navier described a material by the ratio of the force per unit area of the cross section to the elongation per unit length (TIMO, PDF p. 81-82). The elongation per unit length is our strain (1.1). How he arrived at this ratio we will tell in section 2.2.

During his visits to the Venetian arsenal, Galileo Galilei noticed that larger things are weaker than smaller ones of the same shape. In his words, a small obelisk or column can be set up or laid down without danger, but very large ones collapse at the slightest push, and only because of their own weight (TIMO, PDF p. 19). To prove this, in his book published in 1638 he first took a bar that is pulled along its length, and found that the strength of the bar is proportional to the area of its cross section and does not depend on its length (TIMO, PDF p. 19). Why? A bar with twice the cross section is like two equal bars side by side, which share the force. A longer bar, however, is not weaker, because each of its cross sections is pulled by the same force as in a shorter bar, if we neglect the weight of the bar (section 1.2). Then he built the same bar with one end into a wall, so that it stuck out horizontally, and loaded it at the free end. It breaks, he wrote, at the edge of the wall, around which the bar turns like a lever around its support (figure 1.6, left) (TIMO, PDF p. 19-20). He assumed that at the break the whole cross section at the wall resists equally (TIMO, PDF p. 20). A force tends to break the bar off the more strongly, the larger it is and the farther from the edge it acts, as with a lever. Galileo enlarged the bar in his mind by the same factor in all dimensions, say twice (figure 1.6, right). Its weight becomes eight times larger, because the bar is twice as long, twice as wide and twice as high, and it acts twice as far from the edge, so it tends to break the bar off sixteen times more strongly. The resistance of the cross section grows with its area, which becomes four times larger, and with the distance from the edge to the middle of the cross section, which becomes twice as large, so only eight times in all (TIMO, PDF p. 21). A larger bar is therefore weaker, and a big enough one breaks already under its own weight (TIMO, PDF p. 21). So in his view ships, palaces and temples of any size cannot be built (TIMO, PDF p. 21).

In 1678 Robert Hooke published a treatise on springs, the first published treatise on how materials change their shape under a force and return to their original shape when unloaded (TIMO, PDF p. 26). He fixed the upper end of a wire 20 to 40 feet long, about 6 to 12 m, to a nail, and hung a pan for weights from its lower end. He put weights into the pan and measured by how much the wire stretched (figure 1.7). The elongations were always in the same ratio as the weights that caused them (TIMO, PDF p. 26, 28). From such experiments with wires, springs and wood he concluded that the change of shape is proportional to the force (SADD, PDF p. 7, TIMO, PDF p. 28). When bending a strip of wood he also noticed that the fibres on the convex side are stretched and those on the concave side are compressed (figure 1.8, first view) (TIMO, PDF p. 28). Mariotte corrected Galileo's calculation, because he took into account that the fibres stretch (TIMO, PDF pp. 29-30). In the cross section of a bent beam one part of the fibres is in tension and the other part in compression (figure 1.8, second to fourth view) (TIMO, PDF p. 29-31).

So lengthening and shortening came from pulled wires and bent beams. The second kind of change came from sliding. In 1773 Charles-Augustin Coulomb presented to the French Academy a memoir that dealt, among other things, with why masonry pillars and the soil behind retaining walls fail (TIMO, PDF p. 55). He assumed that a pillar pressed from above breaks along an inclined plane, along which one piece slides over the other (figure 1.9, left). In his view the failure happens when the part of the force that lies in this plane becomes larger than the resistance of the material to sliding along it (TIMO, PDF p. 59). Why does a force that presses the pillar straight down have a part in an inclined plane at all? Let us cut the pillar in our mind along an inclined flat surface and look only at the upper piece (figure 1.10). We neglect the weight of the pillar. Then only two things act on the upper piece: the load, which pushes it down along the axis of the pillar, and the lower piece across the cut. The upper piece is at rest, so the lower piece must push it up with a force of the same size, also along the axis, just as the pulls on the two cuts of a piece cut out of the bar pulled by a force at its lower end are equal (figure 1.12, middle). But a force along the axis is not perpendicular to the inclined cut. So we can split it into a part perpendicular to the cut and a part lying in the cut, although nobody pushes the pillar sideways. With the part in the cut the lower piece holds the upper one back from sliding down along the cut. If the material cannot carry that much, the upper piece slides, as on the left of figure 1.9. The force at which this happens, calculated in this way, agreed well with his experiments on brick (TIMO, PDF p. 59). The slide was resisted by the material sticking together across the plane, which we call cohesion (kohezija), and by friction (trenje) along it (TIMO, PDF p. 59). For the soil behind a retaining wall he likewise assumed that it slides along some flat plane (TIMO, PDF p. 69). In 1784 he determined how a wire resists twisting from the oscillations of a metal cylinder hung on it (TIMO, PDF p. 59), and in a twisted wire, too, parts of the material shift relative to each other, as we will see in chapter 16. So lengthening and shortening on one side and sliding on the other were at first two separate kinds of failure.

Why there are exactly two kinds was shown by Cauchy, who by the autumn of 1822 already had the idea of the force per unit area at a point of a body (SADD, PDF p. 7, LOVE, PDF p. 25). In doing so he generalised the notion of hydrostatic pressure (LOVE, PDF p. 25).

Let us return to the numbers with two indices by which we will describe the deformation of a material around a point: some measure changes of lengths, others changes of right angles, as in the deck of cards. Why there are exactly two kinds of change is shown by Cauchy's generalisation of hydrostatic pressure, with which the story ended. Let us see what such pressure is. Water at rest presses on every surface perpendicular to it, however the surface is tilted. Such a force per unit area is called pressure (tlak) (CM §8.1.1, PDF p. 384). Why is pressure perpendicular to the surface? A solid body can resist a force that tries to shift one part of it relative to another, but a fluid cannot. Under such a force a fluid deforms without end, that is, it flows (CM §8.1.1, PDF p. 384). If the force between the water and the surface were not perpendicular to the surface, it would also have a part lying in the surface, and this part would shift the water next to the surface along it. The water would flow. A fluid at rest therefore acts on a surface only with pressure, with no part lying in the surface (CM §8.1.1, PDF p. 384). Let us ask what happens if in a solid body the force can point in any direction. We cut the body in our minds with a flat surface and ask with what force per unit area one part of the body acts on the other across this surface (figure 1.9, right). Such a force has a size and a direction. Every force can be split into a part perpendicular to the surface and a part lying in the surface. The first part pulls or pushes, as in a bar that we pull. The second tries to shift one part of the body relative to the other, as in the deck of cards. So there are two kinds of failure because a force has only these two parts with respect to a surface. The change of shape is similar. A short piece of material can change its length, and two pieces that were perpendicular can change the angle between them.

So the material close to a point can change its shape in two ways. Its lengths can change: in some direction the material gets longer when we pull it, or shorter when we push it together, which is called compression (stiskanje). Or the right angles between directions can change, as in the leaning deck, where the cards slide past each other. This is called shear (strig). Each of the numbers with two indices measures one of these two changes.

Definition 1.3 Normal and shear strain (normalna in strižna deformacija)

A normal strain (normalna deformacija) in a direction is the change of length of a short piece of material lying in that direction, divided by its original length. It is positive when the material gets longer and negative when it gets shorter. A shear strain (strižna deformacija) of two perpendicular directions is a number that describes how the right angle between them changes. It is positive when the right angle between the positive directions gets smaller. Which number exactly measures this change we settle in section 1.17.

Source: SADD §2.2 (PDF pp. 42-43).

From history

Cauchy's memoir was presented to the Academy in September 1822 but was not published. Its contents appeared in the 1827 volume of his Exercices de mathématique (LOVE, PDF p. 25). He showed that the force per unit area at a point is determined by six numbers. He described the change of shape by six numbers too (LOVE, PDF p. 25).

The six numbers that describe the change of shape at a point are three normal strains, one for each axis, and three shear strains, one for each pair of axes. Together they describe completely how the material close to a point is deformed, as long as the deformation is small (SADD §2.2, PDF p. 43). We will derive them when we describe strain in space, in section 1.17.

Which of the two changes we see depends on the directions we look along. In the leaning deck the cards keep their length, and only the right angle between the directions \(x\) and \(y\) changes. But a line drawn on the side face of the deck from one bottom corner to the opposite top corner gets longer, and the line between the other two corners gets shorter. Along these two directions the same deformation is stretching and compression. We will check this with numbers on a sheared cube in section 1.6.2. Cauchy also showed that at a point there are three perpendicular surfaces on which the force is perpendicular to them, with no part lying in the surface (LOVE, PDF p. 25). The same holds for the change of shape: for every small deformation there are three mutually perpendicular directions in which there is no shear at all, only stretching or compression (LOVE, PDF p. 25, SADD §2.4, PDF p. 49). We will meet them in definition 2.62. We will prove that such directions exist in chapter 2, in section 2.11.4.

We will meet Cauchy's cut in chapter 2, in section 2.5, the split of the force into two parts in definition 2.18 and the surfaces without shear in section 2.11. Karl Culmann (CAJORI, PDF p. 312) in 1866 (TIMO, PDF p. 224) and Otto Mohr later represented the force per unit area at a point by a circle, which engineers still draw today (SADD, PDF p. 71), and we tell their story in section 2.12.3. For the history in more detail, SADD recommends the books by Isaac Todhunter and Karl Pearson, by Love and by Timoshenko (SADD, PDF p. 7).

How large are strains? A steel bar 2 m long that stretches by 1 mm has the strain

\[\varepsilon = \frac{0{,}001\ \text{m}}{2\ \text{m}} = 0{,}0005 ,\]

five ten-thousandths. A rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm has the strain \(5\ \text{cm} / 10\ \text{cm} = 0{,}5\), a thousand times more. For structures one more number matters. If ordinary structural steel is stretched by more than about one thousandth of its length, it does not return to its original length when we let go, but stays permanently longer. This bound follows from the data for steel in BOWER (Tables 3.1 and 3.9, PDF pp. 100 and 156). We will see how to compute it once we know how the strain of a bar depends on the force that pulls it. So the strains in steel structures are almost always smaller than \(0{,}001\). This is one of the most important facts in this book, because many simplifications will rest on it.

For a compressed bar \(\Delta L\) is negative, so the strain is negative too. A positive strain means lengthening, a negative one shortening.

The number \(\Delta L / L\) is not the only measure of stretching, only the simplest. Books use others too, and we will meet them when we need them. The stretch (razmerje dolžin) \(\lambda = (L + \Delta L)/L\) compares the new length with the old one and equals \(1 + \varepsilon\). The Green-Lagrange strain \(\big((L + \Delta L)^2 - L^2\big)/(2L^2)\) compares the squares of the lengths and equals \(\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/2\) (CM (3.4.15), PDF p. 131). The logarithmic strain is the logarithm of the ratio \((L + \Delta L)/L\) (BOWER, PDF p. 589). For \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) the Green-Lagrange strain is \(0{,}0010005\) and the logarithmic strain \(0{,}0009995\), both differ from \(\varepsilon\) by half a per mille of its value. For the rubber band with \(\varepsilon = 0{,}5\) they are \(0{,}625\) and \(0{,}405\). So for small strains all the measures give almost the same number, for large strains they differ a lot, and then we must say which measure we use. Until we say otherwise, the strain of a bar means \(\Delta L / L\).

The formula \(\varepsilon = \Delta L / L\) has a hidden assumption. When we divided the longer bar into two halves, we assumed that both stretch the same. More than that, we assumed that every centimetre of the bar stretches the same as every other. What if this is not so?

1.2 When a bar does not stretch the same everywhere

Hang a steel bar from the ceiling and let it hang. Apart from the ceiling that holds its top end, only its own weight acts on it. The top part of the bar has to carry the weight of the whole bar below it. The bottom end carries almost nothing. So we expect the top centimetres to stretch more than the bottom ones. If we measure the total elongation \(\Delta L\) and divide it by \(L\), we get some average, which does not tell us how the material is stretched at the top and how at the bottom. We want to know how the material is stretched close to each point of the bar, separately for every point.

Figure 1.12 shows the difference. Before loading we draw marks on the bar at equal distances, like the marks on a ruler. If we pull the bar by a force at its lower end, and its weight is negligible compared with the force, every piece between two neighbouring marks is pulled by the same force, and all the gaps grow equally. Under its own weight the top gap grows the most, because the piece at the top carries the whole bar below it, and every gap lower down grows a little less. The lowest piece carries only its own weight and hardly gets longer. The two loaded bars in the figure have the same total elongation, so the same average \(\Delta L / L\), and yet the material in them is stretched very differently.

Why is the pull the same everywhere in the first bar but not in the second? Let us cut out one piece between two marks in thought, as drawn to the right of each loaded bar. The part of the bar above the piece pulls it up, the part below pulls it down. The piece is at rest, so the forces on it balance (EP (2.5.3)). In the bar pulled at its end nothing else acts on the piece, so the pull from above is exactly as large as the pull from below. This holds for every piece, and the lowest one is pulled by the force at the end, so every piece is pulled by that same force. In the hanging bar the piece also has its own weight. The pull from above must carry both the pull from below and the weight of the piece, so it is larger by exactly this weight. Going up the bar, the pull grows by the weight of one piece at every mark, from zero at the bottom end to the weight of the whole bar at the top (BARBER (1.33)). So the difference lies in where the load acts. The force at the end acts at one place only, the weight acts on every piece of the material. Books call a force that acts on every bit of the material, like weight, a body force (prostorninska sila), and a force that acts on the surface of a body, like the pull at the end, a surface force (površinska sila) (SADD §3.1, PDF p. 63). We will write the balance of forces exactly in chapter 2. The forces in the figure are drawn to scale: the force at the end is half the weight of the bar. The pull in the hanging bar falls evenly from the weight of the whole bar at the top to zero at the bottom, so on average it is half the weight. If a piece stretches in proportion to the force that pulls it, as we will see for steel, both bars therefore stretch by the same total amount.

How do we describe that? We follow the points of the bar. We label a point by its distance \(x\) from the top end of the bar, measured on the bar before loading. Books that distinguish the position before loading from the position after it often write this distance with a capital \(X\) and the new position with a small \(x\). The top of the bar is at \(x = 0\), the bottom end at \(x = L\). When the bar hangs, every point moves down a little. How far the point that was at distance \(x\) moves, we write as \(u(x)\) and call the displacement (pomik) of that point. So the displacement is the difference between the new and the old position of the point. The top of the bar is fixed to the ceiling, so it does not move: \(u(0) = 0\). Points lower down move more, because the elongations of all the parts of the bar above them add up.

Now pick a short piece of the bar between the points \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) (figure 1.13). Its initial length is \(\Delta x\). The top end of the piece moves by \(u(x)\), the bottom end by \(u(x + \Delta x)\). If the bottom end moves more than the top end, the piece has become longer, by the difference of the two displacements:

\[\Delta u = u(x + \Delta x) - u(x) .\]

The piece is a bar too, and the formula (1.1) holds for it at any length: its strain is the elongation \(\Delta u\) divided by the length \(\Delta x\). It has to be short because we want to know how the material is stretched close to the point \(x\), not an average over a longer part of the bar. The formula (1.1) has a hidden assumption, that every part of the bar stretches the same. Only then does the number \(\Delta L / L\) tell how the material is stretched in every part of the bar, and so also at the point \(x\), otherwise it is only an average. In the whole hanging bar the assumption does not hold, but in a short piece it nearly does. As with the pieces between the marks, the pull at the top end of the piece is larger than the pull at the bottom end by exactly the weight of the piece. In a hanging bar of uniform thickness, 10 m long, this weight is a tenth of the pull at the top for a piece 1 m long at the top, and only a thousandth for a piece 1 cm long. So almost the same force pulls every part of a short piece, and since steel, as we will see, stretches in proportion to the force, all its parts stretch almost the same as the material at its top end, close to the point \(x\). The strain of the piece therefore tells almost exactly how the material is stretched close to the point \(x\):

\[\varepsilon \approx \frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} . \tag{1.2}\]

The sign \(\approx\) means "approximately equal". Even within the piece the strain changes a little from top to bottom, so this is still an average, only over a shorter part of the bar. The shorter the piece, the less the strain changes within it, and the better the number describes how the material is stretched close to the point \(x\). The point itself has no length, so it cannot be stretched. Only the material near it can, and the shorter the piece we take, the closer to the point we look.

Let us try this with numbers. In chapters 2 and 3 we will compute that a steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m, equally thick everywhere and made of one steel, hanging under its own weight, stretches so that the displacement of the point at distance \(x\) from the ceiling is

\[u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2), \qquad a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

The constant \(a\) depends only on how heavy steel is and how strongly it resists stretching (BARBER (1.39) with the data for mild steel from BOWER, Table 3.1). We do not need to understand it now, we will only compute with it. The top of the bar is at \(x = 0\), where \(u(0) = 0\), as it must be. The bottom end moves by \(u(10\ \text{m}) = a \cdot 100\ \text{m}^2 = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, two hundredths of a millimetre. A ten-metre steel bar stretches under its own weight by less than the thickness of a sheet of paper.

Let us compute the strain of the piece (1.2) at the top of the bar (\(x = 0\)) and at the middle (\(x = 5\) m) for shorter and shorter pieces:

length of the piece \(\Delta x\) at the top at the middle
1 m \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}757 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
0,1 m \(3{,}884 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}932 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
0,01 m \(3{,}902 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}950 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
0,001 m \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\)

The numbers settle. At the top they approach about \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), at the middle about \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), exactly half. The material at the top is stretched twice as much as at the middle, which agrees with our expectation that the top part carries more weight. Why exactly half? Every cross section of the bar carries the weight of the part of the bar below it. The cross section at the top carries the whole bar, the one at the middle only the lower half, so half the weight. The bar is equally thick everywhere, and in steel the elongation of a short piece is proportional to the force that pulls it, as long as we do not stretch it beyond about \(0{,}001\), the value from section 1.1: half the force gives half the elongation. We will learn this when we connect the force in a bar with its strain, and the formula for \(u(x)\) above is derived from it (BARBER (1.39)). The same reasoning predicts more. The weight carried by a cross section decreases evenly from the top to the bottom, in proportion to the length of the bar below the cross section, and at the bottom end it is zero. The strain should change in the same way. We will confirm this by calculation in section 1.4.

So it seems that every point has its own strain, the number that the strains of shorter and shorter pieces approach. But what exactly does "approach" mean? A table cannot be the answer. It shows only a few rows, and from them we do not know for certain how the numbers behave further on. And we cannot shrink the piece to nothing, because in the formula (1.2) we would get \(0/0\), a division by zero. We need an exact meaning of the words "the number that the ratio approaches as \(\Delta x\) gets smaller and smaller", and a way to compute that number without tables. This is a job for mathematics, and the next section does it.

1.3 Mathematics: limit and derivative

In this section we forget the bar for a moment. We have a rule that assigns a number \(u(x)\) to every number \(x\), and we ask how fast \(u(x)\) changes as we change \(x\). The answer will be a new number. Once we can compute it, we return to the bar.

When computing we use the school rules for real numbers: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, and working with inequalities. The absolute value \(|a|\) of a number \(a\) is the distance of the number from zero: \(|3| = 3\), \(|-3| = 3\). Precisely, \(|a| = a\) if \(a \ge 0\), and \(|a| = -a\) if \(a < 0\) (LEBL1 §1.3, PDF p. 36). So the distance between the numbers \(a\) and \(b\) is \(|a - b|\).

1.3.1 Function

From history

In 1718 Johann Bernoulli defined a quantity that depends on a variable as a quantity composed in any manner of that variable and of constants (CAJORI, PDF p. 227). Such a quantity is an expression that we write with a formula, for example \(x^2 + 5\).

This definition became too narrow in problems of physics. In 1747 Jean le Rond d'Alembert was led, by the vibrating taut string, to an equation containing rates of change in two variables, in place along the string and in time (CAJORI, PDF p. 257-258). In solving it he restricted himself to quantities that can be expanded in an infinite sum of powers, while Leonhard Euler held that the restriction was not necessary and that they could be arbitrary, even with jumps (CAJORI, PDF p. 267). A quantity that can be expanded in a sum of powers has no jumps, so the restriction would exclude every quantity with a jump. The dispute was judged by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, who decided for Euler (CAJORI, PDF p. 267). It was ended by Joseph Fourier. He first announced his discovery before the Paris Academy in 1807, and in his treatise on the conduction of heat in solid bodies, published in 1822, he wrote that an arbitrary quantity, given by a graph, can be written as an infinite sum of sines and cosines, and gave formulas for the numbers in the sum (CAJORI, PDF p. 286). A sum of sines and cosines can have a jump, while a sum of powers cannot, so Fourier's form also covered the quantities that d'Alembert's restriction excluded. A general proof that the sum really gives the value of the quantity it came from he did not have (CAJORI, PDF p. 286). In problems on the conduction of heat the values are given at the boundary of a body. Such problems lead to the definition that Euler called the second: the relation between two numbers cannot necessarily be written with a formula. This idea strongly influenced Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet (CAJORI, PDF p. 286).

The story showed that the relation between two numbers need not be written with a formula, so the definition that we need asks only for a rule that assigns a number to a number.

A set (množica) is a collection of objects, called its elements (elementi), for example the set of all numbers between \(0\) and \(L\) (LEBL1 Def. 0.3.1, PDF p. 8).

Definition 1.4 Function (funkcija)

A function (funkcija) \(f\) is a rule that assigns to every element \(x\) of some set exactly one element \(f(x)\) of another set. The set whose elements the rule assigns something to is the domain (definicijsko območje) of the function, and \(f(x)\) is the value of the function at \(x\). For now both sets will be sets of numbers: the function assigns to every number \(x\) from some set of numbers exactly one number \(f(x)\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 0.3.11 (PDF p. 14), EP §6.2.4 (p. 281).

The displacement \(u(x)\) is a function. For the hanging bar its domain is the set of all \(x\) between \(0\) and \(L\), that is, of all points of the bar, and the value \(u(x)\) is the displacement of the point \(x\). Why does the definition ask for exactly one number? So that the symbol \(f(x)\) means one definite number that we can calculate with. In the next section we will calculate the difference \(u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)\). These are the displacements of two different points, \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\), and the difference makes sense only because each of the two symbols is one number. A rule that assigned to the number \(4\) both numbers whose square is \(4\), that is, \(2\) and \(-2\), would not be a function: the symbol \(f(4)\) would not say which number is meant, and we could not calculate with it. For the displacement the requirement holds by itself, because after loading every point of the bar is in one place only.

From history

The word function began to be used in 1694 by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, but not in the modern sense (CAJORI, PDF p. 227).

Functions whose input is one number and whose output is one number, like the displacement \(u(x)\), are only the simplest kind. The elements of the two sets can be anything: points, triples of numbers or even other functions (LEBL1 Example 0.3.12). Soon we will describe the position of every point of a body by three numbers, and section 1.5.1 explains how. The displacement of a point in space will also be given by three numbers, which say how far the point moves in each of three directions. The rule whose input is the three numbers that give the position of a point and whose output is the three numbers that give its displacement will be a function too, only both of its sets will be sets of triples of numbers. The general definition asks only that every element of the first set gets exactly one element of the second. Mathematicians even write a function as a set of pairs (input, value) (LEBL1 Def. 0.3.11), which we will not need.

1.3.2 Ratio of changes

The ratio we computed in the table has a general form. In mathematics the numbers at the input of a function are often called points, because we picture them as points on a straight line. For a function \(f\), a point \(x\) and a small change \(\Delta x \neq 0\),

\[\frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} \tag{1.3}\]

is the change of the value divided by the change of the input \(x\). It tells us by how much \(f\) changed on average per unit change of \(x\). We call it the difference quotient (diferenčni količnik). For the bar it is the strain of the piece. For a car journey, where \(f(t)\) is the distance covered up to the time \(t\), it is the average speed over the time \(\Delta t\).

We can also draw the quotient. We draw a function by placing, above every point \(x\) of a horizontal line, a point at the height \(f(x)\). These points form a curve, called the graph (graf) of the function. In figure 1.14 the points of the graph above \(x\) and above \(x + \Delta x\) are joined by a straight line. On the way from the first to the second we move \(\Delta x\) horizontally and \(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\) vertically. The difference quotient is the ratio of these two paths, so it says how much the line rises per unit of horizontal path. This number is called the slope (strmina) of the line. If the line falls, the slope is negative.

For \(\Delta x = 0\) the quotient is not defined, because we would divide by zero. So we treat it as a function of the change \(\Delta x\), defined for all small \(\Delta x\) except \(\Delta x = 0\), when \(f\) is defined on both sides of the point \(x\). At an end of the domain, as for the displacement at the ends of the bar, the quotient is defined only for small \(\Delta x\) of one sign, and we deal with this case at the close of section 1.3.3. We ask what it approaches as \(\Delta x\) approaches zero.

1.3.3 Limit

From history

Pierre de Fermat looked for the \(x\) at which a quantity that depends on \(x\) is largest or smallest. He relied on Johannes Kepler's observation that a quantity hardly changes near its largest or smallest value (CAJORI, PDF p. 179-180). So in the expression for the quantity he replaced \(x\) by \(x + e\), set the two values equal (figure 1.15), divided the equation by \(e\) and then took \(e = 0\). The solutions of the equation obtained in this way are the sought \(x\). He had this rule in 1629 (CAJORI, PDF p. 180). He also based on it a way of drawing the line that touches a curve at a given point (CAJORI, PDF p. 180). We may divide by \(e\) only while \(e\) is not zero, but in the expression he got by dividing, Fermat then set \(e = 0\). This is exactly the difficulty of our quotient (1.3): at \(\Delta x = 0\) it is not defined, because we would divide by zero.

By his own account Newton conceived the method of fluxions in 1665 and 1666 and used it to find areas under curves (CAJORI, PDF p. 208). He did not regard quantities as made of very small parts but as described by continuous motion, just as a line is drawn by a moving point (CAJORI, PDF p. 213). He called the rate at which such a quantity grows a fluxion (fluksija). In his words, the ratio of two fluxions equals, as exactly as we like, the ratio of the increments of the two quantities over the same time, taken as short as possible (CAJORI, PDF p. 213). As an example he took the line through two points of a curve. When the second point moves into the first, the line turns into the line that touches the curve (CAJORI, PDF p. 213-214). In 1684 Leibniz published his first paper on the differential calculus. Its rules of calculation are stated without proof, and it does not make clear what \(\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\mathrm{d}y\) are (CAJORI, PDF p. 226).

Bishop George Berkeley pointed out the difficulty in 1734 in his Analyst. He took an increment \(i\) of the variable \(x\) that is expressly supposed to be something and so not zero, and found that the quotient of the increment of the power \(x^n\) and the increment \(i\) equals \(n x^{n-1} + \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} x^{n-2} i + \dots\) If we now take \(i = 0\), the hypothesis is shifted, and keeping a result obtained on the supposition that \(i\) is not zero is a sophism (CAJORI, PDF p. 235). He called the vanishing quantities the ghosts of departed quantities (CAJORI, PDF p. 235). We met the same difficulty with \(\Delta x\): the difference quotient (1.3) is defined only for \(\Delta x \neq 0\). We need not look for the value of the quotient at \(\Delta x = 0\), which does not exist, but for the number that the quotient approaches.

Lagrange wanted to found the calculus without this kind of approaching. He defined the rate of change of a function as the coefficient of \(h\) in the expansion of \(f(x + h)\) in powers of \(h\), but he used infinite sums without checking that these sums have a finite value at all, and his proof of the expansion has serious defects (CAJORI, PDF p. 273). The solution came from Cauchy, who in 1821, in his textbook Cours d'analyse, improved the foundations of the differential calculus by a precise treatment of what the quantities approach and by his new theory of functions without jumps (section 1.12) (CAJORI, PDF p. 385).

We look for the number that the difference quotient (1.3) approaches as \(\Delta x\) approaches zero, and for this we must say precisely what approaching means. What does it mean that some function \(g(h)\) approaches a number \(d\) as \(h\) approaches zero? It means that \(g(h)\) is as close to \(d\) as we wish, provided \(h\) is close enough to zero. Set an allowed error, say \(0{,}001\). Is there a band around zero so narrow that for every \(h\) in the band, except \(h = 0\), the value \(g(h)\) differs from \(d\) by less than \(0{,}001\)? If there is one for the error \(0{,}001\), for the error \(0{,}000001\), and for every other error we can think of, then \(g(h)\) really approaches \(d\). For a smaller error the band may be narrower, but it must exist.

We write this exactly. We call the allowed error \(\eta\) (the Greek letter eta) and the distance the band reaches on each side of zero \(\delta\) (the small Greek letter delta). Unlike the capital letter \(\Delta\), the small letter \(\delta\) does not mean a change. In mathematics books the allowed error is usually written \(\varepsilon\). For the permitted error, Karl Weierstrass began to use the letter \(\varepsilon\) in his early papers, as Cauchy had already done in 1821 (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 280). The definition 1.5 of the limit, with a permitted error and a strip around the point, comes from this tradition. We keep \(\varepsilon\) for strain.

Definition 1.5 Limit of a function (limita funkcije)

Let the function \(g\) be defined for all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) for some \(r > 0\). The function \(g\) has the limit (limita) \(d\) at the point \(0\), written

\[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = d , \tag{1.4}\]

if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - d| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 3.1.3 (PDF p. 114), written for the point \(0\) and with \(\eta\) instead of \(\varepsilon\).

The condition \(0 < |h|\) leaves out the point \(h = 0\), where \(g\) may not be defined at all, like our quotient. The limit tells what \(g\) approaches, not what it is at the point itself. The number \(r\) makes sure that the points the condition talks about really are in the domain. How? The condition talks about the points \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\). If \(\delta \le r\), every such point is also among the points with \(0 < |h| < r\), where \(g\) is defined by assumption, so the value \(g(h)\) exists. And we can always take the band that narrow. If the condition holds for some \(\delta\), it also holds for every smaller \(\delta\), because a narrower band only checks some of the same points. So we may always take \(\delta \le r\). The number \(r\) ensures one more thing: every band around \(0\), however narrow, contains points where \(g\) is defined. We will need this in step 4 of the proof below that the limit is unique, where we must actually pick such a point.

We have defined the limit only at the point \(0\), because the difference quotient needs it only there. This is a narrowing of a more general notion. The limit of a function \(f\) at any point \(c\) is defined in the same way, with the distance \(|x - c|\) between \(x\) and \(c\) in place of \(|h|\) (LEBL1 Def. 3.1.3). LEBL1 also allows functions that are not defined everywhere near \(c\), only at some points that come arbitrarily close to \(c\). The definition uses only distances, \(|g(h) - d|\) and \(|h|\), so it works wherever we can measure distances, for example between points of space. A more general form is the limit of a function between sets in which a distance between the elements is given, called metric spaces (LEBL1 Def. 7.5.15).

Let us try the definition on the simplest example. Let \(g(h) = 5 - h\). We look for its limit at the point \(0\), that is, the number that \(g(h)\) approaches as \(h\) approaches zero. We expect it to be \(5\), since for small \(h\) the value \(5 - h\) is close to \(5\). The function \(g\) is defined for every \(h\), so all the points the condition talks about are in the domain, however wide the band is.

First we write the definition out for this case, with \(g(h) = 5 - h\) and \(d = 5\). We must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|(5 - h) - 5| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\).

  1. Pick any error \(\eta > 0\). For it we must find a band \(\delta\).
  2. Simplify the difference that the condition bounds. The fives cancel, \((5 - h) - 5 = -h\), so \(|(5 - h) - 5| = |{-h}|\).
  3. The numbers \(-h\) and \(h\) are equally far from zero, so \(|{-h}| = |h|\). So the condition we must reach is \(|h| < \eta\).
  4. We choose the band so that this condition holds: we take \(\delta = \eta\). It is a positive number, as the definition requires.
  5. Check. For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) we have \(|h| < \delta = \eta\), so by steps 2 and 3, \(|(5 - h) - 5| = |h| < \eta\).
  6. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely and found a band for it. The condition of the definition holds, so the limit of \(g\) at the point \(0\) is \(5\), \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} (5 - h) = 5\).

For the error \(0{,}001\) the band is \(0{,}001\) wide on each side, for the error \(0{,}000001\) only \(0{,}000001\). A smaller allowed error needs a narrower band, as we expected.

The notation \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = d\) claims that there is only one limit. Otherwise the word "limit" could mean two different numbers. Let us check that this is so.

The idea is simple. If \(g(h)\) approached two numbers at once, then for small \(h\) the value \(g(h)\) would be close to both, and so the two numbers would be close to each other. But only equal numbers can be closer to each other than every error.

The step "so the two numbers would be close to each other" needs a rule about distances between numbers. The distance between the numbers \(p\) and \(q\) is \(|p - q|\) (introduction of section 1.3). If we go from the number \(p\) to the number \(s\) by way of a third number \(q\), we cover the distance \(|p - q| + |q - s|\), and this is not smaller than the distance \(|p - s|\) that we cover going straight. As an equation:

\[|p - s| \le |p - q| + |q - s| .\]

Let us test it on the numbers of figure 1.17. For \(p = 1\), \(q = 3\) and \(s = 4\) the number \(q\) lies between \(p\) and \(s\), and the two sides are equal: \(|1 - 4| = 3\) and \(|1 - 3| + |3 - 4| = 2 + 1 = 3\). For \(q = 6\) the number \(q\) lies outside, the path through \(q\) covers the stretch from \(4\) to \(6\) twice, and it is longer: \(|1 - 6| + |6 - 4| = 5 + 2 = 7 > 3\). Since \(p - s = (p - q) + (q - s)\), the inequality is a special case of the inequality \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) for the numbers \(a = p - q\) and \(b = q - s\). We prove that inequality in the next lemma. Along with it we prove the rule for how the absolute value behaves for a product of two numbers. We will need it whenever we compare a distance multiplied by a number with an allowed error.

Lemma 1.6 Triangle inequality and the absolute value of a product (trikotniška neenakost in absolutna vrednost zmnožka)

For any real numbers \(a\) and \(b\):

  1. \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\), the triangle inequality for numbers (trikotniška neenakost za števila),
  2. \(|a\,b| = |a|\,|b|\), the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values.
Proof

We have to show both items. We use only the definition of the absolute value, \(|t| = t\) for \(t \ge 0\) and \(|t| = -t\) for \(t < 0\) (introduction of section 1.3), and the school rules for inequalities.

1. Triangle inequality.

  1. Let \(t \ge 0\). Then \(|t| = t\), so \(t \le |t|\) and \(-|t| = -t \le 0 \le t\). So the number \(t\) lies between \(-|t|\) and \(|t|\): \(-|t| \le t \le |t|\).
  2. Let \(t < 0\). Then \(|t| = -t\), so \(-|t| = t\) and \(t < 0 < -t = |t|\). Here too \(-|t| \le t \le |t|\).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, used for \(t = a\) and for \(t = b\), we have \(-|a| \le a \le |a|\) and \(-|b| \le b \le |b|\).
  4. We add the inequalities of step 3, the left sides together and the right sides together. The sum of two non-strict inequalities in the same direction is again such an inequality, so \(-(|a| + |b|) \le a + b \le |a| + |b|\).
  5. Let \(c = |a| + |b|\). If \(a + b \ge 0\), then \(|a + b| = a + b\), and by the right inequality of step 4, \(|a + b| \le c\).
  6. If \(a + b < 0\), then \(|a + b| = -(a + b)\). We multiply the left inequality of step 4, \(-c \le a + b\), by \(-1\), which reverses it: \(-(a + b) \le c\). So here too \(|a + b| \le c\).
  7. The sum \(a + b\) is either nonnegative or negative, so by steps 5 and 6 we always have \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\).

2. Absolute value of a product.

  1. For every number \(t \le 0\) we have \(|t| = -t\). For \(t < 0\) the definition says so, for \(t = 0\) both sides are zero.
  2. Let \(a \ge 0\) and \(b \ge 0\). A product of nonnegative numbers is nonnegative, so \(|a\,b| = a\,b = |a|\,|b|\).
  3. Let \(a < 0\) and \(b < 0\). Then \(-a\) and \(-b\) are positive, and \(a\,b = (-a)(-b) > 0\). So \(|a\,b| = (-a)(-b) = |a|\,|b|\).
  4. Let \(a < 0\) and \(b \ge 0\). Then \((-a)\,b \ge 0\), so \(a\,b = -\big((-a)\,b\big) \le 0\). By step 1, \(|a\,b| = -a\,b = (-a)\,b = |a|\,|b|\).
  5. Let \(a \ge 0\) and \(b < 0\). As in step 4, with the roles of the numbers \(a\) and \(b\) exchanged, \(a\,b \le 0\) and \(|a\,b| = a\,(-b) = |a|\,|b|\).
  6. Every pair of numbers \(a\), \(b\) falls under one of the cases of steps 2 to 5, so always \(|a\,b| = |a|\,|b|\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 1.3.1, items (iii), (v) and (vi), and Prop. 1.3.2 (PDF pp. 36-37). The proof follows the source.

Both rules are simple, but we will use them in almost every estimate in the book. The first says that a sum of two errors is, in size, at most the sum of their sizes. The second says that we may take a constant factor out of the absolute value, as in \(|a\,\Delta x| = a\,|\Delta x|\) with a positive number \(a\). The name triangle inequality comes from geometry: in a triangle no side is longer than the sum of the other two. We prove the same inequality for points of space in chapter 2 (section 2.3). Now we can prove that the limit is unique.

Lemma 1.7 Uniqueness of the limit (enoličnost limite)

Let the function \(g\) be defined for all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) for some \(r > 0\). Then \(g\) has at most one limit at the point \(0\).

Proof

We have to show that two numbers \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) that both satisfy the definition of the limit are equal.

  1. Pick any error \(\eta > 0\). We will show that \(|d_1 - d_2| < \eta\).
  2. Since \(d_1\) is a limit, the definition gives for the error \(\eta/2\) a band \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - d_1| < \eta/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\). We take half the error because in step 6 we will add two such errors.
  3. Since \(d_2\) is a limit, for the same error \(\eta/2\) there is a band \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - d_2| < \eta/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_2\).
  4. Take an \(h\) that is nonzero and smaller than both bands, for example half of the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) and \(r\). For this \(h\) both inequalities of steps 2 and 3 hold.
  5. Write the difference \(d_1 - d_2\) through the value \(g(h)\), which we know: \(d_1 - d_2 = (d_1 - g(h)) + (g(h) - d_2)\).
  6. The distance between \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) is not larger than the distance from \(d_1\) to \(g(h)\) plus the distance from \(g(h)\) to \(d_2\). This is the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1), for \(a = d_1 - g(h)\) and \(b = g(h) - d_2\):
    \[|d_1 - d_2| \le |d_1 - g(h)| + |g(h) - d_2| < \tfrac{\eta}{2} + \tfrac{\eta}{2} = \eta .\]
  7. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely, so \(|d_1 - d_2|\) is smaller than every positive number.
  8. A nonnegative number that is smaller than every positive number is zero: if it were positive, it would be smaller than itself. So \(|d_1 - d_2| = 0\) and \(d_1 = d_2\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 3.1.4 (PDF pp. 114-115).

The proof showed a pattern that we will meet many times: when we want a sum of two errors to be small, we allow each of them half.

So far the function \(g\) was defined on both sides of the point \(0\). For the bar this does not hold everywhere. The displacement of the bar is defined only for \(x\) between \(0\) and \(L\). At the top, at \(x = 0\), the difference quotient of the displacement is therefore defined only for \(\Delta x > 0\), since the point \(x + \Delta x\) must lie on the bar. At the bottom end, at \(x = L\), it is defined only for \(\Delta x < 0\). Such a function does not satisfy the condition \(0 < |h| < r\) of the definition of the limit 1.5. So we also write the definition with a band that reaches to one side of zero only.

Definition 1.8 One-sided limit (enostranska limita)

Let the function \(g\) be defined for all \(h\) with \(0 < h < r\) for some \(r > 0\). The function \(g\) has the limit from the right (limita z desne) \(d\) at the point \(0\), written \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} g(h) = d\), if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - d| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\). If \(g\) is defined for all \(h\) with \(-r < h < 0\), the limit from the left (limita z leve) is defined in the same way, only the condition holds for every \(h\) with \(-\delta < h < 0\), and we write \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^-} g(h) = d\). Both are called one-sided limits (enostranski limiti).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 3.1.16 (PDF p. 119), written for the point \(0\) and with \(\eta\) instead of \(\varepsilon\).

The sign \(^+\) says that \(h\) approaches zero from the positive side, the sign \(^-\) from the negative side. A limit from the right is unique too, because the proof of lemma 1.7 on the uniqueness of the limit works without change: the \(h\) of step 4, half of the smallest of the positive numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) and \(r\), is positive. For a limit from the left we take \(-h\). If a function is defined on both sides of zero and has the limit \(d\) there, it also has both one-sided limits, equal to \(d\), since the condition for all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) contains both one-sided conditions.

1.3.4 Derivative

Now we can say what the number is that the strain of the piece approached in the table.

Definition 1.9 Derivative (odvod)

Let the function \(f\) be defined for all numbers whose distance from \(x\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). The function \(f\) is differentiable at the point \(x\) if the difference quotient (1.3) has a limit as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero. This limit is the derivative (odvod) of the function \(f\) at the point \(x\):

\[f'(x) = \lim_{\Delta \mathrm{x} \to 0} \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} . \tag{1.5}\]

If \(x\) is the smallest number in the domain of \(f\) and \(f\) is defined for all numbers \(t\) with \(x \le t < x + r\), the derivative at the point \(x\) is the one-sided limit of the difference quotient from the right as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero (definition 1.8). If \(x\) is the largest number in the domain and \(f\) is defined for all numbers \(t\) with \(x - r < t \le x\), the derivative is the limit from the left. Such a derivative is called a one-sided derivative (enostranski odvod).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 4.1.1 (PDF p. 155), which also allows a point at the end of the domain. The notation with \(\Delta x\) follows BARBER (1.35)-(1.36), where it is \(\delta x\).

So the derivative is a rate of change: by how much \(f\) changes per unit change of \(x\) when the change is very small. We read \(f'(x)\) as "\(f\) prime of \(x\)". In books you will also find the derivative written as \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}\). This notation recalls the quotient \(\Delta f / \Delta x\) from which the derivative comes. The notation is Leibniz's (CAJORI, PDF p. 227).

This is the derivative of a function whose input is one number, \(x\), and whose output is one number, \(f(x)\), like the displacement \(u(x)\) of the bar. For now this is the only kind we need. In a body, however, a point is given by three numbers, which say where it lies, and its displacement is given by three numbers too, which say how far it moves in each of three directions. There we will look at how one of the output numbers changes when only one of the three input numbers changes and the other two stay fixed. We will define such a derivative in section 1.7.2 (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.8). A more general derivative, however, is no longer a single number. Take a function whose input is a group of \(n\) numbers and whose output is a group of \(m\) numbers. For the displacement in a body \(n = 3\) and \(m = 3\): the input is three numbers that give the position of the point, the output three numbers that give its displacement. The derivative of such a function at a point is a rule that tells, for every small change of the \(n\) input numbers, approximately how much each of the \(m\) output numbers changes (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.1). We will need such a derivative of the displacement when we describe strain in space.

On the graph the derivative has a clear picture. As \(\Delta x\) gets smaller, the point of the graph above \(x + \Delta x\) moves along the graph towards the point above \(x\), and the lines through the two points turn towards the line that has the slope \(f'(x)\) and passes through the point of the graph above \(x\) (figure 1.18). This line is called the tangent (tangenta) of the graph at the point \(x\). The slopes of the lines through two points are difference quotients, and their limit, the derivative, is the slope of the tangent.

Let us compute the derivative of the displacement of the hanging bar, \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), where \(a > 0\) and \(L\) are given numbers (for the steel bar \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\)). The way has two parts. First we simplify the difference quotient so that \(\Delta x\), which we must not set to zero, disappears from the denominator. Then we find the limit of the simplified expression from the definition.

  1. The value at \(x + \Delta x\): \(u(x + \Delta x) = a\,(2L(x + \Delta x) - (x + \Delta x)^2)\).
  2. Expand the square, \((x + \Delta x)^2 = x^2 + 2x\,\Delta x + \Delta x^2\), and multiply out \(2L(x + \Delta x) = 2Lx + 2L\,\Delta x\). So
    \[u(x + \Delta x) = a\,(2Lx + 2L\,\Delta x - x^2 - 2x\,\Delta x - \Delta x^2) .\]
  3. Subtract \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\). The terms \(2Lx\) and \(-x^2\) cancel, and what remains is
    \[u(x + \Delta x) - u(x) = a\,(2L\,\Delta x - 2x\,\Delta x - \Delta x^2) .\]
  4. All three terms in the bracket have the factor \(\Delta x\), so we take it out: \(a\,\Delta x\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x)\).
  5. Divide by \(\Delta x \neq 0\). The factor \(\Delta x\) cancels:
    \[\frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} = a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) .\]

The first part of the way is done. Before we take the limit, let us see what the equation of step 5 tells us. It holds for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\), but its two sides behave differently at \(\Delta x = 0\).

On the left side the numerator would be \(u(x + 0) - u(x) = u(x) - u(x) = 0\), and the denominator \(0\):

\[\frac{u(x + 0) - u(x)}{0} = \frac{0}{0} .\]

This is not a number. The quotient \(c/b\) is the number that gives \(c\) when multiplied by \(b\). For \(0/0\) it would have to be a number that gives \(0\) when multiplied by \(0\). Every number does that, so there is no single number we could call \(0/0\). The left side has no value at \(\Delta x = 0\), and that is why we could not shrink the piece to nothing in section 1.2.

On the right side there is no division any more. It disappeared in step 5, when the factor \(\Delta x\) cancelled. So we may put \(\Delta x = 0\) into the right side:

\[a\,(2L - 2x - 0) = a\,(2L - 2x) .\]

This is an ordinary number, which we can compute for every point \(x\).

Now we split the right side of step 5 into this number and the rest. We multiply the bracket by \(a\) and group the first two terms again: \(a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) = a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x\). So the strain of the piece is

\[\frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} = a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x . \tag{1.6}\]

The first term does not depend on the length \(\Delta x\) of the piece. It is the same for long and short pieces. The second term, \(a\,\Delta x\), is all that separates the quotient from the number \(a\,(2L - 2x)\), and it is proportional to the length of the piece: a piece ten times shorter is ten times closer to the number. Because \(a\,\Delta x\) is subtracted, the strains of pieces with a positive \(\Delta x\) are smaller than the number and grow towards it as \(\Delta x\) gets smaller.

This explains the table of section 1.2, where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) and \(L = 10\) m. At the top, at \(x = 0\), the number \(a\,(2L - 2x)\) is \(a \cdot 20\ \text{m} = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and at the middle, at \(x = 5\) m, it is \(a \cdot 10\ \text{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). These are the two numbers at which the columns of the table settled. For a piece 1 m long the difference is \(a\,\Delta x = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 1\ \text{m} = 0{,}1952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and indeed \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6} - 0{,}1952 \cdot 10^{-6} = 3{,}7088 \cdot 10^{-6}\), rounded to four digits \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the first number in the table. In every following row the piece is ten times shorter, so the difference is ten times smaller: \(0{,}1952\), \(0{,}01952\), \(0{,}001952\) and \(0{,}0001952\), each times \(10^{-6}\). The table shows four digits, and the last one stands for \(0{,}001 \cdot 10^{-6}\). In the last row the difference is too small to show in the rounded last digit, so the table shows \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) itself. So the numbers settle when the difference falls below the last digit shown.

The difference \(a\,\Delta x\) does not contain \(x\), so it is the same at the top and at the middle. The table shows this too: in each row both numbers lie equally far below their final values, for example \(1{,}952 - 1{,}757 = 0{,}195\) at the middle and \(3{,}904 - 3{,}709 = 0{,}195\) at the top. The difference comes from the term \(-a\,\Delta x^2\) of step 2, the part of the square \((x + \Delta x)^2\) that does not contain \(x\). After the division by \(\Delta x\) in step 5 it becomes \(-a\,\Delta x\).

So the difference \(a\,\Delta x\) goes to zero as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero, and we expect the limit to be the number \(a\,(2L - 2x)\). But a table, as we said in section 1.2, shows only a few rows. The equation (1.6) has exactly the form of the example \(g(h) = 5 - h\) of section 1.3.3: the number \(a\,(2L - 2x)\) stands in place of \(5\), the change \(\Delta x\) in place of \(h\), and the subtracted term has an extra factor \(a\). So we show the limit with the same steps as there. Because of the factor \(a\), the band will be \(\delta = \eta / a\) instead of \(\delta = \eta\).

  1. Let us show from the definition of the limit 1.5 that the limit of the quotient is \(d = a\,(2L - 2x)\). The definition, written out for the quotient of step 5 as a function of the change \(\Delta x\) (which plays the role of \(h\)) and for this number \(d\), demands: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) - a\,(2L - 2x)| < \eta\) for every \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\). The formula \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) is defined for every number \(x\), not only for the points of the bar between \(0\) and \(L\), so the quotient of step 5 is defined for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and all the points the condition talks about are in the domain. What this means for the displacement of the bar, which is defined only for the points of the bar, we say in section 1.4.
  2. Pick any error \(\eta > 0\). For it we must find a band \(\delta\).
  3. Simplify the difference. By the equation (1.6), \(a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) = a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x\), so the difference is \(a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x - a\,(2L - 2x) = -a\,\Delta x\).
  4. The numbers \(-a\,\Delta x\) and \(a\,\Delta x\) are equally far from zero, and since \(a > 0\), \(|a\,\Delta x| = a\,|\Delta x|\). So \(|{-a\,\Delta x}| = a\,|\Delta x|\), and the condition we must reach is \(a\,|\Delta x| < \eta\).
  5. We divide the inequality by the positive number \(a\), so it does not turn around: the condition holds exactly when \(|\Delta x| < \eta / a\). So we take the band \(\delta = \eta / a\), which is positive.
  6. Check. For every \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\) we have \(|\Delta x| < \eta / a\), so \(a\,|\Delta x| < \eta\), and by steps 8 and 9 this is the difference between the quotient and \(d\).
  7. We picked the error freely and found a band for it. The condition of the definition holds, so the limit of the quotient is \(a\,(2L - 2x)\), and
    \[u'(x) = a\,(2L - 2x) = 2a\,(L - x) .\]

Step 5 was the heart of the computation. As \(\Delta x\) goes to zero, both the numerator \(u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)\) and the denominator \(\Delta x\) go to zero. If only one of them did, the outcome would be clear. A numerator going to zero over a fixed denominator gives quotients that go to zero. A fixed nonzero numerator over a denominator going to zero gives quotients whose size grows beyond every bound. When both go to zero together, the quotient can approach an ordinary number, and which number depends on how fast the numerator shrinks compared with the denominator. Step 4 showed how fast: the numerator is \(\Delta x\) times \(a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x)\), and the factor that remains approaches \(a\,(2L - 2x)\). When this number is not zero, the numerator therefore shrinks as fast as \(\Delta x\) itself. At the bottom end, at \(x = L\), however, \(a\,(2L - 2x) = 0\), the factor that remains is \(-a\,\Delta x\) and the numerator \(-a\,\Delta x^2\). There the numerator shrinks faster than the denominator, and the quotient \(-a\,\Delta x\) goes to zero. In the hanging bar the numerator and the denominator are the elongation and the length of the piece (figure 1.19). At the top of the bar the piece of 1 m stretches by \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\) m, the piece of 0,001 m only by \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m. The elongation of a piece is its length times its strain from the table:

\[3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m} = 1\ \text{m} \cdot 3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6} , \qquad 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-9}\ \text{m} = 0{,}001\ \text{m} \cdot 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6} .\]

The lengths differ by a factor of 1000, the strains only a little, so the elongation of the long piece is \(1000 \cdot 3{,}709 / 3{,}904 = 950\) times larger, almost a thousand times. The strains differ a little because the long piece reaches from the top down to \(x = 1\) m, and lower down the material is stretched less. By step 12, very short pieces at \(x = 1\) m have strains close to \(a\,(2L - 2x) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 18\ \text{m} = 3{,}514 \cdot 10^{-6}\), less than \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) at the top. The strain of the long piece, \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\), lies between the two, exactly halfway, \((3{,}904 + 3{,}514)/2 = 3{,}709\), because the strain falls evenly along the piece. The shorter the piece, the less its strain differs from the one at the top, and the closer the ratio of the elongations comes to the ratio of the lengths. The elongation and the length vanish together, and their ratio, the strain, approaches a definite number. With patient algebra we cancelled the common factor \(\Delta x\) in step 5 and turned the difference quotient into an expression that is defined at \(\Delta x = 0\) too, and after that the limit was easy. We will compute derivatives this way later as well, until we derive rules in section 1.14.2 that do this work once and for all.

On the graph of the displacement the same limit is the turning of the lines through two points of the graph into the tangent (figure 1.18).

1.4 Strain at a point

Let us return to the bar. The strain of the piece between \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) is the difference quotient of the displacement, and as the length of the piece goes to zero it approaches the derivative of the displacement. This derivative is the measure we were looking for.

Definition 1.10 Strain at a point (deformacija v točki)

Let \(u(x)\) be the displacement of the point of the bar that was at distance \(x\) from a chosen end before loading. The strain (deformacija) of the bar at the point \(x\) is the derivative of the displacement:

\[\varepsilon(x) = u'(x) = \lim_{\Delta \mathrm{x} \to 0} \frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} . \tag{1.7}\]

Source: BARBER (1.35), (1.36) (PDF p. 33), ONATE1 §2.2 (PDF p. 66). In books it is often written \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) or \(e_{\mathrm{xx}}\), where \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the displacement in the direction \(x\) (why two indices, see section 1.1). The sign \(\partial\) writes the derivative when the displacement depends not only on one distance \(x\) but on the position of the point in space. We will meet it when we describe strain in space.

So the strain at a point is, like the strain of a bar (1.1), a number without a unit, an elongation per unit length. The difference is that we do not compute it for the whole bar, but for shorter and shorter pieces around the point, and take the number that their strains approach. So the name strain at a point is a shorthand. It does not mean that the point itself stretches, since it has no length. It describes the material close to the point, in pieces that can be as short as we like. For a bar that stretches the same everywhere, the two strains are equal. Indeed, if the displacement is \(u(x) = \varepsilon_0\,x\) with a constant \(\varepsilon_0\), the difference quotient is \(\varepsilon_0\,\Delta x / \Delta x = \varepsilon_0\) for every \(\Delta x\), its limit is \(\varepsilon_0\), and the total elongation is \(u(L) - u(0) = \varepsilon_0 L\), so \(\Delta L / L = \varepsilon_0\).

For the hanging bar we have already computed the derivative:

\[\varepsilon(x) = 2a\,(L - x) .\]

We computed it for the formula \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), which is defined for every number \(x\). The displacement of the bar, however, is defined only for the points of the bar, for \(x\) between \(0\) and \(L\). At a point between the two ends of the bar this changes nothing. For all \(\Delta x\) for which the point \(x + \Delta x\) stays on the bar, the quotient of the displacement equals the quotient of the formula, and we may always take the band so narrow that these are all the \(\Delta x\) in the band (section 1.3.3). At the ends of the bar, however, the points of the bar lie on one side only. There the strain is the one-sided derivative of definition 1.9: at the top, at \(x = 0\), the limit from the right, for \(0 < \Delta x < \delta\), at the bottom end, at \(x = L\), the limit from the left, for \(-\delta < \Delta x < 0\). The condition of the one-sided limit is part of the condition that we checked in steps 7 to 11 of the computation in section 1.3.4 for all \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\). So at the ends too \(\varepsilon(x) = 2a\,(L - x)\).

At the top, at \(x = 0\), the strain is \(2aL = 2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 10 = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\). At the middle, at \(x = 5\) m, it is \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and at the bottom end zero. These are exactly the numbers the columns of the table approached. The strain falls evenly from top to bottom, just as the weight carried by each cross section falls: the top carries the whole bar, the middle half of it, the bottom end nothing.

The total elongation of the bar is the displacement of the bottom end, \(\Delta L = u(L) - u(0) = aL^2 = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, and the average strain is \(\Delta L / L = aL = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). This is exactly the strain at the middle. When the strain changes evenly along the bar, the average really is the value at the middle. But the most stretched material, at the top, is stretched twice as much as the average. If we judged by the average whether the bar holds, we would be wrong by a factor of two.

One more simple but important observation. Suppose the ceiling sags by 1 mm for some reason. Then every point of the bar moves by an extra millimetre, and the new displacement is \(u(x) + 0{,}001\) m. The strain does not change. In the difference quotient the extra millimetre cancels, \((u(x + \Delta x) + 0{,}001) - (u(x) + 0{,}001) = u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)\). A displacement that is the same for all points does not deform the body, it only moves it as a whole. To give such moves a name, we imagine a body that cannot be deformed at all.

Definition 1.11 Rigid body and rigid-body displacement (togo telo in togi premik)

A rigid body (togo telo) is a body in which the distance between any two points stays the same, whatever forces act on it. A displacement of a body that does not change the distance between any two of its points is called a rigid-body displacement (togi premik).

Source: CM §3.3.1 (PDF p. 118), CM §3.8.1.1 (PDF p. 154), BARBER §1.1.6 (PDF p. 32).

No real body is rigid, since every body changes its shape under a force, as we saw at the start of the chapter. A rigid body is the picture of a body that deforms so little that its change of shape does not matter for the question at hand. The name rigid-body displacement says that this is the only kind of displacement a rigid body can undergo (BARBER §1.1.6, PDF p. 32). The extra millimetre from the sagging ceiling is a rigid-body displacement: it moves all points of the bar by the same distance, so the distances between them stay the same. But a rigid-body displacement need not be the same for all points. A body can also be turned as a whole without any distance changing, and we will meet this in section 1.6 (CM §3.8.1.1, PDF p. 156).

Since a displacement that is the same for all points does not change the strain, we can never compute the displacement completely from the strain: we can always add such a displacement. For the hanging bar it is fixed by the condition that the top is attached to the ceiling, \(u(0) = 0\) (BARBER (1.39)). That this is the only freedom, that is, that two displacements with the same strain at every point differ only by such a constant shift, we will prove in section 1.14.6.

So far the bar has been just a line: every point moved along the same straight line, and the displacement was a single number. But the bar is a body, and like every body it has a length, a width and a height. A point in a body can move in any direction, and a small piece of the body can at the same time stretch in one direction, shorten in another, and twist. One number is not enough to describe displacements in space. We need quantities that have a size and a direction, and we start the next section with them.

1.5 Mathematics: points and vectors

Once again we put mechanics aside for a moment. To describe displacements in space we need two things. First we must say with numbers where a point is. Then we must say with numbers where and how far it has moved. We will build both from an experience everyone has, measuring a room with a tape measure.

1.5.1 Coordinates

How do we tell someone over the phone where a lamp hangs in a room? We can say: start in the corner of the room, walk 2 m along one wall, then 3 m along the other wall, and then 2 m up. Three numbers, \(2\), \(3\) and \(2\), fix the position of the lamp exactly, provided we have agreed on three things beforehand: at which point we start, in which three directions we walk, and in what order we list the numbers. We choose the directions perpendicular to each other, like the edges where the floor and the two walls meet in the corner of the room, and we measure distances along all three with the same tape.

From history

Apollonius of Perga had already related the points of a conic, that is, a curve obtained when a cone is cut by a plane, to the points of a straight line that he called the diameter. From the diameter he measured distances at a constant angle (figure 1.21), and the length of each was determined by the position of the point on the diameter (CAJORI, PDF p. 191). In 1637 René Descartes published, in his Discourse on Method, an essay of 106 pages on geometry (CAJORI, PDF p. 190). He noticed: if a problem has a finite number of solutions, it leads to an equation with one unknown. An equation with two unknowns, however, is satisfied by infinitely many points, so one must find the line on which all of them lie (CAJORI, PDF p. 190). He chose a straight line and associated each of its points with a point of the line sought, in such a way that it can be constructed once the first point is known (CAJORI, PDF p. 191). The new feature was an equation with two unknowns, from which for each value of one length the other can be computed (CAJORI, PDF p. 191). Such an equation does not give one number but a line, because each value of the first length gives the other length, and there are infinitely many such pairs, all lying together on a line.

The angle between the two lengths was usually a right angle with Descartes, but he wrote explicitly that it need not be (CAJORI, PDF p. 191). He never formally introduced another line perpendicular to the first. Descartes and Fermat, and their successors down to the middle of the eighteenth century, used measuring at an oblique angle, that is, not at a right angle, more often than later mathematicians did (CAJORI, PDF p. 191). Fermat set down similar ideas in a treatise Ad locos planos et solidos isagoge (Introduction to Plane and Solid Loci), which was not published until 1679 (CAJORI, PDF p. 190). The agreement on three things that we described for the lamp has a name of its own. It is the simplest of several kinds of such agreements, and we will talk about the others at the end of this subsection.

Definition 1.12 Rectangular Cartesian coordinate system and coordinates (pravokotni kartezični koordinatni sistem in koordinate)

A rectangular Cartesian coordinate system (pravokotni kartezični koordinatni sistem) consists of a chosen point \(O\), called the origin (izhodišče), and three mutually perpendicular straight lines through \(O\), the coordinate axes (koordinatne osi) \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). On each axis a positive direction is chosen, and lengths are measured in the same unit on all three axes.
