The position of a point \(P\) is described by three numbers, its coordinates (koordinate) \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\): we reach \(P\) if, starting at the origin, we walk the distance \(x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), then the distance \(y\) in the direction of the axis \(y\), and then the distance \(z\) in the direction of the axis \(z\). A negative number means walking in the opposite direction. We write \(P = (x, y, z)\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1, Fig. 167 (PDF p. 382).

The words coordinate and axes of coordinates were first used by Leibniz, who introduced the word coordinate in 1692 (CAJORI, PDF p. 191, 227).

Let us return to the lamp of the room. Coordinates are numbers, and the coordinate system is the agreement that gives these numbers their meaning. The lamp of our example is the point \((2, 3, 2)\) if the axes \(x\) and \(y\) lie along the walls, the axis \(z\) points vertically up and the units are metres (figure 1.22). The order matters: the point \((3, 2, 2)\) is a different point, 3 m along the first wall and 2 m along the second. That is why we say that coordinates are an ordered triple (urejena trojica) of numbers. It matters which number stands in which place, because each place belongs to its own axis.

In another coordinate system the same lamp has other coordinates. If we start in the opposite corner of the room, all three numbers change, while the lamp stays where it is. So coordinates always belong to a point together with a coordinate system. In each problem we will choose the system once and keep it. Other books often write coordinates as \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\) or, for the position before loading, \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(X_3\) (CM §3.2.1, PDF p. 111), because with numbered axes the calculations that repeat for all three directions are easier to write. As long as we can, we will stay with \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

The system we have described is the simplest, but not the only one. A system whose axes are straight and each carries a fixed unit is called Cartesian (kartezičen), and one with perpendicular axes and the same unit on all three rectangular Cartesian (pravokoten kartezičen) (EP §1.2, p. 16). The axes can also be oblique, and then too every point gets its own triple of numbers (EP §1.2). But coordinates need not be distances along straight axes at all. For a pipe it is more natural to say how far a point is from the axis of the pipe, at what angle around the axis it lies and how high it is. These are cylindrical coordinates (cilindrične koordinate) \((r, \theta, z)\). For a ball we give the distance from the centre and two angles, much like latitude and longitude on the Earth. These are spherical coordinates (sferične koordinate) (SADD (1.9.1), (1.9.2), PDF p. 29).

All these systems share a single requirement. A coordinate system in some part of our space is a rule that assigns to every point exactly one triple of numbers, different triples to different points, and nearby triples to nearby points, and in which nearby triples also belong to nearby points (CM (2.4.7), (2.4.8), PDF pp. 70-71, SADD §1.9). Cylindrical coordinates break this requirement in two places. On the axis \(z\) the distance from the axis is zero, and every angle \(\theta\) describes the same point. Where the angle completes a full turn and starts again at zero, two neighbouring points on either side get very different angles. That is why a coordinate system often covers only a part of space.

We need three numbers because our space has three dimensions, not because coordinates have to come in threes. The same requirement works with any number of coordinates. On a line one number is enough, the distance from a chosen point. On a curved surface, where there are no straight axes at all, two are enough (VK §11.1, PDF p. 308). On the Earth these are latitude and longitude. The number of numbers a space needs is called its dimension (razsežnost). The precise definition for flat spaces is given by KREYSZIG §7.4 (PDF p. 312), and for curved surfaces by SPONG §12.1.1 (PDF p. 432). The set of all ordered \(n\)-tuples of real numbers is written \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (KREYSZIG §7.9, PDF p. 335). So a coordinate system gives every point of a space with \(n\) dimensions its own element of \(\mathbb{R}^n\): our space corresponds to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), a plane to \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Nothing stops at three. \(\mathbb{R}^4\), the set of all ordered quadruples of numbers, is as good a set as \(\mathbb{R}^3\), only we cannot draw it. In mechanics such spaces turn up by themselves. The position of a mechanism with several moving parts is described by as many numbers as it has independent ways to move, its degrees of freedom (prostostne stopnje). These numbers are called generalized coordinates (posplošene koordinate) (GR §1.2.3, PDF p. 38). A pendulum swinging in a plane needs only one, its angle (GR, Figure 1.5). The positions of a mechanism with \(n\) degrees of freedom form a space with \(n\) dimensions (SPONG §1.1.2, PDF p. 28), and it needs \(n\) coordinates, also when \(n\) is larger than three. We will meet them in chapter 8. The most general form of a coordinate system, for spaces with any number of dimensions and also for curved spaces, is called a chart (karta) in mathematics, and it is the starting point of differential geometry (SPONG §12.1.1, PDF p. 432).

What we derive next, the move from one point to another as the differences of their coordinates and the formula that tells from the coordinates how far apart two points are, holds only in a rectangular Cartesian system. In cylindrical coordinates, for example, two points with the same difference of angles are further apart the further from the axis they lie, so the distance does not come from the differences of the coordinates in the same way (SADD (1.9.4)). Until we say otherwise, a coordinate system in this book means a rectangular Cartesian system.

1.5.2 Vector

Now let a point move. A fly sits on the lamp \(P = (2, 3, 2)\). It flies off and lands on the floor at the point \(Q = (3, 5, 0)\). How do we say with numbers where it has moved? Let us compare the coordinates. The coordinate \(x\) has increased by \(1\), the coordinate \(y\) by \(2\), and the coordinate \(z\) has decreased by \(2\). The triple of changes \((1, 2, -2)\) tells where the fly ended its flight relative to where it began: 1 m further in the direction of the axis \(x\), 2 m further in the direction of the axis \(y\) and 2 m lower. It does not tell where the fly started. A fly that flew from the point \((0, 0, 2)\) to the point \((1, 2, 0)\) would have the same triple of changes, although it flew somewhere else. Nor does the triple tell along which path the fly flew, only where it ended. Such a triple is a new kind of object. It does not describe a position but a move.

From history

Two forces that act at the same point act together as one force along the diagonal of the parallelogram that they span. This principle of statics was stated already by Galileo, but he did not fully recognize its scope (CAJORI, PDF p. 188). Two forces are therefore not added like numbers, and we must take their directions into account too. Calculating with directions grew out of a search. For several years William Rowan Hamilton considered what the product of each pair of perpendicular directed line segments should be (CAJORI, PDF p. 349). A directed line segment is a segment that has a direction as well as a length, like the move of a fly from point \(P\) to point \(Q\). The idea of quaternions (kvaternioni), a calculus with three units \(i\), \(j\) and \(k\), came to him on 16 October 1843 on a walk along the Royal Canal in Dublin. He carved the basic formula \(i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1\) in a stone of Brougham Bridge (CAJORI, PDF p. 349). From this formula it follows that the order of multiplication matters, which we show ourselves. If we multiply \(ijk = -1\) by \(k\) on the right and use \(k^2 = -1\), we get \(-ij = -k\), so \(ij = k\). The reversed product gives \((ji)(ij) = j\,i^2\,j = -j^2 = 1\), so \((ji)\,k = 1\), and after multiplying by \(k\) on the right \(-ji = k\), so \(ji = -k\). Swapping the order changes the sign. He wrote a point as \(p = ix + jy + kz\), where \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) are units in three mutually perpendicular directions (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 156-157). The three numbers \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), multiplied by the units, therefore determine a directed line segment from the origin to the point, just as the triple \((1, 2, -2)\) determines the move of the fly. At about the same time Hermann Günther Grassmann and George Boole also arrived at algebras in which the order of multiplication matters. Grassmann's Ausdehnungslehre appeared in 1844 (BALL, PDF p. 501).

We write the move of a fly, a directed line segment, simply as a triple of numbers, and calculating with them is calculating with numbers (section 1.5.3).

Definition 1.13 Vector (vektor)

In a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system we write a vector (vektor) \(\vek a\) as an ordered triple of real numbers, \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\). The numbers \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components (komponente) of the vector. Two vectors are equal if they agree in all three components. The vector \(\vek 0 = (0, 0, 0)\) is the zero vector (ničelni vektor).

The vector from the point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) to the point \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{Q}}, y_{\mathrm{Q}}, z_{\mathrm{Q}})\) has the differences of the coordinates as its components:

\[\overrightarrow{PQ} = (x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}},\ y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}},\ z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}) . \tag{1.8}\]

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (1) (PDF p. 382), CM §2.2.1 (PDF p. 39).

For the fly, \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (3 - 2,\ 5 - 3,\ 0 - 2) = (1, 2, -2)\). So a vector, like a point, is an ordered triple of numbers, but it means something else. A point tells where something is. A vector tells how to get from one point to another. Bold type, \(\vek a\), distinguishes vectors from numbers. On paper we write a vector with an arrow over the letter, \(\vec a\).

We draw a vector as an arrow from the point \(P\) to the point \(Q\). The same vector can be drawn from any starting point, just as both flies in the example above had the same vector (figure 1.23): the two arrows start at different places, but both point 1 m in the direction \(x\), 2 m in the direction \(y\) and 2 m down. The vector from the origin \(O = (0, 0, 0)\) to the point \(P\) has the coordinates of \(P\) as its components, because the coordinates of the origin are zero. Books call it the position vector (krajevni vektor) of the point \(P\).

The components of a vector depend on the coordinate system, just like the coordinates of points. The arrow itself, however, does not depend on the coordinate system. The fly made the same flight however we placed the axes. The triple of numbers is only how the arrow is written in the chosen system, just as the coordinates are how the position of a point is written, and if we turn the axes, the same vector has other components. So when we say that a vector is a triple of numbers, we always mean how it is written in the chosen system. Other books also write the components as \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\) (CM) or \([a_1, a_2, a_3]\) (KREYSZIG (1)).

1.5.3 Calculating with vectors

On the floor the fly crawls a little further, 2 m in the direction of the axis \(x\), that is, by the vector \((2, 0, 0)\). Where is it now? Each coordinate changes by the corresponding component, and from \(Q = (3, 5, 0)\) it gets to the point \((5, 5, 0)\). From the lamp \(P = (2, 3, 2)\) to there the vector is \((5 - 2,\ 5 - 3,\ 0 - 2) = (3, 2, -2)\). We get the same vector if we add the components of the two parts of the path: \(1 + 2 = 3\), \(2 + 0 = 2\) and \(-2 + 0 = -2\). So two moves one after the other have the same effect as a single move whose components are the sums of the components. This is the model for adding vectors. The difference and the multiple are defined in the same way.

Definition 1.14 Sum, difference and multiple of vectors (vsota, razlika in večkratnik vektorjev)

For vectors \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\vek b = (b_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{z}})\) and a number \(k\), the sum (vsota), the difference (razlika) and the multiple (večkratnik) are the vectors

\[\begin{aligned} \vek a + \vek b &= (a_{\mathrm{x}} + b_{\mathrm{x}},\ a_{\mathrm{y}} + b_{\mathrm{y}},\ a_{\mathrm{z}} + b_{\mathrm{z}}) , \\ \vek a - \vek b &= (a_{\mathrm{x}} - b_{\mathrm{x}},\ a_{\mathrm{y}} - b_{\mathrm{y}},\ a_{\mathrm{z}} - b_{\mathrm{z}}) , \\ k\,\vek a &= (k\,a_{\mathrm{x}},\ k\,a_{\mathrm{y}},\ k\,a_{\mathrm{z}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.9}\]

A vector is added to a point in the same way: for a point \(P = (x, y, z)\), \(P + \vek a = (x + a_{\mathrm{x}},\ y + a_{\mathrm{y}},\ z + a_{\mathrm{z}})\) is the point we reach from \(P\) by the move \(\vek a\). The difference of points \(Q - P\) is the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) of (1.8).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (3), (5) (PDF pp. 383-384), CM §2.2.1.1 and §2.2.1.2 (PDF p. 40).

All these operations are calculated component by component: the component \(x\) of the result is obtained from the components \(x\) only, and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). We draw the sum (figure 1.24) by attaching the arrow of the vector \(\vek b\) to the tip of the arrow of the vector \(\vek a\). The sum is the arrow from the start of the first to the tip of the second. If we draw both arrows from the same point, the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram that the two arrows span, a four-sided figure whose opposite sides are parallel (KREYSZIG §9.1, Fig. 172, PDF p. 383).

The multiple \(2\,\vek a\) is the move we get if we make the move \(\vek a\) twice in a row, since component by component \(\vek a + \vek a = 2\,\vek a\). The multiple \((-1)\,\vek a\) undoes the move \(\vek a\), since \(\vek a + (-1)\,\vek a = \vek 0\). It is the move back. The difference \(\vek a - \vek b\) is the vector we must add to the vector \(\vek b\) to get \(\vek a\), and the difference of points \(Q - P\) is the vector we must add to the point \(P\) to reach the point \(Q\).

We will calculate with vectors as we do with numbers: move the terms of a sum around, shift brackets and factor out numbers. Are we allowed to? The operations are defined component by component, and the components are numbers, for which we know these rules. So we expect the rules to hold for vectors too. Let us check.

Lemma 1.15 Rules of vector arithmetic (računska pravila za vektorje)

For all vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) and all numbers \(k\), \(m\):

  1. \(\vek a + \vek b = \vek b + \vek a\),
  2. \((\vek a + \vek b) + \vek c = \vek a + (\vek b + \vek c)\),
  3. \(\vek a + \vek 0 = \vek a\) and \(\vek a - \vek a = \vek 0\),
  4. \(k\,(\vek a + \vek b) = k\,\vek a + k\,\vek b\) and \((k + m)\,\vek a = k\,\vek a + m\,\vek a\),
  5. \(k\,(m\,\vek a) = (k\,m)\,\vek a\) and \(1\,\vek a = \vek a\).
Proof

We must show that for each rule the vectors on the left and on the right are equal.

  1. Two vectors are equal if they agree in all three components (definition 1.13). So we check each rule separately for the components \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).
  2. All operations in the rules are defined component by component ((1.9)), so the component \(x\) of each side is calculated only from the components \(x\) of the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) and from the numbers \(k\), \(m\).
  3. Rule 1. The component \(x\) of the left side is \(a_{\mathrm{x}} + b_{\mathrm{x}}\), of the right side \(b_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{x}}\). The two numbers are equal, because the order of adding numbers does not change the sum.
  4. Rule 2. The component \(x\) of the left side is \((a_{\mathrm{x}} + b_{\mathrm{x}}) + c_{\mathrm{x}}\), of the right side \(a_{\mathrm{x}} + (b_{\mathrm{x}} + c_{\mathrm{x}})\). The two numbers are equal, because when adding three numbers it does not matter which two we add first.
  5. Rule 3. The component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a + \vek 0\) is \(a_{\mathrm{x}} + 0 = a_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a\). The component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a - \vek a\) is \(a_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), which is the component \(x\) of the zero vector.
  6. Rule 4. The component \(x\) of the vector \(k\,(\vek a + \vek b)\) is \(k\,(a_{\mathrm{x}} + b_{\mathrm{x}})\), and the component \(x\) of the vector \(k\,\vek a + k\,\vek b\) is \(k\,a_{\mathrm{x}} + k\,b_{\mathrm{x}}\). The two numbers are equal by the rule for multiplying a sum by a number. The component \(x\) of the vector \((k + m)\,\vek a\) is \((k + m)\,a_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the component \(x\) of the vector \(k\,\vek a + m\,\vek a\) is \(k\,a_{\mathrm{x}} + m\,a_{\mathrm{x}}\). These two numbers are equal by the same rule.
  7. Rule 5. The component \(x\) of the vector \(k\,(m\,\vek a)\) is \(k\,(m\,a_{\mathrm{x}})\), and the component \(x\) of the vector \((k\,m)\,\vek a\) is \((k\,m)\,a_{\mathrm{x}}\). The two numbers are equal, because when multiplying three numbers it does not matter which two we multiply first. The component \(x\) of the vector \(1\,\vek a\) is \(1 \cdot a_{\mathrm{x}} = a_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the component \(x\) of the vector \(\vek a\).
  8. For the components \(y\) and \(z\) the calculation is the same, with \(x\) replaced everywhere by \(y\) or \(z\).
  9. The left and the right side of each rule agree in all three components, so by step 1 they are equal.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (4), (6) (PDF p. 384), CM §2.2.1.1 (PDF p. 40).

The proof has shown a principle we will use all the time: we check an equality of two vectors by checking three equalities of numbers, one for each component. Every rule for adding, subtracting and multiplying by a number that we will need will be checked in this way.

These rules matter more than they seem to. Mathematics turns them around. It takes any set in which we can add two elements and multiply an element by a real number so that the result is again an element of the set. Then it requires that all the rules of vector arithmetic of lemma 1.15 hold. Only in rule 3 no difference is given in advance, so instead of \(\vek a - \vek a = \vek 0\) it requires that every element has an opposite element which, added to it, gives the zero element.

Definition 1.16 Vector space (vektorski prostor)

Let \(X\) be a set in which to every two elements \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) there belongs an element \(\vek a + \vek b\) of \(X\), their sum, and to every element \(\vek a\) and every real number \(k\) an element \(k\,\vek a\) of \(X\), a multiple. The set \(X\) together with these two operations is a vector space (vektorski prostor) if for all elements \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) of \(X\) and all real numbers \(k\), \(m\):

  1. \(\vek a + \vek b = \vek b + \vek a\),
  2. \((\vek a + \vek b) + \vek c = \vek a + (\vek b + \vek c)\),
  3. there is an element \(\vek 0\) of \(X\), the zero element, with \(\vek a + \vek 0 = \vek a\) for every \(\vek a\), and for every \(\vek a\) there is an element \(-\vek a\) of \(X\), the opposite element, with \(\vek a + (-\vek a) = \vek 0\),
  4. \(k\,(\vek a + \vek b) = k\,\vek a + k\,\vek b\) and \((k + m)\,\vek a = k\,\vek a + m\,\vek a\),
  5. \(k\,(m\,\vek a) = (k\,m)\,\vek a\) and \(1\,\vek a = \vek a\).

The elements of a vector space are called vectors (vektorji).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 8.1.1 (PDF p. 8), KREYSZIG §7.9, definition of a real vector space (PDF pp. 335-336).

Triples of numbers with addition and multiplication by a number component by component ((1.9)) are a vector space. Rules 1, 2, 4 and 5 are the rules of lemma 1.15. The zero element is the zero vector \(\vek 0 = (0, 0, 0)\), since \(\vek a + \vek 0 = \vek a\) by rule 3 of the lemma. The opposite element of the vector \(\vek a\) is \((-1)\,\vek a\), since component by component \(a_{\mathrm{x}} + (-1)\,a_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), and the same for \(y\) and \(z\). So whether something is a vector does not depend on that object alone. It depends on the set in which we look at it, and on how we add and multiply by numbers in that set. If only one rule fails, for example \(1\,\vek a = \vek a\), the set is not a vector space. If in the definition we take complex numbers instead of real ones, we get a complex vector space (KREYSZIG §7.9, PDF p. 336), which we will not need in this book.

Arrows in space are only one example. Vectors in this sense are also functions defined for all numbers between two given numbers, which we add by adding their values and multiply by a number by multiplying all their values by it (KREYSZIG §7.9, PDF p. 335, LEBL2 Example 8.1.4, PDF p. 9, for functions without jumps defined for all numbers between \(0\) and \(1\)), and tables of numbers of size \(2 \times 2\) (KREYSZIG §7.9, Example 1). So whatever we derive from these rules alone will hold for all such objects at once. In mechanics, however, the word vector says more than this. What more, we will see in section 1.5.5, when we look at how the components change if we turn the axes.

1.5.4 Length of a vector

How far did the fly travel when it flew from the lamp to the floor by the vector \((1, 2, -2)\)? Not \(1 + 2 + 2 = 5\) m, because that would be the path along the axes: first 1 m in the direction \(x\), then 2 m in the direction \(y\) and then 2 m down. But the fly flies straight. We work out the distance in two steps (figure 1.26).

First we look only at the floor. The point on the floor directly below the fly moves \(1\) m in the direction \(x\) and \(2\) m in the direction \(y\). These two paths are the legs of a right triangle, since the axes are perpendicular, and the straight path of the point on the floor is its hypotenuse. By the Pythagorean theorem from school, the square of the hypotenuse is the sum of the squares of the legs, \(1^2 + 2^2 = 5\), so the point on the floor moves \(\sqrt 5\) m.

Then we add the height. The fly has come down \(2\) m vertically, and the vertical is perpendicular to every direction on the floor. So the straight path of the point on the floor and the vertical descent are the legs of a second right triangle, whose hypotenuse is the path of the fly. The square of the fly's path is \(5 + 2^2 = 9\), and the path itself is \(\sqrt 9 = 3\) m.

The two steps together say that the square of the distance is the sum of the squares of all three components, \(1^2 + 2^2 + (-2)^2 = 9\). The sign of a component makes no difference, because the square of a negative number is positive.

Definition 1.17 Length of a vector and distance (dolžina vektorja in razdalja)

The length (dolžina) or magnitude (velikost) of the vector \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\) is the number

\[|\vek a| = \sqrt{a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2} . \tag{1.10}\]

The distance (razdalja) between the points \(P\) and \(Q\) is the length of the vector between them, \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (2) (PDF p. 382), CM §2.2.1 (PDF p. 39).

So the length is a number that is never negative, and it has the same unit as the components. We do not prove the Pythagorean theorem in this book. We measure coordinates with the same tape along three mutually perpendicular axes, and for such coordinates school geometry gives us the formula (1.10), as we saw with the fly. From now on this formula is what the word length means, and everything we claim about lengths we will derive from it. It holds only for components in a rectangular Cartesian system, where the axes are perpendicular and the units equal.

Length too has a more general form. Mathematics calls a norm (norma) any rule that assigns a number to a vector so that three requirements hold: the number is never negative and is zero only for the zero vector, for a multiple of a vector it is multiplied by the absolute value of the number, and the norm of a sum is not larger than the sum of the norms (LEBL2 Def. 8.2.1, PDF p. 20). Our length is an example of a norm, called the Euclidean norm (LEBL2, PDF p. 20). More general still is a distance between the elements of any set, which must meet similar requirements (LEBL1 Def. 7.1.1, PDF p. 255).

For a vector with a single nonzero component, for example \((a_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\), the length is \(\sqrt{a_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\), the nonnegative number whose square is \(a_{\mathrm{x}}^2\). This is exactly the absolute value \(|a_{\mathrm{x}}|\), the distance of the number \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\) from zero from section 1.3. That is why we use the same sign for the length of a vector as for the absolute value. The length of a vector measures distances in space as the absolute value measures them on the number line.

The distance between the lamp \(P = (2, 3, 2)\) and the point \(Q = (3, 5, 0)\) on the floor is the length of the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (1, 2, -2)\), that is, \(3\) m. This is exactly what we will need in section 1.6: the distance between two points of a body before and after loading.

1.5.5 Unit vectors and steps along the axes

With the length we can separate the two things an arrow carries: how long it is and where it points. The flight of the fly \(\vek a = (1, 2, -2)\) is \(3\) m long. If we multiply it by \(1/3\), we get the vector \(\tfrac13 (1, 2, -2) = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, -\tfrac23)\). It points the same way, and its length is \(\sqrt{\tfrac19 + \tfrac49 + \tfrac49} = 1\). Such a vector carries only the direction.

Definition 1.18 Unit vector (enotski vektor)

A unit vector (enotski vektor) is a vector of length \(1\).

Source: CM §2.2.1 (PDF p. 39).

Every vector except the zero vector can be shortened or lengthened into a unit vector that points the same way.

Lemma 1.19 Unit vector in the direction of a vector (enotski vektor v smeri vektorja)

For every vector \(\vek a \neq \vek 0\) the vector

\[\hat{\vek a} = \frac{1}{|\vek a|}\,\vek a \tag{1.11}\]

is a unit vector, and \(\vek a = |\vek a|\,\hat{\vek a}\).

Proof

We compute the length of \(\hat{\vek a}\) from its components.

  1. Since \(\vek a \neq \vek 0\), at least one component of \(\vek a\) is not zero, since two vectors are equal only if they agree in all components (definition of a vector 1.13). Its square is positive and the squares of the other two are not negative, so \(a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2 > 0\) and \(|\vek a| > 0\). So we may divide by \(|\vek a|\).
  2. By the definition of the multiple ((1.9)), \(\hat{\vek a} = (a_{\mathrm{x}}/|\vek a|,\ a_{\mathrm{y}}/|\vek a|,\ a_{\mathrm{z}}/|\vek a|)\).
  3. The square of a quotient is the quotient of the squares, so the squares of the components are \(a_{\mathrm{x}}^2/|\vek a|^2\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}^2/|\vek a|^2\) and \(a_{\mathrm{z}}^2/|\vek a|^2\).
  4. Quotients with the same denominator are added by adding the numerators: the sum of the squares is \((a_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + a_{\mathrm{z}}^2)/|\vek a|^2\).
  5. By (1.10) the numerator is \(|\vek a|^2\), so the sum of the squares is \(1\), and by the same formula \(|\hat{\vek a}| = \sqrt 1 = 1\).
  6. By rule 5 of the rules of vector arithmetic (lemma 1.15), \(|\vek a|\,\hat{\vek a} = (|\vek a| \cdot \tfrac{1}{|\vek a|})\,\vek a = 1\,\vek a = \vek a\).

Source: CM (2.2.1), (2.2.2) (PDF p. 39).

So every vector except the zero vector is its length times a unit vector that gives its direction. The hat over the letter is the usual mark of a unit vector (CM (2.2.1)). For the fly, \(\hat{\vek a} = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, -\tfrac23)\) and \(\vek a = 3\,\hat{\vek a}\).

We described the flight of the fly \((1, 2, -2)\) in words as three moves: 1 m in the direction of the axis \(x\), 2 m in the direction of the axis \(y\) and 2 m down. With the sum and the multiple we can now write this with vectors. The unit vector in the positive direction of the axis \(x\) is \((1, 0, 0)\): it points along the axis \(x\), and its length is \(\sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2} = 1\). In the same way \((0, 1, 0)\) is the unit vector along the axis \(y\) and \((0, 0, 1)\) along the axis \(z\). The flight of the fly is one such step in the direction of the axis \(x\), two in the direction of the axis \(y\) and two against the direction of the axis \(z\):

\[1\,(1, 0, 0) + 2\,(0, 1, 0) + (-2)\,(0, 0, 1) = (1, 0, 0) + (0, 2, 0) + (0, 0, -2) = (1, 2, -2) .\]

So the components of a vector are the numbers of steps along the individual axes from which the vector is made. We will need these three vectors often, so they get a name.

Definition 1.20 Unit vectors of the axes (enotski vektorji osi)

In a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system the unit vectors of the axes (enotski vektorji osi) are the vectors

\[\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0) , \quad \vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0) , \quad \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1) . \tag{1.12}\]

Each of them is the unit vector in the positive direction of its axis.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (8), (9) (PDF p. 385), SADD §1.2 (PDF p. 12).

Every vector can be made from such steps, and in only one way.

Lemma 1.21 A vector as a sum of steps along the axes (vektor kot vsota korakov vzdolž osi)

For every vector \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\)

\[\vek a = a_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + a_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + a_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} . \tag{1.13}\]

If \(\vek a = k\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + m\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + n\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) for some numbers \(k\), \(m\) and \(n\), then \(k = a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(m = a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(n = a_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Proof

First we calculate the right side, then we compare components.

  1. By the definition of the multiple ((1.9)), \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 1,\ a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 0,\ a_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 0) = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\).
  2. In the same way, \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, a_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) and \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, a_{\mathrm{z}})\).
  3. By the definition of the sum, \((a_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0) + (0, a_{\mathrm{y}}, 0) = (a_{\mathrm{x}} + 0,\ 0 + a_{\mathrm{y}},\ 0 + 0) = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\).
  4. We add \((0, 0, a_{\mathrm{z}})\) and get \((a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\), that is, \(\vek a\). We write no brackets in the sum of three vectors, because by rule 2 of the rules of vector arithmetic (lemma 1.15) it does not matter which two we add first. This proves the first claim.
  5. For the second claim we repeat steps 1 to 4 with the numbers \(k\), \(m\), \(n\) in place of \(a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{z}}\) and get \(k\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + m\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + n\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (k, m, n)\).
  6. By assumption this vector equals the vector \(\vek a = (a_{\mathrm{x}}, a_{\mathrm{y}}, a_{\mathrm{z}})\). Two vectors are equal if they agree in all three components (definition 1.13), so \(k = a_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(m = a_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(n = a_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.1 (8) (PDF p. 385).

The lemma says two things. The components are exactly the numbers of steps along the axes that make up the vector. And there are no other numbers that give the same vector, so the components in the chosen system tell everything about the vector and nothing more. Many books write the unit vectors of the axes as \(\vek i\), \(\vek j\), \(\vek k\), and the flight of the fly there would be \(\vek i + 2\,\vek j - 2\,\vek k\) (KREYSZIG (8), PDF p. 385). Others write them \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\), \(\vek e_3\) (SADD §1.2, PDF p. 12), and so will we, once we need digits instead of the letters \(x\), \(y\), \(z\).

Now let us show what we only claimed after the definition of a vector 1.13: the arrow is one, but its components depend on the coordinate system. Let us turn the axes about the vertical axis \(z\) by a quarter turn, so that the new axis \(x\) points where the old axis \(y\) pointed, the new axis \(y\) points opposite to the old axis \(x\), and the axis \(z\) stays as it was. We mark the unit vectors of the new axes with a bar on top. Written in the old system they are

\[\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, 0) , \quad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 0, 0) , \quad \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1) .\]

The flight of the fly is one step along the old axis \(x\), two along the old axis \(y\) and two down. The old axis \(y\) is now the new axis \(x\), so two steps along the old axis \(y\) are two steps along the new axis \(x\). The old axis \(x\) points opposite to the new axis \(y\), so one step along the old axis \(x\) is one step back along the new axis \(y\). The vertical part does not change. Let us check:

\[2\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} + (-1)\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} + (-2)\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 2, 0) + (1, 0, 0) + (0, 0, -2) = (1, 2, -2) .\]

So by lemma 1.21 on a vector as a sum of steps along the axes, applied in the turned system, where \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the unit vectors of the axes, the same flight has the components \((2, -1, -2)\) in the turned system. The arrow is the same, its length \(\sqrt{2^2 + (-1)^2 + (-2)^2} = 3\) m is the same, but the numbers are different. How the components change under any turn of the axes we will derive when we need it.

Nor are the unit vectors of the axes the only triple from which every vector can be made. Any three vectors that, drawn from one point, do not lie in one plane serve equally well, for example vectors along axes that are not perpendicular. Every vector is in exactly one way a sum of their multiples, and the numbers in this sum are the components of the vector with respect to these three vectors (CM (2.2.30), PDF p. 48). The unit vectors of rectangular axes are the simplest choice, because the components with respect to them are simply the differences of coordinates of (1.8). Until we say otherwise, a component of a vector always means a component with respect to the unit vectors of the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system.

Now we can also answer the question that the vector space left open: is every triple of numbers a vector? In the mathematical sense yes, since we add triples and multiply them by numbers component by component, and all the rules hold. In mechanics, however, the word vector says more. Take the masses of three parts of a machine, for example \((2, 5, 1)\) kg. Two such machines together have \((4, 10, 2)\) kg, so it makes sense to add such triples and multiply them by numbers. But they are not arrows. When we turn the axes, the components of the fly's flight change from \((1, 2, -2)\) to \((2, -1, -2)\), while the masses of the machine parts stay as they are. A vector in mechanics is a quantity with a size and a direction, an arrow, whose components change in a definite way when the axes are turned, while the arrow itself stays the same (SADD (1.4.6), PDF p. 17, BARBER §1.1.4, PDF p. 26). So three numbers that come out of some calculation may or may not be the components of a vector. We decide by how they change when we turn the axes (BOWER Appendix B.1.3, PDF p. 758).

1.6 Displacement in space

Let us return to mechanics, where we left it at the end of section 1.4: to the bar and to bodies with three dimensions. When we load a body, every point of it moves from its old position to a new one. For the bar we described this move by a single number, because the points moved only along the bar. In a body a point can move in any direction, so we describe its move by a vector.

Definition 1.22 Displacement vector (vektor pomika)

If a point of a body moves under loading from the position \(P\) to a new position, its displacement vector (vektor pomika) \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) is the vector from the old position to the new one. So the new position is \(P + \vek u\). The components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) say how far the point moves in the direction of the axis \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Source: CM (3.2.7) (PDF p. 117), BARBER (1.32) (PDF pp. 31-32), SADD §2.1 (PDF p. 39).

How does the bar of the first sections fit into this? There we labelled a point of the bar by its distance \(x\) from the ceiling, measured before loading, and its displacement by a single number \(u(x)\), how far the point moved down. To write this displacement as a vector, we choose a coordinate system that fits the bar. We put the origin at the top end of the bar and point the axis \(x\) down along the bar. Then the coordinate \(x\) of a point on the axis of the bar is exactly its distance \(x\) from the ceiling, and a move down by \(u(x)\) is a move in the direction of the axis \(x\). So the displacement vector of this point is

\[\vek u = \big(u(x),\ 0,\ 0\big) .\]

Its component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the number \(u(x)\) of the previous sections. The components \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero, because this point moves only along the axis \(x\).

This holds for the points on the axis of the bar, that is, for the line we have looked at so far. A bar that we stretch also gets a little thinner. When a steel bar gets longer by a thousandth of its length, its thickness decreases by about \(0{,}3\) thousandths of the thickness (BOWER §3.2, PDF p. 102, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). So the points off the axis of the bar also move a little sideways, toward the axis, and for them \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are not zero. We have not taken this into account so far. In a body all three components of the displacement are in general different from zero.

Can we explain the thinning by the volume? Suppose the material kept its volume exactly. A cube of the material with edge \(1\) becomes a block with the edge \(1{,}001\) along the axis and the edges \(1 - d\) across it, and its volume is \(1{,}001\,(1 - d)^2\) (BARBER §1.3.2, PDF p. 40). This equals \(1\) only for \(d = 1 - 1/\sqrt{1{,}001} \approx 0{,}0005\): the thickness would decrease by half a thousandth. Steel gets thinner by less, \(0{,}0003\), so its volume grows a little, \(1{,}001 \cdot 0{,}9997^2 \approx 1{,}0004\), that is, by about \(0{,}04\) %. So steel does not keep its volume exactly. Keeping the volume is a limiting case. With the measure \(\Delta L / L\), a material that keeps its volume exactly has the ratio of the relative decrease of thickness to the relative increase of length close to \(0{,}5\): at the strain \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) it is \(0{,}49963\), and in general \(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{3}{8}\varepsilon + \dots\), so for a smaller strain it comes still closer to \(0{,}5\). With the logarithmic strain the ratio is exactly \(0{,}5\) for every elongation, because the volume is the product of the ratios of the three edges and the logarithm turns a product into a sum: \(\ln 1{,}001 + 2 \ln (1 - d) = \ln 1 = 0\), so the lateral logarithmic strain is exactly \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) of the axial one. The value \(0{,}5\) that BOWER gives is the small-strain value (BOWER §3.2, PDF p. 102). Rubber, with \(0{,}49\), comes very close to it (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). If the ratio were \(0\), the bar would not get thinner at all (BOWER p. 102). For most materials it lies between these two cases, typically between \(0{,}2\) and \(0{,}49\), and around \(0{,}3\) for metals (BOWER p. 102). How much a material gets thinner is therefore a property of the material, which we measure in a test. Books call this ratio Poisson's ratio (Poissonovo število), and we will meet it in chapter 3.

Books also write the components of the displacement vector as \(u_1\), \(u_2\), \(u_3\) (CM) or \(u\), \(v\), \(w\) (SADD §2.1, PDF p. 39). In this book the index says the direction, as with the components of every vector.

Every point of the body has its own displacement vector, and different points move differently. For the hanging bar the displacement depended on the position \(x\). In a body it depends on the position of the point, that is, on three coordinates.

Definition 1.23 Displacement field (polje pomikov)

The displacement field (polje pomikov) of a body is the rule that assigns to every point \((x, y, z)\) of the body, taken in its position before loading, its displacement vector

\[\vek u(x, y, z) = \big(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z),\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z),\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z)\big) . \tag{1.14}\]

Source: CM (3.2.8) (PDF p. 117), SADD §2.1 (PDF p. 39).

The displacement field is a rule of the same kind as a function of definition 1.4, except that it has three numbers at the input and three at the output. At the input are the coordinates of the point before loading, at the output the components of its displacement. Each component on its own, for example \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\), is a rule whose input is three numbers and whose output is one number. The numbers at the input are called variables (spremenljivke), so such a rule is called a function of three variables (funkcija treh spremenljivk). The word field comes from a picture: if we draw at every point of the body the arrow of its displacement, the body is covered with arrows like a field with blades of grass.

How do we tell from the displacement field whether the body is deformed? If the displacement is the same vector at all points, all points move equally, and the body only moves as a whole. This is the rigid-body displacement of section 1.4, now in space. But the body can also be turned as a whole without being deformed. Then the points move differently, while the distances between them stay the same, so this too is a rigid-body displacement. Every rigid-body displacement is a move of all points by the same vector, a turn of the body, or both one after the other (CM (3.8.12), PDF p. 156, for small turns SADD (2.2.10), PDF p. 45). So displacements that differ from point to point do not yet mean deformation. Deformation is a change of the distances between points, and that is why we will measure it with lengths.

1.6.1 Fibres

For the bar we looked at a small piece between two points. In a body we do the same, except that the piece can lie in any direction.

Definition 1.24 Material fibre (vlakno)

A material fibre (vlakno) is a straight segment between two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of a body, that is, a straight line that starts at \(P\), ends at \(Q\) and lies wholly in the body, which we imagine drawn into the material so that its points move together with the material. Before loading the fibre is described by the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\).

Source: CM §3.3.1 (PDF pp. 118-119, material line element), SADD §2.2 (PDF p. 42, fibers).

A fibre is like a very thin bar inside the body. So we calculate its strain as the strain of a bar (1.1): the elongation divided by the length before loading. The length before loading is \(L_0 = |\overrightarrow{PQ}|\), the length after loading \(L_1\) is the distance between the new positions of the ends, and the elongation is \(L_1 - L_0\). After loading a fibre is in general no longer perfectly straight. A short fibre bends only a little, so we take the distance between the new positions of the ends as the new length. How accurate this is we will see when we shorten the fibre towards zero, as we did with the piece of the bar. For the cube below the fibres stay straight, and there it is exact.

Where does the fibre go? The end \(P\) moves by \(\vek u(P)\), which means the displacement vector at the point \(P\), and the end \(Q\) by \(\vek u(Q)\). The new positions of the ends are \(P_1 = P + \vek u(P)\) and \(Q_1 = Q + \vek u(Q)\). The index \(1\), as in \(L_1\), means the state after loading. We calculate the vector of the fibre after loading, \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}\), component by component, the way we checked the rules of vector arithmetic in the proof of lemma 1.15. Let \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{Q}}, y_{\mathrm{Q}}, z_{\mathrm{Q}})\).

  1. The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(Q_1\) is \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} + u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q)\), and that of the point \(P_1\) is \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\), because a vector is added to a point in the same way as in the sum of vectors, by adding to each coordinate the corresponding component (definition 1.14).
  2. The component \(x\) of the vector \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}\) is the difference of these two coordinates ((1.8)), \((x_{\mathrm{Q}} + u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q)) - (x_{\mathrm{P}} + u_{\mathrm{x}}(P))\).
  3. We remove the brackets and rearrange the terms by the rules for numbers: \((x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}) + (u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P))\). The first bracket is the component \(x\) of the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) ((1.8)), the second the component \(x\) of the difference \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\) ((1.9)).
  4. For the components \(y\) and \(z\) the calculation is the same. So the two vectors agree in all three components, and by definition 1.13 that is what equality of vectors means, so
    \[\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = \overrightarrow{PQ} + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) . \tag{1.15}\]

So a fibre changes only by the difference of the displacements of its ends (figure 1.32). This is the same difference as \(\Delta u = u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)\) for the piece of the bar, except that it is now a vector. If the displacement is the same at all points, the difference is the zero vector, and every fibre stays as it was.

1.6.2 A sheared cube

Let us try all this on one simple body. We glue a steel cube with an edge of 10 mm to a table by its bottom face and push its top face sideways, so that it moves by 10 µm (figure 1.33). A micrometre, µm, is a thousandth of a millimetre, so the shift is a thousandth of the edge. The cube leans over like the deck of cards of section 1.1: every horizontal layer slides a little relative to the layer below it. Books call such a deformation simple shear (enostavni strig) (CM (3.3.14), PDF p. 123). The word shear describes exactly this, layers sliding past each other like the blades of scissors.

We place the coordinate system at the bottom front left corner of the cube: the axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(y\) along the other bottom edge, and the axis \(z\) vertically up. We measure lengths in micrometres, so the edge of the cube is \(10\,000\) µm. How far does each point move? The bottom layer is glued and does not move at all. The top layer, at the height \(10\,000\) µm, moves by \(10\) µm. A layer in between moves in proportion to its height, by a thousandth of it: the layer at the height \(5\,000\) µm by \(5\) µm, the layer at the height \(z\) by \(0{,}001\,z\) (figure 1.34). All points move only in the direction \(x\). So the displacement field is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = 0{,}001\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = 0 , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) = 0 . \tag{1.16}\]

At the bottom face, where \(z = 0\), the displacement is zero, as it must be, since the face is glued down. The field does not depend on \(x\) and \(y\): all points of one layer move equally.

This field is an idealization, a simple model of the sheared cube. We get it exactly only if, besides the push on the top face and the glue on the bottom one, we also pull along the two side faces that are perpendicular to the axis \(x\): the one we push towards upward, the opposite one downward. The push at the top and the glue at the bottom pull in opposite directions at different heights, and on their own they would tend to turn the cube. If we push only the top face, the field does not hold near these two side faces. Which forces the field needs we compute in chapter 3.

Is it reasonable that the layers move only sideways and not also up or down? One reason is that this way the cube keeps its volume. The front face \(ABCD\) becomes a parallelogram with the same base \(AB\) and the same height, \(10\,000\) µm, and the area of a parallelogram is its base times its height, so the area of the face does not change. The depth of the cube stays the same as well, so its volume does not change either. This holds although the slanted edges get a little longer, as we will compute for the edge \(AD\) below. A deformation that keeps the volume of every piece of a body is called an isochoric deformation (izohorna deformacija), and simple shear is one (CM §3.3.2, PDF pp. 121-122). For small deformations this holds in general: the change of volume of a small piece depends only on its normal strains, while shear changes only the shape, not the volume (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF pp. 51-52).

To see how the material is stretched, we follow four fibres on the front face of the cube, where \(y = 0\) (figure 1.35). Its corners are \(A = (0, 0, 0)\), \(B = (10\,000, 0, 0)\), \(C = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) and \(D = (0, 0, 10\,000)\). The fibres are the bottom edge \(AB\), the vertical edge \(AD\), and the two diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\). The bottom corners do not move, \(\vek u(A) = \vek u(B) = \vek 0\), and the top ones move by \(\vek u(C) = \vek u(D) = (10, 0, 0)\). For each fibre we calculate its vector after loading by (1.15), its two lengths by (1.10) and its strain by (1.1).

Let us show the calculation for the vertical edge \(AD\). Before loading \(\overrightarrow{AD} = (0, 0, 10\,000)\), with length \(L_0 = 10\,000\) µm. The difference of the displacements of the ends is \(\vek u(D) - \vek u(A) = (10, 0, 0)\), so the vector after loading is \((0, 0, 10\,000) + (10, 0, 0) = (10, 0, 10\,000)\). Its length is

\[L_1 = \sqrt{10^2 + 0^2 + 10\,000^2} = \sqrt{100\,000\,100} = 10\,000{,}005\ \text{µm} ,\]

and the strain is \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0 = 0{,}005/10\,000 = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The other fibres are calculated in the same way. Before loading both diagonals are \(\sqrt{2 \cdot 10\,000^2} = 14\,142{,}136\) µm long, after loading \(AC\) is \(14\,149{,}208\) µm long and \(BD\) is \(14\,135{,}066\) µm long.

fibre vector before loading vector after loading strain
bottom edge \(AB\) \((10\,000, 0, 0)\) \((10\,000, 0, 0)\) \(0\)
vertical edge \(AD\) \((0, 0, 10\,000)\) \((10, 0, 10\,000)\) \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \((10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\) \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \((-10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) \((-9\,990, 0, 10\,000)\) \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

The table shows three things that we could not see with the bar.

  1. The diagonal \(AC\) has become longer by five ten-thousandths, and the diagonal \(BD\) shorter by almost exactly as much (figure 1.37). The same material and the same loading, and yet the material is stretched in one direction and shortened in another. How much the material is stretched depends on the direction in which we measure it.
  2. The edges have hardly changed. The bottom edge has stayed the same, and the vertical one has become longer by only \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), a thousand times less than the diagonals.
  3. The vertical edge has tilted, since its top has moved sideways and its bottom has not. So the right angle between the edges \(AB\) and \(AD\) at the corner \(A\) has become a little smaller. This is the change of a right angle that a shear strain describes (definition 1.3), here between the directions \(x\) and \(z\). The front face, which was a square, has become a parallelogram, a leaning four-sided figure with parallel opposite sides.

What happens if we push the top face twice as far, by 20 µm? The displacement field is then \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}002\,z\), and when we repeat the calculation, the diagonals get the strains \(+1{,}0005 \cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(-0{,}9995 \cdot 10^{-3}\), twice as much as before. The vertical edge, however, gets \(2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\), four times as much as before. The strain of the diagonals grows in proportion to the shift of the top face, and the strain of the vertical edge with the square of the shift.

These numbers show two patterns that need an explanation. The two diagonals change by almost the same amount with opposite signs, namely by half the ratio between the shift of the top face and the height of the cube: \(0{,}0005\) for the ratio \(10/10\,000 = 0{,}001\). The vertical edge changes a thousand times less, and when the shift doubles, its strain grows four times, so it grows with the square of the shift. Where does this come from? We call the height of the cube \(h\) and the shift of the top face \(s\), so \(h = 10\,000\) µm and \(s = 10\) µm. The ratio \(s/h\) is a ratio of two lengths, a number without a unit.

What gets in the way of the calculation is the square root in the lengths. We get rid of it with one move that we will need again.

  1. We multiply and divide the strain \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0\) by \(L_1 + L_0\). We may, because \(L_1 + L_0 > 0\), and the value does not change.
  2. The numerator becomes \((L_1 - L_0)(L_1 + L_0)\). When we multiply out the brackets, the terms \(L_1 L_0\) and \(-L_0 L_1\) cancel, and \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\) remains. So
    \[\varepsilon = \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{L_0\,(L_1 + L_0)} . \tag{1.17}\]
    This equality is exact. The squares of the lengths are sums of squares of components ((1.10)), so there are no roots in the numerator.
  3. The denominator of (1.17), \(L_0\,(L_1 + L_0)\), still contains the new length \(L_1\), which we compute with a square root. We would like to get rid of this root too. If the length of the fibre did not change, we would have \(L_1 = L_0\) and the denominator \(L_0\,(L_0 + L_0) = 2L_0^2\). We check how far the true denominator is from this value. From \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0\) we get \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\), so \(L_1 + L_0 = L_0\,(2 + \varepsilon)\), and the true denominator is \(L_0 \cdot L_0\,(2 + \varepsilon) = 2L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon/2)\). So it differs from \(2L_0^2\) only by the factor \(1 + \varepsilon/2\). For strains smaller than a thousandth in size, \(|\varepsilon| < 0{,}001\), this factor differs from \(1\) by less than half a thousandth. So if we replace the denominator \(L_0\,(L_1 + L_0)\) by \(2L_0^2\), we are wrong by less than half a thousandth of the calculated value:
    \[\varepsilon \approx \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} .\]
    So the strain is about half the relative change of the square of the length. Why half? The new length is \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\), so its square is \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2\). The square \((1 + \varepsilon)^2\) is just the product \((1 + \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon)\) written out: multiplying every term of the first bracket by every term of the second gives \(1 + \varepsilon + \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2 = 1 + 2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2\). So the relative change of the square of the length is \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/L_0^2 = 2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2\). The last term is the product \(\varepsilon \cdot \varepsilon\), and for \(|\varepsilon| < 0{,}001\) it is smaller than a thousandth of \(\varepsilon\) in size, for example \(\varepsilon^2 = 0{,}000001\) for \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\). Without it, the relative change of the square is \(2\varepsilon\), twice the strain, and the strain is half of it.
  4. The bottom end of each of our three fibres does not move, and the top end moves sideways by \(s\). So the vertical part of each fibre stays \(h\), and its horizontal part changes by \(s\).
  5. The vertical edge \(AD\) has no horizontal part before loading and gets the horizontal part \(s\). The square of its length grows from \(h^2\) to \(h^2 + s^2\), and step 3 gives \(\varepsilon \approx s^2/(2h^2)\). For our cube this is \(10^2/(2 \cdot 10\,000^2) = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\).
  6. The diagonal \(AC\) has the horizontal part \(h\), which grows to \(h + s\). The square of its length grows from \(h^2 + h^2 = 2h^2\) to \((h + s)^2 + h^2 = 2h^2 + 2hs + s^2\), so by \(2hs + s^2\). The part \(s^2\) is only \(s/(2h) = 0{,}0005\) times the part \(2hs\), so we leave it out, and \(\varepsilon \approx 2hs/(2 \cdot 2h^2) = s/(2h) = 0{,}0005\). The diagonal \(BD\) points the other way, its horizontal part shrinks from \(h\) to \(h - s\), the square of its length shrinks by about \(2hs\), and \(\varepsilon \approx -s/(2h) = -0{,}0005\).

Let us put the three fibres side by side.

fibre change of the square of the length strain
edge \(AD\) \(s^2\) \(\approx s^2/(2h^2) = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \(2hs + s^2\) \(\approx s/(2h) = 5 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \(-2hs + s^2\) \(\approx -s/(2h) = -5 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

The changes are made of two kinds of terms: terms with the shift \(s\) itself, namely \(\pm 2hs\), and terms with its square, \(s^2\). The term \(s^2\) is \(s/(2h) = 0{,}0005\) times the term \(2hs\), so it is 2000 times smaller. Where there is a term with \(s\), as for the diagonals, we may leave out the term \(s^2\), and we are wrong by less than a thousandth. Where there is no term with \(s\), as for the vertical edge, which only tilts, the term \(s^2\) is all that is left. That is why the change of the edge is a thousand times smaller than that of the diagonals and grows with the square of the shift: twice the shift, four times the strain. The term \(s^2\) that we left out and the small error of step 3 cause the small difference between \(5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\) in the table of the exactly computed strains.

We will use this rule all the time with small deformations. Next to a term with a small number itself, a term with its square is smaller roughly by the factor of that small number, as long as the numbers in front of the two terms are of similar size, as here. So we may leave it out.

Is the front face special? It is not. The difference of the displacements of two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of the cube is \(\big(0{,}001\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}),\ 0,\ 0\big)\). It depends only on how much higher \(Q\) lies than \(P\), not on where in the cube the two points are. By (1.15), two fibres with the same vector before loading therefore also have the same vector after loading, and the same strain, wherever in the cube they lie (figure 1.39). The whole cube is deformed in the same way at every point, and what we saw on the front face holds everywhere in it. Such a deformation is called a homogeneous deformation (homogena deformacija) (CM §3.3.2, PDF p. 122).

The cube has taught us two things. First, how the material is stretched close to a point is not described by a single number. We saw this by following four fibres of the front face and computing the strain of each from its lengths before and after loading (the table with the vectors of the fibres). The diagonal \(AC\) has the strain \(+5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the diagonal \(BD\) the strain \(-5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the bottom edge \(AB\) zero and the vertical edge \(AD\) only \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The edge \(AD\) also tilted, so the right angle between the edges \(AB\) and \(AD\) became smaller. These four fibres do not all pass through one point. The diagonals cross at the centre of the front face, and through the centre also pass a horizontal fibre with the same vector as \(AB\) and a vertical fibre with the same vector as \(AD\). The cube is deformed in the same way everywhere, so these two fibres get the same vectors after loading as the edges, and with them the same strains and the same change of the right angle between them. So the fibres through the centre of the face are stretched in one direction, shortened in another, almost unchanged in a third, and the angles between them change too. Second, we can calculate all of this from the displacement field. For every fibre we used only the field (1.16). It gave the displacements of the ends, the equation (1.15) turned their difference into the vector of the fibre after loading, and from the vectors before and after loading we got the two lengths and the strain. We needed nothing else.

For the cube the field was very clear, since the displacement was only horizontal and proportional to the height. So the difference of the displacements of the ends of a fibre depended only on the vector of the fibre, and the strain of a fibre only on its direction, not on where it lies or how long it is. A fibre in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) that is half as long has half the difference of displacements, a vector after loading half as long, and therefore the same strain. That is why the whole edges and diagonals of the cube were enough. In a general body, however, the displacement changes from point to point in a complicated way, as for the hanging bar, where the piece of 1 m at the top had the strain \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and the piece of 0,001 m the strain \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Now the displacement changes in three directions and depends on three coordinates. For the bar we helped ourselves with a piece that we shortened towards zero, and with the derivative. In space we will do the same. For this we will need derivatives of functions of three variables, and a way of writing that gives the strain of a fibre for every direction. We continue with them in the next section.

1.7 Mathematics: partial derivatives

At the end of the previous section we found that in a general body the displacement changes from point to point in all three directions. For the bar we measured how fast the displacement changes along the bar with the derivative (definition 1.9). In this section we extend the derivative to functions of three variables. First we look at a body that needs this extension: the hanging bar, this time with all three components of its displacement. Then we define the derivative in which only one of the three coordinates changes, compute it for this bar and look at what the numbers tell us.

1.7.1 The hanging bar in space

A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs from the ceiling and stretches under its own weight. Let it have a round cross section with a diameter of 10 mm. How it is held matters for its field, so let us say it exactly (figure 1.40, left). The field we will take from the books holds for a bar of which only one point is fixed, the centre \(O\) of its top end, which does not move (CM (7.3.16), PDF p. 305). The books set no other condition for the top face. Their solution, though, implies that every cross section carries the part of the bar below it evenly over its whole face, the top one included (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305, SADD Example 5.1, PDF p. 115). So the weight of the bar is carried by a force that acts upward on the top face and is spread evenly over it, the same on every square millimetre. The fixed point \(O\) carries no weight and only keeps the bar from moving as a whole. That the bar does not turn as a whole either, CM ensures with one more condition: the material right next to the point \(O\) does not turn (CM, PDF p. 306). The top face is not glued to anything, so, like every cross section, it can get a little narrower and, as we will see, curve a little. No real ceiling holds a bar like this. This way of holding is an idealization that gives a simple field. How other ways of holding change the field near the ceiling, we look at at the end of this section.

We set up the coordinate system as in section 1.6: the origin \(O\) is at the centre of the top end of the bar, the axis \(x\) points vertically down along the axis of the bar, and the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are horizontal, perpendicular to the bar. So the coordinate \(x\) of a point is its depth below the ceiling, and the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) say how far from the axis of the bar it lies and on which side.

In section 1.2 we used, for the points on the axis of the bar, the downward displacement

\[u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2) , \qquad a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

In section 1.6 we saw that a bar that stretches also gets thinner: when a steel bar gets longer by a thousandth of its length, its thickness decreases by about \(0{,}3\) thousandths. So the points off the axis also move toward the axis. The whole displacement field of the hanging bar, that is, the rule that assigns to every point of the bar its displacement vector (definition 1.23), is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z . \end{aligned} \tag{1.18}\]

The number \(0{,}3\) is the ratio of thinning to stretching for steel, Poisson's ratio from section 1.6. For another material its own ratio would stand here. Where the other numbers in the field come from, we explain below.

We took the field from SADD (5.7.4) (PDF p. 115) and CM (7.3.20) (PDF p. 306), where it is written in differently placed axes and with symbols for properties of steel. CM (7.3.20) lacks a constant term in the component of the displacement along the bar, which CM determines just before from the condition that the point \(O\) does not move (CM, PDF p. 306). How the field is derived we will see in chapter 11. The two books derive it under these assumptions. The steel is the same everywhere and behaves the same in all directions. After unloading it returns to its original shape. The strains are small, below about a thousandth, and the displacements are small compared with the bar. The weight acts on every small piece vertically downward, and the bar is held in the idealized way we described (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF pp. 305-306, SADD Example 5.1, PDF p. 115). Where one of the assumptions does not hold, for example near a real ceiling or under a load so large that the steel deforms permanently, the field does not hold. For now we take it as given and look at what it says.

On the axis of the bar \(y = 0\) and \(z = 0\). Putting them into (1.18) gives

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, 0, 0) &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(0^2 + 0^2) = a\,(2Lx - x^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 0, 0) &= 0 , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, 0, 0) &= 0 . \end{aligned}\]

So a point on the axis moves only down, by \(u(x)\), and its displacement vector is \(\big(u(x), 0, 0\big)\), as we wrote in section 1.6.

Off the axis the points also move sideways (figure 1.41). Look at the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\). The numbers \(a\) and \(L - x\) are not negative, so \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) has the opposite sign to \(y\). A point to the right of the axis, with \(y > 0\), moves to the left, and a point to the left of the axis, with \(y < 0\), moves to the right. So both move toward the axis. The displacement is proportional to \(y\): a point twice as far from the axis moves twice as much. That is why the bar gets thinner. The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) says the same for the direction of the axis \(z\). The factor \(L - x\) says that the bar gets thinner more at the top than lower down, and not at all at the lower end, where \(x = L\). This also agrees with what we know. In section 1.4 the strain along the bar was \(2a\,(L - x)\), largest at the top and zero at the lower end, at both ends as a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9). The bar gets thinner where it stretches.

Figure 1.42 shows a cross section from below. Every point of the cross section moves toward its centre, the more the farther from the centre it lies, and the circle shrinks into a smaller circle.

By how much does a point move toward the axis, and where does the number \(0{,}6\) come from? Look at a small piece of material at the depth \(x\) (figure 1.43). Along the bar it is stretched by the strain \(\varepsilon = 2a\,(L - x)\), which we computed in section 1.4. So its height \(\Delta x\) grows to \((1 + \varepsilon)\,\Delta x\). Across the bar it contracts by \(0{,}3\) times that: its width \(\Delta y\) decreases to \((1 - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon)\,\Delta y\). We met the thinning rule in section 1.6 for a whole bar, but it also holds for such a small piece, because the neighbouring parts of the bar pull it only up and down and do not squeeze it sideways (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). The fraction by which it contracts is

\[0{,}3\,\varepsilon = 0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x) = 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) .\]

The formula for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) says exactly this: a point at the distance \(y\) from the axis comes closer to the axis by this fraction of the distance \(y\),

\[u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x) \cdot y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y .\]

So the number \(0{,}6\) is \(0{,}3\) times the \(2\) from the strain \(2a\,(L - x)\). The same holds for \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the direction of the axis \(z\). The number \(0{,}3\) in the second term of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the other hand, is half of \(0{,}6\). Why exactly half, we will see at the end of section 1.7.2: with this term the right angle between a fibre along the bar and a fibre across it stays a right angle.

How large are these displacements? Take the point \(P\) at the depth 5 m, 4 mm to the right of the axis, in the plane \(z = 0\). So its coordinates are \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0{,}004\) m and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\). By (1.18) it moves down by

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) &= a\,(2 \cdot 10 \cdot 5 - 5^2)\ \text{m}^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(0{,}004^2 + 0^2)\ \text{m}^2 \\ &= 1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m} - 9{,}4 \cdot 10^{-13}\ \text{m} \end{aligned}\]

and sideways by

\[u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) = -0{,}6\,a\,(10 - 5)\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = -2{,}342 \cdot 10^{-9}\ \text{m} ,\]

while \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(P) = 0\). It moves down by \(14{,}64\) µm and toward the axis by \(2{,}342\) nm. A nanometre, nm, is a billionth of a metre, \(10^{-9}\) m, that is, a thousandth of a micrometre. The displacement toward the axis is more than six thousand times smaller than the downward one, which is why figure 1.41 exaggerates it much more.

The second term of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), says that a point off the axis moves down a little less than the point on the axis at the same depth. At the point \(P\) the difference is only \(9{,}4 \cdot 10^{-13}\) m, more than ten million times less than the downward displacement. So a cross section that was flat before loading becomes very slightly curved: its centre moves a little lower than its rim (figure 1.44).

Where does this shape come from? We might expect the opposite, that the rim of the cross section sags more than the centre, like the rim of an umbrella held at its middle. But in this field the bar does not hang from the point \(O\): its weight is carried by the force spread evenly over the top face, and every cross section carries the part of the bar below it evenly over its whole face (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). The curving has another source, the thinning, which changes with depth (figure 1.45). Higher up the bar gets thinner more than lower down, so a point at the distance \(y\) from the axis moves toward the axis more when it lies higher. A vertical fibre at the distance \(y\) from the axis therefore leans: its upper end moves toward the axis more than its lower end. The material, though, is not sheared, and the right angle between a vertical fibre and a horizontal fibre of the cross section stays a right angle, up to a negligibly small correction. The reason is that neighbouring parts of the bar pass each other only vertical forces, no sideways ones (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). We will show it by computation at the end of section 1.7.2. For the angle to stay a right angle, the horizontal fibre of the cross section must turn by the same amount as the vertical fibre next to it, so its outer end rises. Farther from the axis the vertical fibres lean more, because there the points move toward the axis more. So the cross section rises more and more toward the rim and takes the shape of the letter U. The same holds for the top face: it curves too, its centre \(O\) stays in place and its rim rises a little (figure 1.40, left).

Let us return to how the bar is held. The field (1.18) describes a bar that is fixed only at the point \(O\): this point does not move, since \(\vek u(0, 0, 0) = (0, 0, 0)\). The other points of the top face move: a point on the rim of the top face, 5 mm from the axis, moves toward the axis by \(0{,}6\,a \cdot 10\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}005\ \text{m} = 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m. A real ceiling holds the bar differently. If the bar is welded to the ceiling over its whole top face (figure 1.40, right), the face can neither narrow nor curve. If it were attached so that it could slide along the ceiling, which is rare, it would stay flat and at the same height, but it could narrow. In each case the field near the ceiling would differ a little from (1.18). Far from the place where the body is held, though, the field is almost the same however exactly the forces holding it are spread, as long as together they pull equally (SADD §5.6, PDF pp. 114-115). How far, the book says only in words: the differences die out with the distance from the place where the body is held, but it gives no exact distance. In figure 1.40 the outlines of the two bars are the same lower down.

Now we can ask what we asked for the bar with the derivative: how fast does the displacement change as we move away from a point? In a body we can move in any direction. Let us start with the directions of the axes.

1.7.2 Partial derivative

For the bar the displacement was a function of one variable, \(u(x)\), and the rate at which it changes was the derivative (definition 1.9), the limit of the difference quotient \((u(x + \Delta x) - u(x))/\Delta x\) as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero. Now each component of the displacement is a function of three variables, whose input is the three coordinates of a point and whose output is one number.

Suppose we move down from the point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), along the vertical line through \(P\) (figure 1.46, left). On this line only the coordinate \(x\) changes, while the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) stay \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\). So on it the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is a function of a single variable, which assigns to the number \(x\) the number

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}}) = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2) .\]

The second term is the same fixed number along the whole line. The derivative of this function tells how fast the downward displacement changes as we move down from \(P\). On its graph it is the slope of the tangent above \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) (figure 1.46, middle), just as the derivative in figure 1.18 was the slope of the tangent. In the same way, on the horizontal line through \(P\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) only the coordinate \(y\) changes. On it the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is a function of one variable, which assigns to the number \(y\) the number \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y, z_{\mathrm{P}}) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}})\,y\). Its graph is a straight line (figure 1.46, right).

From history

Derivatives of functions of several variables in which only one variable changes were computed already by Newton, Leibniz and the Bernoulli family, but as a rule without a special notation (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 244). In 1728 Euler used the letters \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) for them, for the derivatives with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 245). Jean le Rond d'Alembert was led to equations with derivatives in several variables in 1744 by the equilibrium and motion of fluids, in 1746 by the winds and in 1747 by the vibrating string that we met in section 1.3.1 (CAJORI, PDF p. 257-258). In 1755 Euler wrote the derivative of the function \(P\) with respect to \(y\) in parentheses. The notation meant that the function \(P\) is differentiated with only \(y\) changing, and the resulting change is divided by \(\mathrm{d}y\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 245). In 1786 Adrien-Marie Legendre wrote that, to avoid all ambiguity, he would denote by \(\partial v/\partial x\) how much the function \(v\) changes per unit change of \(x\) when only \(x\) changes, and by \(\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}x\) the complete change of the function \(v\) divided by \(\mathrm{d}x\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 249). The following year he no longer used the notation. Perhaps also because the letter d was claimed in other fields of mathematics, the notation did not catch on at once (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 249-250). Lagrange wrote such derivatives with a prime, just like the derivative of a function of one variable, for example \(F'(x)\), \(F'(y)\) and \(F'(z)\) for the derivatives of the function \(F(x, y, z)\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 253). The danger of this notation is that \(F'(x)\) could be read as the derivative of a function of the single variable \(x\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 253). In 1841 Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi wrote that Lagrange's notation fails if, for a function of three or more variables, we want to differentiate twice or more (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 253). We see the reason as follows. In \(F'(x)\) the name of the variable in the brackets says with respect to which one we differentiate. For a second derivative we would have to give two variables and their order, while the primes say only that we differentiate, not with respect to what. Stäckel remarked in 1896 that this defect can be removed with several indices (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 253).

Back to the displacement in the bar. A derivative in which we change one variable, for example \(x\) in \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), and hold the other two fixed has a name of its own.

Definition 1.25 Partial derivative (parcialni odvod)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, that is, a function whose input is three numbers \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), the coordinates of a point, and whose output is one number \(f(x, y, z)\). Let \(f\) be defined at all points whose distance from the point \((x, y, z)\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). The partial derivatives (parcialni odvodi) of the function \(f\) with respect to \(x\), to \(y\) and to \(z\) at the point \((x, y, z)\) are the limits

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z) &= \lim_{\Delta \mathrm{x} \to 0} \frac{f(x + \Delta x, y, z) - f(x, y, z)}{\Delta x} , \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x, y, z) &= \lim_{\Delta \mathrm{y} \to 0} \frac{f(x, y + \Delta y, z) - f(x, y, z)}{\Delta y} , \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x, y, z) &= \lim_{\Delta \mathrm{z} \to 0} \frac{f(x, y, z + \Delta z) - f(x, y, z)}{\Delta z} , \end{aligned} \tag{1.19}\]

if they exist. So the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is the derivative of the function of one variable that we get by holding \(y\) and \(z\) fixed, and the same for the other two variables.

Source: LEBL2 Def. 8.3.8 (PDF p. 39), for functions of \(n\) variables. KREYSZIG Appendix A3.2, (1) and (2) (PDF p. 1210), for functions of two variables, for three variables on PDF p. 1211.

So a partial derivative is an ordinary derivative from definition 1.9. The only new thing is that a function of three variables has three variables we can change, and so three partial derivatives at every point. Each tells how fast \(f\) changes as we move away from the point along one of the axes. Partial derivatives of functions of any number of variables are defined in the same way: each time we change one variable and hold the others fixed (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.8).

We read \(\partial f / \partial x\) as "the partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(x\)". The sign \(\partial\) is a rounded d. It recalls the notation \(\mathrm{d}f / \mathrm{d}x\) for the ordinary derivative from section 1.3.4, and its different shape warns that \(f\) also depends on other variables, which we hold fixed while differentiating. This also gives a meaning to the notation \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) that we mentioned with the definition of the strain at a point 1.10.

The notation with the rounded d is called the Legendre-Jacobi notation in textbooks (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 251).
