Some books write the partial derivative more briefly with a subscript, \(f_{\mathrm{x}}\) (KREYSZIG Appendix A3.2, PDF p. 1209), or with a comma in the subscript, \(u_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}}\) (SADD (2.1.4), PDF p. 40). In our book the subscript of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) already means the component of the displacement vector in the direction of the axis \(x\) (definition 1.22). So we will always write partial derivatives with the sign \(\partial\). The notation \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) thus means the rate at which the component \(x\) of the displacement changes as we move in the direction of the axis \(y\).

Why does the definition require \(f\) to be defined at all points whose distance from \((x, y, z)\) is less than \(r\)? The difference quotient with respect to \(x\) uses the values at the points \((x + \Delta x, y, z)\) for all \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < r\), and these points must be in the domain of the function, as the definition of the limit 1.5 requires. In a body this holds at points around which there is still some material in all directions. We call such points interior points (notranje točke) of the body. The point \(P\) is interior: it is 1 mm from the surface of the bar and 5 m from both ends, so we can take \(r = 1\) mm. On the surface of a body, though, a step outward leaves the body, and the definition as written does not apply there. That is why LEBL2 defines partial derivatives only on sets in which every point is interior, the so-called open sets (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.8, PDF p. 39). In this section we compute only at interior points of the bar.

Let us compute the partial derivatives of the hanging bar. The difference quotients we will get all have the same form as the quotient of the displacement \(u(x)\) in section 1.3.4: a fixed number with a multiple of the change added. There we found the limit of such an expression with steps 6 to 12. So that we do not repeat the steps for every quotient, we do them once for a general expression.

Lemma 1.26 Limit of a number plus a multiple (limita vsote števila in večkratnika)

For any numbers \(d\) and \(c\),

\[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \,(d + c\,h) = d . \tag{1.20}\]
Proof

The function \(g(h) = d + c\,h\) is defined for every \(h\), so all the points the definition of the limit 1.5 talks about are in its domain. We write the definition out for this function. We must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|(d + c\,h) - d| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\).

  1. Pick any error \(\eta > 0\). For it we must find a band \(\delta\).
  2. Simplify the difference that the condition bounds. The numbers \(d\) cancel, \((d + c\,h) - d = c\,h\).
  3. The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values, \(|c\,h| = |c|\,|h|\) (lemma 1.6, item 2). So the condition we must reach is \(|c|\,|h| < \eta\).
  4. If \(c = 0\), then \(|c|\,|h| = 0 < \eta\) for every \(h\). The condition holds for any band, so we take, for example, \(\delta = 1\).
  5. If \(c \neq 0\), then \(|c| > 0\). We divide the inequality \(|c|\,|h| < \eta\) by the positive number \(|c|\), so it does not turn around, and it holds exactly when \(|h| < \eta / |c|\). We take the band \(\delta = \eta / |c|\), which is positive.
  6. Check the case \(c \neq 0\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) we have \(|h| < \eta / |c|\), so \(|c|\,|h| < \eta\), and by steps 2 and 3 this is \(|(d + c\,h) - d|\).
  7. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely and found a band for it in both cases. The condition of the definition holds, so the limit of the expression \(d + c\,h\) at the point \(0\) is \(d\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. It follows the example \(g(h) = 5 - h\) of section 1.3.3, which is the case \(d = 5\), \(c = -1\) of this lemma.

We will use the lemma as follows. A difference quotient is defined only for \(\Delta x \neq 0\). If for every such \(\Delta x\) it equals the expression \(d + c\,\Delta x\), with numbers \(d\) and \(c\) that do not depend on \(\Delta x\), it has the same limit as this expression, because the definition of the limit looks only at the values for \(\Delta x \neq 0\). The change \(\Delta x\) plays the role of \(h\). So the limit is \(d\).

We start with the partial derivative of the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\) at any interior point \((x, y, z)\) of the bar. We keep \(y\) and \(z\) fixed and change only \(x\), as the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 prescribes.

  1. We get the value at the point \((x + \Delta x, y, z)\) from (1.18) by putting \(x + \Delta x\) in place of \(x\) and leaving \(y\) and \(z\): \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x + \Delta x, y, z) = a\,(2L(x + \Delta x) - (x + \Delta x)^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\).
  2. We subtract \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). The term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) is the same in both values, because \(y\) and \(z\) did not change, so it cancels. What remains is \(a\,(2L(x + \Delta x) - (x + \Delta x)^2) - a\,(2Lx - x^2)\).
  3. This is the same difference as in steps 1 to 4 of section 1.3.4 for the displacement \(u(x)\). We repeat the computation. We expand the square, \((x + \Delta x)^2 = x^2 + 2x\,\Delta x + \Delta x^2\), and multiply out \(2L(x + \Delta x) = 2Lx + 2L\,\Delta x\). The terms \(2Lx\) and \(-x^2\) cancel, and what remains is \(a\,(2L\,\Delta x - 2x\,\Delta x - \Delta x^2) = a\,\Delta x\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x)\).
  4. We divide by \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and the factor \(\Delta x\) cancels:
    \[\frac{u_{\mathrm{x}}(x + \Delta x, y, z) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)}{\Delta x} = a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) = 2a\,(L - x) + (-a)\,\Delta x .\]
  5. The quotient has the form \(d + c\,\Delta x\) with the numbers \(d = 2a\,(L - x)\) and \(c = -a\), which do not depend on \(\Delta x\). By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, its limit is \(d\):
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z) = 2a\,(L - x) .\]

The partial derivative does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\). At every depth the downward displacement changes with depth equally fast, on the axis and off it. On the axis of the bar \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, 0, 0) = u(x)\), and the partial derivative is the derivative \(u'(x) = 2a\,(L - x)\), the strain at a point (1.7) that we computed in section 1.4. At the point \(P\), at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, it is \(2a\,(10 - 5)\ \text{m} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\).

Next, the partial derivative of the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with respect to \(y\). We hold \(x\) and \(z\) fixed and change only \(y\).

  1. From (1.18), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y + \Delta y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,(y + \Delta y)\).
  2. We subtract \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\). We multiply out the bracket \((y + \Delta y)\), the terms with \(y\) cancel, and what remains is
    \[u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y + \Delta y, z) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y . \tag{1.21}\]
  3. We divide by \(\Delta y \neq 0\). The quotient is \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) for every \(\Delta y \neq 0\). This is the form \(d + c\,\Delta y\) with \(d = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and \(c = 0\).
  4. By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple,
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) .\]

Here the quotient is the same for every change \(\Delta y\), long or short, because the graph of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) along the horizontal line is a straight line (figure 1.46, right). At the point \(P\) it is \(-0{,}6\,a\,(10 - 5)\ \text{m} = -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\).

Let us compare the two partial derivatives. At every depth \(x < L\) their ratio is

\[\frac{-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)}{2a\,(L - x)} = -0{,}3 .\]

What does this mean? At the depth \(x\) take the point on the axis, \((x, 0, 0)\), and the point \((x, \Delta y, 0)\), which lies \(\Delta y\) to the right of it. By (1.21) with \(y = 0\), the components \(y\) of their displacements differ by \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y\). So their separation in the direction of the axis \(y\), \(\Delta y\) before loading, is \(\Delta y - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y\) after loading. It decreases by the fraction \(0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x)\), that is, by \(0{,}3\) times the strain along the bar at that depth. This is the thinning from section 1.6: a bar that gets longer by a thousandth gets thinner by \(0{,}3\) thousandths, and now we see that this holds at every depth separately.

We compute two more partial derivatives in steps, because in them the component of the displacement and the variable do not have the same direction. First \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(y\). We hold \(x\) and \(z\) fixed.

  1. In the difference \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y + \Delta y, z) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\) the term \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) cancels, because \(x\) did not change, and so does the term with \(z^2\). What remains is \(-0{,}3\,a\,\big((y + \Delta y)^2 - y^2\big)\).
  2. We expand the square, \((y + \Delta y)^2 = y^2 + 2y\,\Delta y + \Delta y^2\), the terms \(y^2\) cancel, and what remains is \(-0{,}3\,a\,(2y\,\Delta y + \Delta y^2) = -0{,}3\,a\,\Delta y\,(2y + \Delta y)\).
  3. We divide by \(\Delta y \neq 0\). The quotient is \(-0{,}3\,a\,(2y + \Delta y) = -0{,}6\,a\,y + (-0{,}3\,a)\,\Delta y\), of the form \(d + c\,\Delta y\) with \(d = -0{,}6\,a\,y\) and \(c = -0{,}3\,a\).
  4. By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple,
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,y .\]

So as we move right, away from the axis, the downward displacement decreases a little. This is the curving of the cross section that we noticed above: the rim of the cross section moves down less than its centre. At the point \(P\) it is \(-0{,}6\,a \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\).

Then \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with respect to \(x\). We hold \(y\) and \(z\) fixed.

  1. From (1.18), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x + \Delta x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,y\).
  2. We split the bracket, \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta x\). When we subtract \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\), what remains is \(0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta x\).
  3. We divide by \(\Delta x \neq 0\). The quotient is \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\), of the form \(d + c\,\Delta x\) with \(d = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) and \(c = 0\).
  4. By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple,
    \[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,y .\]

So as we move down, the displacement toward the axis decreases, because lower down the bar gets thinner less. At the point \(P\) it is \(0{,}6\,a \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\).

We get the remaining five partial derivatives with the same steps. Where the variable we differentiate with respect to does not appear in the function, the value does not change when this variable changes. The difference is zero, the quotient is zero for every change, and by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, with \(d = 0\) and \(c = 0\) the partial derivative is zero. For example, \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z + \Delta z) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = 0\), because \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(z\), and so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\). The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) has the same form as \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), only with \(z\) in place of \(y\), and the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) contains \(z\) in the same way as \(y\). So we get \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,z\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,z\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial y = 0\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\).

In all the computations the variables we held fixed behaved like fixed numbers. So we compute a partial derivative as an ordinary derivative in which we treat the other variables as numbers.

Let us collect all nine partial derivatives in a table. The row gives the component of the displacement, the column the variable we differentiate with respect to.

w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(2a\,(L - x)\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0\)
\(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,z\) \(0\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\)

At the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) these partial derivatives have the following values. All of them are numbers without a unit, since a displacement in metres is divided by a distance in metres.

at the point \(P\) w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\) \(0\)
\(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\) \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(0\)
\(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) \(0\) \(0\) \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

The table has two patterns. The first is on the diagonal, where the direction of the component matches the direction of the variable. Along the bar we have \(2a\,(L - x)\), and in both directions across it \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), which is \(-0{,}3\) times as much. This is the thinning we explained above. The bar gets thinner in the direction of the axis \(z\) as much as in the direction of the axis \(y\). The reason is not the round cross section, since the field holds for a bar with any cross section that is the same along the whole length (SADD Example 5.1, PDF p. 115). The reason is that steel behaves the same in all directions across the bar and that nothing squeezes the bar from the side.

The second pattern is the pairs off the diagonal: \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,y\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) are equal in size and opposite in sign, and so are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\). Let us see in words what such a pair means. From the point \(P\) draw two short fibres, one down in the direction of the axis \(x\), the other sideways in the direction of the axis \(y\). The lower end of the first fibre moves a little sideways relative to \(P\), and the side end of the second moves a little up relative to \(P\). Because the two partial derivatives are equal in size, the two fibres lean by the same ratio of the sideways shift of the end to the length of the fibre, and because they have opposite signs, the two fibres turn the same way. So the right angle between the fibres stays a right angle. More precisely, the fibres do not lean by quite the same ratio, because their lengths also change a little: the vertical fibre gets longer by the fraction \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\), the horizontal one shorter by the fraction \(-\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\). So the difference between the ratios is about \(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big)\), at the point \(P\) equal to \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} \cdot 2{,}538 \cdot 10^{-6} \approx 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-15}\), more than a hundred thousand times smaller than the partial derivatives themselves. For small displacements we neglect such a product, as we neglected the square of the shift for the sheared cube in section 1.6.2. So the material near the point \(P\) only turns a little, and it is not sheared. Now we also see why the second term of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the number \(0{,}3\), half of \(0{,}6\). The partial derivative of the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,y^2\) with respect to \(y\) is \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\), exactly the opposite of \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\). This half is not a property of steel. For every material the number in the second term of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is its ratio of thinning, and the number in \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is twice this ratio (CM (7.3.20), PDF p. 306). So the number in \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is always half the number in \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the right angle stays a right angle for every material. The books also find that the shear strains of the hanging bar are zero (CM Example 7.3.2, Eq. (3), PDF p. 305, SADD (5.7.3), PDF p. 115). We will check this exactly when we compute the strains of short fibres in any direction, in section 1.17.4.

The partial derivatives tell how fast the displacement changes as we move away from a point along one of the axes. But a fibre can lie in any direction. How does the displacement change when we take a short step from the point \(P\) in any direction? We can split the step into three steps along the axes, just as we split a vector in lemma 1.21 on a vector as a sum of steps along the axes, and each of them changes only one coordinate. We continue with this in the next part of this section.

1.7.3 A step in any direction

In this section we find by how much the displacement changes over a short step in any direction, and we show on the hanging bar that for a short step this change is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the step. For a general field we prove it in section 1.15.3. Let us return to the fibre of section 1.6.1. A fibre between the points \(P\) and \(Q\) of a body changes under loading only by the difference of the displacements of its ends,

\[\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = \overrightarrow{PQ} + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) ,\]

where \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\) are the positions of the ends after loading ((1.15)). So for a short fibre in any direction we need the difference of displacements \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\). Let \(P = (x, y, z)\) be an interior point of the body, that is, a point with some material around it in all directions, and let the fibre reach to the point \(Q = (x + \Delta x,\ y + \Delta y,\ z + \Delta z)\). The vector of the fibre is then \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) ((1.8)). We compute each component of the difference of displacements separately. To begin, take the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\).

We can also get from \(P\) to \(Q\) in three steps along the axes, just as in lemma 1.21 on a vector as a sum of steps along the axes we wrote a vector as a sum of steps (figure 1.47). First we step by \(\Delta x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) to the point \(A = (x + \Delta x,\ y,\ z)\), then by \(\Delta y\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) to the point \(B = (x + \Delta x,\ y + \Delta y,\ z)\), and finally by \(\Delta z\) in the direction of the axis \(z\) to the point \(Q\). Each step changes only one coordinate.

We split the difference \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\) into three changes, one for each step.

  1. We add and subtract the values at the intermediate points, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(A) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(A) = 0\). Adding zero does not change the value:
    \[u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) + u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(A) + u_{\mathrm{x}}(A) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) .\]
  2. We arrange the terms in pairs, read from \(P\) toward \(Q\):
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = {} & \big(u_{\mathrm{x}}(A) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\big) + \big(u_{\mathrm{x}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(A)\big) \\ & + \big(u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(B)\big) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.22}\]

This equality is exact and holds for every function of three variables that is defined at the points \(P\), \(A\), \(B\) and \(Q\), not only for a displacement. For a displacement all these points are in the body if the fibre is shorter than the number \(r\) up to which there is still material in all directions around the interior point \(P\). This is because the distances \(|PA| = |\Delta x|\) and \(|PB| = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\) are not larger than the length of the fibre \(|PQ|\). Each bracket is the change in one step along one axis. The first bracket starts at \(P\) and changes only \(x\). It is the numerator of the difference quotient from which, by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) at the point \(P\) arises. The second bracket changes only \(y\), but it starts not at \(P\) but at \(A\). So it is the numerator of the quotient for \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) at the point \(A\). The third bracket changes only \(z\) and starts at \(B\), so it is the numerator of the quotient for \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z\) at the point \(B\).

Let us try this on the hanging bar, where

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z . \end{aligned}\]

The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) teaches the most, so we start with it. We write equality (1.22) for it in the same way as for \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\).

  1. The first step, from \(P\) to \(A\), changes only \(x\). As in the computation of \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) in section 1.7.2,
    \[u_{\mathrm{y}}(A) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y = 0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta x .\]
    This is exactly \(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x\), since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\).
  2. The second step, from \(A\) to \(B\), changes only \(y\), but at the depth \(x + \Delta x\), where \(A\) lies:
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{y}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(A) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,(y + \Delta y) + 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,y \\ &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,\Delta y . \end{aligned}\]
  3. We split the bracket \((L - x - \Delta x)\) into \((L - x)\) and \(-\Delta x\):
    \[-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\,\Delta y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y + 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y .\]
    The first part is \(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y\), since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\). The second part, \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), is there because the step starts at \(A\), at the depth \(x + \Delta x\). There the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) is \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x - \Delta x)\), not \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) as at \(P\) (figure 1.48).
  4. The third step, from \(B\) to \(Q\), changes only \(z\). The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(z\), so \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(B) = 0\), which is \(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z\), since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\).
  5. We add the three changes by (1.22):
    \[u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) = 0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta x - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y + 0 \cdot \Delta z + 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y .\]

For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) we take the same steps. In \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) does not change with \(x\), so the second and third steps are the same as if they started at \(P\). We computed the changes in all three steps already in section 1.7.2, before taking the limit: \(a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x)\,\Delta x\), \(-0{,}3\,a\,(2y + \Delta y)\,\Delta y\) and \(-0{,}3\,a\,(2z + \Delta z)\,\Delta z\). In \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) the second step is zero, because \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) does not depend on \(y\), and the third starts at \(B\) at the depth \(x + \Delta x\), just like the second step for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\). Multiplying out the brackets and adding the changes, we get for all three components

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) &= 2a\,(L - x)\,\Delta x - 0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta y - 0{,}6\,a\,z\,\Delta z \\ &\quad - a\,\Delta x^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta y^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta z^2 , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) &= 0{,}6\,a\,y\,\Delta x - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta y + 0 \cdot \Delta z \\ &\quad + 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{z}}(P) &= 0{,}6\,a\,z\,\Delta x + 0 \cdot \Delta y - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\Delta z \\ &\quad + 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta z . \end{aligned} \tag{1.23}\]

Each line starts with three products. The numbers in front of \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z\) are the partial derivatives from the matching row of the table in section 1.7.2, taken at the point \(P\). After them come terms that are products of two components of the step, \(\Delta x^2\), \(\Delta x\,\Delta y\) and the like. We call these terms the remainder (ostanek). In general we define it as everything that is left when we subtract the three products with the partial derivatives at \(P\) from the difference:

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{x}} , \tag{1.24}\]

and in the same way for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and for \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) with the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\). This is only a way of writing that holds for every field that has all three partial derivatives at the point \(P\): \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\) is what is left over. For the hanging bar, by (1.23),

\[\begin{aligned} R_{\mathrm{x}} &= -a\,\Delta x^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta y^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta z^2 , \\ R_{\mathrm{y}} &= 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y , \\ R_{\mathrm{z}} &= 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta z . \end{aligned}\]

Books often write the difference of displacements without the remainder (SADD (2.1.1), PDF p. 39) and say that they dropped the higher-order terms because the components of the step are small (SADD, PDF p. 40). But how small is the remainder? Take a fibre from the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = \big(\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23\big)\), which has the length \(\sqrt{1/9 + 4/9 + 4/9} = 1\). A fibre of length \(h\) has the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). For two lengths, let us compute for \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) the part with the partial derivatives and the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\):

length of the fibre \(h\) part with the partial derivatives remainder \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\)
1 mm \(6{,}504 \cdot 10^{-10}\) m \(-7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-14}\) m
0,1 mm \(6{,}504 \cdot 10^{-11}\) m \(-7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-16}\) m

For a fibre ten times shorter the part with the partial derivatives is ten times smaller, but the remainder a hundred times smaller. Why? In the part with the partial derivatives each term is the product of a fixed number and one component of the step, for example \(2a\,(L - x)\,\Delta x\), and each component is proportional to \(h\). In the remainder, though, each term is a product of two components, for example \(\Delta x\,\Delta y\), and so it is proportional to \(h \cdot h = h^2\). This is the same rule we met at the sheared cube in section 1.6.2: next to a small number, its square is smaller by roughly a factor of that small number.

We can write this exactly. A fibre in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) has the components \(\Delta x = h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta y = h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Delta z = h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). For \(h > 0\) it points in the direction of the vector \(\vek n\), for \(h < 0\) in the opposite direction. We allow negative \(h\) because the definition of the limit 1.5 looks at numbers \(h\) on both sides of zero. The length of the fibre is \(|h|\), since \(\sqrt{h^2 n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + h^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + h^2 n_{\mathrm{z}}^2} = |h|\,\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2} = |h|\). We take \(0 < |h| < r\), so that the fibre stays in the body. Let us show that the remainder divided by \(h\) goes to zero as we shorten the fibre.

  1. We put the components of the step into \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\). Each term gets the factor \(h^2\), which we take out:
    \[R_{\mathrm{x}} = -a\,h^2 n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,h^2 n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,h^2 n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = -a\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\big)\,h^2 .\]
  2. We divide by \(h\):
    \[\frac{R_{\mathrm{x}}}{h} = -a\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\big)\,h .\]
    This is the form \(d + c\,h\), where \(d = 0\) and \(c = -a\,(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\), a number that does not depend on \(h\).
  3. By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, the limit is \(d = 0\). The length of the fibre, though, is \(|h|\), not \(h\). The quotients \(R_{\mathrm{x}}/h\) and \(R_{\mathrm{x}}/|h|\) differ at most in sign, so they are equally far from zero, and the band \(\delta\) that the lemma gives for an error \(\eta\) works for \(R_{\mathrm{x}}/|h|\) too. So the remainder divided by the length \(|h|\) of the fibre goes to zero.
  4. We get the same for the other two remainders: \(R_{\mathrm{y}} / h = 0{,}6\,a\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\,h\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}} / h = 0{,}6\,a\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\,h\) have the form \(0 + c\,h\), so they go to zero.

What does this tell us about the difference of displacements? We divide (1.24) by \(h\) and put in \(\Delta x = h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta y = h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\Delta z = h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\):

\[\frac{u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)}{h} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,n_{\mathrm{z}} + \frac{R_{\mathrm{x}}}{h} .\]

The first three terms do not depend on \(h\), and the last one is \(c\,h\). By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, the quotient approaches the sum of the first three terms as \(h\) goes to zero. At the point \(P\) and in the direction \(\vek n\) this sum is \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot \tfrac13 - 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} \cdot \tfrac23 + 0 \cdot \tfrac23 = 6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7}\), while the quotient is \(6{,}5028 \cdot 10^{-7}\) for \(h = 1\) mm and \(6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7}\) for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm (figure 1.49). It is the same picture as for the hanging bar in section 1.4, where the strain of ever shorter pieces approached the derivative. So for the hanging bar the difference of displacements of a short fibre, divided by its length, is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives at \(P\) with the components of the direction. We will need this for the strain of a short fibre in any direction.

For the hanging bar we computed the remainder exactly, because each component of its field is a sum of terms with at most two coordinate factors, like \(x^2\) and \(x\,y\). That is why the remainder was exactly a number times \(h^2\). A field with a term like \(x^3\) would also give terms with \(h^3\) in the remainder. But what about a general field? Equality (1.22) is true for every field. The first bracket starts at \(P\), so by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 its quotient approaches the partial derivative at \(P\). The second and third brackets, though, start at the points \(A\) and \(B\), which move as we shorten the fibre. For the bar this gave terms like \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\). For a general field two facts would finish the job.

  1. For a function of one variable that has a derivative at every point between two numbers and no jump at the end points, the change between the numbers equals the derivative at some point between them times the difference of the two numbers. We will prove this statement in section 1.14. For the second bracket this function is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) along the step from \(A\) to \(B\), where only \(y\) changes. If \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) has a partial derivative with respect to \(y\) at all points from \(A\) to \(B\), which the assumption of item 2 ensures, by this statement the change equals the partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) at some point between \(A\) and \(B\), times \(\Delta y\). The same holds for the third bracket, where only \(z\) changes from \(B\) to \(Q\).
  2. We assume that the partial derivatives exist at all points near \(P\) and change there without jumps: at points close enough to \(P\) they differ only a little from those at \(P\). This is an assumption about the field, which has to be checked for every field. Then the partial derivative at the point between \(A\) and \(B\) differs a little from the one at \(P\), and the remainder is small compared with the length of the fibre.

With these two facts LEBL2 proves that the remainder divided by the length of the step goes to zero for every field whose partial derivatives have no jumps (LEBL2 Prop. 8.4.6, PDF pp. 48-49). For a graph the first fact looks self-evident: between two points of a graph without jumps or sharp corners there is a point where the tangent is parallel to the line through both points. A proof, though, must show that such a point really exists, and it turns out to depend on the fact that the number line has no holes.

So for a few sections we now turn to mathematics. First we look at why the number line has no holes. Then we look at endless strings of numbers that approach some number, then at functions whose graph has no jumps, and finally at the statement about the derivative at a point in between. Then we return to the fibre and show that the remainder divided by the length of the fibre goes to zero for every such field.

1.8 Mathematics: numbers without holes

At the end of the previous section we needed a statement about functions of one variable: the change of a function between two numbers equals the derivative at some point between them times the difference of the two numbers. On a picture of the graph it looks self-evident, but its proof depends on the fact that the number line has no holes. In this section we say what exactly this means and what follows from it. First we find a hole among the fractions. Then we give a name to the bound up to which a set of numbers reaches, so that we can describe the hole without the number that is missing. Then we require that the real numbers have no such holes, and from this requirement we derive the first consequences: how the elements of a set come close to its bound, that the natural numbers grow past every bound, and that every nonnegative number has a square root.

1.8.1 A hole among the fractions

To begin, some notation that we will use from now on. A set is made up of its elements (the definition of a function 1.4 speaks of sets and their elements). The notation \(x \in A\) means that \(x\) is an element of the set \(A\), and the notation \(A \subseteq B\) means that every element of the set \(A\) is also an element of the set \(B\). We write the set of all elements that satisfy some condition with curly brackets. So \(\{t \in \mathbb R : t^2 < 3\}\) is the set of all real numbers \(t\) whose square is less than \(3\). We write a finite set as the list of its elements, for example \(\{1, 2, 3\}\). A set that has no element is empty, and a set with at least one element is nonempty. The sign \(\mathbb R\) denotes the set of all real numbers, that is, of all points of the number line. The natural numbers are \(1, 2, 3, \dots\), and we write their set \(\mathbb N\). The integers \(\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots\) form the set \(\mathbb Z\). A fraction, or rational number (racionalno število), is a number \(p/q\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are integers and \(q \neq 0\). We write the set of all fractions \(\mathbb Q\) (LEBL1 §0.3, PDF pp. 8-10).

About numbers we assume what we know from school. First, how we add, multiply, divide and compare them by size (LEBL1 Def. 1.1.5 and 1.1.7, PDF pp. 25-26, where these rules are collected as the rules of addition, multiplication and order). Second, two properties of the integers: an integer can be divided with a remainder, and every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element (LEBL1 §0.3.2, PDF p. 12, which accepts this property without proof). Division with a remainder we know from school, and LEBL1 uses it without stating it. The rules of arithmetic from the first part also hold for fractions: the sum, difference, product and quotient of fractions are again fractions. So these rules do not tell the real numbers apart from the fractions. We will see that the fractions do differ from the real numbers after all, and exactly in the statement we need.

Take the function \(f(t) = t^3\) between the numbers \(0\) and \(1\) (figure 1.50). The line through the points of the graph above \(0\) and above \(1\) has the slope

\[\frac{f(1) - f(0)}{1 - 0} = \frac{1 - 0}{1} = 1 .\]

The statement we need says that somewhere between \(0\) and \(1\) a tangent also has the slope \(1\), that is, that there is a \(\xi\) between \(0\) and \(1\) with \(f'(\xi) = 1\). The Greek letter \(\xi\) (xi) denotes this point in between. For this we need the derivative of the function \(f\). Let us compute it by the definition of the derivative 1.9 at any point \(t\). First we simplify the difference quotient, as for the hanging bar in section 1.3.4.

  1. We expand the square of the sum: \((t + \Delta t)^2 = t^2 + 2t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2\).
  2. The cube is the square multiplied once more by \(t + \Delta t\). We multiply each term of the square by \(t\) and by \(\Delta t\) and add the like terms:
    \[(t + \Delta t)^3 = (t^2 + 2t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2)(t + \Delta t) = t^3 + 3t^2\,\Delta t + 3t\,\Delta t^2 + \Delta t^3 .\]
  3. We subtract \(f(t) = t^3\). The terms \(t^3\) cancel: \((t + \Delta t)^3 - t^3 = 3t^2\,\Delta t + 3t\,\Delta t^2 + \Delta t^3\).
  4. We divide by \(\Delta t \neq 0\). Every term has the factor \(\Delta t\), which cancels:
    \[\frac{(t + \Delta t)^3 - t^3}{\Delta t} = 3t^2 + 3t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2 .\]

The candidate for the limit is \(3t^2\), the value of the right side at \(\Delta t = 0\). Lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple is not enough here, because the last term, \(\Delta t^2\), is not a multiple of the change \(\Delta t\) with a fixed factor. So we show the limit by the definition of the limit 1.5. It requires: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|(3t^2 + 3t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2) - 3t^2| < \eta\) for every \(\Delta t\) with \(0 < |\Delta t| < \delta\).

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). The difference that the condition bounds is \((3t^2 + 3t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2) - 3t^2 = 3t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2 = \Delta t\,(3t + \Delta t)\).
  2. The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, item 2): \(|\Delta t\,(3t + \Delta t)| = |\Delta t|\,|3t + \Delta t|\).
  3. By the triangle inequality for numbers \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1) we have \(|3t + \Delta t| \le 3|t| + |\Delta t|\). Multiplying the inequality by the nonnegative number \(|\Delta t|\) keeps it: \(|\Delta t|\,|3t + \Delta t| \le |\Delta t|\,(3|t| + |\Delta t|)\).
  4. The factor \(3|t| + |\Delta t|\) changes with \(\Delta t\), so we first bound it by a fixed number. For \(|\Delta t| < 1\) we have \(3|t| + |\Delta t| < 3|t| + 1\). The number \(1\) is an arbitrary choice, and any positive number would do as well. So for \(0 < |\Delta t| < 1\) we have \(|\Delta t|\,(3|t| + |\Delta t|) < |\Delta t|\,(3|t| + 1)\).
  5. The last expression is smaller than \(\eta\) if \(|\Delta t| < \eta/(3|t| + 1)\). So for the band \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(1\) and \(\eta/(3|t| + 1)\), which are both positive. For \(0 < |\Delta t| < \delta\) both requirements hold, \(|\Delta t| < 1\) and \(|\Delta t| < \eta/(3|t| + 1)\), and by steps 5 to 8
    \[|3t\,\Delta t + \Delta t^2| \le |\Delta t|\,(3|t| + |\Delta t|) < |\Delta t|\,(3|t| + 1) < \frac{\eta}{3|t| + 1}\,(3|t| + 1) = \eta .\]
  6. We picked the error freely and found a band for it. So the limit is \(3t^2\), and \(f'(t) = 3t^2\).

The tangent has the slope \(1\) where \(3\xi^2 = 1\), that is, \(\xi^2 = \tfrac13\). Between \(0\) and \(1\) this is the number \(\xi = 1/\sqrt 3 = 0{,}577\dots\) That such a real number really exists we will prove in section 1.8.6. Would this point exist if we knew only the fractions? Only if some fraction had the square \(\tfrac13\). Let us show that none has. It is enough to show that no fraction has the square \(3\). For if the fraction \(p/q\) had the square \(\tfrac13\), the fraction \(3p/q\) would have the square \(9 \cdot \tfrac13 = 3\).

From history

That the side and the diagonal of a square have no common measure was, historians believe, proved already by the Pythagoreans. Two lengths have a common measure if there is a length that goes a whole number of times into the first and a whole number of times into the second. This discovery is said to have led the Greeks to banish number and measurement from geometry (BALL, PDF p. 52). If we measure a length by counting how many times the unit goes into it, the diagonal of a square cannot be measured with its side as the unit. Theodorus of Cyrene is said to have proved geometrically that lengths whose square is a number from 3 to 17 that is not the square of a whole number have no common measure with the unit (BALL, PDF p. 58). Eudoxus gave the Greeks a doctrine of proportion that also applies to quantities without a common measure (CAJORI, PDF p. 47).

Back to the question of whether the number with square \(3\) is a fraction. A length has a common measure with the unit exactly when it is a fraction of the unit, and that the length whose square is 3 is not a fraction we shall show in lemma 1.27.

Lemma 1.27 No rational number has square 3 (noben ulomek nima kvadrata 3)

There are no integers \(p\) and \(q \neq 0\) for which \((p/q)^2 = 3\).

Proof

We prove this by contradiction: we assume that such a fraction exists and derive something that cannot hold.

  1. Suppose that \((p/q)^2 = 3\) for integers \(p\) and \(q \neq 0\). We may take \(q > 0\): if \(q < 0\), we write the fraction with \(-p\) and \(-q\), since \((-p)/(-q) = p/q\).
  2. Among all such ways of writing it with a positive denominator we choose the one with the smallest denominator \(q\). It exists, because every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element.
  3. We multiply the equation \((p/q)^2 = 3\) by \(q^2\) and get \(p^2 = 3q^2\). So the number \(p^2\) is divisible by \(3\).
  4. On division by \(3\) every integer gives the remainder \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\), so \(p = 3k\), \(p = 3k + 1\) or \(p = 3k + 2\) for some integer \(k\). In the second and the third case we expand the square:
    \[\begin{aligned} (3k + 1)^2 &= 9k^2 + 6k + 1 = 3\,(3k^2 + 2k) + 1 , \\ (3k + 2)^2 &= 9k^2 + 12k + 4 = 3\,(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1 . \end{aligned}\]
    In both cases \(p^2\) gives the remainder \(1\) on division by \(3\) and is not divisible by \(3\), which contradicts step 3. What remains is \(p = 3k\).
  5. We put \(p = 3k\) into \(p^2 = 3q^2\): \(9k^2 = 3q^2\), and after dividing by \(3\), \(q^2 = 3k^2\). So the number \(q^2\) is divisible by \(3\), and by the reasoning of step 4, \(q = 3m\) for some integer \(m\). Since \(q > 0\), we have \(m > 0\) and \(m < q\).
  6. Then \(p/q = 3k/(3m) = k/m\), so \((k/m)^2 = 3\), and the denominator \(m\) is positive and smaller than \(q\). This contradicts the choice in step 2, where \(q\) was the smallest. So the assumption of step 1 is false.

Source: LEBL1 Example 1.1.4 (PDF pp. 24-25) gives the same proof for the square \(2\), with even and odd numbers in place of the remainders on division by \(3\). For the square \(3\) the proof is not from the source.

So there is no fraction with the square \(\tfrac13\), and if we knew only the fractions, the point \(\xi\) would not exist. At the fractions \(t\) with \(3t^2 < 1\) the tangent would be less steep than the line through the end points, at those with \(3t^2 > 1\) steeper, and there is no fraction with \(3t^2 = 1\). Among the fractions there would be no equally steep tangent anywhere. The statement we need would not hold among the fractions.

Where is the hole? Let us draw the nonnegative fractions on the number line (figure 1.51). Those with the square below \(3\), such as \(1\), \(1{,}7\) and \(1{,}73\), we draw grey, and those with the square above \(3\), such as \(1{,}74\) and \(2\), blue. Every nonnegative fraction gets a colour, because by lemma 1.27 no rational number has square 3. Every grey fraction lies to the left of every blue one. Why? For this we need a simple fact about squares.

Lemma 1.28 A larger nonnegative number has a larger square (večje nenegativno število ima večji kvadrat)

For nonnegative numbers \(s\) and \(t\), \(s < t\) holds exactly when \(s^2 < t^2\), and \(s \le t\) exactly when \(s^2 \le t^2\).

Proof

We must show that \(s < t\) implies \(s^2 < t^2\) and the other way round, and the same for \(\le\).

  1. Let \(0 \le s < t\). We write the difference of the squares as a product: \(t^2 - s^2 = (t - s)(t + s)\).
  2. The factor \(t - s\) is positive, because \(s < t\). The factor \(t + s\) is positive, because \(t > s \ge 0\), so \(t > 0\), and \(s \ge 0\). A product of positive numbers is positive, so \(t^2 - s^2 > 0\) and \(s^2 < t^2\).
  3. Conversely, let \(s^2 < t^2\). If \(t \le s\), then either \(t = s\), and then \(t^2 = s^2\), or \(t < s\), and then by steps 1 and 2 with the roles swapped \(t^2 < s^2\). Both contradict \(s^2 < t^2\). So \(s < t\).
  4. The inequality \(s \le t\) holds exactly when \(t < s\) does not hold. By steps 1 to 3 with the roles swapped, \(t < s\) holds exactly when \(t^2 < s^2\) holds, and this holds exactly when \(s^2 \le t^2\) does not hold. So \(s \le t\) exactly when \(s^2 \le t^2\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 1.2.3 (PDF p. 30) uses the first implication for the uniqueness of the root. The proof is not from the source.

For a grey fraction \(s\) and a blue fraction \(t\) we have \(s^2 < 3 < t^2\), so by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(s < t\). The grey and the blue fractions come close to the same bound from both sides: \(1{,}732^2 = 2{,}999824\) is below \(3\) and \(1{,}733^2 = 3{,}003289\) above \(3\), and even more tightly \(1{,}73205^2 = 2{,}9999972\dots\) is below \(3\) and \(1{,}73206^2 = 3{,}0000318\dots\) above \(3\). By the same lemma a number with the square \(3\) would lie to the right of all the grey fractions and to the left of all the blue ones, that is, at the bound between them. Among the fractions there is none. That is where the hole is.

From history

It was not satisfactory to calculate with numbers that are not fractions as if they were fractions. The question of what these numbers actually are demanded greater rigour in the nineteenth century (CAJORI, PDF p. 412). In his textbook Cours d'analyse, which we mentioned in section 1.3.3, Cauchy wrote that such a number is a number approached by fractions with better and better approximations (CAJORI, PDF p. 412). But if we know only fractions, such a number does not exist when it is not a fraction, so the description is circular (CAJORI, PDF p. 412). It is the same for us: the grey fractions approach a bound, but at the bound there is nothing among the fractions to be approached. So people wanted to define such numbers without approaching. Four men achieved this independently and almost at the same time (CAJORI, PDF p. 412-413). Charles Méray published first, in 1869, Weierstrass's presentation was first printed in 1872, and in 1872 Richard Dedekind and Georg Cantor also published (CAJORI, PDF p. 413). Dedekind's treatise is called Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen (Continuity and Irrational Numbers). In it he declared every division of the fractions into a left and a right group, of the kind we describe precisely below, to be a number, and the divisions with no fraction at the boundary between the groups are new numbers that are not fractions (CAJORI, PDF p. 413).

Back to our grey and blue fractions with the hole between them. A cut (rez) is a division of all fractions into a left and a right group such that every fraction of the left group is smaller than every fraction of the right group. It is open if the left group has no largest fraction and the right group no smallest one. Such are our grey and blue fractions if we add to the grey ones also zero and all the negative fractions.

The rules of arithmetic do not notice this hole, because they also hold for fractions. If we want to say that the real numbers have no holes, we must require it separately. Before that, though, we must describe the hole, and without the number that is missing, since there is no such number among the fractions. We describe it by the bound up to which the grey fractions reach.

1.8.2 Upper bound and supremum

The grey fractions do not reach past the number \(2\): each of them is smaller than it, because \(2\) has the square \(4 > 3\). Nor do they reach past \(1{,}74\) or past any blue fraction. The numbers that a set does not reach past get a name.

Definition 1.29 Upper bound and bounded set (zgornja meja in omejena množica)

Let \(A \subseteq \mathbb R\) be a set of real numbers. A number \(b\) is an upper bound (zgornja meja) of the set \(A\) if \(x \le b\) for every \(x \in A\), and a lower bound (spodnja meja) if \(x \ge b\) for every \(x \in A\). A set is bounded above (navzgor omejena) if it has some upper bound, bounded below (navzdol omejena) if it has some lower bound, and bounded (omejena) if it is both.

Source: LEBL1 Def. 1.1.2 (PDF pp. 23-24).

So an upper bound is a number, while being bounded is a property of a set. There is not just one upper bound. For \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) the numbers \(3\), \(3{,}5\) and \(100\) are upper bounds, because no element is larger than them. The number \(2{,}5\), though, is not an upper bound, because the element \(3\) is larger than it. Every number \(c\) larger than an upper bound \(b\) is again an upper bound: for every element \(x\), from \(x \le b < c\) it follows that \(x < c\). An upper bound also need not be an element of the set: \(2\) is an upper bound of the grey fractions, but it is not grey itself. The set of all real numbers \(\mathbb R\) is not bounded above: for every number \(b\), \(b + 1\) is a real number larger than \(b\), so \(b\) is not an upper bound.

Among the upper bounds of the grey fractions, \(2\) tells less precisely how far they reach than \(1{,}74\), and this one in turn less precisely than \(1{,}733\). The closer an upper bound comes to the set, the better it describes it. The hole would be filled by the least upper bound: a number that no grey fraction exceeds, while every smaller number is exceeded by some grey fraction.

Definition 1.30 Supremum and infimum (supremum in infimum)

Let \(A \subseteq \mathbb R\). The supremum (supremum) of the set \(A\), written \(\sup A\), is a number \(s\) that is an upper bound of the set \(A\) and is not larger than any of its upper bounds: \(x \le s\) for every \(x \in A\) and \(s \le b\) for every upper bound \(b\) of the set \(A\). The infimum (infimum) \(\inf A\) is a lower bound \(i\) of the set \(A\) that is not smaller than any of its lower bounds. If the supremum lies in the set, \(\sup A \in A\), we call it the maximum (maksimum) of the set, \(\max A\), and if the infimum lies in it, the minimum (minimum), \(\min A\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 1.1.2 (PDF pp. 23-24), maximum and minimum §1.2.4 (PDF p. 34).

So the supremum is the least upper bound, and the infimum the greatest lower bound. Both names are Latin: supremum means "the highest", infimum "the lowest". The maximum is the largest element of a set, the minimum the smallest. The definition of the supremum has two parts with different tasks. The first requires that no element of the set lies above \(s\). The second requires that \(s\) is the smallest among the upper bounds. So a number below \(s\) is no longer an upper bound, and some element of the set exceeds it.

We defined upper bounds and the supremum for sets of real numbers. They are defined in the same way in every ordered set (urejena množica), that is, a set in which for any two elements \(x\) and \(y\) exactly one of \(x < y\), \(x = y\) and \(y < x\) holds, and \(x < y\) and \(y < z\) imply \(x < z\) (LEBL1 Def. 1.1.1 and 1.1.2, PDF pp. 23-24). The fractions on their own are such a set too. An upper bound of a set of fractions among the fractions is a fraction that the set does not go beyond, and its supremum among the fractions is the smallest such fraction, if there is one. We will need such a supremum at the end of section 1.8.6.

Let us try the definition on the set \(A = \{x \in \mathbb R : 0 \le x < 1\}\) (figure 1.52). The number \(1\) is an upper bound, because every element is smaller than \(1\). Is \(0{,}9\) an upper bound? It is not, because \(0{,}95\) is an element of the set and larger than \(0{,}9\). It is the same with every number \(b\) with \(0 \le b < 1\): the midpoint \(c = \tfrac12(b + 1)\) is larger than \(b\), since \(c - b = \tfrac12(1 - b) > 0\), and it is an element of the set \(A\), since \(c > b \ge 0\) and \(1 - c = \tfrac12(1 - b) > 0\). Numbers below \(0\) are not upper bounds at all, because \(0 \in A\). So every upper bound is at least \(1\), and \(\sup A = 1\). But the number \(1\) is not an element of the set, so \(A\) has no maximum: for every element \(x\), \(\tfrac12(x + 1)\) is a larger element, by the same computation with \(x\) in place of \(b\). The set has no largest element, but it has a supremum. This is exactly the concept we were looking for: a bound that the set comes arbitrarily close to without reaching it. The infimum of this set is \(0\): the number \(0\) is a lower bound, because every element is at least \(0\), and it is an element of the set, so no lower bound is larger than it. So it is the minimum of the set.

The notation \(\sup A\) claims that the supremum is a single number. Let us check.

Lemma 1.31 Uniqueness of the supremum (enoličnost supremuma)

A set of real numbers has at most one supremum and at most one infimum.

Proof

We must show that two suprema of the same set are equal, and the same for the infimum.

  1. Let \(s\) and \(s'\) be suprema of the set \(A\).
  2. The number \(s'\) is an upper bound of the set \(A\), and \(s\) is not larger than any upper bound. So \(s \le s'\).
  3. With the roles of the numbers \(s\) and \(s'\) swapped we get \(s' \le s\).
  4. From \(s \le s'\) and \(s' \le s\) it follows that \(s = s'\).
  5. Let \(i\) and \(i'\) be infima of the set \(A\). The number \(i'\) is a lower bound, and \(i\) is not smaller than any lower bound, so \(i \ge i'\).
  6. With the roles swapped we get \(i' \ge i\), and from the two inequalities it follows that \(i = i'\).

Source: LEBL1, the paragraph after Def. 1.1.2 (PDF p. 24).

The proof showed a general way of showing that two numbers are equal: we prove \(a \le b\) and \(b \le a\).

1.8.3 Completeness axiom

Now we can describe the hole among the fractions without the number that is missing. The grey fractions form a nonempty set that is bounded above, for example by the number \(2\). Its supremum would have to stand at the place of the hole. At the end of this section we will see that this supremum would have to have the square \(3\), so it is not among the fractions. We want the real numbers to have no such holes. The rules of arithmetic do not contain this requirement, because they also hold for fractions, so we accept it as an axiom, that is, as a statement that we do not prove.

Definition 1.32 Completeness axiom (aksiom polnosti)

Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above, that is, a set with at least one element and with an upper bound, has a supremum.

Source: LEBL1 Def. 1.1.3 (PDF p. 24) and Thm 1.2.1 (PDF p. 29). LEBL1 calls the property the least-upper-bound property (lastnost najmanjše zgornje meje).

The completeness axiom is a statement about the set of real numbers as a whole, not about a single number. The name says that the number line is complete, without holes. The requirement is also called Dedekind completeness, after Dedekind, who described the holes among the fractions by cuts (LEBL1, PDF p. 24). Together with the rules of arithmetic and the properties of the integers from section 1.8.1, this is all we assume about numbers. The rules of arithmetic also hold for fractions, but the completeness axiom does not, so it is exactly what tells the real numbers apart from the fractions. That numbers with all these properties exist at all is a theorem, which mathematicians prove by building the real numbers from the fractions. The construction goes beyond this book (LEBL1 Thm 1.2.1, PDF p. 29, refers to other books for it).

Why does the axiom require both conditions? A set that is not bounded above, for example \(\mathbb R\), has no upper bound at all, so it has no least one either. The empty set, which has no element, has too many upper bounds, on the other hand. Since it has no elements, no element is larger than the number \(b\), so every real number is its upper bound. But there is no smallest real number, since \(b - 1\) is smaller than \(b\). Without either condition the axiom would require something that no numbers satisfy.

1.8.4 Properties of the supremum

The axiom speaks only about the supremum of sets that are bounded above. Let us derive from it two tools that we will need all the time.

The first is the infimum. Do we need a new axiom for it? No. If we change the sign of all the elements, the inequalities turn around. The lower bounds of the set \(A\) become upper bounds of the set \(-A = \{-x : x \in A\}\), and the greatest lower bound becomes the least upper bound, which exists by the axiom. For \(A = \{1, 2, 3\}\) we have \(-A = \{-3, -2, -1\}\), \(\sup(-A) = -1\) and \(\inf A = 1 = -\sup(-A)\).

The second makes use of the word least. A number just below the supremum, for example \(\sup A - 0{,}001\), is no longer an upper bound, so some element of the set exceeds it. So the elements of the set come arbitrarily close to the supremum (figure 1.53). For \(A = \{x \in \mathbb R : 0 \le x < 1\}\) and the error \(0{,}001\) such an element is \(0{,}9995\).

Theorem 1.33 Properties of the supremum and infimum (lastnosti supremuma in infimuma)

Let \(A \subseteq \mathbb R\) be a nonempty set.

  1. If \(A\) is bounded below, it has an infimum, and \(\inf A = -\sup(-A)\), where \(-A = \{-x : x \in A\}\).
  2. If \(A\) is bounded above, then for every \(\eta > 0\) there is an \(x \in A\) with \(\sup A - \eta < x \le \sup A\). If \(A\) is bounded below, then for every \(\eta > 0\) there is an \(x \in A\) with \(\inf A \le x < \inf A + \eta\).
Proof

We must show both statements of the theorem.

1. Existence of the infimum.

  1. The set \(A\) is bounded below, so it has a lower bound \(b\): \(x \ge b\) for every \(x \in A\).
  2. We multiply the inequality \(x \ge b\) by \(-1\), which turns it around: \(-x \le -b\). The elements of the set \(-A\) are exactly the numbers \(-x\) with \(x \in A\), so \(-b\) is an upper bound of the set \(-A\).
  3. The set \(-A\) is nonempty, because \(A\) is nonempty. So by the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum \(c = \sup(-A)\).
  4. Let \(x \in A\). Then \(-x \in -A\), and since \(c\) is an upper bound of the set \(-A\), we have \(-x \le c\). We multiply by \(-1\): \(x \ge -c\). This holds for every \(x \in A\), so \(-c\) is a lower bound of the set \(A\).
  5. Let \(b\) be any lower bound of the set \(A\). By step 2, \(-b\) is an upper bound of the set \(-A\), and since \(c\) is not larger than any upper bound, \(c \le -b\). We multiply by \(-1\): \(b \le -c\).
  6. The lower bound \(-c\) (step 4) is thus not smaller than any lower bound (step 5), so it is the infimum: \(\inf A = -c = -\sup(-A)\).

2. Approaching the supremum.

  1. Let \(A\) be bounded above and \(\eta > 0\). By the completeness axiom 1.32 the supremum \(\sup A\) exists.
  2. Since \(\eta > 0\), we have \(\sup A - \eta < \sup A\).
  3. So the number \(\sup A - \eta\) is not an upper bound of the set \(A\). If it were, then by the definition of the supremum 1.30 the supremum would not be larger than it, which contradicts step 2.
  4. That \(\sup A - \eta\) is not an upper bound means that it is not true that \(x \le \sup A - \eta\) for every \(x \in A\). So there is an \(x \in A\) with \(x > \sup A - \eta\).
  5. For the same \(x\) we have \(x \le \sup A\), because the supremum is an upper bound.
  6. For a set that is bounded below we use item 1. The set \(-A\) is bounded above (step 2 of item 1), so by steps 1 to 5 there is an element \(-x \in -A\) with \(\sup(-A) - \eta < -x\). We multiply the inequality by \(-1\), which turns it around: \(x < -\sup(-A) + \eta = \inf A + \eta\). The number \(x\) is an element of the set \(A\), and \(x \ge \inf A\), because the infimum is a lower bound.

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 1.1.11 and 1.2.8 (PDF pp. 27 and 33). The source leaves the proof of Prop. 1.2.8 to the reader.

Item 2 is the tool we will use most often: the elements of the set are arbitrarily close to the supremum.

We will need one more tool, which does not come from the completeness axiom but only from the rules of arithmetic. It tells how we prove inequalities. If a number \(x\) is not larger than any positive number, it cannot be positive: a positive \(x\) would be larger than its half \(x/2\), which is also positive. We used a similar argument in step 8 of the proof of lemma 1.7 on the uniqueness of the limit. There the inequality was strict and it was enough to compare the number with itself, here it is not strict, so we take half.

Lemma 1.34 An inequality tested with all positive numbers (neenakost z vsemi pozitivnimi števili)

If a real number \(x\) satisfies \(x \le \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\), then \(x \le 0\). If in addition \(x \ge 0\), then \(x = 0\).

Proof

We must show that \(x\) is not positive, and that it equals zero when \(x \ge 0\).

  1. Let \(x \le \eta\) hold for every \(\eta > 0\). We argue by contradiction: suppose that \(x > 0\).
  2. We choose \(\eta = x/2\). This number is positive, because \(x > 0\).
  3. We have \(x - \eta = x - x/2 = x/2 > 0\), so \(x > \eta\). This contradicts the assumption \(x \le \eta\) for this \(\eta\). So \(x > 0\) does not hold, and \(x \le 0\).
  4. If in addition \(x \ge 0\), then from \(x \le 0\) and \(x \ge 0\) it follows that \(x = 0\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 1.2.2 (PDF p. 29).

The lemma turns an inequality into a test with all positive numbers: we prove the inequality \(x \le 0\) by showing \(x \le \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). In the same way we prove that two numbers are equal. If the distance \(|x - y|\) between them is at most \(\eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\), then by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers \(|x - y| = 0\), and \(x = y\).

1.8.5 Archimedean property

In proofs with limits we require that some quantity is smaller than every allowed error \(\eta > 0\), for example than \(0{,}01\) or than \(0{,}000001\). For this we will need that every positive number, however small, is larger than some fraction \(1/n\). For \(\eta = 0{,}000001\) the number \(n = 1\,000\,001\) will do, but at \(n = 1\,000\,000\) the fraction \(1/n\) would be equal to \(\eta\), not smaller. Does such an \(n\) exist for every \(\eta\)? The inequality \(1/n < \eta\) holds exactly when \(n > 1/\eta\), so this is the same question as whether the natural numbers grow past every bound, or whether there might be a real number that is larger than all natural numbers. Intuition says there is not. But about the real numbers we have assumed only the rules of arithmetic and the completeness axiom, so the answer must come from them.

From history

The Greeks avoided quantities smaller than every given quantity but not zero in rigorous proofs. The great geometers of that time resorted to an extreme measure: they excluded such infinitely small quantities from proofs by a postulate, that is, by a requirement that they do not prove. This was done by Eudoxus, Euclid and Archimedes (CAJORI, PDF p. 51). In the preface to the Quadrature of the Parabola Archimedes stated a requirement that he attributed to Eudoxus: when two quantities are unequal, the difference can be added to itself so often that every finite quantity is exceeded (CAJORI, PDF p. 51). Euclid wrote it in Elements V, 4 as a definition of ratio: two magnitudes have a ratio when the lesser can be multiplied so as to exceed the other (CAJORI, PDF p. 51). The same requirement is Axiom V of Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder of 225 BC (LEBL1, PDF p. 31). The Greeks may nevertheless have used infinitely small quantities in the search for truths. Archimedes' book The Method, discovered in 1906, shows that he regarded them as scientific enough to hint to him what the theorems state, but not firm enough to prove with them (CAJORI, PDF p. 51). Mathematicians took no interest in the requirement that every quantity is exceeded until the real numbers were built from the fractions. Otto Stolz showed that it follows from Dedekind's requirement on cuts of fractions (CAJORI, PDF p. 51).

We shall derive the requirement that the natural numbers exceed every real number from the completeness axiom.

The proof is by contradiction. If the natural numbers were bounded above, they would have a supremum \(b\) by the completeness axiom. The number \(b - 1\) is smaller than the least upper bound, so some natural number \(m\) exceeds it. But then \(m + 1\) is a natural number above \(b\), and \(b\) is not an upper bound at all.

Theorem 1.35 Archimedean property (Arhimedova lastnost)

The set of natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) is not bounded above. So for real numbers \(x > 0\) and \(y\) there is a natural number \(n\) with \(n\,x > y\), and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a natural number \(N\) such that \(1/n < \eta\) for every natural number \(n \ge N\).

Proof

We must show that \(\mathbb N\) is not bounded above, and derive the other two statements from this.

The set \(\mathbb N\) is not bounded above.

  1. We argue by contradiction. Suppose that \(\mathbb N\) is bounded above.
  2. The set \(\mathbb N\) is nonempty, because it contains \(1\). So by the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum \(b = \sup \mathbb N\).
  3. By theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 2, with \(\eta = 1\) there is a natural number \(m\) with \(m > b - 1\).
  4. We add \(1\) to the inequality and get \(m + 1 > b\). The number \(m + 1\) is natural.
  5. So the natural number \(m + 1\) is larger than \(b\), and \(b\) is not an upper bound of the set \(\mathbb N\). This contradicts step 2, where \(b\) is the supremum and so an upper bound. The assumption of step 1 is false.

A multiple exceeds every number.

  1. Let \(x > 0\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Since \(x \neq 0\), the number \(y/x\) exists.
  2. By the first part, \(y/x\) is not an upper bound of the set \(\mathbb N\), so there is an \(n \in \mathbb N\) with \(n > y/x\).
  3. We multiply the inequality by the positive number \(x\), which does not turn it around: \(n\,x > y\).

The fractions \(1/n\) are smaller than \(\eta\) from some point on.

  1. Let \(\eta > 0\). We use the previous part with \(x = \eta\) and \(y = 1\): there is a natural number \(N\) with \(N\eta > 1\).
  2. We multiply the inequality by the positive number \(1/N\) and get \(\eta > 1/N\).
  3. Let \(n \ge N\). Then \(1/n \le 1/N\), because for positive numbers a larger denominator gives a smaller fraction: \(1/N - 1/n = (n - N)/(nN) \ge 0\).
  4. From \(1/n \le 1/N\) and \(1/N < \eta\) it follows that \(1/n < \eta\), for every \(n \ge N\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 1.2.4 (i) and Cor. 1.2.5 (PDF pp. 31-32).

The theorem says that among the real numbers there is no number larger than all natural numbers, and no positive number smaller than all fractions \(1/n\). The second statement reads: however small the steps of length \(x > 0\) we take, with enough steps we pass every number \(y\) (figure 1.54). The third says that every positive number is larger than \(1/n\) when \(n\) is large enough, and not just for one \(n\), but for every one from some \(N\) on.

Now we can find the infimum of the set \(\{1/n : n \in \mathbb N\}\). The number \(0\) is a lower bound, because \(1/n > 0\) for every \(n\). But no number \(b > 0\) is a lower bound, because by the theorem there is an \(n\) with \(1/n < b\). For \(b = 0{,}001\) this is, for example, \(n = 1001\). So every lower bound is at most \(0\), and \(\inf\{1/n : n \in \mathbb N\} = 0\) (LEBL1 Cor. 1.2.5, PDF p. 32). The infimum is not an element of the set, because \(1/n \neq 0\), so the set has no minimum. It was the same with the set \(\{x : 0 \le x < 1\}\) and its supremum: the set comes arbitrarily close to its bound without reaching it.

1.8.6 Square root

Now we can fill the hole with which this section began, and for every nonnegative number \(x\), not only for \(3\). At the same time we fill a gap that the book has carried since section 1.5.4: there we computed the length of a vector with a square root, without knowing that the root exists.

As the candidate for \(\sqrt x\) we take the bound up to which the nonnegative numbers with the square below \(x\) reach, that is, the supremum \(r\) of the set \(A = \{t \in \mathbb R : t \ge 0,\ t^2 < x\}\) (figure 1.55). For \(x > 0\) the set \(A\) is nonempty, because it contains \(0\), and bounded above, as we show in the proof, so by the completeness axiom it has a supremum. We treat the case \(x = 0\) separately. It remains to show \(r^2 = x\), and we do this by ruling out the other two possibilities. If the square were too small, \(r^2 < x\), we could increase \(r\) by a small \(h > 0\), and \(r + h\) would still be in \(A\). Then \(r\) would not be an upper bound. If the square were too large, \(r^2 > x\), we could decrease \(r\) by a small \(h > 0\), and \(r - h\) would still be an upper bound. Then \(r\) would not be the least upper bound. All the work lies in finding a small enough \(h\).

Let us try with numbers for \(x = 3\). Can \(r = 1{,}73\) be the supremum? Its square \(2{,}9929\) is below \(3\). The number \(1{,}732\) has the square \(2{,}999824\), still below \(3\), so it is an element of the set \(A\) and larger than \(1{,}73\). So the number \(1{,}73\) is not even an upper bound. Can \(r = 1{,}74\) be the supremum? Its square \(3{,}0276\) is above \(3\). The number \(1{,}733\) has the square \(3{,}003289\), still above \(3\), so by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, every element of the set \(A\) is smaller than it. So the number \(1{,}733\) is an upper bound smaller than \(1{,}74\), and \(1{,}74\) is not the least upper bound. The proof does the same with a general \(h\), chosen so that it works for every square that is too small or too large.

Theorem 1.36 Existence of square roots (obstoj kvadratnega korena)

For every real number \(x \ge 0\) there is exactly one number \(r \ge 0\) with \(r^2 = x\). This number is the square root (kvadratni koren) \(\sqrt x\).

Proof

We must show that such a number \(r\) exists and that there is only one.

Uniqueness.

  1. Let \(r \ge 0\) and \(s \ge 0\) be numbers with \(r^2 = s^2 = x\). Then \(0 = r^2 - s^2 = (r - s)(r + s)\).
  2. A product is zero only if one of the factors is zero. If \(r - s = 0\), then \(r = s\). If \(r + s = 0\), the nonnegative numbers \(r\) and \(s\) are both zero, since otherwise the sum would be positive, and again \(r = s\).

The case \(x = 0\).

  1. For \(x = 0\) the number is \(r = 0\), because \(0 \ge 0\) and \(0^2 = 0\).

A candidate for the root.

  1. Let \(x > 0\) and \(A = \{t \in \mathbb R : t \ge 0,\ t^2 < x\}\).
  2. The set \(A\) is nonempty, because it contains \(0\): we have \(0 \ge 0\) and \(0^2 = 0 < x\).
  3. The number \(1 + x\) is an upper bound of the set \(A\). For \(t \ge 1 + x\), by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(t^2 \ge (1 + x)^2\). Since \((1 + x)^2 - x = 1 + x + x^2 > 0\), we have \(t^2 > x\). Such a \(t\) is not in \(A\), so every element of the set \(A\) is smaller than \(1 + x\). Why do we not simply take \(x\)? Because for \(x < 1\) it is not an upper bound: for \(x = 0{,}25\) we have \(0{,}4 \in A\), since \(0{,}4^2 = 0{,}16 < 0{,}25\), and \(0{,}4 > 0{,}25\).
  4. By the completeness axiom 1.32 there is \(r = \sup A\). We have \(r \ge 0\), because \(0 \in A\) and \(r\) is an upper bound. We will show \(r^2 = x\) by ruling out the possibilities \(r^2 < x\) and \(r^2 > x\).

The square is not smaller than \(x\).

  1. Suppose, on the contrary, that \(r^2 < x\). We will find an \(h > 0\) for which still \((r + h)^2 < x\).
  2. We expand the square of the sum and take out \(h\): \((r + h)^2 - r^2 = 2rh + h^2 = h\,(2r + h)\).
  3. For \(0 < h < 1\) we have \(2r + h < 2r + 1\), and multiplying by the positive \(h\) we get \(h\,(2r + h) < h\,(2r + 1)\).
  4. By steps 2 and 3 it is enough to find an \(h\) with \(0 < h < 1\) and \(h\,(2r + 1) < x - r^2\).
  5. The numbers \(1\) and \((x - r^2)/(2r + 1)\) are positive, because \(x - r^2 > 0\) and \(2r + 1 > 0\). For \(h\) we take half of the smaller of them. Half, so that both inequalities of step 4 are strict.
  6. The number \(h\) is positive, because it is half of a positive number, and it is smaller than that number, which is larger neither than \(1\) nor than \((x - r^2)/(2r + 1)\). So \(0 < h < 1\) and \(h < (x - r^2)/(2r + 1)\). Multiplying by the positive \(2r + 1\) we get \(h\,(2r + 1) < x - r^2\).
  7. By steps 2, 3 and 6,
    \[(r + h)^2 - r^2 = h\,(2r + h) < h\,(2r + 1) < x - r^2 ,\]
    and adding \(r^2\) gives \((r + h)^2 < x\). Since also \(r + h \ge 0\), we have \(r + h \in A\).
  8. Since \(h > 0\), we have \(r + h > r\). So the element \(r + h\) of the set \(A\) is larger than \(r\), which contradicts \(r\) being an upper bound. So \(r^2 < x\) does not hold.

The square is not larger than \(x\).

  1. Suppose, on the contrary, that \(r^2 > x\). We will find an \(h > 0\) for which \(r - h\) is still an upper bound of the set \(A\).
  2. We have \(r \neq 0\), because \(r^2 > x > 0\). Since also \(r \ge 0\), we have \(r > 0\).
  3. Let \(h = (r^2 - x)/(2r)\). It is chosen so that \(2rh = r^2 - x\). We have \(h > 0\), because the numerator and the denominator are positive, and \(h < r/2 < r\), because \(r^2 - x < r^2\). So \(r - h > 0\).
  4. We expand the square of the difference and use \(2rh = r^2 - x\):
    \[(r - h)^2 = r^2 - 2rh + h^2 = x + h^2 > x ,\]
    because \(h^2 > 0\).
  5. Let \(t \in A\). If \(t \ge r - h\), then by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(t^2 \ge (r - h)^2 > x\). This contradicts the condition \(t^2 < x\). So \(t < r - h\).
  6. This holds for every \(t \in A\), so \(r - h\) is an upper bound of the set \(A\). Since \(h > 0\), we have \(r - h < r\), but the supremum \(r\) is not larger than any upper bound. This is impossible, so \(r^2 > x\) does not hold.

Conclusion.

  1. Of the three possibilities \(r^2 < x\), \(r^2 = x\) and \(r^2 > x\), what remains is \(r^2 = x\). So the number \(r \ge 0\) is the root we were looking for.

Source: LEBL1 Example 1.2.3 (PDF pp. 29-30) for \(x = 2\), with the same conditions on the first \(h\) and the same second \(h\). Taking half of the smaller number, the general \(x\) and the upper bound \(1 + x\) are not from the source. The source leaves the general \(x\) to the reader (PDF p. 30).

The proof showed how we test a candidate for the supremum: if we can move it up a little and it stays in the set, or down a little and it stays an upper bound, it is not the supremum. For the square that was too small we chose a small enough \(h\) as half of the smaller of two numbers, each of which takes care of one requirement. This move will come back in almost every proof that follows.

For fractions the theorem does not hold, and the proof says why. If \(x\) and \(r\) are fractions, both numbers \(h\) that the proof chooses are fractions too. Suppose the set of grey fractions \(\{t \in \mathbb Q : t \ge 0,\ t^2 < 3\}\) had a least upper bound \(r\) among the fractions. The same steps would rule out \(r^2 < 3\) and \(r^2 > 3\), because \(r + h\) and \(r - h\) would again be fractions. What remains is \(r^2 = 3\), but by lemma 1.27 no rational number has square 3. So the set of grey fractions has no supremum among the fractions, and the completeness axiom does not hold for the fractions (LEBL1 Example 1.1.4, PDF pp. 24-25, shows this for the square \(2\)). This is the precise form of the hole we saw in figure 1.51.

Among the real numbers, however, there is no hole: \(\sqrt 3\) exists, and with it the point \(\xi = 1/\sqrt 3\), where the tangent to the graph of the function \(t^3\) has the slope \(1\). All the lengths of vectors from section 1.5.4 exist too. But that such a point in between exists for every function with a derivative we will prove only in the next sections. For this we need endless strings of numbers that approach some number. We continue with them.

1.9 Mathematics: sequences and their limits

At the end of the previous section we announced endless strings of numbers that approach some number. We have met them already. In section 1.2 we computed, for the hanging bar, the strain of ever shorter pieces at the top, and the strains approached the number \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\). In this section such a string of approximations, which follow one another without end, gets a name and a precise definition. Then we say when such a string approaches a number, and we show that it cannot approach two numbers at once and that its numbers are then bounded. We will need such strings for the proofs in the next sections, because with them we can catch a point as the place that a string of points approaches.

1.9.1 Sequence

Let us return to the hanging bar of section 1.7.1: a steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m stretches under its own weight. It is fixed only at the centre \(O\) of its top end, and its weight is carried by a force that pulls the top face up evenly, which is an idealization (figure 1.40). A point on the axis of the bar at the depth \(x\) moves down by \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Above the point at the top there is no material, so we take pieces below it. At the top let us take a piece of length \(1\) m, then \(\tfrac12\) m, \(\tfrac13\) m, \(\tfrac14\) m and so on, each time a piece of length \(1/n\) m for the next natural number \(n\) (figure 1.56, left). By (1.6), written for \(x = 0\) and \(\Delta x = 1/n\) m, the strain of the \(n\)-th piece is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{u(1/n) - u(0)}{1/n} = a\,(2L - 1/n) = 2aL - \frac{a}{n} ,\]

where \(1/n\) means the length of the piece in metres. The first few values are \(\varepsilon_1 = 3{,}7088 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(\varepsilon_2 = 3{,}8064 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(\varepsilon_3 = 3{,}8389 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(\varepsilon_{10} = 3{,}8845 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and \(\varepsilon_{1000} = 3{,}9038 \cdot 10^{-6}\) (figure 1.56, right). To every natural number \(n\) belongs one strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}\), and it matters which strain belongs to which \(n\): the strain at \(n = 2\) is the strain of the piece of length \(\tfrac12\) m.

Definition 1.37 Sequence (zaporedje)

A sequence (zaporedje) of real numbers is a function whose input is a natural number \(n\) and whose output is a real number, which we write \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) and call the \(n\)-th term (člen) of the sequence. We write the whole sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) or \(x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots\) A sequence is bounded (omejeno) if the set of its terms \(\{x_{\mathrm{n}} : n \in \mathbb N\}\) is a bounded set (definition 1.29).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 2.1.1 (PDF p. 51).

So a sequence is a function as in definition 1.4, whose domain is the set of natural numbers. The number \(n\) is the place of the term in the sequence, and \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the term at this place.
