The strains of the pieces are a sequence \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}})\), and its third term is \(\varepsilon_3 = 3{,}8389 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Another example is the sequence \((1/n)\) with the terms \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\), which we can draw in two ways (figure 1.57). As the graph of a function these are dots above the numbers \(1, 2, 3, \dots\), which we do not join with a line, because the sequence has no values in between. On the number line they are the points \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\), which crowd together toward \(0\).

A sequence is not the set of its terms. The sequence \(((-1)^n)\), that is, \(-1, 1, -1, 1, \dots\), has infinitely many terms, but the set of its terms is \(\{-1, 1\}\). In a sequence what counts is the place of each term and the fact that a term repeats.

1.9.2 Limit of a sequence

What exactly does it mean that the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}\) approach the number \(2aL\)? It is not enough that the distance to \(2aL\) decreases, since the distance to the number \(4 \cdot 10^{-6}\) decreases too, and the strains do not reach this number and do not come arbitrarily close to it. We require that the distance eventually becomes smaller than every allowed error and stays so.

From history

A distance that decreases at every step, while the steps never end, is a difficulty older than our strains. In the fifth century BC Zeno of Elea argued that Achilles cannot overtake a tortoise. He must first reach the place from which the tortoise started, and by then the tortoise has moved on a little way. Achilles must traverse that too, and the tortoise is ahead again, he is always nearer but never makes up to it (CAJORI, PDF p. 39). None of Zeno's writings have come down to us, and we know him through his critics (CAJORI, PDF p. 39).

Back to the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}\) that approach the number \(2aL\). Let us see why Achilles does overtake the tortoise after all: his total distance too approaches a bound. Let Achilles be ten times faster than the tortoise and let the tortoise have a head start of 100 m. When Achilles runs these 100 m, the tortoise has gone 10 m. When Achilles runs these 10 m as well, the tortoise has gone 1 m, then 0.1 m and so on. Achilles' distances are therefore 100 m, 10 m, 1 m, 0.1 m and so on, each a tenth of the previous one (figure 1.58). After the first step 100 m have been run, after the second 110 m, after the third 111 m, after the fourth 111.1 m. The total distance approaches \(1000/9 \approx 111{,}11\) m. There Achilles and the tortoise are at the same place at the same time, since in the time in which Achilles runs 111.11 m the tortoise has covered a tenth of this distance and is \(100 + 11{,}11 = 111{,}11\) m from the start. The total distance never reaches this place at any step, since after the fourth step about 0.011 m is still missing, after the fifth about 0.0011 m and so on, always something.

From history

Gregory St. Vincent (1584 to 1667), whose large book Opus geometricum appeared in Antwerp in 1647 (CAJORI, PDF p. 197-198), was the first to treat the problem of Achilles as the summation of infinitely many ever smaller distances, and the first to state the exact time and place at which Achilles overtakes the tortoise. He thought of the number that the sum approaches as an obstacle against further advance, like a rigid wall. It did not bother him that the sum never reaches it (CAJORI, PDF p. 198).

The abbreviation lim, which we write from section 1.3.3 on, as far as is known, did not exist before Simon Lhuilier (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 278). In the same textbook Cauchy also wrote: when the successive values attributed to a variable approach a fixed value indefinitely, so as to end by differing from it as little as is wished, this fixed value is called the limit of all the others (CAJORI, PDF p. 412).

Let us return to numbers that approach a bound, as the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}\) approach the number \(2aL\). The definition that follows says the same as Cauchy's description, but with a permitted error \(\eta\) and a place \(N\) in the sequence from which on the distance is smaller than \(\eta\). This is the same idea as for the limit of a function in section 1.3.3, except that instead of "close enough to zero" we say "far enough along the sequence".

Definition 1.38 Limit of a sequence (limita zaporedja)

A sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges (konvergira) to a number \(d\) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a natural number \(N\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\). The number \(d\) is then the limit (limita) of the sequence, and we write

\[\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} = d . \tag{1.25}\]

A sequence that converges to some number is convergent (konvergentno), otherwise it is divergent (divergentno).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 2.1.2 (PDF p. 52).

The definition is a game of two players. The first chooses an allowed error \(\eta\), however small. The second must find a place \(N\) from which on all terms are closer to the number \(d\) than \(\eta\). The sequence converges if the second player always wins. In figure 1.59 this is the band between \(d - \eta\) and \(d + \eta\): from the place \(N\) on all dots are in the band, while before it they may be outside. The place \(N\) depends on \(\eta\). A narrower band usually requires a later place (figure 1.60). We read \(n \to \infty\) as "when \(n\) goes past every bound". The sign \(\infty\) (infinity) is not a number, and the notation only says that we look at ever later terms.

The limit is a property of the tail of the sequence, that is, of the terms from some place on. The first few terms do not affect it, because the definition speaks only of \(n \ge N\). Nor does any term have to reach the limit.

The simplest example is the constant sequence \(c, c, c, \dots\) It converges to \(c\), because \(|c - c| = 0 < \eta\) for every \(n\), so for every \(\eta\) the place \(N = 1\) will do. We need the next example in almost every computation that follows.

Lemma 1.39 Limit of the sequence 1/n (limita zaporedja 1/n)

The sequence \((1/n)\) converges to \(0\): \(\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} 1/n = 0\).

Proof

We must show that for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a place \(N\) from which on \(|1/n - 0| < \eta\).

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\).
  2. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(N\) such that \(1/n < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\).
  3. For every \(n\) we have \(1/n - 0 = 1/n > 0\), so \(|1/n - 0| = 1/n\).
  4. By steps 2 and 3, \(|1/n - 0| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so the limit of the sequence is \(0\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 2.1.4 (PDF p. 53).

For the error \(\eta = 0{,}01\), for example, \(N = 101\): for \(n \ge 101\) we have \(1/n \le \tfrac{1}{101} < 0{,}01\), while at \(n = 100\) we have \(1/n = 0{,}01\), which is not less than \(0{,}01\).

Now we can say exactly what the strains of the pieces approach. Let us show that \(\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = 2aL\).

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\).
  2. The distance of a term from the number \(2aL\) is \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} - 2aL| = |{-a/n}| = a/n\), because \(a > 0\).
  3. The condition \(a/n < \eta\) holds exactly when \(1/n < \eta/a\). The number \(\eta/a\) is positive, so by the Archimedean property 1.35 there is an \(N\) such that \(1/n < \eta/a\) for every \(n \ge N\).
  4. So for every \(n \ge N\) we have \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} - 2aL| = a/n < \eta\). We picked the error freely, so \(\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = 2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\).

This is the strain at the point at the top of the bar, which in section 1.4 we got as a derivative. There we required that the strain of a piece approach the derivative for all short enough pieces, not only for chosen lengths. Here we took only the lengths \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\) m and got the same number. A single chosen sequence of lengths does not prove that the derivative exists, since the quotient could behave differently for other lengths. That every such sequence approaches the derivative, when the derivative exists, we will show in one of the next sections. At the very top this limit is one-sided. There is no material above the top, so the length \(\Delta x\) of the piece approaches zero only from the positive side, and the strain at the top is the limit of the quotient from the right (definition 1.8), that is, the one-sided derivative of definition 1.9. The number \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) at the very top holds for the idealized way of holding the bar. For a bar welded to the ceiling it would be different near the ceiling.

1.9.3 A sequence without a limit

Does every sequence have a limit? No. The sequence \(((-1)^n)\), that is, \(-1, 1, -1, 1, \dots\), jumps between \(-1\) and \(1\) and does not settle at any number. Why can it not converge to any number \(d\)? Neighbouring terms are \(2\) apart. If both were closer to the number \(d\) than \(\tfrac12\), they would be closer to each other than \(1\) (figure 1.61).

Lemma 1.40 A sequence without a limit (zaporedje brez limite)

The sequence \(((-1)^n)\) is bounded and divergent.

Proof

We must show that the terms are bounded and that the sequence does not converge to any number.

  1. The term \((-1)^n\) is \(1\) if \(n\) is even, and \(-1\) if \(n\) is odd. So \(-1 \le (-1)^n \le 1\) for every \(n\), and the sequence is bounded.
  2. We prove the divergence by contradiction. Suppose that the sequence converges to some number \(d\).
  3. We use the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 with the error \(\eta = \tfrac12\): there is an \(N\) such that \(|(-1)^n - d| < \tfrac12\) for every \(n \ge N\). We choose the error \(\tfrac12\) because the sum of two such errors is \(1\), which is less than the distance \(2\) between the terms \(1\) and \(-1\).
  4. Let \(n = 2N\). This number is even and at least \(N\), and the number \(n + 1\) is odd and also at least \(N\). So \((-1)^n = 1\) and \((-1)^{n+1} = -1\), and by step 3, \(|1 - d| < \tfrac12\) and \(|-1 - d| < \tfrac12\).
  5. We estimate the distance between \(1\) and \(-1\) through the number \(d\). We write \(1 - (-1) = (1 - d) + (d - (-1))\). By the triangle inequality for numbers \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1),
    \[2 = |1 - (-1)| \le |1 - d| + |d - (-1)| .\]
  6. The numbers \(d - (-1)\) and \(-1 - d\) are opposite, so they have the same absolute value, \(|d - (-1)| = |-1 - d|\). So by step 4 the right side of the inequality of step 5 is smaller than \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1\), and it follows that \(2 < 1\).
  7. This is not true. The assumption of step 2 is false, so the sequence does not converge to any number.

Source: LEBL1 Example 2.1.5 (PDF pp. 53-54).

So the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) is bounded, and still it has no limit. Being bounded is not enough for convergence.

1.9.4 Uniqueness of the limit

The notation \(\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} = d\) claims that there is only one limit. Let us check that a sequence cannot converge to two different numbers. The idea is the same as for the limit of a function in lemma 1.7 on the uniqueness of the limit. If the terms approached two numbers, late terms would be close to both, so the two numbers would be close to each other, closer than every error (figure 1.62).

Lemma 1.41 Uniqueness of the limit of a sequence (enoličnost limite zaporedja)

A convergent sequence has only one limit.

Proof

We must show that two numbers \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) to which the same sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges are equal.

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). We will show that \(|d_1 - d_2| < \eta\).
  2. Since \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d_1\), the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 gives for the error \(\eta/2\) a place \(N_1\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_1| < \eta/2\) for every \(n \ge N_1\). We take half the error because in step 5 we will add two such errors.
  3. Since \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d_2\), for the same error \(\eta/2\) there is a place \(N_2\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_2| < \eta/2\) for every \(n \ge N_2\).
  4. Let \(n\) be the larger of the numbers \(N_1\) and \(N_2\). Since \(n \ge N_1\) and \(n \ge N_2\), both inequalities of steps 2 and 3 hold for this \(n\).
  5. We write the difference through the term \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(d_1 - d_2 = (d_1 - x_{\mathrm{n}}) + (x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_2)\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) and since \(|d_1 - x_{\mathrm{n}}| = |x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_1|\), we have
    \[|d_1 - d_2| \le |x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_1| + |x_{\mathrm{n}} - d_2| < \tfrac{\eta}{2} + \tfrac{\eta}{2} = \eta .\]
  6. We picked the error freely, so \(|d_1 - d_2| \le \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). Since \(|d_1 - d_2| \ge 0\), by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers \(|d_1 - d_2| = 0\), and so \(d_1 = d_2\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 2.1.6 (PDF p. 53).

The proof repeated the pattern of the proof of the uniqueness of the limit of a function: when the sum of two errors must be small, we allow each of them half. The only new thing is that the two requirements each held from their own place on, and both hold at once from the larger of the two places on.

1.9.5 Boundedness of a convergent sequence

The sequence \(((-1)^n)\) showed that a bounded sequence need not be convergent. The converse, however, does hold: a convergent sequence is always bounded. Why? From some place \(N\) on the terms are close to the limit, say closer than \(1\), and so they are bounded. Before this place there are only finitely many terms, \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{N}-1}\), and finitely many numbers can be caught by one bound (figure 1.63).

Lemma 1.42 A convergent sequence is bounded (konvergentno zaporedje je omejeno)

If a sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges, there is a number \(B\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le B\) for every \(n\). So the sequence is bounded, with the lower bound \(-B\) and the upper bound \(B\).

Proof

We must show that one bound \(B\) bounds all the terms.

  1. Let the sequence converge to \(d\). We use the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 with the error \(\eta = 1\): there is an \(N\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < 1\) for every \(n \ge N\). The size of the error does not matter. We only need some bound for the terms from \(N\) on.
  2. For \(n \ge N\) we write \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}} - d) + d\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le |x_{\mathrm{n}} - d| + |d| < 1 + |d|\).
  3. As the bound we take the sum of the absolute values of the terms before \(N\) and of the number \(1 + |d|\):
    \[B = |x_1| + |x_2| + \dots + |x_{\mathrm{N}-1}| + 1 + |d| .\]
    For \(N = 1\) there are no terms before \(N\), and \(B = 1 + |d|\).
  4. Let \(n < N\). Then \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}|\) is one of the terms of the sum \(B\), and all the other terms of the sum are not negative. So \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le B\).
  5. Let \(n \ge N\). By step 2, \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| < 1 + |d|\), and \(1 + |d| \le B\), because the other terms of the sum \(B\) are not negative. So \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| < B\).
  6. Every \(n\) is smaller than \(N\) or at least \(N\), so by steps 4 and 5, \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le B\) for every \(n\). The inequality \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le B\) means \(-B \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le B\), so \(B\) is an upper bound and \(-B\) a lower bound of the set of terms.

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 2.1.7 (PDF p. 54). The source takes as the bound the largest of the numbers \(|x_1|, \dots, |x_{\mathrm{N}-1}|, 1 + |d|\). The sum that we take is larger, but just as good as a bound, and it does not need a proof that finitely many numbers have a largest one.

For the strains of the pieces of the hanging bar the bound is simple. All terms are smaller than \(2aL\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = 2aL - a/n\), and positive, because \(2L = 20\) m is more than \(1/n \le 1\) m. So \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}}| \le 2aL\) for every \(n\).

The next section tells how we compute limits and when a sequence converges without our knowing the limit in advance. The completeness axiom will appear there again.

1.10 Mathematics: when a sequence converges

In section 1.9 we always knew the limit in advance. For the strains of the pieces of the hanging bar it was \(2aL\), for the sequence \((1/n)\) the number \(0\), and each time we checked the definition of the limit with a computation of its own. On the road ahead it will be different. The statement that we have needed since the end of section 1.7.3 says that the change of a function between two numbers equals the derivative at some point between them times the difference of the two numbers. Its proof will find such a point as the limit of a sequence that we build step by step, and it will have no formula for the limit. So we need two things: a way to get new limits from known ones without a new computation with \(\eta\) and \(N\), and a guarantee that a sequence converges even when we cannot name its limit.

We develop both on one example, the search for the number \(\sqrt 3\) by bisection, which computes only with fractions. Along the way we meet a way of proving statements for all natural numbers at once, a rule that gets the limit of a sequence trapped between two sequences from their limits, the rule that a non-strict inequality between the terms carries over to the limits, and a theorem about sequences that only increase or only decrease. In this theorem the completeness axiom appears again. About numbers we assume the same as in section 1.8.1: the school rules of arithmetic, division of integers with a remainder, the fact that every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element, and the completeness axiom 1.32.

1.10.1 Search by bisection

In section 1.8.6 we proved that the number \(\sqrt 3\) exists: it is the supremum of the set of nonnegative numbers with the square below \(3\) (theorem 1.36 on the existence of square roots). But the proof does not tell how large \(\sqrt 3\) is. How would we compute it if we can compute exactly only with fractions? Take the numbers \(1\) and \(2\). We have \(1^2 = 1 < 3\) and \(2^2 = 4 > 3\), so by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(\sqrt 3\) lies between them. We look at the number in the middle, \(1{,}5\). Its square \(2{,}25\) is below \(3\), so \(\sqrt 3\) lies between \(1{,}5\) and \(2\). We look at the new middle, \(1{,}75\). Its square \(3{,}0625\) is not below \(3\), so \(\sqrt 3\) lies between \(1{,}5\) and \(1{,}75\). We go on like this. Each step halves the distance over which we search, so we call the procedure bisection (razpolavljanje).

We need a name for all the numbers between two numbers.

Definition 1.43 Interval (interval)

Let \(a < b\) be real numbers. The closed interval (zaprti interval) \([a, b]\) is the set \(\{x \in \mathbb R : a \le x \le b\}\), the open interval (odprti interval) \((a, b)\) is the set \(\{x \in \mathbb R : a < x < b\}\), and the half-open intervals (polodprta intervala) are the sets \([a, b) = \{x \in \mathbb R : a \le x < b\}\) and \((a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb R : a < x \le b\}\). The numbers \(a\) and \(b\) are the endpoints (krajišči) of the interval, the number \(b - a\) is its length (dolžina), and the number \(\tfrac12(a + b)\) is its midpoint (središče).

Source: LEBL1 §1.4 (PDF p. 41). The length and the midpoint are not from the source.

A square bracket says that the endpoint belongs to the interval, and a round one that it does not (figure 1.64). So the set \(\{x \in \mathbb R : 0 \le x < 1\}\) from section 1.8.2 is the half-open interval \([0, 1)\). An interval contains all real numbers between its endpoints, not only the fractions. The requirement \(a < b\) makes the length positive and keeps an interval from being a single point, as the closed interval \([a, a] = \{a\}\) would be for \(a = b\). The notation \((a, b)\) for the open interval is the same as the notation for a pair of numbers, for example a point in the plane, and the text tells which is meant. The midpoint lies strictly between the endpoints, because it is half the length away from each of them:

\[\tfrac12(a + b) - a = \tfrac12(b - a) > 0 , \qquad b - \tfrac12(a + b) = \tfrac12(b - a) > 0 .\]

So every interval is nonempty. The intervals of the definition are bounded, because \(a\) and \(b\) are numbers. We will need unbounded intervals later, for example the set of all numbers \(x \ge a\), which we write \([a, \infty)\) (LEBL1 §1.4, PDF p. 41).

Let us now write the search as a rule. We start with the interval \([a_1, b_1] = [1, 2]\). Suppose that for some natural number \(k\) the interval \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, b_{\mathrm{k}}]\) is already determined, and let \(m_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{k}} + b_{\mathrm{k}})\) be its midpoint.

  • If \(m_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3\), the next interval is the right half: \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = b_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  • If \(m_{\mathrm{k}}^2 \ge 3\), the next interval is the left half: \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\).

The rule determines the first interval, and from each interval the next one. The left endpoints \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots\) form a sequence, and so do the right endpoints. The rule uses only addition, division by \(2\), multiplication and comparison of fractions. It does not use the number \(\sqrt 3\) anywhere. The table shows the first eight steps, and figure 1.65 shows the intervals.

\(k\) \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(m_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) next interval
1 1 2 1 1,5 2,25 right half
2 1,5 2 0,5 1,75 3,0625 left half
3 1,5 1,75 0,25 1,625 2,640625 right half
4 1,625 1,75 0,125 1,6875 2,8476… right half
5 1,6875 1,75 0,0625 1,71875 2,9541… right half
6 1,71875 1,75 0,03125 1,734375 3,0080… left half
7 1,71875 1,734375 0,015625 1,7265625 2,9810… right half
8 1,7265625 1,734375 0,0078125 1,73046875 2,9945… right half

The endpoints are fractions with the denominators \(1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\), so they have finite decimal expansions, and the table gives them exactly. The squares of the midpoints that end in three dots are cut off after four decimal places, and the others are exact.

The table shows four properties that hold for every \(k\).

  1. The left endpoint has a square below \(3\), and the right one a square of at least \(3\): \(a_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). At \(k = 1\) we have \(1 < 3 \le 4\). The rule replaces the left endpoint only by a midpoint whose square is below \(3\), and the right one only by a midpoint whose square is at least \(3\).
  2. The left endpoints do not decrease, and the right ones do not increase: \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\). This is because a new endpoint is an old endpoint or the midpoint, which lies between the old endpoints, since the left endpoint is smaller than the right one (by the third property \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = 1/2^{k-1} > 0\)).
  3. The length of the interval is \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = 1/2^{k-1}\). At \(k = 1\) the length is \(1 = 1/2^0\), and each step halves it, because the midpoint is half the length away from both endpoints.
  4. All endpoints are fractions in the interval \([1, 2]\). At \(k = 1\) they are \(1\) and \(2\). A new endpoint is an old endpoint or the midpoint of two fractions from \([1, 2]\), which is again a fraction and lies between them.

From the first property it follows that \(\sqrt 3\) is in every bisection interval. By the fourth property the endpoints are positive, so by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(a_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3 = (\sqrt 3)^2\) gives \(a_{\mathrm{k}} < \sqrt 3\), and \((\sqrt 3)^2 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) gives \(\sqrt 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\).

The table shows even more. The left endpoints increase and crowd together below \(1{,}732\), and the right ones decrease toward the same value. Do they really approach some number, and is it \(\sqrt 3\)? If we were allowed to use \(\sqrt 3\), the answer would be short. In the proofs ahead of us, though, there will be no such number. There bisection will search for a point about which we know nothing in advance. So we will first show that the left endpoints converge without using \(\sqrt 3\), and only then that their limit is \(\sqrt 3\). For this we need four tools. The first one is already hidden in the four properties: we showed each of them by the argument that it holds at \(k = 1\) and that every step preserves it. Does such an argument really prove the statement for every \(k\)?

1.10.2 Induction

The argument for the properties of bisection was the same each time. The property holds at \(k = 1\), and if it holds at some \(k\), it also holds at \(k + 1\). Why does it follow that it holds at every \(k\)? Since it holds at \(1\), it holds at \(2\). Since it holds at \(2\), it holds at \(3\). We can go on like this, but in finitely many steps we do not reach all natural numbers. We need an argument that covers all natural numbers at once.

From history

Mathematicians before us knew the same difficulty. In his edition of Euclid of 1260 Giovanni Campano of Novara (in Latin Campanus) proved that the ratio in which the whole segment is to the greater part as the greater part to the lesser (the golden section) cannot be written as a fraction. The argument went back to smaller numbers and led to a contradiction, but not in order from \(n\) to \(n - 1\) and \(n - 2\), rather by leaps over several whole numbers (CAJORI, PDF p. 158). The discovery of such an argument by a sequence of steps is attributed to Francesco Maurolico (in Latin Franciscus Maurolycus, 1494 to 1575) of Messina. It appears in the introduction to his Opuscula mathematica (Venice, 1575) (CAJORI, PDF p. 157-158). In 1656 John Wallis, in his Arithmetica infinitorum, inferred from several cases to all, as is the custom in natural science (CAJORI, PDF p. 347). Blaise Pascal used the argument by steps in his Traité du triangle arithmétique in 1662 (CAJORI, PDF p. 158). In 1686 Jakob Bernoulli rejected Wallis's procedure because it is not logically binding (CAJORI, PDF p. 347). A statement may hold for the first few numbers and fail at the next.

An inference from a few cases to all natural numbers does not always hold. Let us look at an example that we add ourselves: divide a circle by all possible segments between \(n\) points on the circle, so that no three of them meet in the same point. For \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) we get \(1, 2, 4, 8, 16\) parts, which suggests \(2^{n-1}\), but for \(n = 6\) there are 31 and not 32 (figure 1.66). Instead of Wallis's procedure Bernoulli proposed a proof from \(n\) to \(n + 1\) (CAJORI, PDF p. 347). One must show that the statement holds at \(n = 1\) and that from its validity at some \(n\) its validity at \(n + 1\) follows. From these two facts we get the statement for all natural numbers at once.

That such an argument is allowed is shown by the property of the natural numbers that we assumed in section 1.8.1: every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element. We write a claim that depends on a natural number as \(P(n)\). It is a statement that for every natural number \(n\) is either true or not, for example the statement \(b_{\mathrm{n}} - a_{\mathrm{n}} = 1/2^{n-1}\) about the length of the \(n\)-th bisection interval.

Theorem 1.44 Principle of induction (načelo indukcije)

Let \(P(n)\) be a statement that depends on the natural number \(n\). Suppose that:

  1. basis (začetek): the statement \(P(1)\) is true,
  2. induction step (indukcijski korak): for every natural number \(n\) the truth of the statement \(P(n)\) implies the truth of the statement \(P(n + 1)\).

Then the statement \(P(n)\) is true for every natural number \(n\).

Proof

We must show that there is no natural number for which the statement \(P(n)\) is false.

  1. Let \(S\) be the set of all natural numbers \(n\) for which the statement \(P(n)\) is not true. We argue by contradiction: suppose that \(S\) is not empty.
  2. Every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element (section 1.8.1). Let \(m\) be the smallest element of the set \(S\).
  3. By the basis \(P(1)\) is true, so \(1\) is not in \(S\), and \(m \neq 1\). Since \(m\) is a natural number different from \(1\), we have \(m \ge 2\), and \(m - 1\) is a natural number.
  4. The number \(m - 1\) is smaller than \(m\). Since \(m\) is the smallest element of the set \(S\), the number \(m - 1\) is not in \(S\), and the statement \(P(m - 1)\) is true.
  5. So by the induction step with \(n = m - 1\) the statement \(P(m - 1 + 1)\), that is, \(P(m)\), is true as well. Then \(m\) is not in \(S\), which contradicts step 2.
  6. The assumption of step 1 is false. The set \(S\) is empty, and \(P(n)\) is true for every natural number \(n\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 0.3.6 (PDF p. 12). The source accepts the property of the smallest element as an axiom (the well ordering property) and says in a remark that the argument also needs \(m - 1\) to be a natural number for every natural number \(m > 1\), which we accept with the school properties of the integers.

From history

The name mathematical induction first appears, as far as is known, in an article by Augustus De Morgan of 1838, and it was popularized by Todhunter in his Algebra (CAJORI, PDF p. 347).

Induction works like a row of dominoes (figure 1.67). The first domino falls, and this is the basis. Every domino that falls knocks over the next one, and this is the induction step. The proof tells why none of them can stay standing: among the standing dominoes there would be a first one, \(m\), and right before it the fallen domino \(m - 1\), which would have had to knock it over.

Let us write the proof of the third property of bisection by induction, because we will need it in a computation. The statement \(P(k)\) is \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = 1/2^{k-1}\).

  1. Basis. We have \(b_1 - a_1 = 2 - 1 = 1\) and \(1/2^0 = 1\), so \(P(1)\) is true.
  2. Induction step. Let \(P(k)\) be true, that is, \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = 1/2^{k-1}\). The midpoint \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(m_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{k}} + b_{\mathrm{k}}) - a_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}})\) away from the left endpoint and \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - m_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}})\) away from the right one.
  3. The next interval is \([m_{\mathrm{k}}, b_{\mathrm{k}}]\) or \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, m_{\mathrm{k}}]\). In both cases, by step 2, its length is
    \[\tfrac12(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}}) = \frac12 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} = \frac{1}{2^k} ,\]
    which is the statement \(P(k + 1)\).
  4. By the principle of induction 1.44, \(P(k)\) is true for every natural number \(k\).

The first and the fourth property have the same structure: a basis at \(k = 1\) and a step that preserves the property. The second property speaks only about one step of the rule. It needs induction only through the third property, which guarantees \(a_{\mathrm{k}} < b_{\mathrm{k}}\) at every \(k\). Induction also tells why the bisection rule determines an interval for every \(k\): the first interval is given, and from every determined interval the rule determines the next one. We will build sequences in the same way later too (LEBL1 Example 2.2.8, PDF p. 66, shows by induction that all terms of such a sequence are defined).

We will also need that the lengths \(1/2^{k-1}\) go to zero. We will compare them with the fractions \(1/k\), which go to zero by lemma 1.39 on the limit of the sequence 1/n. For this we need the inequality \(2^{k-1} \ge k\). The numbers show that \(2^{k-1}\) is much larger than \(k\). At \(k = 10\), for example, \(2^9 = 512\).

Lemma 1.45 Powers of 2 are at least as large as the natural numbers (potence števila 2 so vsaj tolikšne kot naravna števila)

For every natural number \(k\) we have \(2^{k-1} \ge k\).

Proof

We use the principle of induction 1.44 for the statement \(P(k)\): \(2^{k-1} \ge k\).

  1. Basis. At \(k = 1\) we have \(2^0 = 1 \ge 1\).
  2. Induction step. Let \(2^{k-1} \ge k\) hold. We multiply the inequality by the positive number \(2\), which does not reverse it, and get \(2^k = 2 \cdot 2^{k-1} \ge 2k\).
  3. We have \(2k = k + k \ge k + 1\), because \(k \ge 1\). The inequalities of step 2 and of this step form a chain, so \(2^k \ge k + 1\), which is the statement \(P(k + 1)\).
  4. By the principle of induction, \(2^{k-1} \ge k\) for every natural number \(k\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 0.3.7 (PDF p. 13) proves \(2^{n-1} \le n!\) in the same way. The lemma is not from the source.

The induction step multiplied the inequality for \(k\) by \(2\) and compared the result with \(k + 1\). We will meet such a step, which turns the claim for \(k\) into the claim for \(k + 1\) with one computation, many more times.

1.10.3 A trapped sequence

Do the lengths of the bisection intervals, that is, \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \dots\), go to zero? We could repeat the computation from the proof of lemma 1.39 on the limit of the sequence 1/n and find a place \(N\) for every error \(\eta\). There is a shorter way, though. The lengths are positive, and by lemma 1.45 on the powers of 2 they are not larger than the fractions \(1/k\). So every length is trapped between \(0\) and \(1/k\) (figure 1.68). From below they are held by the constant number \(0\), from above by the fractions \(1/k\), which go to \(0\). The lengths have no choice but to go to \(0\). The next lemma writes this idea down for any sequences.

Lemma 1.46 Squeeze lemma (lema o sendviču)

Let \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((z_{\mathrm{n}})\) be sequences such that \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le z_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\). If the sequences \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((z_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to the same number \(d\), the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) also converges to \(d\).

Proof

We must show that from some place on all terms \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) are closer to the number \(d\) than a given error.

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\).
  2. Since \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d\), by the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 there is a place \(N_1\) such that \(|y_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N_1\). The inequality \(|y_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) means \(-\eta < y_{\mathrm{n}} - d < \eta\), and its left half gives \(d - \eta < y_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  3. Since \((z_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d\), there is a place \(N_2\) such that \(|z_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N_2\). The right half of the inequality \(-\eta < z_{\mathrm{n}} - d < \eta\) gives \(z_{\mathrm{n}} < d + \eta\).
  4. Let \(N\) be the larger of the numbers \(N_1\) and \(N_2\). For \(n \ge N\) steps 2 and 3 hold at once. With the assumption \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le z_{\mathrm{n}}\) the inequalities form a chain:
    \[d - \eta < y_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le z_{\mathrm{n}} < d + \eta .\]
  5. We subtract \(d\) from all sides and get \(-\eta < x_{\mathrm{n}} - d < \eta\), that is, \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d\).

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 2.2.1 (PDF p. 61).

From each of the two sequences the proof needed only one side of the band (figure 1.69). From the place \(N_1\) on, the lower sequence does not let the terms \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) below the band, and from the place \(N_2\) on, the upper one does not let them above it. From the larger of the two places on, both sides are closed. The name of the lemma gives the same picture: the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is squeezed between two sequences like the filling between two slices of bread.

The lemma needs both bounds to converge to the same number. The terms of the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) are trapped between the constant sequences \(-1, -1, \dots\) and \(1, 1, \dots\), and still they have no limit (lemma 1.40 on a sequence without a limit). Bounds with different limits let the terms jump between them.

Now we apply the lemma to the lengths of the bisection intervals.

Corollary 1.47 Limit of the powers of one half (limita potenc polovice)

The sequence \((1/2^{k-1})\), that is, \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \dots\), converges to \(0\).

Proof

We must show that the sequence is trapped between two sequences with the limit \(0\), and use the squeeze lemma.

  1. For every \(k\) we have \(1/2^{k-1} > 0\), because \(2^{k-1} > 0\).
  2. For every \(k\) we have \(1/2^{k-1} \le 1/k\). We write the difference over a common denominator,
    \[\frac1k - \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} = \frac{2^{k-1} - k}{k \cdot 2^{k-1}} .\]
    By lemma 1.45 on the powers of 2 the numerator is not negative, and the denominator is positive, so the difference is not negative.
  3. By steps 1 and 2, \(0 \le 1/2^{k-1} \le 1/k\) for every \(k\).
  4. The constant sequence \(0, 0, 0, \dots\) converges to \(0\) (section 1.9.2), and the sequence \((1/k)\) does so by lemma 1.39 on the limit of the sequence 1/n. So by the squeeze lemma 1.46 with the lower sequence \(0, 0, 0, \dots\) and the upper sequence \((1/k)\), the sequence \((1/2^{k-1})\) also converges to \(0\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 2.2.2 (PDF pp. 61-62) proves in the same way that \(1/(n\sqrt n)\) goes to \(0\). The corollary is not from the source.

The comparison with \(1/k\) is rough, but it is enough. At \(k = 11\) the length of the interval is \(1/2^{10} = 1/1024 < 0{,}001\), while the fraction \(1/11 = 0{,}0909\dots\) is almost a hundred times larger. The squeeze lemma only needs the upper sequence to lie above the sequence of lengths and to go to the same limit. How tightly it follows the sequence does not matter.

1.10.4 Limit and inequalities

By the fourth property the left endpoints of the bisection all lie in the interval \([1, 2]\). If they converge, does their limit lie in it too? We expect that it does, since the terms come arbitrarily close to it and all of them are in the interval. Let us show that this is so, and let us look at where the expectation breaks down.

Lemma 1.48 Limits preserve non-strict inequalities (limita ohrani nestroge neenakosti)

Let the sequences \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge.

  1. If \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le y_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\), then \(\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} \le \lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} y_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. If \(a\) and \(b\) are numbers such that \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) for every \(n\), then \(a \le \lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\).
Proof

We must show both items. The second follows from the first, applied with constant sequences.

1. Inequality between the limits.

  1. Let \(x = \lim x_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(y = \lim y_{\mathrm{n}}\). We argue by contradiction: suppose that \(x > y\).
  2. As the error we take half the distance between the limits, \(\eta = \tfrac12(x - y)\), which is positive. Then
    \[x - \eta = \tfrac12(x + y) = y + \eta ,\]
    so the band of width \(\eta\) around \(x\) and the band of width \(\eta\) around \(y\) touch in the middle, at \(\tfrac12(x + y)\) (figure 1.70).
  3. Since \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(x\), by the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 there is a place \(N_1\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - x| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N_1\). The left half of the inequality \(-\eta < x_{\mathrm{n}} - x < \eta\) gives \(x_{\mathrm{n}} > x - \eta = \tfrac12(x + y)\).
  4. Since \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(y\), there is a place \(N_2\) such that \(|y_{\mathrm{n}} - y| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N_2\). The right half of the inequality \(-\eta < y_{\mathrm{n}} - y < \eta\) gives \(y_{\mathrm{n}} < y + \eta = \tfrac12(x + y)\).
  5. Let \(n\) be the larger of the numbers \(N_1\) and \(N_2\). By steps 3 and 4, \(y_{\mathrm{n}} < \tfrac12(x + y) < x_{\mathrm{n}}\), so \(x_{\mathrm{n}} > y_{\mathrm{n}}\). This contradicts the assumption \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le y_{\mathrm{n}}\). So \(x > y\) does not hold, and \(x \le y\).

2. Bounds of the terms are bounds of the limit.

  1. The constant sequence \(a, a, a, \dots\) converges to \(a\) (section 1.9.2). Since \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\), item 1, applied with this constant sequence in place of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) and with the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) in place of the sequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\), gives \(a \le \lim x_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. The constant sequence \(b, b, b, \dots\) converges to \(b\). Since \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) for every \(n\), item 1 gives \(\lim x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\).

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 2.2.3 and Cor. 2.2.4 (PDF p. 62). The source proves the first item without contradiction, by showing \(x - y < \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). The proof by contradiction is not from the source.

The proof used the same picture as the proof of the uniqueness of the limit (figure 1.62). Two bands around two different numbers, each as wide as half the distance between the numbers, do not overlap. There, late terms of the same sequence cannot be in both bands. Here the late terms \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) would be in the upper band and the late terms \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) in the lower one, so \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) would be above \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\).

For the left endpoints of the bisection, item 2 says: if they converge, their limit is in the interval \([1, 2]\), because all \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) are in it.

A limit, however, does not necessarily preserve a strict inequality. Take again the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m that hangs under its own weight, and the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = 2aL - a/n\) of its top pieces of length \(1/n\) m from section 1.9.1. All of them are smaller than \(2aL\), because \(a/n > 0\). Their limit, though, is \(2aL\) (section 1.9.2). The dots in figure 1.56 approach the line \(2aL\) without reaching it. Of the strict inequalities \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} < 2aL\) only \(2aL \le 2aL\) remains in the limit. That is why the lemma speaks of non-strict inequalities. From the strict inequalities \(x_{\mathrm{n}} < y_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\) we may conclude only \(\lim x_{\mathrm{n}} \le \lim y_{\mathrm{n}}\), because every strict inequality is also a non-strict one.

So it matters whether an interval contains its endpoints (figure 1.71). The terms of the sequence \((1/n)\) lie in the half-open interval \((0, 1]\), but their limit \(0\) does not, because it is not larger than \(0\). With a closed interval this cannot happen: if all terms of a convergent sequence are in \([a, b]\), then by item 2 the limit is there too. We will need this when we search for points as limits. The point we find must lie in the interval in which we search.

1.10.5 Monotone sequences

Let us return to the left endpoints of the bisection: \(1\), \(1{,}5\), \(1{,}5\), \(1{,}625\), \(1{,}6875\), \(1{,}71875\), \(1{,}71875\), \(1{,}7265625\) and so on. No term is smaller than the previous one, and none is larger than \(2\). Such terms cannot go back down and cannot get past \(2\). It seems that they must pile up somewhere. Where? At the smallest number that no term exceeds, that is, at the supremum of the set of terms. Here the completeness axiom appears again, and it guarantees that this supremum exists without our knowing it. First let us name the sequences that do not turn back.

Definition 1.49 Monotone sequence (monotono zaporedje)

A sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is increasing (naraščajoče) if \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) for every \(n\), and decreasing (padajoče) if \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \ge x_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) for every \(n\). A sequence is monotone (monotono) if it is increasing or decreasing. A sequence is strictly increasing (strogo naraščajoče) if \(x_{\mathrm{n}} < x_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) for every \(n\), and strictly decreasing (strogo padajoče) if \(x_{\mathrm{n}} > x_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) for every \(n\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 2.1.9 (PDF p. 55), the strictly increasing sequence at Def. 2.1.16 (PDF p. 58).

So an increasing sequence allows equal consecutive terms, and a strictly increasing one does not. Some books mean strictly increasing by the word increasing, so when reading the sources it is worth checking the definition. The left endpoints of the bisection are an increasing sequence by the second property from section 1.10.1, but not a strictly increasing one, because \(a_2 = a_3 = 1{,}5\). At \(k = 2\) the rule kept the left half and moved only the right endpoint. The right endpoints are a decreasing sequence, and \(b_1 = b_2 = 2\). The strains of the pieces of the hanging bar are strictly increasing:

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} = \Big(2aL - \frac{a}{n+1}\Big) - \Big(2aL - \frac{a}{n}\Big) = \frac{a}{n} - \frac{a}{n+1} = \frac{a}{n(n+1)} > 0 .\]

The sequence \((1/n)\) is strictly decreasing. A constant sequence is increasing and decreasing at once. The sequence \(((-1)^n)\) is not monotone, because \(x_1 = -1 < 1 = x_2\), but \(x_2 = 1 > -1 = x_3\).

The definition compares only neighbouring terms. In proofs we will need that in an increasing sequence no later term is smaller than any earlier one. This is a claim about infinitely many places, so we prove it by induction.

Lemma 1.50 Terms of a monotone sequence (členi monotonega zaporedja)

If the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is increasing, then \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{m}}\) for any natural numbers \(n \le m\). If it is decreasing, then \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \ge x_{\mathrm{m}}\) for any natural numbers \(n \le m\).

Proof

We must show that a later term of an increasing sequence is not smaller than an earlier one. We keep the place \(n\) fixed and step forward by induction.

  1. Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be increasing and \(n\) a natural number. For a natural number \(j\) let \(P(j)\) be the statement \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}-1}\). The term \(x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}-1}\) is \(j - 1\) places after the term \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\), so as \(j\) runs through \(1, 2, 3, \dots\), we cover all terms from \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) on.
  2. Basis. The statement \(P(1)\) is \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}}\), which is true.
  3. Induction step. Let \(P(j)\) hold, that is, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}-1}\). Since the sequence is increasing, \(x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}-1} \le x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}}\). The inequalities form a chain, so \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{j}}\), which is the statement \(P(j + 1)\).
  4. By the principle of induction 1.44, \(P(j)\) holds for every natural number \(j\). For \(m \ge n\) we take \(j = m - n + 1\) and get \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  5. For a decreasing sequence steps 1 to 4 are the same, only with \(\ge\) in place of \(\le\).

Source: LEBL1 uses the claim in the proof of Thm 2.1.10 (PDF p. 55) and says that it follows by induction. The proof is not from the source.

The lemma builds a comparison of any two terms from comparisons of neighbouring ones. Between \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{m}}\) stands a chain of \(m - n\) comparisons of neighbouring terms, and induction joins them all.

Now we can say where an increasing sequence goes if it cannot get past some bound (figure 1.72). Let \(s\) be the supremum of the set of its terms. No term is above \(s\). The number \(s - \eta\), which for a given error \(\eta > 0\) is smaller than \(s\), is no longer an upper bound, though, so some term \(x_{\mathrm{N}}\) exceeds it. Since the sequence increases, all later terms are at least as large as \(x_{\mathrm{N}}\), so they are above \(s - \eta\), and at the same time at most \(s\). From the place \(N\) on all of them are in the band between \(s - \eta\) and \(s\).

Theorem 1.51 Monotone convergence theorem (izrek o monotonih zaporedjih)

A monotone sequence converges if and only if it is bounded. If the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is increasing and bounded, then

\[\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} = \sup\{x_{\mathrm{n}} : n \in \mathbb N\} ,\]

and if it is decreasing and bounded, then

\[\lim_{\mathrm{n} \to \infty} x_{\mathrm{n}} = \inf\{x_{\mathrm{n}} : n \in \mathbb N\} .\]
Proof

We must show that a convergent monotone sequence is bounded, and that a bounded monotone sequence converges to the supremum or the infimum of the set of its terms.

A convergent monotone sequence is bounded.

  1. By lemma 1.42 on the boundedness of a convergent sequence every convergent sequence is bounded, so every convergent monotone sequence is bounded too.

An increasing bounded sequence converges to the supremum.

  1. Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be increasing and bounded, and let \(A = \{x_{\mathrm{n}} : n \in \mathbb N\}\) be the set of its terms. The set \(A\) is nonempty, because it contains \(x_1\), and bounded above, because the sequence is bounded (definition 1.37).
  2. By the completeness axiom 1.32, \(A\) has a supremum \(s\). We will show that the sequence converges to \(s\).
  3. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 2, there is an element of the set \(A\) that is larger than \(s - \eta\). The elements of the set \(A\) are the terms of the sequence, so there is a place \(N\) such that \(x_{\mathrm{N}} > s - \eta\).
  4. Let \(n \ge N\). By lemma 1.50 on the terms of a monotone sequence, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \ge x_{\mathrm{N}}\), and so by step 3, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} > s - \eta\).
  5. The term \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) is an element of the set \(A\), and the supremum \(s\) is an upper bound of this set, so \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le s\).
  6. By steps 4 and 5, \(s - \eta < x_{\mathrm{n}} \le s\). So the difference \(s - x_{\mathrm{n}}\) is not negative and is smaller than \(\eta\), that is, \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - s| = s - x_{\mathrm{n}} < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so the sequence converges to \(s\).

A decreasing bounded sequence converges to the infimum.

  1. Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be decreasing and bounded, and let \(A = \{x_{\mathrm{n}} : n \in \mathbb N\}\). The set \(A\) is nonempty and bounded below, so by theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 1, it has an infimum \(i\).
  2. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). By item 2 of the same theorem there is an element of the set \(A\) that is smaller than \(i + \eta\), that is, a place \(N\) such that \(x_{\mathrm{N}} < i + \eta\).
  3. Let \(n \ge N\). By lemma 1.50 on the terms of a monotone sequence, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \le x_{\mathrm{N}}\), and so by step 2, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} < i + \eta\).
  4. The infimum \(i\) is a lower bound of the set \(A\), so \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \ge i\).
  5. By steps 3 and 4, \(i \le x_{\mathrm{n}} < i + \eta\), so \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - i| = x_{\mathrm{n}} - i < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so the sequence converges to \(i\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 2.1.10 (PDF pp. 55-56). The source leaves the decreasing case to the reader.

Where is the completeness axiom in the proof? In step 2 of the second part. It guarantees the number \(s\) to which the sequence converges. We did not know the limit in advance, and the proof named it as the supremum of the set of terms. An increasing sequence always has the lower bound \(x_1\), because by lemma 1.50 on the terms of a monotone sequence \(x_1 \le x_{\mathrm{n}}\) for every \(n\). So it is enough to check that it is bounded above (LEBL1, PDF p. 56). We will use the theorem every time we must show that some number exists without being able to write it down. So it is one of the results that carry the road to the statement about the change of a function between two numbers.

The strains of the pieces of the hanging bar are strictly increasing and all smaller than \(2aL\), so by the theorem they converge even before we compute the limit. The limit is unique and equal to \(2aL\), so the theorem also tells us that \(2aL\) is the supremum of the set of strains: the smallest number that no strain of a piece exceeds. Boundedness is needed. The sequence \(1, 2, 3, \dots\) is strictly increasing, but it is not bounded, because by the Archimedean property 1.35 the set of natural numbers is not bounded above. So by the first part of the theorem it does not converge.

Now we can answer the question from section 1.10.1. Let us show that the left endpoints of the bisection converge to \(\sqrt 3\) (figure 1.73). Let us recall what we know about them: \(a_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}^2\), \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = 1/2^{k-1}\), and all endpoints are in the interval \([1, 2]\). First we show that the left endpoints converge, without using \(\sqrt 3\).

  1. The sequence \((a_{\mathrm{k}})\) is increasing by the second property and bounded by the fourth, because all its terms are in \([1, 2]\).
  2. So by the monotone convergence theorem 1.51 it converges to the number \(c = \sup\{a_{\mathrm{k}} : k \in \mathbb N\}\).
  3. The number \(c\) lies in every bisection interval. Since the supremum is an upper bound, \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le c\). Let us also show \(c \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let \(j\) be any natural number. For \(j \le k\) we have \(a_{\mathrm{j}} \le a_{\mathrm{k}} < b_{\mathrm{k}}\) by lemma 1.50 on the terms of a monotone sequence and by the third property, which gives \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\). For \(j > k\) we have \(a_{\mathrm{j}} < b_{\mathrm{j}} \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\) by the third property and by the same lemma for the decreasing sequence \((b_{\mathrm{k}})\). So the number \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) is an upper bound of all the left endpoints, and the supremum \(c\) is not larger than any upper bound. So \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le c \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Up to here we have used nothing about the number \(\sqrt 3\). Let us now show that \(c = \sqrt 3\).

  1. The number \(\sqrt 3\) lies in every bisection interval, \(a_{\mathrm{k}} < \sqrt 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\), as we showed in section 1.10.1.
  2. Two numbers in the same interval are at most its length apart. From \(c \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le \sqrt 3\) it follows that \(c - \sqrt 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}}\), and from \(\sqrt 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le c\) that \(\sqrt 3 - c \le b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}}\). So by the third property
    \[|c - \sqrt 3| \le b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\]
    for every natural number \(k\).
  3. On the left side of the inequality stands a constant sequence, which converges to \(|c - \sqrt 3|\), and on the right side a sequence that converges to \(0\) by corollary 1.47 on the limit of the powers of one half. By lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 1, \(|c - \sqrt 3| \le 0\). An absolute value is not negative, so \(|c - \sqrt 3| = 0\) and \(c = \sqrt 3\).

So the left endpoints of the bisection converge to \(\sqrt 3\). At \(k = 12\), for example, \(a_{12} = 3547/2048 = 1{,}73193359375\), and this is less than \(1/2^{11} = 0{,}000488\dots\) away from \(\sqrt 3 = 1{,}7320508\dots\), in fact \(0{,}000117\dots\) away.

Why was the completeness axiom needed? All the left endpoints are fractions, but their limit \(\sqrt 3\) is not a fraction, because by lemma 1.27 no rational number has square 3. If we knew only the fractions, \((a_{\mathrm{k}})\) would be an increasing bounded sequence of fractions that has no limit among the fractions. A limit that was a fraction would be equal to \(\sqrt 3\) by lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence. So the monotone convergence theorem does not hold among the fractions, and the gap is exactly in the step where its proof uses the completeness axiom. The hole among the fractions from figure 1.51 shows up here as a sequence that finds no limit among the fractions.

Bisection worked because at every step we knew which half to keep: the one that contains \(\sqrt 3\), which we recognized by the square of the midpoint. The next section applies bisection to an arbitrary bounded sequence. We will keep the half that contains infinitely many terms, and in this way choose from the sequence infinitely many terms that converge.

1.11 Mathematics: subsequences

Section 1.10 ended with bisection, which found the number \(\sqrt 3\). At every step we knew which half to keep, and the left endpoints converged to \(\sqrt 3\). In this section we apply bisection to a sequence that does not converge. We cannot get a limit out of such a sequence, but we can choose from it infinitely many terms that converge. We will prove that this is possible for every bounded sequence. This theorem is one of the results that carry the road to the statement about the change of a function between two numbers from section 1.7.3.

Why do we need it? The proof of that statement will need a point at which the value of a function on an interval is largest. We will not be able to compute such a point. We will find a sequence of points at which the values of the function approach the largest one, and choose from it terms that converge. Their limit will be the point we are looking for. The question has a physical side too. Let us take again the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m that stretches under its own weight. It is fixed only at the centre \(O\) of its top end, and its weight is carried by a force that pulls the top face up evenly, which is an idealization (section 1.7.1). The strain along its axis at the depth \(x\) is \(2a\,(L - x)\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 1.4). From the formula we see that it is largest at the top, where \(x = 0\). When we have no formula, we must first prove that a point where the material is stretched most exists at all. We will need the same tool in chapter 2, where among all planes through a point of a body we will look for the one on which the forces pull the material apart most strongly.

The route of the section is as follows. First we give the chosen terms a name and show two things: the \(k\)-th chosen term stands at least at the place \(k\) in the sequence, and if the sequence converges, the chosen terms converge to the same limit. Then we say precisely what it means that a set holds infinitely many terms, and we show that at least one of the two halves of an interval has this property. At the end we carry out bisection on an example and prove the theorem. About numbers we assume the same as in section 1.10: the rules of school arithmetic and the properties of the integers, the fact that every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element, and the completeness axiom 1.32.

1.11.1 Subsequence

Let us take the sequence

\[x_{\mathrm{n}} = (-1)^n \Big(1 + \frac1n\Big) ,\]

that is, \(x_1 = -2\), \(x_2 = \tfrac32\), \(x_3 = -\tfrac43\), \(x_4 = \tfrac54\), \(x_5 = -\tfrac65\) and so on (figure 1.74). The factor \((-1)^n\) is \(1\) for even \(n\) and \(-1\) for odd \(n\), as in the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) from section 1.9.3. The factor \(1 + 1/n\) is larger than \(1\) and approaches \(1\). So the terms at even places are \(1 + 1/n\) and approach \(1\) from above, and the terms at odd places are \(-(1 + 1/n)\) and approach \(-1\) from below. The sequence is bounded. Since \(0 < 1/n \le 1\), we have \(1 < 1 + 1/n \le 2\), so \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| = 1 + 1/n \le 2\) and \(-2 \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le 2\) for every \(n\). But it does not converge, because it jumps between values close to \(1\) and values close to \(-1\), much like the sequence \(((-1)^n)\). We will prove this in section 1.11.2. If we take only the terms at even places, \(x_2, x_4, x_6, \dots\), we get the sequence \(\tfrac32, \tfrac54, \tfrac76, \dots\), which approaches \(1\). From a sequence that does not converge we have chosen terms that approach a number. We write such a choice precisely through the places of the chosen terms.

Definition 1.52 Subsequence (podzaporedje)

Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a sequence of real numbers and let \((n_{\mathrm{k}})\) be a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers, that is, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} < n_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) for every natural number \(k\), or \(n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \dots\) The sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) whose \(k\)-th term is \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\), that is, the sequence \(x_{\mathrm{n}_1}, x_{\mathrm{n}_2}, x_{\mathrm{n}_3}, \dots\), is a subsequence (podzaporedje) of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 2.1.16 (PDF p. 58).

A subsequence is again a sequence: its input is a natural number \(k\), its output the term \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\). The indices \(k\) and \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) have different jobs. The number \(k\) counts the chosen terms: \(x_{\mathrm{n}_1}\) is the first chosen term, \(x_{\mathrm{n}_2}\) the second. The number \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) tells at which place of the original sequence the \(k\)-th chosen term stands. For the terms at even places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k\): the first chosen term is \(x_2\), the second \(x_4\), the \(k\)-th \(x_{2\mathrm{k}}\). The sequence of places \(2, 4, 6, \dots\) is strictly increasing, because \(2(k + 1) = 2k + 2 > 2k\). In figure 1.75 the chosen places are \(2, 3, 6, 7, 10\) and \(12\), irregularly spaced. The chosen terms are renumbered. The term \(x_6\) is the third chosen term, so in the subsequence it stands at the place \(k = 3\): \(x_{\mathrm{n}_3} = x_6 = \tfrac76\).

What is the requirement that the places increase strictly for? The chosen terms keep the order they have in the sequence, and no term is chosen twice. So the subsequence moves ever further along the sequence, and this is exactly what we will need when we go from the limit of the sequence to the limit of the chosen terms. The sequence \(x_2, x_1, x_4, x_3, \dots\) is not a subsequence of \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\), because it swaps the order. Nor is the sequence \(x_1, x_1, x_1, \dots\), which takes the same term several times, since the places \(1, 1, 1, \dots\) do not increase strictly. Values may repeat, though. The sequence \(1, 1, 1, \dots\) is a subsequence of the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) with the places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k\), because \((-1)^{2k} = 1\). As with the sequence itself, what counts is the place of a term, not only its value.

Since the places are natural numbers and each is larger than the previous one, with every chosen term we move at least one place forward. The first chosen term stands at least at the place \(1\), the second at least at the place \(2\), and so on. This is a claim for all natural numbers \(k\), so we prove it by induction.

Lemma 1.53 Indices of a subsequence (indeksi podzaporedja)

If \((n_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers, then \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\) for every natural number \(k\).

Proof

We must show that the \(k\)-th chosen place is not before the place \(k\). We use the principle of induction 1.44 for the statement \(P(k)\): \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\).

  1. Basis. The number \(n_1\) is natural, and the natural numbers are \(1, 2, 3, \dots\), so \(n_1 \ge 1\).
  2. Induction step. Let \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\) hold. The sequence of places increases strictly, so \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1} > n_{\mathrm{k}}\). The inequalities form a chain, \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1} > n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\), so \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1} > k\).
  3. The numbers \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and \(k\) are integers, and there is no integer between the integers \(k\) and \(k + 1\) (school properties of the integers, section 1.8.1). So an integer larger than \(k\) is at least \(k + 1\). Hence \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1} \ge k + 1\), which is the statement \(P(k + 1)\).
  4. By the principle of induction, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\) for every natural number \(k\).

Source: LEBL1 states the claim in the proof of Prop. 2.1.17 (PDF p. 58) and leaves the proof by induction to the reader. The proof is not from the source.

The lemma says that the \(k\)-th chosen term does not stand before the place \(k\) (figure 1.76). For the places of figure 1.75, \(n_1 = 2 \ge 1\), \(n_3 = 6 \ge 3\) and \(n_6 = 12 \ge 6\). We get the equality \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = k\) at every \(k\) only if we choose all terms, and then the subsequence is just the sequence itself. Every skipped term pushes all the following chosen places one place further from \(k\). In the figure \(n_6 - 6 = 6\), because six places are skipped before the place \(12\), namely \(1, 4, 5, 8, 9\) and \(11\).

1.11.2 The limit of a subsequence

If a sequence converges, its terms from some place on are close to the limit. A subsequence takes only some of these terms, so we expect it to converge to the same limit. The lemma on the indices of a subsequence tells us why this is so: the chosen terms from the \(N\)-th on stand at places from \(N\) on (figure 1.77).

Lemma 1.54 Limit of a subsequence (limita podzaporedja)

If the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to the number \(d\), then every subsequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) of it also converges to \(d\).

Proof

We must show that from some \(k\) on all terms \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) are closer to the number \(d\) than a given error.

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\).
  2. Since \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(d\), by the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 there is a place \(N\) such that \(|x_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\).
  3. Let \(k \ge N\). By lemma 1.53 on the indices of a subsequence, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\), so \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge N\).
  4. By step 2, used for the place \(n = n_{\mathrm{k}}\), we have \(|x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} - d| < \eta\). This holds for every \(k \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so the subsequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(d\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 2.1.17 (PDF p. 58).

The proof used for the subsequence the same place \(N\) as for the sequence. That \(k \ge N\) guarantees \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge N\) is exactly the lemma on the indices of a subsequence. In figure 1.77, \(N = 4\), and the chosen terms from the fourth on, at the places \(7\), \(10\) and \(12\), are in the band. The third chosen term is in the band too, because it stands at the place \(6 \ge N\). The proof does not need it: the bound \(k \ge N\) is only a safe choice that works for every subsequence.

The converse does not hold. A convergent subsequence does not yet mean that the sequence converges (LEBL1 Example 2.1.18, PDF p. 58, shows this with the sequence \(0, 1, 0, 1, \dots\)). But the lemma offers a simple way to show that a sequence does not converge: we find two subsequences with different limits. Let us try it first on the sequence \(((-1)^n)\), whose divergence we proved in lemma 1.40 on a sequence without a limit with the error \(\eta = \tfrac12\).

  1. The subsequence with the places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k\) has the terms \((-1)^{2k} = 1\). This is the constant sequence \(1, 1, 1, \dots\), which converges to \(1\) (section 1.9.2).
  2. The subsequence with the places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k - 1\) has the terms \((-1)^{2k-1} = -1\), so it converges to \(-1\). The places \(2k - 1\) increase strictly, because \(2(k + 1) - 1 = (2k - 1) + 2\).
  3. Suppose that the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) converges to some number \(d\). Then by lemma 1.54 on the limit of a subsequence both subsequences converge to \(d\).
  4. By lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence, each of the two subsequences has only one limit, so \(d = 1\) by step 1 and \(d = -1\) by step 2. Then \(1 = -1\), which is not true. So the sequence \(((-1)^n)\) does not converge.

This proof is shorter than the first one, because the work with the error \(\eta\) has already been done in the proofs of the lemma on the limit of a subsequence and of the lemma on the uniqueness of the limit. In the same way we show that the sequence \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (-1)^n (1 + 1/n)\) does not converge, except that its subsequences are not constant.

  1. At an even place \(n = 2k\) we have \(x_{2\mathrm{k}} = 1 + \frac{1}{2k}\). Let us take the sequence \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = 1 + 1/n\). The distance of its term from \(1\) is \(|y_{\mathrm{n}} - 1| = 1/n = |1/n - 0|\). By lemma 1.39 on the limit of the sequence 1/n, for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a place \(N\) such that \(|1/n - 0| < \eta\) for every \(n \ge N\), and so for the same \(N\) we have \(|y_{\mathrm{n}} - 1| < \eta\). So the sequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(1\).
  2. The terms \(x_{2\mathrm{k}} = y_{2\mathrm{k}}\) form a subsequence of the sequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) with the places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k\). So by the lemma on the limit of a subsequence they converge to \(1\).
  3. At an odd place \(n = 2k - 1\) we have \(x_{2\mathrm{k}-1} = -\big(1 + \frac{1}{2k-1}\big)\). The sequence \(z_{\mathrm{n}} = -(1 + 1/n)\) converges to \(-1\), because \(|z_{\mathrm{n}} - (-1)| = |-1/n| = 1/n\), and for the same \(N\) as in step 1 we have \(|z_{\mathrm{n}} - (-1)| < \eta\). The terms \(x_{2\mathrm{k}-1} = z_{2\mathrm{k}-1}\) form a subsequence of the sequence \((z_{\mathrm{n}})\) with the places \(n_{\mathrm{k}} = 2k - 1\), so they converge to \(-1\).
  4. If the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) converged to a number \(d\), then by the lemma on the limit of a subsequence both subsequences of steps 2 and 3 would converge to \(d\), and by the uniqueness of the limit we would have \(d = 1\) and \(d = -1\). So \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) does not converge.

Figure 1.74 shows both subsequences, the even one with blue dots and the odd one with the others. From a bounded sequence that does not converge we have chosen a convergent subsequence, because we knew the formula for its terms. Can this be done for every bounded sequence, also when we do not know a formula?

1.11.3 Infinitely many terms

How would we find a convergent subsequence without a formula? Bisection suggests itself. All terms of a bounded sequence lie in some interval. We halve it and keep the half in which infinitely many terms lie, then we halve this half, and so on. The intervals shrink, and in each of them there are enough terms to choose from it the next term of the subsequence at a later place than the previous one. Before we carry this out, we must say precisely what it means that a half holds infinitely many terms, and show that at least one of the two halves has this property.

In a sequence we count places, not values. The sequence \(((-1)^n)\) has terms at infinitely many places in the set \(\{1\}\), which has a single element, because every term at an even place equals \(1\). So that a set holds infinitely many terms will mean that terms at arbitrarily late places lie in it.

Definition 1.55 Infinitely many terms in a set (neskončno mnogo členov v množici)

Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a sequence of real numbers and \(A\) a set of real numbers. The set \(A\) holds infinitely many terms (neskončno mnogo členov) of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) if for every natural number \(N\) there is a natural number \(n \ge N\) such that \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \in A\).

Source: LEBL1, in the second proof of Thm 2.3.8 (PDF p. 78), speaks of infinitely many places \(n\) at which \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies in an interval, without defining the notion separately. The definition is not from the source.

The definition is a game of two players, like the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38. The first picks a place \(N\), however late. The second must find a term in \(A\) at the place \(N\) or later. Let us try it on the sequence \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (-1)^n (1 + 1/n)\) (figure 1.78). The interval \(A = [1, 2]\) holds infinitely many terms. For every \(N\) the place \(n = 2N\) is even and at least \(N\), and the term at it is \(1 + \frac{1}{2N}\), which lies between \(1\) and \(\tfrac32\), so in \([1, 2]\). The interval \(B = [-\tfrac52, -\tfrac32]\), though, holds only the term \(x_1 = -2\). The terms at even places are positive, and the terms at odd places from the third on are \(-(1 + 1/n) \ge -(1 + \tfrac13) = -\tfrac43\), which is more than \(-\tfrac32\). So for \(N = 2\) there is no place \(n \ge 2\) with its term in \(B\), and \(B\) does not hold infinitely many terms.

The example of the interval \(B\) shows what it means that a set does not hold infinitely many terms. The definition requires a term in the set for every place \(N\). If this does not hold, there is at least one place \(N\) for which there is no such term, that is, no term at the place \(N\) or later lies in the set. So a set does not hold infinitely many terms exactly when there is a place from which on no term lies in it. The terms that lie in it are then all among \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{N}-1}\).

In bisection we split an interval into two halves, and every number of the interval lies in at least one of them. We need a name for this situation. The union (unija) of the sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cup B\), is the set of all numbers that lie in \(A\) or in \(B\) (LEBL1 Def. 0.3.4, PDF p. 10). The word or allows both here, so the union also contains the numbers that lie in both sets. The closed interval \([a, b]\) with the midpoint \(m = \tfrac12(a + b)\) is the union of its halves,

\[[a, b] = [a, m] \cup [m, b] .\]

Indeed, every number \(t\) with \(a \le t \le b\) satisfies \(t \le m\) or \(t \ge m\), so it lies in the left or in the right half, and every number of either half lies in \([a, b]\). The midpoint \(m\) lies in both halves.

If the union of two sets holds infinitely many terms, does one of the two sets hold infinitely many terms? We expect so. If each of the sets held only terms before some place, both together would also hold only terms before some place. Let us show this precisely.

Lemma 1.56 One of the halves (ena od polovic)

Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a sequence of real numbers and \(A\) and \(B\) sets of real numbers. If the union \(A \cup B\) holds infinitely many terms of the sequence, then \(A\) or \(B\) holds infinitely many terms.

Proof

We must show that terms at arbitrarily late places lie in at least one of the sets \(A\) and \(B\).

  1. We argue by contradiction. Suppose that neither \(A\) nor \(B\) holds infinitely many terms.
  2. Since \(A\) does not hold infinitely many terms, the condition of definition 1.55 of infinitely many terms in a set does not hold for every place. So there is a place \(N_1\) for which there is no \(n \ge N_1\) with \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \in A\): from the place \(N_1\) on no term lies in \(A\).
  3. In the same way there is a place \(N_2\) from which on no term lies in \(B\).
  4. Let \(N\) be the larger of the numbers \(N_1\) and \(N_2\), and let \(n \ge N\). Then \(n \ge N_1\) and \(n \ge N_2\), so by steps 2 and 3, \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies neither in \(A\) nor in \(B\). So it does not lie in \(A \cup B\) either, which contains only numbers from \(A\) or from \(B\).
  5. The set \(A \cup B\) holds infinitely many terms, so by the definition, used with this place \(N\), there is an \(n \ge N\) with \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \in A \cup B\). This contradicts step 4. The assumption of step 1 is false, so \(A\) or \(B\) holds infinitely many terms.

Source: LEBL1 uses the conclusion in the second proof of Thm 2.3.8 (PDF p. 78) without proving it. The proof is not from the source.

The proof again used the larger of two places, like the proof of lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence. From the place \(N_1\) on no term lies in \(A\), from the place \(N_2\) on none in \(B\), and from the larger of the two places on none in either (figure 1.79). Let us try the lemma on the sequence \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (-1)^n (1 + 1/n)\) with the interval \([-2, -1] = [-2, -\tfrac32] \cup [-\tfrac32, -1]\). The interval \([-2, -1]\) holds infinitely many terms, because all terms at odd places lie in it, \(-2 \le -(1 + 1/n) < -1\). The left half holds only the term \(x_1 = -2\), as we saw for the interval \(B\). So by the lemma the right half \([-\tfrac32, -1]\) holds infinitely many terms, and indeed all terms at odd places from the third on lie in it. But the lemma does not say which half has this property, and both may have it. All terms at odd places lie in \([-2, 0]\), all terms at even places in \([0, 2]\).

1.11.4 The Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem

Now let us carry out bisection on the sequence \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (-1)^n (1 + 1/n)\). All its terms lie in the interval \([a_1, b_1] = [-2, 2]\). For some natural number \(k\) let the interval \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, b_{\mathrm{k}}]\), which holds infinitely many terms, be already determined, and let \(m_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{k}} + b_{\mathrm{k}})\) be its midpoint.

  • If the left half \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, m_{\mathrm{k}}]\) holds infinitely many terms, the next interval is the left half: \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  • Otherwise the next interval is the right half: \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = b_{\mathrm{k}}\). By lemma 1.56 on one of the halves it holds infinitely many terms.

From every interval we also choose a term of the subsequence. The first chosen term is \(x_1\), that is, \(n_1 = 1\). When the interval \([a_{\mathrm{k}+1}, b_{\mathrm{k}+1}]\) is determined, we take for \(n_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) the smallest place after the place \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) at which the term lies in this interval. Such a place exists, because the interval holds infinitely many terms. The table shows the first seven steps, and figure 1.80 shows the intervals with the terms in them.

\(k\) \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) terms in the left half next interval
1 \(-2\) \(2\) 1 \(-2\) \(0\) all at odd places left half
2 \(-2\) \(0\) 3 \(-1{,}3333\dots\) \(-1\) all at odd places left half
3 \(-2\) \(-1\) 5 \(-1{,}2\) \(-1{,}5\) only \(x_1\) right half
4 \(-1{,}5\) \(-1\) 7 \(-1{,}1428\dots\) \(-1{,}25\) only \(x_3\) right half
5 \(-1{,}25\) \(-1\) 9 \(-1{,}1111\dots\) \(-1{,}125\) \(x_5\), \(x_7\) right half
6 \(-1{,}125\) \(-1\) 11 \(-1{,}0909\dots\) \(-1{,}0625\) \(x_9\), \(x_{11}\), \(x_{13}\), \(x_{15}\) right half
7 \(-1{,}0625\) \(-1\) 17 \(-1{,}0588\dots\) \(-1{,}03125\) \(x_{17}\), \(x_{19}\), \(\dots\), \(x_{31}\) right half

The endpoints and midpoints are fractions with denominators \(1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\) and are written exactly in the table. The chosen terms \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} = -(1 + 1/n_{\mathrm{k}})\) that end in three dots are cut off after four decimals.

How do we know whether the left half holds infinitely many terms? Here, from the formula. The terms at even places are larger than \(1\). The terms at odd places are \(-1 - 1/n\) and lie below \(-1\), ever closer to \(-1\). At \(k = 1\) and \(k = 2\) the left half contains all terms at odd places. From \(k = 3\) on the right endpoint is \(b_{\mathrm{k}} = -1\), but the left half does not reach \(-1\), because its right endpoint \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) is smaller than \(-1\). The term \(-1 - 1/n\) lies in the left half only if \(-1 - 1/n \le m_{\mathrm{k}}\), that is, only if \(1/n \ge -1 - m_{\mathrm{k}}\). This holds only for the places \(n \le 1/(-1 - m_{\mathrm{k}})\), and from some place on for none. At \(k = 3\) we have \(m_3 = -\tfrac32\) and \(-1 - m_3 = \tfrac12\), so only the places \(n \le 2\) come into question, and the only odd one among them is \(n = 1\). The right half, on the other hand, contains all terms at odd places from some place on.

For a general sequence we have no formula. In bisection for \(\sqrt 3\) we recognized the half by the square of the midpoint, with one computation. Here no check of finitely many terms tells us whether a half holds terms at arbitrarily late places. So the proof of the theorem will not be a procedure for computing. It only tells us that at least one half has this property, and it does so by the lemma on one of the halves, by contradiction.
