So the number \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) is a value of the function \(\varepsilon\) that no other of its values on \([0, L]\) exceeds, and the number \(0\) a value below which none falls. Such values get a name.

Definition 1.70 Maximum and minimum of a function (največja in najmanjša vrednost funkcije)

Let \(f\) be a function with real values, defined on a set \(D\), and let \(c \in D\). The elements of the set \(D\) may be numbers or points of space. The function \(f\) attains at the point \(c\) its largest value or maximum (maksimum) on \(D\) if \(f(x) \le f(c)\) for every \(x \in D\), and its smallest value or minimum (minimum) on \(D\) if \(f(x) \ge f(c)\) for every \(x \in D\). The number \(f(c)\) is then the largest or the smallest value of the function \(f\) on \(D\). Maximum and minimum together are called extrema, and each of them an extremum (ekstrem).

Source: LEBL1 §3.3.1 (PDF p. 130), where they are called the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum.

So the largest value is a number, and the point \(c\) is the place where the function attains it. For the strain of the hanging bar the largest value is \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), attained at the point \(0\), and the smallest value \(0\) is attained at the point \(L\). The definition agrees with the maximum of a set from definition 1.30. The values of the function form the set \(\{f(x) : x \in D\}\). If \(f\) attains its largest value at the point \(c\), then \(f(c)\) is an element of this set and at the same time an upper bound of it. No upper bound is smaller than the element \(f(c)\), so \(f(c)\) is a supremum of the set of values that lies in the set, that is, its maximum. The definition requires that the point \(c\) lies in \(D\). It is not enough that the values come arbitrarily close to some number. It does not require, though, that the point \(c\) is the only one.

Nor is the largest value necessarily at an endpoint of the interval. Let us stay with the hanging bar, held in the idealized way, and take its cross section at the depth \(x = 5\) m. On it we look at the points of the diameter that lies in the plane \(z = 0\), that is, the points \((5\ \text{m}, y, 0)\) with \(-0{,}005\ \text{m} \le y \le 0{,}005\ \text{m}\), since the bar has a diameter of 10 mm. By (1.18) such a point moves down by

\[g(y) = u_{\mathrm{x}}(5\ \text{m}, y, 0) = a\,(2 \cdot 10 \cdot 5 - 5^2)\ \text{m}^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + 0^2) = 75\ \text{m}^2 \cdot a - 0{,}3\,a\,y^2 .\]
  1. For every \(y\) we have \(y^2 \ge 0\), so \(-0{,}3\,a\,y^2 \le 0\) and \(g(y) \le 75\ \text{m}^2 \cdot a = g(0)\). So the function \(g\) attains its largest value at the point \(y = 0\), the centre of the cross section, and this value is \(75\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} = 1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m.
  2. For every \(y\) with \(-0{,}005\ \text{m} \le y \le 0{,}005\ \text{m}\) we have \(|y| \le 0{,}005\) m, and by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(y^2 = |y|^2 \le (0{,}005\ \text{m})^2\). So \(-0{,}3\,a\,y^2 \ge -0{,}3\,a\,(0{,}005\ \text{m})^2\) and \(g(y) \ge g(-0{,}005\ \text{m}) = g(0{,}005\ \text{m})\). The function attains its smallest value at two points, the two ends of the diameter on the rim of the cross section.

The difference between the largest and the smallest value is \(0{,}3\,a\,(0{,}005\ \text{m})^2 = 1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-12}\) m, ten million times less than the displacement itself. This is the U shape from section 1.7.1: the centre of the cross section moves a little lower than its rim, because the bar gets thinner more at the top than lower down, so the vertical fibres lean and the cross section rises toward the rim (figure 1.93). The example shows two things. A function may attain its largest value inside the interval, and an extremum may be attained at several points. In both examples we found the extrema with an inequality, because the functions were simple. The proof in section 1.14, however, will need to know only that an extremum exists.

Does every function attain a largest value? No. Figure 1.94 shows two ways in which this fails.

The first is the function \(f(x) = x\) on the half-open interval \([0, 1)\). Its values are exactly the numbers in \([0, 1)\). For this set we showed in section 1.8.2 that it has the supremum \(1\) and no maximum: for every \(x \in [0, 1)\) the number \(\tfrac12(x + 1)\) is larger than \(x\) and still in \([0, 1)\). So the function attains no largest value at any point. The values do not run off to infinity, they only approach the number \(1\), which the function would reach only at the point \(1\), and this point does not lie in the domain.

The second is the function \(f(x) = 1/x\) on the half-open interval \((0, 1]\). For every number \(B\) there is by the Archimedean property 1.35 a natural number \(n > B\). The point \(1/n\) lies in \((0, 1]\), and there \(f(1/n) = n > B\). So no number is larger than all the values. The set of values is not bounded above, so it has no supremum, let alone a maximum.

The first way is mild: the values are caught between two numbers, and only the point that would carry the largest value is missing. The second is rough: the values are not caught. For this second case we need a name.

Definition 1.71 Bounded function (omejena funkcija)

A function \(f\) with real values, defined on a set \(D\), is bounded (omejena) on \(D\) if there is a number \(B\) such that \(|f(x)| \le B\) for every \(x \in D\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 1.3.6 (PDF p. 38).

The inequality \(|f(x)| \le B\) means \(-B \le f(x) \le B\). So a bounded function has a bounded set of values \(\{f(x) : x \in D\}\) in the sense of definition 1.29, with the upper bound \(B\) and the lower bound \(-B\). The converse holds too. If the set of values has a lower bound \(b_1\) and an upper bound \(b_2\), then \(f(x) \le b_2 \le |b_2| \le |b_1| + |b_2|\) and \(f(x) \ge b_1 \ge -|b_1| \ge -(|b_1| + |b_2|)\), so \(|f(x)| \le |b_1| + |b_2|\) for every \(x \in D\). In the same way we bounded a sequence by a single number in lemma 1.42 on the boundedness of a convergent sequence. The function \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, 1)\) is bounded with \(B = 1\), while the function \(1/x\) on \((0, 1]\) is not bounded.

A bounded function on a nonempty set \(D\) has a supremum of its values by the completeness axiom 1.32, but, as the function \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, 1)\) shows, it does not necessarily attain it. So for continuous functions on a closed interval we will prove two things: that they are bounded, and that they attain the supremum of their values.

1.13.2 A continuous function on a closed interval is bounded

Why would a continuous function on a closed interval be bounded? Continuity at a point \(c\) says (definition 1.58, with the error \(\eta = 1\)) that there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f(x)\) differs from \(f(c)\) by less than \(1\) for every \(x\) in the domain with \(|x - c| < \delta\). So near every point the values are caught in a band of width \(1\) on each side of \(f(c)\) (figure 1.95). The function \(1/x\) on \((0, 1]\) gets around this restriction. Its values grow at the points \(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\), which approach the point \(0\), and this point does not lie in the domain, so there is no band there to hold the values. On a closed interval this way out does not exist. If the values were unbounded, we would find points at which they get ever larger. From these, with the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, we would choose points that approach some point \(c\), and \(c\) would lie in the interval, because the interval is closed. In the band around \(f(c)\) the values would have to be bounded and arbitrarily large at the same time, which is impossible.

Lemma 1.72 A continuous function on a closed interval is bounded (zvezna funkcija na zaprtem intervalu je omejena)

Let \(a < b\) be real numbers and \(f\) a function that is defined and continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\). Then \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\): there is a number \(B\) such that \(|f(x)| \le B\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\).

Proof

We argue by contradiction: we assume that \(f\) is not bounded and derive that the natural numbers would be bounded above.

  1. Suppose that \(f\) is not bounded on \([a, b]\). By definition 1.71 no number \(B\) then works, that is, for every number \(B\) there is an \(x \in [a, b]\) with \(|f(x)| > B\).
  2. For every natural number \(n\) we use step 1 with \(B = n\) and choose a point \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \in [a, b]\) with \(|f(x_{\mathrm{n}})| > n\). We take the bound \(B = n\) so that the values \(|f(x_{\mathrm{n}})|\) grow beyond every bound.
  3. The sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is bounded, because \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) for every \(n\). So by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.57 it has a convergent subsequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\). We denote its limit by \(c\).
  4. For every \(k\) we have \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} \le b\). So by lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, \(a \le c \le b\), that is, \(c \in [a, b]\).
  5. The function \(f\) is continuous at the point \(c\), because \(c \in [a, b]\). The subsequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) lies in \([a, b]\) and converges to \(c\), so by lemma 1.61 on continuity through sequences the sequence of values \((f(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}))\) converges to \(f(c)\).
  6. By lemma 1.42 on the boundedness of a convergent sequence there is a number \(B'\) such that \(|f(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| \le B'\) for every \(k\).
  7. By step 2, \(|f(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| > n_{\mathrm{k}}\), and by lemma 1.53 on the indices of a subsequence, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\). So \(|f(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| > k\) for every \(k\).
  8. By steps 6 and 7, \(k < |f(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| \le B'\), so \(k < B'\) for every natural number \(k\). The number \(B'\) would be an upper bound of the set \(\mathbb N\), but by the Archimedean property 1.35 this set is not bounded above. So the assumption of step 1 is false, and \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\).

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 3.3.1 (PDF p. 130).

The proof used three properties, each in its own step. Because the interval is bounded, the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) was bounded and had a convergent subsequence (step 3). Because the interval is closed, the limit \(c\) stayed in it (step 4). Because \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), the values followed the points (step 5). For the function \(1/x\) on \((0, 1]\) step 4 fails: the points \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = 1/(n + 1)\), at which \(f(x_{\mathrm{n}}) = n + 1 > n\), approach the point \(0\), which does not lie in the interval. The lemma does not say how large the bound \(B\) is, only that it exists.

1.13.3 The extreme value theorem

Fermat's rule from section 1.3.3 looks for the greatest value, if one exists. We prove the rule in section 1.14.3.

From history

That a greatest value exists was not obvious in itself. Archimedes and Zenodorus already discussed the statement that among all closed plane curves of given length the circle encloses the greatest area, but nobody proved it rigorously for two millennia, until Weierstrass and Schwarz did (CAJORI, PDF p. 386). Jakob Steiner thought he had proved this statement for the circle. His argument was that a curve that is not a circle can be improved so that the area increases, so the greatest area must belong to the circle (CAJORI, PDF p. 386). Weierstrass gave a simple general existence theorem that applies to the extremes of continuous functions (CAJORI, PDF p. 386). In 1913 Oskar Perron showed by an example what is wrong with Steiner's proof: let us try to "prove" that \(1\) is the largest natural number. No number larger than \(1\) can be the largest, because its square is larger than itself. Hence \(1\) is the largest. The argument excludes all the other numbers, but it does not say that a largest number exists at all. In the same way Steiner's proof does not show that among the curves of given length there exists one whose area is greatest (CAJORI, PDF p. 386).

We prove Weierstrass's version of the statement that a continuous function on a closed interval attains a greatest and a least value in this section, for functions of one variable.

So a continuous function on a closed interval is bounded, and the set of its values has a supremum \(s\) by the completeness axiom. Does the function attain it? By theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 2, the values come arbitrarily close to the supremum. So for every natural number \(n\) there is a point \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) at which the value is closer to the number \(s\) than \(1/n\). The points \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) themselves, however, need not converge. In figure 1.96 the function has two equally high peaks, and the points \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) may jump from one to the other. So again we choose a convergent subsequence. Its limit lies in the interval, because the interval is closed, and continuity tells us that the value there is exactly \(s\).

Theorem 1.73 Extreme value theorem (izrek o največji in najmanjši vrednosti)

Let \(a < b\) be real numbers and \(f\) a function that is defined and continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\). Then \(f\) attains a largest and a smallest value on \([a, b]\): there are points \(x_{\max}\) and \(x_{\min}\) in \([a, b]\) such that

\[f(x_{\min}) \le f(x) \le f(x_{\max}) \quad \text{for every } x \in [a, b] .\]
Proof

We must show that there is a point at which the value equals the supremum of the values, and a point at which it equals the infimum.

Largest value.

  1. The set of values \(A = \{f(x) : x \in [a, b]\}\) is nonempty, because it contains \(f(a)\), and bounded above, because by lemma 1.72 the function \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\). So by the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum \(s\).
  2. Let \(n\) be a natural number. By theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 2, with the error \(\eta = 1/n\) there is an element of the set \(A\) that is larger than \(s - 1/n\). The elements of the set \(A\) are values of the function, so there is a point \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \in [a, b]\) with \(s - 1/n < f(y_{\mathrm{n}}) \le s\). For every \(n\) we choose one such point. We take the error \(1/n\) because it goes to zero, so the values \(f(y_{\mathrm{n}})\) will approach the number \(s\).
  3. The sequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}})\) is bounded, because \(a \le y_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) for every \(n\). By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.57 it has a convergent subsequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\). We denote its limit by \(x_{\max}\).
  4. For every \(k\) we have \(a \le y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} \le b\), so by lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, also \(a \le x_{\max} \le b\).
  5. The function \(f\) is continuous at \(x_{\max}\), so by lemma 1.61 on continuity through sequences the sequence \((f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}))\) converges to \(f(x_{\max})\).
  6. By step 2, \(s - 1/n_{\mathrm{k}} < f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) \le s\), so \(|f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| = s - f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) < 1/n_{\mathrm{k}}\). By lemma 1.53 on the indices of a subsequence, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\), so \(1/n_{\mathrm{k}} \le 1/k\), since for positive numbers a larger denominator gives a smaller fraction. So \(|f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| < 1/k\) for every \(k\).
  7. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is an \(N\) such that \(1/k < \eta\) for every \(k \ge N\). By step 6, then, \(|f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| < \eta\) for every \(k \ge N\). We picked the error freely, so the sequence \((f(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}))\) converges to \(s\) too (definition 1.38).
  8. By lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence, the limits of steps 5 and 7 are equal: \(f(x_{\max}) = s\).
  9. The supremum \(s\) is an upper bound of the set \(A\), so \(f(x) \le s = f(x_{\max})\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\). The function attains its largest value at the point \(x_{\max}\).

Smallest value.

  1. The function \(-f\), which assigns to every \(x \in [a, b]\) the number \(-f(x)\), is continuous on \([a, b]\). For a point \(c \in [a, b]\) and an error \(\eta > 0\) we take the band \(\delta\) that definition 1.58 gives for the function \(f\). For every \(x \in [a, b]\) with \(|x - c| < \delta\) we then have \(|(-f(x)) - (-f(c))| = |f(x) - f(c)| < \eta\), so the same band works for \(-f\).
  2. By the part on the largest value, applied to the function \(-f\), there is a point \(x_{\min} \in [a, b]\) with \(-f(x) \le -f(x_{\min})\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\).
  3. We multiply the inequality by \(-1\), which reverses it: \(f(x) \ge f(x_{\min})\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\). The function attains its smallest value at the point \(x_{\min}\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 3.3.2 (PDF pp. 130-131). The source proves the smallest value with a sequence that approaches the infimum, instead of with the function \(-f\).

The theorem is one of the results that carry the road to the statement about the change of a function between two numbers (figure 1.97). The proof used the same three properties as the proof of lemma 1.72. The boundedness of the interval gave a convergent subsequence (step 3), closedness kept its limit in the interval (step 4), and continuity carried the limit of the points over to a limit of the values (step 5). The theorem says that the extrema exist, not where they are. For the strain of the hanging bar and for the displacement of the points of a cross section we found them with inequalities. Physically the theorem says this. Every quantity that changes along a bar without jumps has a place on the bar where it is largest and a place where it is smallest, if we look at the whole bar including its two ends. If we left out the ends, the largest value could be missing, as for the function \(x\) on \([0, 1)\).

Without any one of the three assumptions the theorem fails. For each let us show where the proof breaks down.

The interval must be closed. The function \(1/x\) on \((0, 1]\) from figure 1.94, right, is not bounded, as we saw. It is continuous, though. Let us show this at a point \(c \in (0, 1]\). The condition of definition 1.58, written out for this case, is: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|1/x - 1/c| < \eta\) for every \(x \in (0, 1]\) with \(|x - c| < \delta\).

  1. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). We bring the fractions to a common denominator: \(1/x - 1/c = (c - x)/(xc)\), so \(|1/x - 1/c| = |x - c|/(xc)\), because \(x\) and \(c\) are positive.
  2. The denominator \(xc\) changes with \(x\), so first we bound it from below. For \(|x - c| < c/2\) we have \(x > c - c/2 = c/2\), so \(xc > c^2/2\) and \(1/(xc) < 2/c^2\).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, for \(|x - c| < c/2\) the difference is \(|1/x - 1/c| \le 2\,|x - c|/c^2\).
  4. As the band \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the positive numbers \(c/2\) and \(\eta c^2/2\). For every \(x \in (0, 1]\) with \(|x - c| < \delta\) we have \(|x - c| < c/2\) and \(|x - c| < \eta c^2/2\), so by step 3
    \[\Big|\frac1x - \frac1c\Big| \le \frac{2\,|x - c|}{c^2} < \frac{2\delta}{c^2} \le \frac{2}{c^2} \cdot \frac{\eta c^2}{2} = \eta .\]
  5. We picked the error freely and found a band for it, so \(1/x\) is continuous at \(c\). We picked the point \(c \in (0, 1]\) freely, so \(1/x\) is continuous on \((0, 1]\).

So a continuous and unbounded function on \((0, 1]\) exists, and in the proof of lemma 1.72 step 4 fails. The function \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, 1)\) from figure 1.94, left, is continuous and bounded, but it does not attain its supremum \(1\). In the proof of the theorem the points \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) would approach the number \(1\), which does not lie in \([0, 1)\), so step 4 fails.

The interval must be bounded. The function \(f(x) = x\) on the unbounded interval \([0, \infty)\), that is, on the set of all \(x \ge 0\), is continuous, since it is a polynomial (corollary 1.64 on sums and products of continuous functions), and it attains its smallest value \(0\) at the point \(0\). It attains no largest value, because for every \(x \ge 0\) the number \(x + 1\) is a larger value (figure 1.98, left). By the Archimedean property it is not even bounded. In the proof of lemma 1.72 step 3 fails. The points \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(f(x_{\mathrm{n}}) = x_{\mathrm{n}} > n\) run away beyond every bound, and so does every subsequence of them, since \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} > n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\). So by lemma 1.42 on the boundedness of a convergent sequence none of them converges.

The function must be continuous. On the closed interval \([0, 2]\) let us take a function with a jump (figure 1.98, right):

\[f(x) = x \quad \text{for } 0 \le x < 1 , \qquad f(x) = 0 \quad \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 .\]

The function is bounded, because \(0 \le f(x) < 1\) for every \(x \in [0, 2]\). Its values are the numbers in \([0, 1)\), so the supremum of the values is \(1\), but it is not attained. The function is not continuous at the point \(1\). Let us take the points \(y_{\mathrm{n}} = 1 - 1/(2n)\), which lie in \([\tfrac12, 1)\). Their distance from \(1\) is \(1/(2n) < 1/n\), which by the Archimedean property is smaller than any error \(\eta > 0\) from some place on, so the \(y_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to \(1\). The values \(f(y_{\mathrm{n}}) = y_{\mathrm{n}}\), however, converge to \(1\), not to \(f(1) = 0\), and by lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence they do not converge to \(0\). So by lemma 1.61 on continuity through sequences \(f\) is not continuous at the point \(1\). In the proof of the theorem step 5 fails: the points approach the point \(1\), but their values do not approach the value there. This is how, for example, the force carried by a cross section of the bar with the pin and the two blocks from section 1.12.2 jumps as we pass the pin.

The theorem gives sufficient conditions, not necessary ones. A function with a jump can attain a largest value too. The function that equals \(0\) on \([0, 1)\) and \(1\) on \([1, 2]\) jumps at the point \(1\), but it attains its largest value \(1\) at every point of the interval \([1, 2]\). The force carried by a cross section of the bar with the pin and the two blocks attains its largest value at the top in spite of the jump, where the top cross section carries the whole bar and both blocks. The theorem only says that for a continuous function on a closed interval the extrema are never missing.

1.13.4 Closed and bounded sets of points

Now let us return to the second question from the start of the section, the one about fibres. In section 1.6.2 we deformed a steel cube with edge \(h = 10\) mm, glued to a table with its bottom face, by shifting its top face by \(s = 10\) µm in the direction of the axis \(x\). The axis \(z\) points up, and the displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) ((1.16)). The four fibres of the front face stretched differently: the diagonal \(AC\) by \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the diagonal \(BD\) by \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the edge \(AB\) not at all and the edge \(AD\) by \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Is there a direction in which a fibre stretches most? The cube is deformed the same way everywhere, so the strain of a fibre depends only on its direction, not on where it lies or how long it is. We describe a direction by a unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 1.18). A fibre \(PQ\) of length \(L_0\) in this direction has the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = L_0\,\vek n\). Let us compute how the square of its length changes.

  1. By (1.16) the difference of the displacements of the ends is \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) = \big(0{,}001\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}),\ 0,\ 0\big)\). The difference of heights \(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}\) is the component \(z\) of the vector \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = L_0\,\vek n\), that is, \(L_0 n_{\mathrm{z}}\). So \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) = (0{,}001\,L_0 n_{\mathrm{z}},\ 0,\ 0)\).
  2. By (1.15) the vector of the fibre after loading is \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = (L_0 n_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,L_0 n_{\mathrm{z}},\ L_0 n_{\mathrm{y}},\ L_0 n_{\mathrm{z}}) = L_0\,(n_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{z}},\ n_{\mathrm{y}},\ n_{\mathrm{z}})\).
  3. By (1.10) the square of its length is the sum of the squares of the components. We write the square of the first component out as the product \((n_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{z}})(n_{\mathrm{x}} + 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\):
    \[L_1^2 = L_0^2\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 0{,}002\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}000001\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\big) .\]
  4. The vector \(\vek n\) is a unit vector, so \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 1\), and \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,(1 + 0{,}002\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}000001\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\).

So the relative change of the square of the length is

\[q(\vek n) = \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{L_0^2} = 0{,}002\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}000001\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 .\]

Let us check it on the diagonal \(AC\), which has the direction \(\vek n = (1/\sqrt 2, 0, 1/\sqrt 2)\). Then \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac12\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = \tfrac12\), so \(q = 0{,}001 + 0{,}0000005 = 0{,}0010005\) and \(L_1 = L_0 \sqrt{1{,}0010005}\). The strain is \(L_1/L_0 - 1 = \sqrt{1{,}0010005} - 1 = 5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\), as in the table of section 1.6.2. The computation is exact, we neglected nothing. Why do we look at \(q\) instead of the strain? Because \(q\) is a polynomial in the three components \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\), and so by corollary 1.69 it is a continuous function of the point \((n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). For the strain \(\sqrt{1 + q} - 1\) we would also need the continuity of the square root, which we have not proved. From \(L_1 = L_0\sqrt{1 + q(\vek n)}\), though, it follows that for the same length \(L_0\) the fibre is the longer after loading the larger \(q\) is, since by lemma 1.28 a larger nonnegative number has a larger square. So the direction with the largest \(q\) is the direction with the largest strain.

On which points do we look at the function \(q\)? Let us draw the unit vectors from the origin \(O\). Their tips are exactly the points at distance \(1\) from \(O\), and they form the sphere with radius \(1\) and centre \(O\), that is, the surface of a ball. We call it the unit sphere (enotska sfera) (figure 1.99). Every point of the unit sphere is one direction in space. So the question reads: does a continuous function on the unit sphere attain a largest value? The unit sphere is not an interval, so the extreme value theorem 1.73 is not enough. Which properties of the closed interval did the proof really need? Two. Boundedness: every sequence in it was bounded, so it had a convergent subsequence. Closedness: the limit of a convergent sequence from the interval stayed in the interval. Let us write both properties for sets of points.

Definition 1.74 Closed and bounded set of points (zaprta in omejena množica točk)

Let \(K\) be a set of points of space and \(O\) the origin of the coordinate system. The set \(K\) is bounded (omejena) if there is a number \(R\) such that \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every point \(P \in K\). The set \(K\) is closed (zaprta) if for every sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) from \(K\) that converges to some point \(P\) (definition 1.65) the limit \(P\) also lies in \(K\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 7.1.12 (PDF p. 261) for boundedness, Prop. 7.3.12 and 7.3.13 (PDF p. 277) for closedness.

So a bounded set of points lies in the ball of radius \(R + 1\) around the origin, since each of its points is at most \(R\) away from the origin, which is less than \(R + 1\). Instead of the origin we could take any other point, which gives the same notion (LEBL1 Def. 7.1.12 and item (i) after it, PDF p. 261). A closed set is a set from which a sequence of its points cannot escape in the limit. LEBL1 defines a closed set differently, with open sets (Def. 7.2.4, PDF p. 264). From its Propositions 7.3.12 and 7.3.13 (PDF p. 277) and 7.2.19 (PDF p. 270) it follows that this is the same property as ours. Both definitions use only distances, so they work in the same way for sets of numbers, where \(|x|\) stands in place of \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|\). The closed interval \([a, b]\) is closed, because by lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, the limit of a sequence from \([a, b]\) lies in \([a, b]\). It is also bounded, because by the same argument as for bounded functions \(|x| \le |a| + |b|\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\). The half-open interval \((0, 1]\), however, is not closed, because the sequence \((1/n)\) from it converges to \(0\), which does not lie in it (figure 1.71). It is exactly these two properties that the proof of the extreme value theorem needed.

In space too a set is not necessarily closed (figure 1.100). Let us take all points whose distance from the origin is less than \(1\), that is, the ball of radius \(1\) around the origin. The ball does not contain the points at distance exactly \(1\), which form its surface. The points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (1 - 1/n, 0, 0)\) lie in it, because \(|\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}| = 1 - 1/n < 1\). Their coordinates converge to \(1\), \(0\) and \(0\), so by lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate the points converge to the point \((1, 0, 0)\). Its distance from the origin is exactly \(1\), and it does not lie in the set. The set of all points of space, on the other hand, is closed, because the limit of every convergent sequence of points is again a point of space, but it is not bounded, because the point \((n, 0, 0)\) is at distance \(n\) from the origin, and by the Archimedean property the natural numbers exceed every bound \(R\).

How do we show that a set is closed? For the unit sphere, for the cube and for the bar we will use the same argument: the set is given by equations or non-strict inequalities for continuous functions.

Lemma 1.75 Equations and non-strict inequalities give closed sets (enačbe in nestroge neenačbe dajo zaprte množice)

Let \(f\) be a function that is defined and continuous at every point of space (definition 1.67), and \(c\) a number.

  1. The sets of all points \(P\) with \(f(P) = c\), of all points with \(f(P) \le c\) and of all points with \(f(P) \ge c\) are closed.
  2. If the sets \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are closed, then the set of points that lie in both is closed too.
Proof

We must show that the limit of a convergent sequence from each of these sets lies in it.

1. The equation and the two inequalities.

  1. Let \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a sequence of points with \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}}) = c\), and let it converge to a point \(P\).
  2. The function \(f\) is continuous at \(P\), so by lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points the sequence \((f(P_{\mathrm{n}}))\) converges to \(f(P)\).
  3. The sequence \((f(P_{\mathrm{n}}))\) is the constant sequence \(c, c, c, \dots\), which converges to \(c\) (section 1.9.2). By lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence, \(f(P) = c\), so \(P\) lies in the set.
  4. If \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}}) \le c\) for every \(n\), then by step 2 and by lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 1, applied to the sequences \((f(P_{\mathrm{n}}))\) and \(c, c, c, \dots\), \(f(P) \le c\). In the same way \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}}) \ge c\) gives \(f(P) \ge c\).

2. Points that lie in both sets.

  1. Let the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) lie in \(K_1\) and in \(K_2\) and converge to \(P\).
  2. The sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) is a sequence from \(K_1\), and \(K_1\) is closed, so \(P\) lies in \(K_1\). In the same way \(P\) lies in \(K_2\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 7.5.9 (PDF p. 291) for item 1 and Prop. 7.2.8 (ii) (PDF p. 266) for item 2, both with open sets. The proof with sequences is not from the source.

The lemma tells us why it matters that the inequalities are non-strict. A limit preserves only non-strict inequalities, as we saw with the strains of the pieces of the hanging bar, which are all smaller than \(2aL\), while their limit equals \(2aL\). The set of points with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| < 1\) is given by a strict inequality, so a sequence from it could converge to a point on its edge that does not belong to it.

Let us apply the lemma to three sets that we will need.

The unit sphere is the set of all points \(P = (x, y, z)\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| = 1\). A length is nonnegative, so by lemma 1.28, used in both directions, it equals \(1\) exactly when its square equals \(1\), that is, when \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\). The function \(f(P) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\) is a polynomial in the coordinates, so by corollary 1.69 it is continuous at every point of space. By lemma 1.75, item 1, the unit sphere is closed. It is bounded with \(R = 1\).

A box with edges along the axes is the set of all points \((x, y, z)\) with \(a_1 \le x \le b_1\), \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\) and \(a_3 \le z \le b_3\), where \(a_1 < b_1\), \(a_2 < b_2\) and \(a_3 < b_3\) are numbers. We write it as \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), where the sign \(\times\) says that each coordinate lies in its own interval. The sheared cube before loading is such a box, \([0, 10\,000] \times [0, 10\,000] \times [0, 10\,000]\) in micrometres. The box is given by six non-strict inequalities. Each contains one coordinate, which is a polynomial and so a continuous function of the point, so by lemma 1.75, item 1, each of the six sets that the inequalities determine is closed. The box is the set of points that lie in all six, so by item 2, used five times, the box is closed too. It is bounded. As for an interval, \(|x| \le |a_1| + |b_1|\), so by lemma 1.28 \(x^2 \le (|a_1| + |b_1|)^2\), and the same for \(y\) and \(z\). So \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|^2 \le R^2\) with \(R^2 = (|a_1| + |b_1|)^2 + (|a_2| + |b_2|)^2 + (|a_3| + |b_3|)^2\), and by the same lemma \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\). For the cube \(R = \sqrt{3 \cdot 10\,000^2}\ \text{µm} = 17\,320{,}5\) µm, the length of the space diagonal from the corner \(A\) at the origin to the opposite corner.

The hanging bar before loading is the set of all points with \(0 \le x \le L\) and \(y^2 + z^2 \le r^2\), where \(r = 0{,}005\) m is the radius of the cross section. All three inequalities are non-strict and contain polynomials, so by lemma 1.75, item 1 for each inequality and item 2 used twice, the bar is closed. It is bounded, because by lemma 1.28 \(x^2 \le L^2\), and \(y^2 + z^2 \le r^2\), so \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|^2 \le L^2 + r^2\) and \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le \sqrt{L^2 + r^2}\) for every point of it. So both bodies we have computed with in space so far, the sheared cube and the hanging bar, are closed and bounded sets of points together with their surfaces.

1.13.5 The largest value in space

The proof of the extreme value theorem needed the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, which is about sequences of numbers. For sequences of points we get it by using it three times, on each coordinate separately. First we choose a subsequence in which the coordinates \(x\) converge, from it a subsequence in which the coordinates \(y\) converge as well, and from that one a subsequence in which the coordinates \(z\) converge too. Why not all three at once? Because the subsequence that the theorem chooses for the coordinates \(x\) does not take care of the coordinates \(y\) (figure 1.101). Along the way we need that a subsequence chosen from a subsequence is again a subsequence of the original sequence.

Lemma 1.76 A subsequence of a subsequence (podzaporedje podzaporedja)

Let \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) be a subsequence of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\), and \((x_{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}}})\) a subsequence of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\), given by a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers \(k_1 < k_2 < \dots\) Then the sequence of numbers \(m_{\mathrm{j}} = n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}}\) is strictly increasing, so \((x_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\) is a subsequence of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\). The same holds for sequences of points.

Proof

We must show that \(m_{\mathrm{j}} < m_{\mathrm{j}+1}\) for every \(j\).

  1. Let \(j\) be a natural number. Since the sequence \((k_{\mathrm{j}})\) is strictly increasing, \(k_{\mathrm{j}} < k_{\mathrm{j}+1}\), so \(k_{\mathrm{j}} + 1 \le k_{\mathrm{j}+1}\), since both numbers are natural numbers.
  2. The sequence \((n_{\mathrm{k}})\) is strictly increasing (definition 1.52), so \(n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}} < n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j} + 1}\).
  3. A strictly increasing sequence is also increasing (definition 1.49). So by lemma 1.50 on the terms of a monotone sequence and step 1, \(n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j} + 1} \le n_{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{j}+1}}\).
  4. The inequalities of steps 2 and 3 form a chain: \(m_{\mathrm{j}} = n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}} < n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j} + 1} \le n_{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{j}+1}} = m_{\mathrm{j}+1}\).
  5. For sequences of points the proof is the same, since it is only about the indices.

Source: LEBL1 uses the argument in the proof of Thm 7.4.14 (PDF pp. 284-285). The lemma is not from the source.

Lemma 1.77 Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in space (Bolzano-Weierstrassov izrek v prostoru)

Every bounded sequence of points, that is, every sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) for which there is a number \(R\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}| \le R\) for every \(n\), has a convergent subsequence.

Proof

We must show that there is a strictly increasing sequence of indices along which all three coordinates converge. We denote the coordinates of the point \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) by \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, z_{\mathrm{n}})\).

  1. The coordinates are bounded. We have \(x_{\mathrm{n}}^2 \le x_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{n}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = |\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}|^2 \le R^2\), and since \(x_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = |x_{\mathrm{n}}|^2\), by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|x_{\mathrm{n}}| \le R\). In the same way \(|y_{\mathrm{n}}| \le R\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{n}}| \le R\) for every \(n\).
  2. The sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}})\) is bounded, so by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.57 it has a subsequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some number \(x\).
  3. The sequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\), which we index by \(k\), is bounded by step 1, so by the same theorem it has a subsequence \((y_{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}}})\) that converges to some number \(y\). Let \(m_{\mathrm{j}} = n_{\mathrm{k}_\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 1.76 on a subsequence of a subsequence, \((P_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\) is a subsequence of the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\).
  4. The sequence \((x_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\) is a subsequence of the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\), which converges to \(x\). So by lemma 1.54 on the limit of a subsequence the \(x_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}}\) converge to \(x\). By step 3 the \(y_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}}\) converge to \(y\).
  5. The sequence \((z_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\) is bounded by step 1, so it has a subsequence \((z_{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{j}_\mathrm{i}}})\) that converges to some number \(z\). Let \(p_{\mathrm{i}} = m_{\mathrm{j}_\mathrm{i}}\). By lemma 1.76, \((P_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{i}})\) is a subsequence of the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\).
  6. The sequences \((x_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{i}})\) and \((y_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{i}})\) are subsequences of the sequences \((x_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\) and \((y_{\mathrm{m}_\mathrm{j}})\), so by lemma 1.54 they converge to \(x\) and \(y\).
  7. So all three coordinates of the points \(P_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{i}}\) converge, to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate the subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{p}_\mathrm{i}})\) converges to the point \((x, y, z)\).

Source: LEBL1 proof of Thm 7.4.14 (PDF pp. 284-285), where it is written for two coordinates.

The proof repeated the same step three times, and with every choice it kept what it had achieved before: a subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same limit. In a space with more dimensions we would repeat the step as many times as there are coordinates. Now we can carry the proof of the extreme value theorem over to space. The points of the interval are replaced by the points of the set \(K\), the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem by its version for points, and the lemma on preserving inequalities by the closedness of the set.

Theorem 1.78 Extreme value theorem in space (izrek o največji vrednosti v prostoru)

Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.74) and \(f\) a function that is defined and continuous on \(K\) (definition 1.67). Then \(f\) attains a largest and a smallest value on \(K\): there are points \(P_{\max}\) and \(P_{\min}\) in \(K\) such that

\[f(P_{\min}) \le f(P) \le f(P_{\max}) \quad \text{for every } P \in K .\]
Proof

We must show that \(f\) is bounded on \(K\) and that it attains the supremum and the infimum of its values.

Boundedness.

  1. We argue by contradiction. Suppose that \(f\) is not bounded on \(K\) (definition 1.71). Then for every natural number \(n\) there is a point \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) with \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}})| > n\). For every \(n\) we choose one such point.
  2. The set \(K\) is bounded, so \(|\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}| \le R\) for every \(n\). By lemma 1.77, the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in space, the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(P\).
  3. The set \(K\) is closed, so \(P\) lies in \(K\).
  4. The function \(f\) is continuous at \(P\), so by lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points the values \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converge to \(f(P)\).
  5. By lemma 1.42 on the boundedness of a convergent sequence there is a \(B\) with \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| \le B\) for every \(k\).
  6. By step 1 and lemma 1.53 on the indices of a subsequence, \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| > n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\). So by step 5, \(k < B\) for every natural number \(k\), which contradicts the Archimedean property 1.35. The assumption of step 1 is false, and \(f\) is bounded on \(K\).

Largest value.

  1. The set of values \(A = \{f(P) : P \in K\}\) is nonempty, because \(K\) is nonempty, and bounded above by the first part. By the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum \(s\).
  2. For every natural number \(n\), by theorem 1.33 on the properties of the supremum and infimum, item 2, with the error \(1/n\) there is a point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) with \(s - 1/n < f(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \le s\). For every \(n\) we choose one such point.
  3. The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.77 the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point. We denote it by \(P_{\max}\).
  4. The set \(K\) is closed, so \(P_{\max}\) lies in \(K\).
  5. The function \(f\) is continuous at \(P_{\max}\), so by lemma 1.68 the values \(f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converge to \(f(P_{\max})\).
  6. By step 2, \(|f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| = s - f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) < 1/n_{\mathrm{k}}\), and by lemma 1.53, \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\) and so \(1/n_{\mathrm{k}} \le 1/k\). So \(|f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| < 1/k\) for every \(k\).
  7. For every error \(\eta > 0\) there is by the Archimedean property 1.35 an \(N\) such that \(1/k < \eta\) for every \(k \ge N\), and so by step 6, \(|f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - s| < \eta\). So the values \(f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converge to \(s\) too.
  8. By lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence, the limits of steps 5 and 7 are equal: \(f(P_{\max}) = s\).
  9. The supremum \(s\) is an upper bound of the values, so \(f(P) \le s = f(P_{\max})\) for every \(P \in K\).

Smallest value.

  1. The function \(-f\) is continuous on \(K\): for a point \(P \in K\) and an error \(\eta > 0\), the band \(\delta\) that definition 1.67 gives for the function \(f\) works for \(-f\) too, because \(|(-f(Q)) - (-f(P))| = |f(Q) - f(P)|\).
  2. By the part on the largest value, applied to \(-f\), there is a point \(P_{\min} \in K\) with \(-f(P) \le -f(P_{\min})\) for every \(P \in K\). Multiplying by \(-1\) we get \(f(P) \ge f(P_{\min})\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 7.5.6 (PDF p. 290) for nonempty compact sets, together with the Heine-Borel theorem 7.4.14 (PDF p. 284), by which closed and bounded sets in space are compact. Our proof is not from the source, it follows the proof of Thm 3.3.2 (PDF pp. 130-131).

The requirement that \(K\) is nonempty is needed, because in the empty set there is no point to carry the largest value. Now we can answer the question about the fibres of the sheared cube. The function \(q(\vek n) = 0{,}002\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}000001\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous. The unit sphere is nonempty, closed and bounded. So by theorem 1.78 there is a direction \(\vek n_{\max}\) in which \(q\) is largest, and with it a direction in which a fibre through any point of the cube stretches most. There is also a direction in which it shortens most. Among the four fibres of the table, the diagonal \(AC\) has the largest \(q\), \(q = 0{,}0010005\), the edge \(AD\) has \(0{,}000001\), the edge \(AB\) zero and the diagonal \(BD\) the smallest, \(q = -0{,}0009995\). So the largest value on the whole sphere is at least \(0{,}0010005\). Whether the function attains it exactly in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) or in some other direction, the theorem does not say. It says only that the most stretched direction exists before we know how to find it. How to find it we will see in chapter 2, where in the same way we will look for the direction in which the force on a small patch pulls the material hardest.

The property that the proofs of both theorems needed is that every sequence from the set has a subsequence that converges to a point of the same set. Mathematicians call such a set compact (kompaktna). LEBL1 defines compactness differently (Def. 7.4.7, PDF p. 280) and shows in Thm 7.4.11 (PDF p. 282) that it is the same property. In the space \(\mathbb R^n\) with any number of coordinates the compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded sets. This is the Heine-Borel theorem (LEBL1 Thm 7.4.14, PDF p. 284). The direction from closed and bounded to compact we proved for three coordinates with lemma 1.77 and closedness. In more general sets with a distance, however, closedness and boundedness are not enough (LEBL1 Example 7.4.15, PDF p. 285). The extreme value theorem holds for continuous functions on every nonempty compact set (LEBL1 Thm 7.5.6, PDF p. 290).

We now have what the next section needs. Take a function that is continuous on a closed interval and has the same value at both endpoints. By the extreme value theorem 1.73 it attains a largest and a smallest value. If it is not constant, at least one of the extrema lies inside the interval, since the values at the endpoints are equal. In the next section we will show that the tangent is horizontal there, and from this derive the statement about the change of a function between two numbers.

1.14 Mathematics: the mean value theorem

At the end of section 1.7.3 we needed two facts for a fibre in a general field. The first is about functions whose input is one number and whose output is one number, like the displacement \(u(x)\) of a bar: if a function has a derivative at every point between two numbers and no jump at the end points, then its change between the numbers equals the derivative at some point between them times the difference of the two numbers. For the function \(f(t) = t^3\) between \(0\) and \(1\) we found such a point in section 1.8.1, at \(\xi = 1/\sqrt 3\), and saw that it does not exist among the fractions (figure 1.50). In this section we state this fact precisely and prove it for every such function.

The route is short, because the tools of the previous sections do the main work. By the extreme value theorem 1.73, a continuous function on a closed interval attains a largest and a smallest value. We will show that the tangent to the graph at a point where the function attains its largest or smallest value is horizontal, if that point is not an end point of the interval and the function has a derivative there. Together these give the statement for functions that have the same value at both end points: somewhere in between the tangent is horizontal. We then get the general statement by subtracting from the function the straight line through the points of the graph above the end points. For this last step we must be able to differentiate the difference of two functions, so we first derive the rules by which we differentiate sums, multiples and products. They will also spare us the long computations of derivatives from sections 1.3.4 and 1.8.1. The rule for products needs the fact that a differentiable function has no jumps, and this is where we begin. At the end we derive two consequences that we will use for strains.

About the numbers we assume the same as in section 1.8.1: the arithmetic rules from school, division of integers with remainder, the fact that every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element, and the completeness axiom 1.32. The completeness axiom enters this section in one place only, through the extreme value theorem, and we will say where. All functions in this section have one number as input and one number as output.

1.14.1 A differentiable function has no jumps

In section 1.3.4, for the derivative of the displacement of the hanging bar, we noticed that the numerator \(u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)\) and the denominator \(\Delta x\) of the difference quotient go to zero together. Let us turn the question around. Suppose that the function \(f\) has a derivative at the point \(x\). Must the numerator \(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\) then go to zero? It must. For \(\Delta x \neq 0\) the numerator is the quotient times the denominator,

\[f(x + \Delta x) - f(x) = \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} \cdot \Delta x ,\]

and as \(\Delta x\) goes to zero, the first factor stays close to the derivative \(f'(x)\), while the second goes to zero. So the value \(f(x + \Delta x)\) approaches the value \(f(x)\), and the function has no jump at the point \(x\). For the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hanging under its own weight, the numerator and the denominator are the elongation and the length of a piece. The piece of length 0,001 m at the top gets longer by \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m, which is its length times the strain \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) (section 1.3.4). A piece ten times shorter gets longer by about ten times less, and the elongation goes to zero together with the length.

Continuity from section 1.12 expresses exactly this. By the definition of continuity 1.58 a function \(f\) defined on a set \(D\) is continuous at a point \(x\) of \(D\) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|f(y) - f(x)| < \eta\) for every \(y\) in \(D\) with \(|y - x| < \delta\). So the values at points close to \(x\) are close to \(f(x)\), and the function has no jump at \(x\).

By definition 1.9 the derivative is defined at a point around which the function is defined on both sides, and as a one-sided derivative at an endpoint of the domain. So we state the claim for a function on any interval (definition 1.43): at a point between the endpoints the derivative is the ordinary one, at an endpoint that belongs to the interval it is one-sided. In this way we may use it on a closed interval too, for example for the displacement of the hanging bar on \([0, L]\), which has a one-sided derivative at the top and at the lower end (section 1.4).

Lemma 1.79 A differentiable function is continuous (odvedljiva funkcija je zvezna)

Let the function \(f\) be defined on an interval \(I\) and differentiable at the point \(x \in I\), at an endpoint of the interval that belongs to \(I\) with the one-sided derivative of definition 1.9. Then \(f\) is continuous at the point \(x\).

Proof

We write the definition of continuity 1.58 out for the function \(f\) on the set \(D = I\) at the point \(x\). We must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|f(y) - f(x)| < \eta\) for every \(y \in I\) with \(|y - x| < \delta\). We will write a point \(y \neq x\) as \(y = x + \Delta x\).

  1. We choose an arbitrary error \(\eta > 0\). For it we must find a band \(\delta\).
  2. The difference quotient \(q(\Delta x) = (f(x + \Delta x) - f(x))/\Delta x\) is defined for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\) for which \(x + \Delta x\) is in \(I\). We call such \(\Delta x\) admissible.
  3. By the definition of the derivative 1.9, \(q\) approaches \(f'(x)\). We use this with the error \(1\): there is a band \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|q(\Delta x) - f'(x)| < 1\) for every admissible \(\Delta x\) with \(|\Delta x| < \delta_1\). If \(x\) is not an endpoint of the interval, this is the limit of definition 1.5, and we may take the band so narrow that all \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta_1\) are admissible (section 1.3.3). If \(x\) is the left endpoint and belongs to \(I\), only positive \(\Delta x\) are admissible, and this is the limit from the right of definition 1.8, which looks at exactly such \(\Delta x\). At the right endpoint only negative \(\Delta x\) are admissible, and this is the limit from the left. The error \(1\) is an arbitrary choice, any positive number would do equally well.
  4. For such a \(\Delta x\) we bound the quotient by a number that does not depend on \(\Delta x\). By the triangle inequality for numbers \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1)
    \[|q(\Delta x)| = \big|\big(q(\Delta x) - f'(x)\big) + f'(x)\big| \le |q(\Delta x) - f'(x)| + |f'(x)| < 1 + |f'(x)| .\]
  5. The numerator is the quotient times \(\Delta x\): \(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x) = q(\Delta x)\,\Delta x\). The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, item 2), so by step 4, for every admissible \(\Delta x\) with \(|\Delta x| < \delta_1\),
    \[|f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)| = |q(\Delta x)|\,|\Delta x| < \big(1 + |f'(x)|\big)\,|\Delta x| .\]
  6. The right side is smaller than \(\eta\) if \(|\Delta x| < \eta / (1 + |f'(x)|)\). So for the band \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the positive numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\eta / (1 + |f'(x)|)\).
  7. We check. Let \(y \in I\) and \(|y - x| < \delta\). If \(y = x\), then \(|f(y) - f(x)| = 0 < \eta\). If \(y \neq x\), then \(\Delta x = y - x\) is admissible, because \(y\) is in \(I\), and \(|\Delta x| < \delta \le \delta_1\), so by step 5
    \[|f(y) - f(x)| < \big(1 + |f'(x)|\big)\,|\Delta x| < \big(1 + |f'(x)|\big) \cdot \frac{\eta}{1 + |f'(x)|} = \eta .\]
  8. We chose the error arbitrarily and found a band for it. So the function \(f\) is continuous at \(x\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 4.1.6 (PDF p. 157), for a function on any interval, also at an endpoint. The source proves it with the limit of a product. The proof by bounding the quotient is not from the source.

What did the proof show? The inequality of step 5 says that close to the point \(x\) the graph cannot leave the region between the two straight lines through the point of the graph above \(x\) with slopes \(1 + |f'(x)|\) and \(-(1 + |f'(x)|)\) (figure 1.102). Towards this point the region narrows to a tip from both sides, so the graph approaches the point from both sides and cannot jump. At an endpoint of the interval the graph lies on one side of the point only, and the tip catches it from that side. Step 6 then only chose a band so narrow that the tip inside it lies within the allowed error. For the displacement of the hanging bar \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) on \([0, L]\) the lemma turns the one-sided derivative \(2aL\) at the top into continuity at \(x = 0\), which we checked directly in section 1.12.1.

The converse is false: a continuous function need not have a derivative. An example is the absolute value, the function that assigns \(|x|\) to the number \(x\), at the point \(0\) (figure 1.103, left). It is continuous at \(0\), because \(\big||x| - |0|\big| = |x|\) is smaller than \(\eta\) for every \(x\) with \(|x| < \eta\), that is, with the band \(\delta = \eta\). But it has no derivative at \(0\). The difference quotient is

\[\frac{|0 + \Delta x| - |0|}{\Delta x} = \frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta x} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } \Delta x > 0 , \\ -1 & \text{for } \Delta x < 0 \end{cases}\]

(figure 1.103, right). If it had a limit \(d\), the definition of the limit with the error \(\eta = 1\) would give a band \(\delta\) in which all values of the quotient differ from \(d\) by less than \(1\). The band contains the point \(\Delta x = \delta/2\) with the value \(1\) and the point \(\Delta x = -\delta/2\) with the value \(-1\), so \(|1 - d| < 1\) and \(|-1 - d| < 1\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) we would then have

\[2 = |1 - (-1)| = \big|(1 - d) + (d + 1)\big| \le |1 - d| + |d + 1| < 1 + 1 = 2 ,\]

that is, \(2 < 2\), which cannot hold. So there is no limit. The graph has a sharp corner at \(0\): the straight lines through the point of the graph above \(0\) and the points to its left have slope \(-1\), those through the points to its right slope \(1\), and no number is the limit of both slopes (LEBL1 Example 4.1.5, PDF p. 157). For the displacement of a bar such a corner would mean that the material just above the point is stretched differently from the material just below it, for example at the joint of two bars of different materials that stretch differently under the same force (chapter 3). At the point of the joint the strain is not defined.

1.14.2 Rules of differentiation

Section 1.3.4 ended with the promise that we would compute derivatives from the definition until we derived rules that do this work once and for all. Each rule says how we get the derivative of a combined function, for example of the sum or the product of two functions, from the derivatives of its parts. The task is the same for every rule: we must show that the difference quotient of the combined function has a limit, and compute it. We will write the quotient of the combined function with quotients we already know, for example as their sum. So we need a rule that gives, from the limits of two functions, the limit of their sum, and similarly for products. We do not yet have such rules for limits of functions. But we have them for continuous functions: by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions, the sum, a multiple and the product of functions that are continuous at some point are again continuous at that point. So we will translate the limit into continuity.

How? The difference quotient is not defined at \(\Delta x = 0\). Its graph has a hole above \(\Delta x = 0\), as in figure 1.49, where an empty circle said that a fibre of length zero does not exist. If the quotient has the limit \(d\), we fill the hole with the point at height \(d\) (figure 1.104). The function we get is defined at \(\Delta x = 0\) too, and since the values nearby approach \(d\), it has no jump at the point \(0\). For the bar of length \(L\) hanging under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) from the top downwards and the displacement \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), the difference quotient of the displacement at the point \(x\) is, by (1.6),

\[\frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} = a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x \qquad (\Delta x \neq 0) .\]

When we fill the hole with the limit \(a\,(2L - 2x)\), we get a function equal to \(a\,(2L - 2x) - a\,\Delta x\) for every \(\Delta x\), also for \(\Delta x = 0\). Its graph is a whole straight line, without a hole.

We state the claim for any function \(g\) that is defined near zero, except at zero. We use the letter \(h\) as in the definition of the limit 1.5.

Lemma 1.80 Limit and continuity (limita in zveznost)

Let \(d\) be a number.

  1. Let the function \(g\) be defined for all \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) for some \(r > 0\), and let \(G\) be the function on the open interval \((-r, r)\) that has the value \(G(h) = g(h)\) for \(h \neq 0\) and the value \(G(0) = d\) at the point \(0\). Then \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = d\) if and only if \(G\) is continuous at the point \(0\).
  2. Let the function \(g\) be defined for all \(h\) with \(0 < h < r\) for some \(r > 0\), and let \(G\) be the function on the interval \([0, r)\) that has the value \(G(h) = g(h)\) for \(h > 0\) and the value \(G(0) = d\) at the point \(0\). Then \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} g(h) = d\) if and only if \(G\) is continuous at the point \(0\). The same holds for the limit from the left, with the function \(g\) defined for all \(h\) with \(-r < h < 0\) and with the interval \((-r, 0]\).
Proof

We must show both items. We reduce the first to lemma 1.59 on continuity and the limit, and prove the second directly from the definition of continuity.

1. Limit.

  1. The function \(G\) is defined on the interval \((-r, r)\), that is, at all numbers \(h\) with \(|h - 0| < r\). So lemma 1.59 on continuity and the limit applies to it at the point \(c = 0\): \(G\) is continuous at \(0\) if and only if \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} G(0 + h) = G(0)\), that is, \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} G(h) = d\).
  2. The definition of the limit 1.5 looks only at numbers \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), never at \(h = 0\). For all such \(h\) with \(|h| < r\) we have \(G(h) = g(h)\). So the condition of the definition of the limit for the function \(G\) and the number \(d\) is the same as for the function \(g\) and the number \(d\), when we take \(\delta \le r\), which the explanation after the definition of the limit allows. Therefore \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} G(h) = d\) if and only if \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = d\).
  3. Steps 1 and 2 together say: \(G\) is continuous at \(0\) if and only if \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = d\).

2. One-sided limit.

  1. We write the definition of continuity 1.58 out for the function \(G\) on the set \(D = [0, r)\) at the point \(0\): for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|G(h) - d| < \eta\) for every \(h \in [0, r)\) with \(|h| < \delta\).
  2. In the condition of continuity and in the condition of the limit from the right we may take a band \(\delta \le r\), because a condition that holds for some band also holds for every narrower band (section 1.3.3).
  3. At \(h = 0\) we have \(|G(0) - d| = |d - d| = 0 < \eta\), so the condition of continuity holds there for every \(\eta\).
  4. For \(\delta \le r\) the numbers \(h \in [0, r)\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) are exactly the numbers \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\), and for them \(G(h) = g(h)\).
  5. By steps 3 and 4 a band \(\delta \le r\) satisfies the condition of continuity if and only if \(|g(h) - d| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\). This is the condition of the limit from the right of definition 1.8. So \(G\) is continuous at \(0\) if and only if \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0^+} g(h) = d\).
  6. For the limit from the left the steps are the same, with the interval \((-r, 0]\) and with the numbers \(h\) for which \(-\delta < h < 0\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 3.2.2 (ii) (PDF p. 122) in a more general form: at a point that points of the domain approach arbitrarily closely, a function is continuous if and only if it has a limit there equal to its value at that point. Item 2 is the same statement for the set \([0, r)\), on which the limit at the point \(0\) is the limit from the right (LEBL1 Def. 3.1.16, PDF p. 119). LEBL1 uses the difference quotient completed with the derivative in the proof of Prop. 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159).

The lemma says nothing new about the limit, it only translates it into the language of continuity. It is useful because for continuous functions we already know that sums, multiples and products behave well. So we will prove all the rules for sums, multiples and products by the same recipe. We write the difference quotient of the combined function with the completed quotients of its parts, which by the lemma are continuous at \(0\). The function we get is continuous at \(0\) by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions, and by the lemma its value at \(0\) is the limit of the quotient, that is, the derivative.

For the product the area of a rectangle helps (figure 1.105). Let us picture the product of two positive numbers as the area of a rectangle with sides \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\). When \(x\) changes to \(x + \Delta x\), both sides change, by \(\Delta f = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\) and by \(\Delta g = g(x + \Delta x) - g(x)\). The area grows by two strips. The top strip has the area \(f(x + \Delta x)\,\Delta g\), the right one \(\Delta f\,g(x)\):

\[f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\,g(x) = f(x + \Delta x)\,\Delta g + \Delta f\,g(x) .\]

In the proof we will check this equality by a computation that holds for all numbers, not only for positive ones. When we divide it by \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta g / \Delta x\) approaches the derivative \(g'(x)\), \(\Delta f / \Delta x\) the derivative \(f'(x)\), and the factor \(f(x + \Delta x)\) the value \(f(x)\), because by lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous, \(f\) has no jump at \(x\).

We state the rules for functions on any interval, like lemma 1.79: at an endpoint that belongs to the interval the derivative is one-sided. As in section 1.12.5, for every number \(t\) the power \(t^0\) is \(1\), and for a natural number \(n\), \(t^n\) is the product of \(n\) factors \(t\).

Lemma 1.81 Rules of differentiation (pravila odvajanja)

Let the functions \(f\) and \(g\) be defined on an interval \(I\) and differentiable at the point \(x \in I\), at an endpoint of the interval that belongs to \(I\) with the one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), and let \(c\) be a number. At an endpoint the derivatives in items 1 to 3 are one-sided too.

  1. The sum \(f + g\), which assigns \(f(t) + g(t)\) to the number \(t\), is differentiable at \(x\) and \((f + g)'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x)\).
  2. The multiple \(c f\), which assigns \(c\,f(t)\) to the number \(t\), is differentiable at \(x\) and \((c f)'(x) = c\,f'(x)\).
  3. The product \(f g\), which assigns \(f(t)\,g(t)\) to the number \(t\), is differentiable at \(x\) and
    \[(f g)'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x) . \tag{1.29}\]

For functions defined for all numbers, moreover:

  1. A constant function (stalna funkcija), which has the same value \(d\) for every number, has the derivative \(0\) at every point. The function that assigns \(t\) to every number \(t\) has the derivative \(1\) at every point.
  2. For every natural number \(n\) the function that assigns \(t^n\) to every number \(t\) has at every point \(x\) the derivative
    \[n\,x^{n-1} . \tag{1.30}\]
Proof

We must show five items. We prove the first three by the recipe with completed quotients, the fourth with the lemma on the limit of a number plus a multiple, the fifth by induction.

Preparation.

  1. If \(x\) is not an endpoint of the interval \(I\), we take for \(r\) the smaller of the distances from \(x\) to the two endpoints. Then all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(x\) lie in \(I\), and we let \(J = (-r, r)\). If \(x\) is the left endpoint and belongs to \(I\), let \(r\) be the length of the interval and \(J = [0, r)\), and if it is the right endpoint, \(J = (-r, 0]\). In all cases \(x + \Delta x\) is in \(I\) for every \(\Delta x \in J\).
  2. For \(\Delta x \in J\) with \(\Delta x \neq 0\) we denote the difference quotients of the functions \(f\) and \(g\) at the point \(x\):
    \[q_{\mathrm{f}}(\Delta x) = \frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} , \qquad q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x) = \frac{g(x + \Delta x) - g(x)}{\Delta x} .\]
  3. Let \(Q_{\mathrm{f}}\) be the function on \(J\) that equals \(q_{\mathrm{f}}(\Delta x)\) for \(\Delta x \neq 0\) and has the value \(Q_{\mathrm{f}}(0) = f'(x)\) at \(0\). In the same way let \(Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) equal \(q_{\mathrm{g}}\) for \(\Delta x \neq 0\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{g}}(0) = g'(x)\). The derivative \(f'(x)\) is the limit of the quotient \(q_{\mathrm{f}}\), one-sided at an endpoint (definition 1.9), so by lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1 or 2, the function \(Q_{\mathrm{f}}\) is continuous at \(0\). For the same reason \(Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) is continuous at \(0\).

1. Sum.

  1. We rearrange the numerator of the quotient of the sum so that the terms of each function stand together: \(\big(f(x + \Delta x) + g(x + \Delta x)\big) - \big(f(x) + g(x)\big) = \big(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\big) + \big(g(x + \Delta x) - g(x)\big)\). When we divide by \(\Delta x \neq 0\), the quotient of the sum equals \(q_{\mathrm{f}}(\Delta x) + q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x)\).
  2. The function \(Q_{\mathrm{f}} + Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) on \(J\) equals the quotient of the sum for \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and at \(0\) it has the value \(f'(x) + g'(x)\).
  3. By corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions, \(Q_{\mathrm{f}} + Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) is continuous at \(0\).
  4. By lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1 or 2, the quotient of the sum has the limit \(f'(x) + g'(x)\), one-sided at an endpoint. So the sum is differentiable at \(x\), and \((f + g)'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x)\).

2. Multiple.

  1. The numerator of the quotient of the multiple is \(c\,f(x + \Delta x) - c\,f(x) = c\,\big(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\big)\), so the quotient equals \(c\,q_{\mathrm{f}}(\Delta x)\).
  2. The function \(c\,Q_{\mathrm{f}}\) equals this quotient for \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and at \(0\) it has the value \(c\,f'(x)\). By corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions it is continuous at \(0\).
  3. By lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1 or 2, \(c f\) is differentiable at \(x\), and \((c f)'(x) = c\,f'(x)\).

3. Product.

  1. In the numerator \(f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\,g(x)\) both factors change. We add and subtract the term \(f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x)\), so that in each pair only one factor changes, and take out the common factors:
    \[\begin{aligned} f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\,g(x) &= f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x + \Delta x) - f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x) \\ &\quad + f(x + \Delta x)\,g(x) - f(x)\,g(x) \\ &= f(x + \Delta x)\,\big(g(x + \Delta x) - g(x)\big) + \big(f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\big)\,g(x) . \end{aligned}\]
    This is the equality of areas from figure 1.105.
  2. We divide by \(\Delta x \neq 0\). The quotient of the product is \(f(x + \Delta x)\,q_{\mathrm{g}}(\Delta x) + g(x)\,q_{\mathrm{f}}(\Delta x)\).
  3. Let \(F\) be the function on \(J\) given by \(F(\Delta x) = f(x + \Delta x)\). Let us show that it is continuous at \(0\). By lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous, \(f\) is continuous at \(x\): for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|f(y) - f(x)| < \eta\) for every \(y \in I\) with \(|y - x| < \delta\). For \(\Delta x \in J\) with \(|\Delta x| < \delta\) the point \(y = x + \Delta x\) lies in \(I\) by step 1 of the preparation, and \(|y - x| = |\Delta x| < \delta\), so \(|F(\Delta x) - F(0)| = |f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)| < \eta\). This is the condition of the definition of continuity 1.58 for \(F\) on the set \(J\) at the point \(0\).
  4. By step 2 the function \(F\,Q_{\mathrm{g}} + g(x)\,Q_{\mathrm{f}}\) on \(J\) equals the quotient of the product for \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and at \(0\) it has the value \(F(0)\,Q_{\mathrm{g}}(0) + g(x)\,Q_{\mathrm{f}}(0) = f(x)\,g'(x) + g(x)\,f'(x)\).
  5. By corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions the product \(F\,Q_{\mathrm{g}}\) is continuous at \(0\), so is the multiple \(g(x)\,Q_{\mathrm{f}}\), and therefore also their sum.
  6. By lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1 or 2, \(f g\) is differentiable at \(x\), and \((f g)'(x) = f'(x)\,g(x) + f(x)\,g'(x)\).

4. A constant function and the function that assigns \(t\) to the number \(t\).

  1. For the constant function with the value \(d\) the numerator at every point \(x\) is \(d - d = 0\), so the quotient is \(0\) for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\). This has the form \(0 + 0 \cdot \Delta x\), and by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple the limit is \(0\).
  2. For the function that assigns \(t\) to the number \(t\) the numerator is \((x + \Delta x) - x = \Delta x\), so the quotient is \(\Delta x / \Delta x = 1\) for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\). This has the form \(1 + 0 \cdot \Delta x\), and by the same lemma the limit is \(1\).

5. Powers.

  1. We use the principle of induction 1.44 for the statement \(P(n)\): the function that assigns \(t^n\) to the number \(t\) has the derivative \(n\,x^{n-1}\) at every point \(x\).
  2. Basis. For \(n = 1\) this is the function that assigns \(t\) to the number \(t\). By item 4 it has the derivative \(1\) at every point, and this is \(1 \cdot x^0\).
  3. Induction step. Let \(P(n)\) hold. For every number \(t\), \(t^{n+1} = t \cdot t^n\), so the function that assigns \(t^{n+1}\) to the number \(t\) is the product of the function that assigns \(t\) to it and the function that assigns \(t^n\) to it. Both are defined for all numbers, hence on the open interval \((x - 1, x + 1)\). The first has the derivative \(1\) at \(x\) by item 4, the second the derivative \(n\,x^{n-1}\) by the statement \(P(n)\).
  4. By item 3 the derivative of the product at \(x\) is \(1 \cdot x^n + x \cdot n\,x^{n-1} = x^n + n\,x^n = (n + 1)\,x^n\), which is the statement \(P(n + 1)\). Here we used \(x \cdot x^{n-1} = x^n\), which for \(n = 1\) holds because \(x^0 = 1\).
  5. By the principle of induction \(P(n)\) holds for every natural number \(n\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 4.1.7 and 4.1.8 (PDF pp. 157-158), for functions on any interval, powers in Exercise 4.1.3 (PDF p. 160). The source leaves the rule for products and the powers to the reader. LEBL1 uses the completed quotient in the proof of Prop. 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159), and LEBL1 Figure 4.2 (PDF p. 158) shows the areas for the product.

Now let us use the rules on the polynomials of definition 1.63. With the variable \(t\) we write a polynomial as \(b_0 + b_1 t + b_2 t^2 + \dots + b_{\mathrm{m}} t^m\), where \(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{\mathrm{m}}\) are given numbers. It is a sum of a constant function and multiples of powers. By item 4 the constant term has the derivative \(0\), and by items 2 and 5 the term \(b_{\mathrm{k}} t^k\) has the derivative \(k\,b_{\mathrm{k}}\,x^{k-1}\). We build the polynomial by adding one term after another, and by item 1, used at each addition, the polynomial has at every point \(x\) the derivative

\[b_1 + 2b_2\,x + 3b_3\,x^2 + \dots + m\,b_{\mathrm{m}}\,x^{m-1} .\]

The displacement of the hanging bar, \(u(t) = a\,(2Lt - t^2) = 2aL \cdot t + (-a) \cdot t^2\), is a polynomial with \(b_0 = 0\), \(b_1 = 2aL\) and \(b_2 = -a\). So its derivative is

\[u'(x) = 2aL + 2 \cdot (-a)\,x = 2a\,(L - x) ,\]

the strain that we computed from the definition in twelve steps in section 1.3.4. The function \(t^3\) from section 1.8.1 has by item 5 with \(n = 3\) the derivative \(3x^2\), for which we needed ten steps there. The rules did the work with the definition of the limit in their proofs, once and for all.

1.14.3 The derivative at the largest value

Let a function on some interval attain its largest value at a point \(x_0\) that is not an end point of the interval. Then there are points of the interval on both sides of \(x_0\), and at none of them is the value larger than \(f(x_0)\). What does this tell us about the difference quotients at \(x_0\)? To the right of \(x_0\), for \(\Delta x > 0\), the numerator \(f(x_0 + \Delta x) - f(x_0)\) is not positive and the denominator is positive, so the quotient is not positive. The straight lines through the point of the graph above \(x_0\) and the points of the graph to its right therefore fall or are horizontal. To the left of \(x_0\), for \(\Delta x < 0\), the numerator is not positive and the denominator is negative, so the quotient is not negative, and the lines rise or are horizontal (figure 1.106). The tangent is the limit of both kinds of lines, so it can neither rise nor fall. It is horizontal.

Recall that the largest and the smallest value of a function, its maximum and its minimum, are called by one word an extremum (definition 1.70). When a function attains an extremum at a point that is not an end point of the interval, we speak of an interior extremum (notranji ekstrem). Let us write the reasoning above precisely. We will choose the error \(\eta\) in the definition of the limit equal to the size of the derivative, so that the band around the derivative lies on one side of zero.

Lemma 1.82 Derivative at an interior extremum (odvod v notranjem ekstremu)

Let the function \(f\) be defined on an interval with end points \(a < b\) that is closed, open or half-open, and let it attain its largest or smallest value on this interval at a point \(x_0\) with \(a < x_0 < b\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\), then \(f'(x_0) = 0\).

Proof

First we treat the largest value, then we reduce the smallest value to it.

1. Largest value.

  1. By the definition of the maximum 1.70, \(f(y) \le f(x_0)\) for every point \(y\) of the interval.
  2. Let \(r\) be the smaller of the positive numbers \(x_0 - a\) and \(b - x_0\). For \(0 < |\Delta x| < r\) the point \(x_0 + \Delta x\) lies strictly between \(a\) and \(b\), hence in the interval, and by step 1, \(f(x_0 + \Delta x) - f(x_0) \le 0\).
  3. So the difference quotient \(q(\Delta x) = (f(x_0 + \Delta x) - f(x_0))/\Delta x\) is nonpositive for \(0 < \Delta x < r\), because we divide a nonpositive number by a positive one. For \(-r < \Delta x < 0\) it is nonnegative, because we divide a nonpositive number by a negative one.
  4. Suppose that \(f'(x_0) > 0\). The definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(\eta = f'(x_0)\) gives a band \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|q(\Delta x) - f'(x_0)| < f'(x_0)\) for every \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\). From the left half of the inequality \(-f'(x_0) < q(\Delta x) - f'(x_0) < f'(x_0)\) it follows that \(q(\Delta x) > 0\) for all such \(\Delta x\).
  5. Let \(\Delta x\) be half of the smaller of the numbers \(\delta\) and \(r\). This \(\Delta x\) is positive and smaller than both, so by step 4 \(q(\Delta x) > 0\), and by step 3 \(q(\Delta x) \le 0\). Both cannot hold, so \(f'(x_0) > 0\) is false.
  6. Suppose that \(f'(x_0) < 0\). The definition of the limit with the error \(\eta = -f'(x_0) > 0\) gives a band \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|q(\Delta x) - f'(x_0)| < -f'(x_0)\) for every \(\Delta x\) with \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\). From the right half of the inequality \(f'(x_0) < q(\Delta x) - f'(x_0) < -f'(x_0)\) it follows that \(q(\Delta x) < 0\) for all such \(\Delta x\).
  7. Let \(\Delta x\) be the negative of half of the smaller of the numbers \(\delta\) and \(r\). This \(\Delta x\) is negative and \(0 < |\Delta x| < \delta\), so by step 6 \(q(\Delta x) < 0\), and by step 3 \(q(\Delta x) \ge 0\). So \(f'(x_0) < 0\) is false too.
  8. What remains is \(f'(x_0) = 0\).

2. Smallest value.

  1. Let \(f\) attain its smallest value at \(x_0\), that is, \(f(y) \ge f(x_0)\) for every point \(y\) of the interval. Then \(-f(y) \le -f(x_0)\), and the function \(-f\), which assigns \(-f(t)\) to the number \(t\), attains its largest value at \(x_0\).
  2. The function \(f\) is defined on the open interval \((a, b)\), which contains \(x_0\). By lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, item 2 with \(c = -1\), \(-f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\) and \((-f)'(x_0) = -f'(x_0)\).
  3. By the first part of the proof \((-f)'(x_0) = 0\), so \(f'(x_0) = 0\).
