Source: LEBL1 Lemma 4.2.2 (PDF pp. 162-163), for an extremum that is the largest or smallest value only among the points close to \(x_0\). The source argues with sequences. The proof by direct use of the definition of the limit is not from the source.

The proof used points on both sides of \(x_0\), to the right in step 5 and to the left in step 7. At an end point of the interval there are no points on one side, and the lemma says nothing there. An example is the strain of a steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hanging under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) from the top downwards: \(\varepsilon(x) = 2a\,(L - x)\) on the interval \([0, L]\), where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) is not an end point of an interval but the number from the displacement of the bar. It is largest at the top, at \(x = 0\), where it is \(2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), because the top carries the whole bar. By the rules of differentiation the polynomial \(2aL - 2a\,x\), defined for all numbers, has the derivative \(-2a\) at every point. The function \(\varepsilon\) is defined only on \([0, L]\), so its derivative at \(x = 0\) is one-sided, a limit from the right (definition 1.9). A limit on both sides of zero is also a limit from the right (section 1.3.3), so this one-sided derivative equals \(-2a\), and it is not zero. The tangent at the largest value is horizontal only when that value is attained in the interior of the interval.

The converse is false too: a zero derivative does not yet mean an extremum. The function \(t^3\) has the derivative \(3 \cdot 0^2 = 0\) at \(0\), but on no interval around \(0\) does it have its largest or smallest value at \(0\), because it is negative to the left of \(0\) and positive to the right, for example \((-0{,}1)^3 = -0{,}001 < 0 < 0{,}001 = 0{,}1^3\) (LEBL1, PDF p. 166). The lemma only tells where an extremum can be: at a point where the derivative is zero, at a point where there is no derivative, and at an end point (LEBL1, PDF p. 163). The absolute value \(|x|\), for example, has its smallest value at \(0\), where it has no derivative.

1.14.4 Rolle's theorem

From history

Michel Rolle (1652 to 1719) looked for limits between which lie the places where the value of a polynomial is zero. His theorem did not arise from graphs but from equations. It is not yet in his Traité d'algèbre of 1690, it appears in his Méthode pour résoudre les égalités (Paris, 1691) (CAJORI, PDF p. 240). He transformed the polynomial and arranged it by powers, and equated the coefficients of the powers to zero. He called these equations cascades (kaskade). They are the derivative of the original polynomial, the derivative of the derivative and so on, each put equal to zero. He solved them from the lowest degree upward, which is very laborious (CAJORI, PDF p. 240-241). He started from a statement that in modern form reads: between two successive places where the derivative is zero there is no more than one place where the value of the polynomial is zero (CAJORI, PDF p. 241). This statement follows from another one: between two places where the value of the polynomial is zero lies a place where the derivative is zero, that is, a place with a horizontal tangent. If two places with value zero lay between successive places with derivative zero, there would have to be one more place with derivative zero between them, and the places would not be successive. At first Rolle rejected the differential calculus and held it to be a collection of ingenious fallacies (BALL, PDF p. 346), and he had a controversy about it with Pierre Varignon (CAJORI, PDF p. 236). He obtained the cascades, which are derivatives in content, by arranging in powers, that is, by algebra and not by calculus.

The statement about the horizontal tangent that Rolle used for polynomials we can now prove for a function that has the same value at both end points of an interval. Its graph begins and ends at the same height. If the function is not constant, somewhere in between it rises above this height or falls below it, and then it must come back. At the highest or lowest place in between the tangent is horizontal (figure 1.107). That the highest place exists is guaranteed by the extreme value theorem 1.73, and that the tangent is horizontal there by lemma 1.82 on the derivative at an interior extremum.

A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at each of its points (definition of continuity 1.58), and differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at each of its points, at an endpoint that belongs to the interval with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9). The theorem requires continuity on the closed interval because the extreme value theorem needs it, and a derivative only at the points between the end points because the lemma on the derivative at an interior extremum speaks only about them. The theorem does not need one-sided derivatives at the end points. But a function that is differentiable on the whole closed interval is also continuous on it by lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous, so both hypotheses hold for it.

Theorem 1.83 Rolle's theorem (Rolleov izrek)

Let the function \(f\) be continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\), and let \(f(a) = f(b)\). Then there is a point \(\xi \in (a, b)\) at which \(f'(\xi) = 0\).

Proof

We must show that \(f\) has a zero derivative at some point between \(a\) and \(b\). We will look for it among the points where \(f\) attains its largest and its smallest value.

  1. The function \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\), so by the extreme value theorem 1.73 there are points \(x_{\max}\) and \(x_{\min}\) in \([a, b]\) such that \(f(x_{\min}) \le f(y) \le f(x_{\max})\) for every \(y \in [a, b]\).
  2. Let \(K = f(a) = f(b)\). At least one of three cases holds: (A) there is a \(y \in [a, b]\) with \(f(y) > K\), (B) there is a \(y \in [a, b]\) with \(f(y) < K\), (C) \(f(y) = K\) for every \(y \in [a, b]\). Indeed, if neither (A) nor (B) holds, every value is at once at most \(K\) and at least \(K\), which is (C).
  3. Case (A). By step 1, \(f(x_{\max}) \ge f(y) > K\), so \(f(x_{\max})\) differs from \(f(a)\) and from \(f(b)\). So the point \(x_{\max}\) is neither \(a\) nor \(b\), but lies in \((a, b)\). There \(f\) is differentiable, and by lemma 1.82 on the derivative at an interior extremum \(f'(x_{\max}) = 0\). For \(\xi\) we take \(x_{\max}\).
  4. Case (B). By step 1, \(f(x_{\min}) \le f(y) < K\), so \(x_{\min}\) lies in \((a, b)\), and by the same lemma \(f'(x_{\min}) = 0\). For \(\xi\) we take \(x_{\min}\).
  5. Case (C). For \(\xi\) we take the midpoint \(\tfrac12(a + b)\). For \(0 < |\Delta x| < \tfrac12(b - a)\) the point \(\xi + \Delta x\) lies in \((a, b)\), the numerator of the difference quotient is \(K - K = 0\), and the quotient is \(0 + 0 \cdot \Delta x\). By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, \(f'(\xi) = 0\).
  6. In each of the cases we have found \(\xi \in (a, b)\) with \(f'(\xi) = 0\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 4.2.3 (PDF pp. 163-164).

From history

The name Rolle's theorem was first used by Moritz Wilhelm Drobisch in 1834 and by Giusto Bellavitis in 1846 (CAJORI, PDF p. 240).

Where does the completeness axiom enter the proof of Rolle's theorem? In step 1. The extreme value theorem rests on the supremum and on the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.57, and both rest on the completeness axiom. The other steps use only the arithmetic rules and the definition of the limit, which hold for fractions too. That we cannot do without the axiom is shown by the function \(g(t) = t^3 - t\) on the interval \([0, 1]\). The values at the end points are equal, \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g(1) = 1 - 1 = 0\). The function is a polynomial, so it is continuous by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions and differentiable by lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, with the derivative \(g'(t) = 3t^2 - 1\). The derivative is zero when \(t^2 = \tfrac13\). On \((0, 1)\) the only such point is \(\xi = 1/\sqrt 3 = 0{,}577\dots\), because by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, there is only one nonnegative number with the square \(\tfrac13\). This is the same point as in figure 1.50, and in section 1.8.1 we showed that it is not a fraction. If we knew only fractions, the function \(g\) would have the value \(0\) at both end points, but its derivative would be zero at no point. The conclusion of the theorem would be false, and since the other steps hold among fractions, the proof would break down exactly in step 1.

Among the real numbers the point \(\xi\) exists, and the proof finds it in case (B). The value there is

\[g(\xi) = \xi\,(\xi^2 - 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt 3} \cdot \Big({-\frac23}\Big) = -\frac{2\sqrt 3}{9} = -0{,}3849\dots ,\]

less than the value \(0\) at the end points. By the extreme value theorem, \(g\) attains a smallest value somewhere on \([0, 1]\). It is not at an end point, because \(g(\xi)\) is smaller than the values at the end points. So by the lemma on the derivative at an interior extremum it is at a point with zero derivative, and the only such point is \(\xi\).

Both hypotheses of the theorem are needed (figure 1.108). The first example is the absolute value \(|x|\) on the interval \([-1, 1]\), which has equal values at the end points, \(|-1| = |1| = 1\). For \(x > 0\) and \(0 < |\Delta x| < x\) we have \(x + \Delta x > 0\), so \(|x + \Delta x| - |x| = \Delta x\), the quotient is \(1\), and by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple the derivative is \(1\). In the same way the derivative is \(-1\) for \(x < 0\). At \(0\) there is no derivative, as we showed in section 1.14.1, but the function is continuous there. At every other point it is continuous by lemma 1.79, because it has a derivative there. So the function is continuous on \([-1, 1]\), but it has no point with zero derivative. The hypothesis that fails is differentiability at every point of \((-1, 1)\): the function attains its smallest value exactly at the corner, where the lemma on the derivative at an interior extremum says nothing. The second example is the function that equals \(x\) for \(0 \le x < 1\) and has the value \(0\) at \(1\). The values at the end points are equal, both \(0\), and at every point of \((0, 1)\) the derivative is \(1\). Again there is no point with zero derivative. Here continuity at the end point \(1\) fails: the values just left of \(1\) are close to \(1\), but the value at \(1\) is \(0\). So the function has no largest value on \([0, 1]\), and step 1 of the proof fails. Indeed, at every point \(m < 1\) the value \(m\) is smaller than the value \(\tfrac12(m + 1)\) at the point \(\tfrac12(m + 1)\), which lies between \(m\) and \(1\), and the value \(0\) at the point \(1\) is smaller than the value \(\tfrac12\) at the point \(\tfrac12\). Exactly such a jump is excluded by the requirement from section 1.7.3 that the function has no jump at the end points.

1.14.5 The mean value theorem

Rolle's theorem is a special case of the fact we are looking for. When \(f(a) = f(b)\), the straight line through the points of the graph above the end points is horizontal, and a point with a horizontal tangent is a point where the tangent is parallel to this line. But what if the line is tilted (figure 1.109)? The idea is to straighten it. From each value \(f(t)\) we subtract the height of the line above \(t\). What remains are the vertical distances between the graph and the line, which are zero at both end points (figure 1.110). Rolle's theorem holds for the new function, and the point where its tangent is horizontal is the point where the tangent of the old graph is parallel to the line.

The straight line through the points of the graph above \(a\) and above \(b\) has the slope

\[k = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} ,\]

and above the point \(t\) it is at the height \(\ell(t) = f(a) + k\,(t - a)\): at the point \(a\) at the height \(f(a)\), and every step to the right raises it by \(k\) times the length of the step.

Theorem 1.84 Mean value theorem (izrek o srednji vrednosti)

Let the function \(f\) be continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\). Then there is a point \(\xi \in (a, b)\) for which

\[f(b) - f(a) = f'(\xi)\,(b - a) . \tag{1.31}\]
Proof

We must show that at some point \(\xi\) the tangent has the slope \(k = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)\) of the straight line through the points of the graph above the end points. We subtract this line from \(f\) and use Rolle's theorem.

  1. Let \(\ell(t) = f(a) + k\,(t - a)\) be the height of the line above the point \(t\). At the end points \(\ell(a) = f(a) + k \cdot 0 = f(a)\) and \(\ell(b) = f(a) + k\,(b - a) = f(a) + \big(f(b) - f(a)\big) = f(b)\).
  2. Let \(g(t) = f(t) - \ell(t)\) for \(t \in [a, b]\). By step 1, \(g(a) = f(a) - f(a) = 0\) and \(g(b) = f(b) - f(b) = 0\).
  3. The function \(\ell\) is a polynomial, \(\ell(t) = (f(a) - k\,a) + k\,t\), so by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions it is continuous at every point. It is also continuous as a function on \([a, b]\), because the definition of continuity 1.58 on a smaller set checks only some of the same points. Since \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), by the same corollary the difference \(g = f + (-1)\,\ell\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) too.
  4. By lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, items 1, 2 and 4, \(\ell\) has the derivative \(0 + k \cdot 1 = k\) at every point.
  5. Let \(x \in (a, b)\). The functions \(f\) and \(\ell\) are defined on the open interval \((a, b)\) and differentiable at \(x\). By items 1 and 2 of the same lemma, \(g\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(g'(x) = f'(x) + (-1) \cdot k = f'(x) - k\).
  6. The function \(g\) satisfies the hypotheses of Rolle's theorem 1.83: it is continuous on \([a, b]\) by step 3, differentiable at every point of \((a, b)\) by step 5, and \(g(a) = g(b)\) by step 2. So there is a \(\xi \in (a, b)\) with \(g'(\xi) = 0\), that is, \(f'(\xi) - k = 0\) and \(f'(\xi) = k\).
  7. We multiply the equality \(f'(\xi) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)\) by \(b - a\) and get \(f(b) - f(a) = f'(\xi)\,(b - a)\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 4.2.4 (PDF pp. 164-165).

The quotient \((f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)\) is the average change of the function per unit change of \(t\) between \(a\) and \(b\), and the derivative is the change per unit just at a point. The theorem says that the average is attained at some point in between. Hence the name: the mean value here is the average. When driving a car, where \(f(t)\) is the distance travelled up to the time \(t\) (section 1.3.2), the theorem says that at some moment the car was going exactly at the average speed of the whole trip (LEBL1, PDF p. 165). The theorem is also called Lagrange's theorem (Lagrangeov izrek).

Now we can read the first fact of section 1.7.3 precisely. "A derivative at every point between two numbers" is differentiability at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\). "No jump at the end points" is continuity at \(a\) and at \(b\). Continuity at the points between \(a\) and \(b\) need not be required separately, because there the derivative guarantees it by lemma 1.79. Both hypotheses are needed, as the examples of figure 1.108 show, which are examples for this theorem too.

The theorem does not say where the point \(\xi\) is, only that it exists. Let us look at two examples where we can compute it. For \(f(t) = t^3\) on \([0, 1]\), \(k = (1 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1\), and from \(f'(\xi) = 3\xi^2 = 1\) it follows that \(\xi = 1/\sqrt 3 = 0{,}577\dots\), the point of figure 1.50. For this function the proof subtracted the line \(\ell(t) = t\) and got the function \(g(t) = t^3 - t\), which we met with Rolle's theorem (figure 1.110).

Next the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points from the top downwards, and the displacement of the point at depth \(x\) is \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 1.2). The displacement is a polynomial, so it satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem on every interval. For the whole bar, on \([0, L]\),

\[\frac{u(L) - u(0)}{L} = \frac{a\,(2L^2 - L^2) - 0}{L} = aL = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} .\]

This is the total elongation divided by the length, that is, the average strain \(\Delta L / L\) of section 1.2. The theorem says that it equals the strain \(u'(\xi) = 2a\,(L - \xi)\) at some point \(\xi\) of the bar. From \(2a\,(L - \xi) = aL\) it follows that \(L - \xi = L/2\), so \(\xi = L/2 = 5\) m (figure 1.111). We noticed this already in section 1.4: the average strain of the bar equals the strain at its middle.

The same holds for every piece. For the piece between \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\), by (1.6),

\[\frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} = a\,(2L - 2x - \Delta x) = 2a\,\Big(L - \big(x + \tfrac12 \Delta x\big)\Big) = u'\big(x + \tfrac12 \Delta x\big) ,\]

so \(\xi\) is always the middle of the piece. For the top piece of length 1 m the strain of the piece is \(3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the first number in the table of section 1.2, and this is the strain at the point \(x = 0{,}5\) m, \(2a\,(10 - 0{,}5)\ \text{m} = 19\ \text{m} \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} = 3{,}709 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Why exactly the middle? The strain \(2a\,(L - x)\) decreases evenly along the bar, by \(2a\) per metre, as the weight carried by a cross section does. So at a point some distance above the middle of the piece the strain is larger than the strain at the middle by as much as it is smaller at the point the same distance below the middle. In the average these differences cancel, and the value at the middle remains. For \(t^3\) the derivative \(3t^2\) does not grow evenly, and \(\xi = 0{,}577\dots\) is not the middle of the interval \([0, 1]\).

What does the theorem mean for strains? The strain of a piece, that is, its elongation divided by its length, is exactly the strain at some point of the piece, whenever the displacement satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem:

\[\frac{u(x + \Delta x) - u(x)}{\Delta x} = u'(\xi) \qquad \text{for some } \xi \text{ between } x \text{ and } x + \Delta x .\]

In section 1.2 we took the strain of a piece as an approximation of the strain just at the point \(x\), \(\varepsilon \approx (u(x + \Delta x) - u(x))/\Delta x\) ((1.2)). So this approximation is off only by the difference between the strains at \(\xi\) and at \(x\). The shorter the piece, the closer \(\xi\) is to \(x\). The theorem cannot be used, and its conclusion can fail, when the displacement has a jump in the piece, for example at a crack (razpoka), where the material is torn apart, or when at some point of the piece it has no derivative, as at the joint of two different materials.

1.14.6 Two consequences

The mean value theorem connects the change of a function over a whole interval with the derivative at one point. So what we know about the derivative at all points we can carry over to the change. Two consequences follow, which we will use often for strains.

The first answers the question from section 1.4. There we saw that a displacement that is the same for all points does not change the strain, and that therefore the displacement cannot be computed from the strain completely. Is this the only freedom? If two displacements of a bar have the same strain at every point, do they differ only by such a constant shift? A constant function is, as in lemma 1.81, item 4, a function that has the same value at all points.

Corollary 1.85 A function with zero derivative is constant (funkcija z ničelnim odvodom je stalna)

Let the function \(f\) be continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\), differentiable at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\), and let \(f'(t) = 0\) for every \(t \in (a, b)\). Then \(f(t) = f(a)\) for every \(t \in [a, b]\).

Proof

We must show that the value at every point \(t\) equals the value at \(a\). We use the mean value theorem on the interval \([a, t]\).

  1. For \(t = a\) there is nothing to prove. Let \(a < t \le b\).
  2. The function \(f\) is continuous on \([a, t]\). The definition of continuity 1.58 on the smaller set \([a, t]\) checks only some of the same points as on \([a, b]\), so the condition that holds on \([a, b]\) holds on \([a, t]\) too.
  3. The function \(f\) is differentiable at every point \(s \in (a, t)\) and \(f'(s) = 0\), because \(s\) also lies in \((a, b)\). The difference quotient at \(s\) uses only values at points close to \(s\), so the derivative is the same whether we regard \(f\) on \([a, b]\) or on \([a, t]\).
  4. By the mean value theorem 1.84 on the interval \([a, t]\) there is a \(\xi \in (a, t)\) such that \(f(t) - f(a) = f'(\xi)\,(t - a)\).
  5. The point \(\xi\) lies in \((a, b)\), so \(f'(\xi) = 0\), \(f(t) - f(a) = 0\) and \(f(t) = f(a)\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 4.2.6 (PDF p. 165), for a function that is differentiable on the whole interval.

Let us use it on a bar of length \(L\) with the axis \(x\) along the bar. Let \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) be two displacements, continuous on \([0, L]\), that have the same strain at every point \(x \in (0, L)\), \(u_1'(x) = u_2'(x)\). The difference \(f = u_1 + (-1)\,u_2\) is continuous on \([0, L]\) by corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions, and by lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, items 1 and 2, it has the derivative \(u_1'(x) - u_2'(x) = 0\) at every point \(x \in (0, L)\). By corollary 1.85 it is constant:

\[u_1(x) - u_2(x) = u_1(0) - u_2(0) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [0, L] .\]

So the two displacements differ only by the same shift of all points, by a rigid-body displacement along the bar. Once this shift is fixed, for example by the condition \(u(0) = 0\) for a fixed end, the strain determines the displacement exactly. For the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hanging under its own weight with its top fixed, \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) is therefore the only displacement with the strain \(2a\,(L - x)\) and with \(u(0) = 0\). A bar that has zero strain at every point does not deform, it only moves as a whole (figure 1.112, left). The argument does not need the strains at the ends of the bar, which are one-sided derivatives (definition 1.9), but it needs the displacements to be continuous at the ends. If the two displacements have the same strain at every point of \([0, L]\), the ends included, then by lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous they are continuous on \([0, L]\), and the corollary holds without a further assumption.

Continuity is essential here. Take a bar of length \(L\) lying on a table, with the axis \(x\) along it from the left end. The bar breaks at its middle, and we move the right part away by \(s\) without stretching it (figure 1.112, right). Each part moves as a whole, so the strain is zero at every point except at the break. But the distance between the ends of the bar has grown by \(s\). At the break the displacement has no single value, because the two faces of the break move differently, so the displacement is not a continuous function on \([0, L]\). The corollary does not hold here, because its hypothesis does not hold. Across a crack we cannot infer the displacements from the strains, and this is why we will assume that displacement fields have no jumps.

The second consequence bounds the change of a function when all we know about the derivative is that its size does not exceed some bound.

Corollary 1.86 Bounded derivative (omejen odvod)

Let the function \(f\) be continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of the open interval \((a, b)\), and let \(M\) be a number for which \(|f'(t)| \le M\) for every \(t \in (a, b)\). Then

\[|f(b) - f(a)| \le M\,(b - a) .\]
Proof

We must show that the size of the change is not larger than the bound of the derivative times the length of the interval.

  1. By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a \(\xi \in (a, b)\) such that \(f(b) - f(a) = f'(\xi)\,(b - a)\).
  2. The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, item 2), and \(b - a > 0\), so \(|f(b) - f(a)| = |f'(\xi)|\,(b - a)\).
  3. By the hypothesis \(|f'(\xi)| \le M\). We multiply this inequality by the positive number \(b - a\), which does not reverse it, and get \(|f'(\xi)|\,(b - a) \le M\,(b - a)\).
  4. By steps 2 and 3, \(|f(b) - f(a)| \le M\,(b - a)\).

Source: LEBL1 Exercise 4.2.3 (PDF p. 169), where the claim is left to the reader as an exercise, stated as Lipschitz continuity (LEBL1 Def. 3.4.7, PDF p. 141).

For a bar the corollary says: if the strain at every point of a piece is at most \(M\) in size, the piece gets longer or shorter by at most \(M\) times its length. For the steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hanging under its own weight the strain \(u'(x) = 2a\,(L - x)\) is at most \(M = 2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\). So the total elongation is at most

\[M\,L = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 10\ \text{m} = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m}\]

(figure 1.113). The actual elongation, \(u(L) = aL^2 = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, is half as large, because the strain is that large only at the top and falls evenly to zero towards the bottom. The estimate is rough, but it needs no displacement, only a bound on the strain. This is also how we will use the corollary: when we do not know the displacement exactly but know that its derivative is not too large.

With this the first fact from the end of section 1.7.3 is proved. The road to it led from the hole among the fractions through the completeness axiom, sequences and their subsequences to functions without jumps and their largest value. In the next section we return to the fibre. We will use the mean value theorem on each of the three steps along the axes and show that the remainder divided by the length of the fibre goes to zero for every field whose partial derivatives have no jumps.

1.15 The change of a field over a short step

Now we return to the fibre of section 1.7.3 and finish the work there. Let us recall where we stopped. A fibre between the points \(P\) and \(Q\) of a body changes under loading only by the difference of the displacements of its ends, \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\) ((1.15)). Let \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta x,\ y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y,\ z_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta z)\). We wrote the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the difference of displacements as the sum of three products of the partial derivatives at the point \(P\) with the components of the step \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\), and a remainder (ostanek) \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is everything that is left over:

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{x}}\]

((1.24)). For the hanging bar we computed the remainder exactly. It was a number times the square of the length of the fibre, so the remainder divided by the length of the fibre went to zero as we shortened the fibre. For a general field two facts were missing. The first is the mean value theorem 1.84 of section 1.14: if a function of one variable is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable at every point between its end points, its change between the end points equals the derivative at some point in between times the length of the interval. The second is an assumption about the field, which we can now state precisely: the partial derivatives exist at all points near \(P\) and are continuous at \(P\) (definition 1.67), so at points close enough to \(P\) they differ only a little from those at \(P\).

The goal of this section is to put both facts together into a theorem: for every field with such partial derivatives the remainder is small compared with the length of the step. The route is this. First we say precisely what "small compared with the length of the step" means. Then we carry the mean value theorem over to a step along one axis and use it to prove the theorem. We test the theorem on the hanging bar, where we know the remainder, and on a field with kinks, where the assumptions fail and so does the conclusion. From this we get the assumption that we will make for displacement fields from now on, and we say what it means physically and where it fails. Finally we use the theorem for all three components of the displacement and for a fibre in any direction. Strain in space will be built on this result.

1.15.1 When the remainder is small

What should it mean that the remainder is small? It is not enough that it goes to zero as we shorten the step. The remainder is the difference

\[R_{\mathrm{x}} = \big(u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\big) - \Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z\Big) .\]

If \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous at \(P\), the first bracket already goes to zero (definition 1.67), and so does the second, because every component of the step goes to zero. So the remainder of every such field goes to zero, and that tells us nothing. What matters is how fast it goes to zero compared with the step. The three products in the second bracket are proportional to the length of the step: for a step half as long in the same direction they are half as large. If the remainder were also proportional to the length of the step, it would be comparable with them for every step, and the sum of the three products would not be a good approximation of the change, not even for a very short step. So the remainder must shrink faster than the step: divided by the length of the step, it must go to zero. This is exactly what we need for strain, which is a difference of displacements divided by the length of the fibre. For the hanging bar we saw in section 1.7.3 how this works: for a fibre ten times shorter the part with the partial derivatives was ten times smaller, but the remainder a hundred times smaller.

Let us write this precisely for any function. Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, that is, a function whose input is the three coordinates of a point and whose output is one number, for example one of the components of the displacement. A function that assigns a number or a vector to every point of some part of space is also called a field (polje), just as we called the rule that assigns to every point of a body its displacement vector the displacement field (definition 1.23). The step from \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) to \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta x,\ y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y,\ z_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta z)\) has the length

\[|PQ| = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2} ,\]

the distance between the points from definition 1.17. The remainder \(R(Q)\) is the number that is left when we subtract from the change \(f(Q) - f(P)\) the three products of the partial derivatives at \(P\) with the components of the step. It depends on the point \(Q\), that is, on the three numbers \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\).

We would like to say that the quotient \(R(Q)/|PQ|\) goes to zero as \(Q\) goes to \(P\). But we defined the limit only for functions of one number \(h\) (definition 1.5), while the point \(Q\) can approach \(P\) from all directions. So we write the requirement directly with an error \(\eta\) and a band \(\delta\), as in the definition of the limit: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|PQ| \quad \text{for every point } Q \text{ with } 0 < |PQ| < \delta . \tag{1.32}\]

The number \(\eta\) is the allowed error per unit length of the step. With \(\eta = 10^{-10}\) and a step of length 1 mm the remainder may be at most \(10^{-10} \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 10^{-13}\) m. We divide the inequality by the positive number \(|PQ|\), which does not reverse it, and get \(|R(Q)|/|PQ| \le \eta\). So the quotient differs from zero by at most \(\eta\) at every point \(Q\) whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(\delta\) but which is not \(P\) itself. This is the pattern of the definition of the limit, where \(g(h)\) differed from \(d\) by less than \(\eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\). That we write \(\le\) instead of \(<\) does not matter: if we satisfy the requirement with the error \(\eta/2\), then \(|R(Q)|/|PQ| \le \eta/2 < \eta\).

Figure 1.114 shows what the requirement means. For every point \(Q\) near \(P\) let us draw a dot whose horizontal coordinate is the length of the step \(|PQ|\) and whose vertical coordinate is the size of the remainder \(|R(Q)|\). The line \(\eta\,|PQ|\) passes through the origin, and the part of the plane below it gets lower the closer we are to the origin. The requirement says that the dots of all points \(Q\) closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\) lie below this line. A smaller \(\eta\) gives a flatter line. The allowed error is smaller, so as a rule we must shorten the step more, and \(\delta\) is smaller.

1.15.2 A step along one axis

We will estimate the remainder as in section 1.7.3: we split the step from \(P\) to \(Q\) into three steps along the axes. Each changes only one coordinate, so along it the field is a function of one variable, for which the mean value theorem holds. We write a step with a point to which we add a vector (section 1.5.3). For a point \(S = (x_{\mathrm{S}}, y_{\mathrm{S}}, z_{\mathrm{S}})\) and a number \(t\),

\[S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}} + t,\ z_{\mathrm{S}})\]

is the point we reach from \(S\) by a step \(t\) in the direction of the axis \(y\), where \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (0, 1, 0)\) is the unit vector of the axis \(y\) (definition 1.20). For \(t < 0\) we step the opposite way.

What does the mean value theorem say about such a step? The values of the field at the points of the step are described by the function \(g(t) = f(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\). Its input is one number \(t\), how far we have stepped from \(S\) in the direction of the axis \(y\), and its output is the value of the field at the point we have reached. Along the step only the coordinate \(y\) changes, so the derivative of the function \(g\) is the partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(y\). The mean value theorem therefore says that the change of the field over the step equals the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) at some point of the step times the component of the step \(\Delta y\) (figure 1.115).

Lemma 1.87 Change over a step along an axis (sprememba na koraku vzdolž osi)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, \(S = (x_{\mathrm{S}}, y_{\mathrm{S}}, z_{\mathrm{S}})\) a point and \(\Delta y \neq 0\) a number. Suppose that the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y\) exists at every point \(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = (x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}} + t,\ z_{\mathrm{S}})\) with \(t\) in the closed interval with the end points \(0\) and \(\Delta y\), that is, in \([0, \Delta y]\) for \(\Delta y > 0\) and in \([\Delta y, 0]\) for \(\Delta y < 0\). Then there is a number \(\xi\) strictly between \(0\) and \(\Delta y\) such that

\[f(S + \Delta y\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) - f(S) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(S + \xi\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\,\Delta y . \tag{1.33}\]

The same holds for a step \(\Delta x \neq 0\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) with the partial derivative with respect to \(x\), and for a step \(\Delta z \neq 0\) in the direction of the axis \(z\) with the partial derivative with respect to \(z\).

Proof

We must show that a number \(\xi\) with this property exists. We denote the closed interval with the end points \(0\) and \(\Delta y\) by \(I\).

  1. For every \(t\) for which the point \(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) is in the domain of the function \(f\), let \(g(t) = f(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = f(x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}} + t,\ z_{\mathrm{S}})\). This is a function of one variable.
  2. Let \(t\) be in \(I\). By assumption the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y\) exists at the point \(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). By the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, \(f\) is therefore defined at all points whose distance from this point is less than some number \(r_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\). Among them are the points \(S + (t + s)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(|s| < r_{\mathrm{t}}\), since their distance from \(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) is \(|s|\). So the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers \(t + s\) with \(|s| < r_{\mathrm{t}}\).
  3. The difference quotient of the function \(g\) at \(t\) is
    \[\frac{g(t + s) - g(t)}{s} = \frac{f(x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}} + t + s,\ z_{\mathrm{S}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}} + t,\ z_{\mathrm{S}})}{s} .\]
    This is the quotient from the second line of (1.19) at the point \(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), except that we write the change as \(s\) instead of \(\Delta y\). So its limit as \(s\) goes to zero exists and is the partial derivative at this point. By the definition of the derivative 1.9, \(g\) is differentiable at \(t\) and
    \[g'(t) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(S + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) .\]
  4. Let \(t\) be in \(I\). By step 2, \(g\) is defined on the open interval \((t - r_{\mathrm{t}}, t + r_{\mathrm{t}})\), and by step 3 it is differentiable at \(t\). By lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, it is therefore continuous at \(t\) as a function on this interval. The condition of the definition of continuity 1.58 for the function on the set \(I\) asks for less, since we check it only at the numbers in \(I\), and those among them whose distance from \(t\) is less than \(r_{\mathrm{t}}\) all lie in the interval \((t - r_{\mathrm{t}}, t + r_{\mathrm{t}})\). If we reduce the band \(\delta\) from the continuity on this interval to \(r_{\mathrm{t}}\) where needed, the condition also holds on \(I\). So \(g\) is continuous at every point of \(I\), that is, continuous on \(I\).
  5. By step 3, \(g\) is differentiable at every point strictly between the end points of the interval \(I\).
  6. Let \(\Delta y > 0\), so \(I = [0, \Delta y]\). By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a \(\xi\) strictly between \(0\) and \(\Delta y\) such that \(g(\Delta y) - g(0) = g'(\xi)\,(\Delta y - 0) = g'(\xi)\,\Delta y\).
  7. Let \(\Delta y < 0\), so \(I = [\Delta y, 0]\). By the same theorem there is a \(\xi\) strictly between \(\Delta y\) and \(0\) such that \(g(0) - g(\Delta y) = g'(\xi)\,(0 - \Delta y)\). We multiply both sides by \(-1\) and get \(g(\Delta y) - g(0) = g'(\xi)\,\Delta y\), the same equality as in step 6.
  8. Into the equality of step 6 or 7 we put \(g(\Delta y) = f(S + \Delta y\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\), \(g(0) = f(S)\) and \(g'(\xi)\) from step 3. We get (1.33).
  9. For a step in the direction of the axis \(x\) we take \(g(t) = f(x_{\mathrm{S}} + t,\ y_{\mathrm{S}},\ z_{\mathrm{S}})\), for a step in the direction of the axis \(z\) we take \(g(t) = f(x_{\mathrm{S}},\ y_{\mathrm{S}},\ z_{\mathrm{S}} + t)\), and we repeat steps 1 to 8 with the first or the third line of (1.19).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF p. 49) uses the mean value theorem on a step along one axis in the same way. As a separate statement the lemma is not from the source.

The lemma does not say where on the step the point \(S + \xi\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) lies, only that it exists and lies on the step. For us this will be enough, because every point of a short step will be close to the point \(P\).

1.15.3 The theorem on the change of a field

Now we can write the theorem. Before it, let us state the idea of the proof (figure 1.116). We go from \(P\) to \(Q\) in three steps along the axes, through the points \(A = P + \Delta x\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(B = A + \Delta y\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), as in section 1.7.3. By lemma 1.87 on the change over a step along an axis, the change of the field over the first step equals the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) at some point \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the first step times \(\Delta x\), and likewise over the second and third steps with the points \(T_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{z}}\). So three differences are left in the remainder: the partial derivative at an intermediate point minus the partial derivative at \(P\), times a component of the step. The intermediate points lie on the path from \(P\) to \(Q\), so they are not farther from \(P\) than \(Q\). For a short step they are close to \(P\), and the continuity of the partial derivatives at \(P\) makes the differences small. Each difference is multiplied by a component of the step, which is not longer than the step, so the remainder is small compared with the step.

Theorem 1.88 Change of a field over a short step (sprememba polja na kratkem koraku)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) a point and \(r > 0\) a number such that \(f\) is defined at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\). Suppose that at each of these points all three partial derivatives \(\partial f/\partial x\), \(\partial f/\partial y\), \(\partial f/\partial z\) exist (definition 1.25) and that all three are continuous at the point \(P\) (definition 1.67). For a point \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta x,\ y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y,\ z_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta z)\) with \(|PQ| < r\) let the remainder \(R(Q)\) be the number determined by the equality

\[f(Q) - f(P) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R(Q) . \tag{1.34}\]

Then for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta\) with \(0 < \delta \le r\) such that \(|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|PQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\).

Proof

We must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta\) with \(0 < \delta \le r\) such that \(|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|PQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\).

  1. We choose any error \(\eta > 0\). For it we must find a band \(\delta\).
  2. The partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) is a function that is defined at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\), and it is continuous at \(P\). We write the definition of continuity 1.67 for it with the error \(\eta/3\): there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}} > 0\) such that
    \[\Big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(T) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{3}\]
    for every point \(T\) whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) and less than \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\). We take a third of the error because in step 12 we will add three such errors. In the same way we get a band \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\) for \(\partial f/\partial y\) and a band \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\) for \(\partial f/\partial z\).
  3. As the band \(\delta\) we take the smallest of the four positive numbers \(r\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\), which is positive and not larger than \(r\). Let \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta x,\ y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y,\ z_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta z)\) be any point with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\). We must show that \(|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|PQ|\).
  4. No component of the step is longer than the step. We have \(\Delta x^2 \le \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2 = |PQ|^2\), so by lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|\Delta x| \le |PQ|\). Likewise \(|\Delta y| \le |PQ|\) and \(|\Delta z| \le |PQ|\).
  5. We go from \(P\) to \(Q\) in three steps along the axes, through the points \(A = P + \Delta x\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(B = A + \Delta y\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the last step takes us to \(Q = B + \Delta z\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). No point of this path is farther from \(P\) than \(Q\). The point \(P + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(t\) between \(0\) and \(\Delta x\) has the distance \(|t| \le |\Delta x| \le |PQ|\) from \(P\). The point \(A + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(t\) between \(0\) and \(\Delta y\) has the distance \(\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + t^2}\) from \(P\). Since \(|t| \le |\Delta y|\), by the same lemma \(t^2 \le \Delta y^2\), so \(\Delta x^2 + t^2 \le |PQ|^2\) and the distance is at most \(|PQ|\). Likewise the point \(B + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) with \(t\) between \(0\) and \(\Delta z\) has the distance \(\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + t^2} \le |PQ|\) from \(P\). Since \(|PQ| < \delta \le r\), all points of the path are at a distance less than \(r\) and less than \(\delta\) from \(P\). At them \(f\) is defined and all three partial derivatives exist.
  6. Equality (1.22) holds for every function defined at the points \(P\), \(A\), \(B\) and \(Q\). For \(f\) it reads
    \[f(Q) - f(P) = \big(f(A) - f(P)\big) + \big(f(B) - f(A)\big) + \big(f(Q) - f(B)\big) .\]
  7. The first bracket is the change over the step \(\Delta x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) from the point \(P\). Let \(\Delta x \neq 0\). By step 5 the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) exists at every point \(P + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(t\) in the closed interval with the end points \(0\) and \(\Delta x\). By lemma 1.87 on the change over a step along an axis there is therefore a number \(\xi_{\mathrm{x}}\) strictly between \(0\) and \(\Delta x\) such that for the point \(T_{\mathrm{x}} = P + \xi_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\)
    \[f(A) - f(P) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(T_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta x .\]
    If \(\Delta x = 0\), then \(A = P\) and both sides are zero, so the equality holds with \(T_{\mathrm{x}} = P\).
  8. In the same way we get the second bracket, the step \(\Delta y\) from the point \(A\), and the third, the step \(\Delta z\) from the point \(B\). There are points \(T_{\mathrm{y}} = A + \xi_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{z}} = B + \xi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) on the path such that
    \[f(B) - f(A) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(T_{\mathrm{y}})\,\Delta y , \qquad f(Q) - f(B) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(T_{\mathrm{z}})\,\Delta z .\]
  9. From (1.34) we express the remainder by moving the three products to the left side:
    \[R(Q) = f(Q) - f(P) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y - \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z .\]
  10. In place of \(f(Q) - f(P)\) we put the sum of step 6, with the brackets written as in steps 7 and 8, and we group the terms with the same component of the step:
    \[R(Q) = \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(T_{\mathrm{x}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P)\Big)\Delta x + \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(T_{\mathrm{y}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P)\Big)\Delta y + \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(T_{\mathrm{z}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P)\Big)\Delta z .\]
  11. The points \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{z}}\) lie on the path, so by step 5 their distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) and less than \(\delta\), and \(\delta\) is not larger than any of the bands \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\). By step 2 each of the three brackets in step 10 is therefore less than \(\eta/3\) in absolute value.
  12. By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\), used twice, and because the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, items 1 and 2),
    \[|R(Q)| \le \frac{\eta}{3}\,|\Delta x| + \frac{\eta}{3}\,|\Delta y| + \frac{\eta}{3}\,|\Delta z| .\]
    We write a non-strict inequality because one of the components of the step may be zero.
  13. By step 4 none of the numbers \(|\Delta x|\), \(|\Delta y|\), \(|\Delta z|\) is larger than \(|PQ|\), so
    \[|R(Q)| \le 3 \cdot \frac{\eta}{3}\,|PQ| = \eta\,|PQ| .\]
  14. We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily and found for it a band \(\delta\) that works for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\). This is what we had to show.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF pp. 48-49), for functions of \(n\) variables on an open set, where the partial derivatives are continuous at every point. The source adds the steps along the axes by induction on the number of variables and on each one uses the mean value theorem and the continuity of the partial derivatives at the point, as we do. Since continuity is used only at the point \(P\), continuity at \(P\) is enough. The form with \(\eta\) and \(\delta\) instead of a limit is not from the source.

Figure 1.117 shows steps 5 and 11 of the proof for a step in the plane \(z = z_{\mathrm{P}}\), where \(\Delta z = 0\) and the path consists of two steps. As we go along the path from \(P\) toward \(Q\), the distance from \(P\) only grows. On the first step it is \(|t|\), on the second \(\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + t^2}\), where \(|t|\) grows from \(0\) to \(|\Delta y|\), and at the end it is \(|PQ|\). So the whole path lies in the disc with the centre \(P\) and the radius \(|PQ|\). If \(|PQ|\) is smaller than the band \(\delta\), the points \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{y}}\) are also closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\), and the partial derivatives at them differ from those at \(P\) by less than \(\eta/3\).

The proof showed where we need which assumption. We needed the existence of the partial derivatives at all points near \(P\) in steps 7 and 8, so that we could use the lemma on the change over a step along an axis, and with it the mean value theorem, on each step. We needed continuity at \(P\) in step 11, so that the partial derivatives at the intermediate points are close to those at \(P\). The proof needs no other derivatives. We will meet both moves again several times: the mean value theorem on a step along an axis, and continuity at a point.

What does the theorem mean? For a short step the change of the field equals the sum of the three products of the partial derivatives at \(P\) with the components of the step, up to an error that is only a small part of the length of the step. So three partial derivatives at a single point \(P\) determine how the field changes over every short step in any direction, even though we computed them only along the three axes. The theorem does not say, though, how short the step must be. The band \(\delta\) depends on how fast the partial derivatives change around \(P\): where they change fast, the step must be very short. The theorem cannot be used at points around which not all points closer than some number \(r\) are available, for example on the surface of a body, nor at points where the partial derivatives are not continuous. What goes wrong there we show in section 1.15.5.

The theorem and its proof hold for functions of any number of variables, only there are as many steps along the axes as there are variables (LEBL2 Prop. 8.4.6, PDF pp. 48-49). The property that the theorem proves has its own name in the books. A function is differentiable (odvedljiva) at the point \(P\) if there are three numbers which, used in (1.34) in place of the partial derivatives, give a remainder that is small in the sense of (1.32) (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.1, PDF p. 35). For a function of one variable this is the same as differentiability in the sense of definition 1.9, as LEBL2 shows on the same page. So the theorem says that a function with continuous partial derivatives is differentiable. The mere existence of the partial derivatives is not enough for this (LEBL2, PDF p. 48), as we will see in an example.

1.15.4 A test on the hanging bar

Let us test the theorem on a field whose remainder we know exactly. Take the steel hanging bar of section 1.7.1. It is \(L = 10\) m long, has a round cross section with a diameter of 10 mm and stretches under its own weight. In the model its field comes from, only the point \(O\) at the centre of the top face is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face, which is an idealization. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie horizontally. The displacement field is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

where \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) and the number \(0{,}3\) is the ratio of thinning to stretching of steel.

First we check the assumptions of the theorem at the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\). The point is an interior point: its distance from the surface of the bar is 1 mm, so all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r = 1\) mm are in the bar (section 1.7.2). The formulas of the field are sums of products of numbers and coordinates, so we can evaluate them at every point. The computations of the partial derivatives in section 1.7.2 used only these formulas, so they hold at every point where we use the formulas, also at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\). We got:

w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(2a\,(L - x)\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0\)
\(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) \(0{,}6\,a\,z\) \(0\) \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\)

So all nine exist at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\). All of them are polynomials in \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), that is, sums of products of numbers and coordinates. By corollary 1.69 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space, item 2, they are therefore continuous at every point, also at \(P\). Of course the formulas have a physical meaning only in the bar. Theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step therefore holds for all three components: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that the remainder of every step shorter than \(\delta\) is at most \(\eta\) times its length.

The theorem only says that such a \(\delta\) exists. For the hanging bar we can compute it, because we know the remainders from section 1.7.3:

\[R_{\mathrm{x}} = -a\,\Delta x^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta y^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,\Delta z^2 , \qquad R_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta y , \qquad R_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\,\Delta z .\]

Let us estimate them by the length of the step \(|PQ|\).

  1. The number \(a\) is positive, so none of the three terms of \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\) is positive, and \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| = a\,(\Delta x^2 + 0{,}3\,\Delta y^2 + 0{,}3\,\Delta z^2)\).
  2. Squares are not negative and \(0{,}3 < 1\), so \(0{,}3\,\Delta y^2 \le \Delta y^2\) and \(0{,}3\,\Delta z^2 \le \Delta z^2\). Hence \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le a\,(\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2) = a\,|PQ|^2\).
  3. No component of the step is longer than the step (step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.88), so \(|R_{\mathrm{y}}| = 0{,}6\,a\,|\Delta x|\,|\Delta y| \le 0{,}6\,a\,|PQ|^2 \le a\,|PQ|^2\). Likewise \(|R_{\mathrm{z}}| \le a\,|PQ|^2\).
  4. So all three remainders are at most \(a\,|PQ| \cdot |PQ|\). If \(|PQ| < \eta/a\), then \(a\,|PQ| < \eta\), and the remainders are at most \(\eta\,|PQ|\).
  5. As the band \(\delta\) we therefore take the smaller of the numbers \(\eta/a\) and \(r\). For every step shorter than \(\delta\) each of the three remainders is at most \(\eta\,|PQ|\).

For \(\eta = 10^{-10}\),

\[\frac{\eta}{a} = \frac{10^{-10}}{1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}} = 5{,}123 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m} ,\]

about \(0{,}51\) mm, which is less than \(r = 1\) mm. So every fibre from \(P\) shorter than \(0{,}51\) mm has, in any direction, remainders that are at most a ten-billionth of its length.

Let us check this on the fibre from the table of section 1.7.3, which points from \(P\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\). For the length \(0{,}1\) mm we had \(R_{\mathrm{x}} = -7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-16}\) m, while the limit \(\eta\,|PQ|\) is \(10^{-10} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 10^{-14}\) m. The remainder is more than ten times below the limit. For the length 1 mm, \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| = 7{,}374 \cdot 10^{-14}\) m, and the limit is \(10^{-13}\) m. This fibre is below the limit too, although it is longer than \(0{,}51\) mm (figure 1.118). So the band we got from the estimate \(a\,|PQ|^2\) is not the largest possible one. The estimate holds for all directions at once, while in the direction \(\vek n\) the remainder is smaller. A fibre of length \(h\) has the components \(\Delta x = h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta y = h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\Delta z = h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), so

\[\begin{aligned} |R_{\mathrm{x}}| &= a\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + 0{,}3\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\big)\,h^2 \\ &= a\,\Big(\frac19 + 0{,}3 \cdot \frac49 + 0{,}3 \cdot \frac49\Big)\,h^2 = \frac{3{,}4}{9}\,a\,h^2 = 0{,}3778\,a\,h^2 . \end{aligned}\]

Requirement (1.32) does not look for the largest band, one band that works is enough.

For the bar the remainder is at most \(a\,|PQ|^2\), so it is proportional to the square of the length of the step. This is more than the theorem promises. For a general field the theorem only guarantees that the remainder is smaller than every fraction \(\eta\) of the length of the step if the step is short enough, not that it is proportional to the square. For the bar the estimate with the square held because the components of its field are sums of terms with at most two coordinate factors, as we saw in section 1.7.3.

1.15.5 A field with kinks

Are the two assumptions of the theorem really needed? Perhaps it would be enough for the partial derivatives to exist only at the point \(P\) itself, since only values at \(P\) appear in equality (1.34). The next example shows that it is not. In section 1.12 we already saw a function that has all three partial derivatives at \(O\) but is not even continuous at \(O\). The field we take now is continuous at \(O\), and still the remainder is not small. We built the example ourselves, while LEBL2 (PDF p. 48) states that the existence of the partial derivatives without their continuity is not enough. Take the field

\[f(x, y, z) = |x + y| - |x - y| \tag{1.35}\]

and the point \(P = O = (0, 0, 0)\). The field is continuous at \(O\), since \(f(O) = 0\) and by the triangle inequality for numbers \(|f(Q)| \le |x + y| + |x - y| \le 2\,|x| + 2\,|y| \le 4\,|OQ|\), which is less than \(\eta\) whenever \(|OQ| < \eta/4\). The field does not depend on \(z\), so it is enough to look at it in the plane \(z = 0\). Let us see what it is in the part of the plane where \(x > |y|\), that is, between the lines \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\) on the side where \(x\) is positive. There \(x + y\) and \(x - y\) are positive, because \(x\) is larger than \(y\) and than \(-y\). So \(|x + y| = x + y\) and \(|x - y| = x - y\), and

\[f = (x + y) - (x - y) = 2y .\]

In the same way we get \(f = 2x\) where \(y > |x|\), \(f = -2y\) where \(x < -|y|\), and \(f = -2x\) where \(y < -|x|\). In each of the four parts the graph of the field is a plane. Together they form a roof of four flat triangles that meet along the lines \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\) (figure 1.119). There the graph breaks, just as two sides of a roof meet at the ridge or in the valley. Such a place is called a kink (pregib).

The partial derivatives at \(O\) exist. On the axis \(x\) we have \(f(\Delta x, 0, 0) = |\Delta x| - |\Delta x| = 0\) for every \(\Delta x\). So the difference quotient with respect to \(x\) is zero for every \(\Delta x \neq 0\), and by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple with \(d = 0\) and \(c = 0\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(O) = 0\). Likewise \(f(0, \Delta y, 0) = |\Delta y| - |{-\Delta y}| = 0\), so \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(O) = 0\), and the field does not depend on \(z\), so \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(O) = 0\). Along all three axes the field is zero. Since also \(f(O) = 0\), equality (1.34) at the point \(O\) says

\[f(Q) - 0 = 0 \cdot \Delta x + 0 \cdot \Delta y + 0 \cdot \Delta z + R(Q) , \qquad \text{so} \qquad R(Q) = f(Q) .\]

Now let us step from \(O\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45, 0)\), which has the length \(\sqrt{9/25 + 16/25 + 0} = 1\). The point \(Q = O + h\,\vek n = (\tfrac35 h,\ \tfrac45 h,\ 0)\) has the distance \(|h|\) from \(O\), and

\[f(Q) = \Big|\tfrac35 h + \tfrac45 h\Big| - \Big|\tfrac35 h - \tfrac45 h\Big| = \tfrac75\,|h| - \tfrac15\,|h| = \tfrac65\,|h| .\]

So the remainder is \(R(Q) = \tfrac65\,|OQ|\) for every \(h \neq 0\), no matter how short the step is. The quotient \(R(Q)/|OQ| = \tfrac65\) does not go to zero. Requirement (1.32) fails for every \(\eta < \tfrac65\): in every band \(\delta\) there are points \(Q\) on this line with \(|R(Q)| = \tfrac65\,|OQ| > \eta\,|OQ|\) (figure 1.120). The sum of the three products predicts that the field does not change over a step from \(O\), but in fact over a step in the direction \(\vek n\) it changes by \(\tfrac65\) of the length of the step.

Which assumption of the theorem fails? Let us look at the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) near \(O\).

  1. Let \(t > 0\) and take the point \((t, 0, 0)\) on the axis \(x\). For every \(s\) with \(0 < |s| < t\) the point \((t, s, 0)\) lies in the part where \(x > |y|\), because \(t > |s|\). There \(f = 2y\), so \(f(t, s, 0) = 2s\), while \(f(t, 0, 0) = 0\).
  2. So the difference quotient with respect to \(y\) at the point \((t, 0, 0)\) is \((2s - 0)/s = 2\) for every such \(s\). By lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple with \(d = 2\) and \(c = 0\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(t, 0, 0) = 2\).
  3. The point \((t, 0, 0)\) has the distance \(t\) from \(O\). So for every \(\delta > 0\) there are points \((t, 0, 0)\) with \(0 < t < \delta\), whose distance from \(O\) is less than \(\delta\), and the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) is \(2\) at them but \(0\) at \(O\). For the error \(\eta = 1\) the condition of the definition of continuity 1.67 fails for every \(\delta\), and the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) is not continuous at \(O\).

Existence also fails at some points near \(O\). Take the point \((t, t, 0)\) with \(t > 0\) on the line \(y = x\), where \(f = 2t\). A step \(s > 0\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) takes us into the part where \(y > |x|\) and \(f = 2x = 2t\), so the quotient with respect to \(y\) is \((2t - 2t)/s = 0\). A step \(s < 0\) with \(|s| < 2t\) takes us into the part where \(x > |y|\) and \(f = 2y = 2(t + s)\), so the quotient is \((2t + 2s - 2t)/s = 2\). If the quotient approached some number \(d\), then for the error \(1\) and small \(s\) we would have \(|0 - d| < 1\) and \(|2 - d| < 1\), and by the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) \(2 = |2 - 0| \le |2 - d| + |d - 0| < 2\), which is impossible. So the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) does not exist at the point \((t, t, 0)\). This is the kink.

This is exactly where the proof of the theorem would break down. For the step from \(O\) to \(Q = (\tfrac35 h,\ \tfrac45 h,\ 0)\) with \(h > 0\) the path goes through the point \(A = (\tfrac35 h, 0, 0)\), and the second step, from \(A\) to \(Q\), changes \(y\) from \(0\) to \(\tfrac45 h\). Up to the line \(y = x\), at \(y = \tfrac35 h\), it lies in the part where \(f = 2y\) and the partial derivative with respect to \(y\) is \(2\). Beyond it, it lies in the part where \(f = 2x = \tfrac65 h\) is constant. So the change over this step is \(2 \cdot \tfrac35 h = \tfrac65 h\), and all of it comes from the partial derivative \(2\), which differs from the value \(0\) at \(O\) however short the step is. This is the difference that continuity at \(P\) bounded in step 11 of the proof.

The example shows why the theorem needs its assumptions. The partial derivatives at a point \(P\) look only along the three axes. The theorem uses them to predict the change in all other directions, and this works only if the field does not break anywhere around \(P\). For a displacement field a kink means that the rate at which the displacement changes, from which we will compute the strain, jumps from one value on one side of a line or a surface to another value on the other side. Where this happens in bodies we look at in the next part.

1.15.6 Continuously differentiable fields

For bodies we will make the assumptions of the theorem in advance, for all interior points at once. Recall from section 1.7.2: a point is an interior point of a body if there is still some material around it in all directions, that is, if there is a number \(r > 0\) such that all points whose distance from it is less than \(r\) are in the body. We speak in the same way of the interior points of any set of points. In the hanging bar the point \(P\) was an interior point with \(r = 1\) mm, while a point on the surface is not an interior point, because every ball around it, however small, reaches out of the body (figure 1.121).

We will make the requirement on the displacement field on the set of all interior points of the body. For the theorem to be usable at each of them we need one more property: all points close enough to an interior point are interior points too. For a point with \(r = 1\) mm we expect this, since a point only \(0{,}1\) mm away from it is still quite far from the surface. Let us show that this holds in general.

Lemma 1.89 Neighbourhood of an interior point (okolica notranje točke)

Let \(M\) be a set of points and \(P\) an interior point of it, such that all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r > 0\) are in \(M\). Then every point \(S\) whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r/4\) is also an interior point of the set \(M\): all points whose distance from \(S\) is less than \(r/4\) are in \(M\).

Proof

We must show that every point \(T\) with \(|ST| < r/4\) has a distance less than \(r\) from \(P\), since it is then in \(M\).

  1. Let \(|PS| < r/4\) and \(|ST| < r/4\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1)
    \[|x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}| = |(x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{S}}) + (x_{\mathrm{S}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})| \le |x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{S}}| + |x_{\mathrm{S}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}| .\]
  2. No difference of coordinates is larger than the distance: \(|x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{S}}| \le |ST|\) and \(|x_{\mathrm{S}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}| \le |PS|\), as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.88. By step 1, therefore, \(|x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}| < \tfrac{r}{4} + \tfrac{r}{4} = \tfrac{r}{2}\). Likewise \(|y_{\mathrm{T}} - y_{\mathrm{P}}| < r/2\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{T}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}| < r/2\).
  3. By lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, each square of a difference of coordinates is less than \(r^2/4\), so
    \[|PT|^2 = (x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})^2 + (y_{\mathrm{T}} - y_{\mathrm{P}})^2 + (z_{\mathrm{T}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})^2 < 3 \cdot \frac{r^2}{4} < r^2 .\]
  4. By the same lemma \(|PT| < r\), so \(T\) is in \(M\). We chose the point \(T\) arbitrarily, so \(S\) is an interior point of the set \(M\).

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

Why exactly \(r/4\)? The point \(T\) is less than \(r/4\) from \(S\), and \(S\) less than \(r/4\) from \(P\), so in each coordinate \(T\) differs from \(P\) by less than \(r/2\). There are three coordinates, and the sum of three squares, each less than \(r^2/4\), is less than \(3r^2/4\), hence less than \(r^2\). With \(r/2\) instead of \(r/4\) the sum of the squares would only be less than \(3r^2\), which is not enough. The bound \(r/4\) comes from the method of the proof, not from the property itself. Every point \(S\) with \(|PS| < r\) is in fact interior, because all points closer to \(S\) than \(r - |PS|\) are in \(M\) (LEBL1 Prop. 7.2.9, PDF p. 266). The proof of this needs the triangle inequality for distances between points in space, which we will prove in chapter 2, in section 2.3. For our purpose \(r/4\) is enough. The lemma says that every point of the set of interior points is again surrounded by interior points. In section 1.7.2 we called a set in which every point is an interior point an open set. So the set of interior points of any set is open.

Now we can name a field for which the assumptions of the theorem hold everywhere.

Definition 1.90 Continuously differentiable field (zvezno odvedljivo polje)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, that is, a set in which every point is an interior point: for every point \(P\) of \(D\) there is a number \(r > 0\) such that all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) are in \(D\). A function \(f\) of three variables defined on \(D\) is continuously differentiable (zvezno odvedljiva) on \(D\) if at every point of \(D\) all three of its partial derivatives exist (definition 1.25) and each of them is continuous at every point of \(D\) (definition 1.67). A field of vectors, for example a displacement field, is continuously differentiable on \(D\) if all three of its components are continuously differentiable on \(D\). A function of one variable defined on an interval is continuously differentiable on it if it has a derivative at every point of the interval, at an endpoint that belongs to the interval a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), and this derivative is continuous at every point of the interval (definition 1.58).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 8.4.5 and Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF p. 48), for functions of \(n\) variables. The source defines continuous differentiability through the derivative of a function of several variables, and Proposition 8.4.6 shows that this is the same as the existence and continuity of the partial derivatives. Open set: LEBL1 Def. 7.2.4 (PDF p. 264).

For a continuously differentiable field, theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds at every point \(P\) of the set \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are in \(D\). At all these points the partial derivatives exist, and at \(P\) they are continuous. The field of the hanging bar is continuously differentiable on the set of interior points of the bar, because its partial derivatives exist at every interior point and are polynomials, which are continuous by corollary 1.69, item 2.

The theorem on the change of a field over a short step also shows that a continuously differentiable function has no jumps. As \(Q\) goes to \(P\), all three products and the remainder in (1.34) go to zero, so the difference \(f(Q) - f(P)\) does too. Let us write this precisely, since we will refer to this property several more times.

Lemma 1.91 A continuously differentiable function is continuous (zvezno odvedljiva funkcija je zvezna)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(f\) a function that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). Then \(f\) is continuous at every point of \(D\) (definition 1.67).

Proof

We must show: for every point \(P\) of \(D\) and every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|f(Q) - f(P)| < \eta\) for every point \(Q\) of \(D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\).

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). At these points the partial derivatives of \(f\) exist, and at \(P\) they are continuous, so theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds for \(f\) at \(P\).
  2. By this theorem, used with the error \(1\), there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that the remainder of (1.34) is at most \(|PQ|\) in absolute value for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta_1\).
  3. Let \(M = |\partial f/\partial x\,(P)| + |\partial f/\partial y\,(P)| + |\partial f/\partial z\,(P)|\) and let \(Q\) be a point with \(0 < |PQ|\), where \(|PQ|\) is smaller than \(r\) and than \(\delta_1\). By (1.34), by the triangle inequality for numbers, because the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, items 1 and 2), and because no component of the step is longer than the step (step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.88),
    \[|f(Q) - f(P)| \le M\,|PQ| + |R(Q)| \le (M + 1)\,|PQ| .\]
  4. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take for \(\delta\) the smallest of the positive numbers \(r\), \(\delta_1\) and \(\eta/(M + 1)\). For a point \(Q\) with \(0 < |PQ| < \delta\) step 3 gives \(|f(Q) - f(P)| \le (M + 1)\,|PQ| < \eta\), and for \(Q = P\) the difference is zero. The error \(\eta\) was arbitrary, so \(f\) is continuous at \(P\).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.3.5 (PDF p. 37), for differentiable functions, and Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF p. 48), by which continuously differentiable functions are differentiable. The proof with the theorem on the change of a field is not from the source.

From now on we will assume for every body that its displacement field is continuously differentiable on the set of interior points of the body, which is open by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point. Where the assumption does not hold, we will say so. What does it mean physically? The displacement is defined at every point of the body and, at the interior points, changes from point to point without jumps (lemma 1.91). So the material nowhere tears apart and nowhere slides along some surface inside the body. The partial derivatives, which measure how fast the displacement changes, have no jumps either. The strain that we will compute from them therefore changes continuously from point to point, and the displacement field has no kinks. CM makes this assumption at the start as part of the picture of a material that fills space continuously, without gaps (CM §1.1, PDF p. 30). Real material is made of atoms and grains, so this is an idealization that holds at lengths much larger than these particles. CM adds that these properties hold almost everywhere (skoraj povsod), that is, with exceptions like the ones below (CM §3.1, PDF p. 110).

Where does the assumption fail, and where does it hold only with difficulty? Figure 1.122 shows three cases.

  1. Two materials glued together. Take a bar made of two pieces of equal thickness, one of steel and one of rubber, glued at the joint, and pull it at both ends with equal forces. The rubber stretches much more than the steel. The displacement is continuous at the joint, because the pieces are glued, but its derivative along the bar, the strain, jumps at the joint. The displacement field has a kink there. The books therefore compute the field for each material separately and require at the joint that the displacements match (SADD §5.2, PDF pp. 107-108). We use the theorem in each piece separately.
  2. A crack (razpoka), a surface in the body along which the material is torn apart. Two points that were together on opposite sides of the crack before loading move differently, so the displacement jumps across the crack. This is so for a crack that forms during loading, as in the figure, and there the assumption fails. For a crack that exists before loading, however, its two faces are part of the surface of the body, where we made no assumption, and at the interior points the assumption can hold. At the tip of the crack the strains grow without bound (SADD §10.8, PDF p. 321, and §5.8, PDF pp. 120-121).
  3. A concentrated force (točkovna sila), that is, a force acting at a single point, and sharp corners and notches. When such a point lies on the surface of the body, as the force in the figure and every sharp corner and notch do, we made no assumption there, and at the interior points the assumption can hold. But as an interior point approaches such a point, the strains in the model, and with them the partial derivatives, grow without bound, so the step in theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step must be ever shorter. Real forces are never gathered at a single point and real corners are never infinitely sharp, so such models are approximations (SADD §5.8, PDF pp. 120-121).

These irregularities are confined to the neighbourhood of the joint, the crack, the corner or the point where the force acts (SADD §5.8, PDF p. 120). Elsewhere the assumption holds.

1.15.7 A fibre in any direction

Let us return to the fibre. Let \(P\) be an interior point of a body whose displacement field is continuously differentiable, and let \(r > 0\) be such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body. Such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point. Let the fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta x,\ y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y,\ z_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta z)\) with \(|PQ| < r\). Theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds for each component of the displacement separately. Let us write all three equalities:

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{x}} , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{y}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{y}} , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{z}}(P) &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P)\,\Delta x + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}(P)\,\Delta y + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P)\,\Delta z + R_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned} \tag{1.36}\]

Nine partial derivatives at \(P\) appear in these equalities. Let us collect them in a table, as in section 1.7.2: in a row is a component of the displacement, in a column the variable we differentiate with respect to, and all are taken at the point \(P\).

at the point \(P\) w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z\)
\(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial y\) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial z\)

Each line of equality (1.36) takes one row of the table, multiplies its three numbers by the components of the step \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\) and adds the products.

For every error \(\eta > 0\) the theorem gives a band for each remainder. If we take the smallest of the three, then for every step shorter than it all three remainders are at most \(\eta\,|PQ|\) in absolute value. Then the vector of the remainders \((R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}})\) is also small compared with the step. Its length is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of its components,

\[\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{z}}^2} \le |R_{\mathrm{x}}| + |R_{\mathrm{y}}| + |R_{\mathrm{z}}| \le 3\eta\,|PQ| .\]

We get the first inequality by comparing the squares of the two sides. The square of the right side is \(R_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + R_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2\,|R_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|R_{\mathrm{y}}| + 2\,|R_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|R_{\mathrm{z}}| + 2\,|R_{\mathrm{y}}|\,|R_{\mathrm{z}}|\), which is not less than the square of the left side, because the last three terms are not negative. By lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, the inequality therefore also holds between the two sides. Since \(\eta\) is arbitrary, \(3\eta\) is arbitrarily small too.

For a fibre in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) and of length \(|h|\) we have \(Q = P + h\,\vek n\), with the components of the step \(\Delta x = h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta y = h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\Delta z = h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), as in section 1.7.3.
