\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = (c - 1)\,x - s\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = s\,x + (c - 1)\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 , \qquad c = 0{,}6 , \quad s = 0{,}8 .\]

The numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are the sides of the right triangle with sides \(3\), \(4\) and \(5\), divided by \(5\), so \(c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). The point \((x, y, z)\) moves to the position \((x + u_{\mathrm{x}},\ y + u_{\mathrm{y}},\ z + u_{\mathrm{z}}) = (c\,x - s\,y,\ s\,x + c\,y,\ z)\). The corner \(A\) moves to \(A_1 = (3, 4, 0)\), the corner \(C\) to \((-4, 3, 0)\), and the points on the axis \(z\) do not move (figure 1.138). Is this really a rigid-body displacement (definition 1.11)? Let us check that the distance between no two points changes.

  1. Let the points \(P\) and \(Q\) differ by \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) before loading. We subtract the new positions coordinate by coordinate. Since each new coordinate is a sum of multiples of the old ones, the new positions differ by \((c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y,\ s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y,\ \Delta z)\).
  2. We multiply out the square of the new distance:
    \[\begin{aligned} (c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y)^2 + (s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y)^2 + \Delta z^2 &= c^2\Delta x^2 - 2cs\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + s^2\Delta y^2 \\ &\quad + s^2\Delta x^2 + 2sc\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + c^2\Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2 . \end{aligned}\]
  3. The mixed terms cancel, and we collect the others: \((c^2 + s^2)(\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2) + \Delta z^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2\), because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\).

The distances stay the same, the plate does not deform. The fibre \(OA\) of length \(5\) becomes \(OA_1\) with the length \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). What do the two measures of strain say? The displacement gradient is, at every point,

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} c - 1 & -s & 0 \\ s & c - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(0{,}6^2 + 0{,}8^2 + 0^2 = 1\), the entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and in the same way we find \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). So the Green-Lagrange tensor is exactly zero, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\), and it correctly says that no fibre gets longer. The small strain tensor, however, is

\[\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\big(\mat H + \mat H^\T\big) = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By it every fibre in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) would get shorter by \(40\) %, which is false. Where does the error come from? The number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = c - 1 = -0{,}4\) measures only how the component \(x\) of a fibre along the axis \(x\) changes. The fibre \(OA\) turns into \(OA_1\), its component \(x\) decreases from \(5\) to \(3\), but its length stays \(5\) (figure 1.138). The small strain tensor mistakes the turn for a shortening, because it leaves out the term \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}8^2 = 0{,}32\) and the term \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}4^2 = 0{,}08\). With them, by (1.48), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}4 + 0{,}08 + 0{,}32 = 0\).

How large is the error for a small turn? Take \(s = 0{,}001\) and \(c = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\), so that again \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) and the displacement is rigid. A point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 1 mm. Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). This is about \(-s^2/2\), because \((1 - s^2/2)^2 = 1 - s^2 + s^4/4\), which differs from \(c^2 = 1 - s^2\) only by \(s^4/4\). So the false strain is proportional to the square of the turn. For \(s = 0{,}001\) it is small compared with the strains of steel of about \(0{,}001\). For \(s = 0{,}1\), when a point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 10 cm, however, \(c - 1 = -0{,}0050\). This is five times the strain at which steel already gets permanently longer (section 1.1), although the body does not deform at all.

So the small strain tensor is a good approximation only when all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, that is, when the strains and also the turns are small. In steel structures the strains are small, and when the turns of their parts are small too, this is so. When parts of a body turn a lot while the body deforms little, for example a thin ruler bent into an arc, the Green-Lagrange tensor must be used. The same holds for large strains, for example in rubber. CM warns that smallness must be checked separately in every application, and also shows the opposite example: a field for which the small strain tensor is zero but the Green-Lagrange tensor is not (CM (3.5.16)-(3.5.18), PDF pp. 143-144). The example with the turned plate is not from a source.

1.17.7 Strain relative to the shape after loading

The Green-Lagrange strain tensor and the small strain tensor measure fibres that we choose before loading. We take the point \(P\) and the direction \(\vek n\) on the unloaded body, and we compare the change of the square of the length of the fibre with the square of its length before loading, \(L_0^2\). This is how we have described a body ever since section 1.6: we name every point by the position it had before loading and assign to it its displacement. Books call this the Lagrangian or material description (Lagrangeov ali materialni opis).

Sometimes, however, we know a body mainly after loading. We draw a grid of short marks on an unloaded rubber band, stretch the band and take a photograph. On the photograph we see each mark in its position, direction and length after loading, and by these we also choose it. For a liquid flowing in a pipe, we want to know what happens at a given place in the pipe, not where the bit of liquid that is there now was before. A description in which we name points by their position after loading is the Eulerian or spatial description (Eulerjev ali prostorski opis). CM says that for solid bodies the Eulerian description is less useful, because we do not know the shape of the body after loading in advance, while for the motion of liquids it is the one usually used (CM §3.2.1-§3.2.3, PDF pp. 112-114 and 117).

The goal of this section is a measure of stretching that compares the change of the square of the length of a short fibre with the square of its length after loading, \(L_1^2\), and gives the direction of the fibre after loading. We will find a matrix that gives this measure for every direction, and show how it is related to the Green-Lagrange tensor. The physical model and both assumptions are the same as in the whole of section 1.17: the body is a continuum, its displacement field is continuously differentiable, and the point \(P\) is an interior point of the body. We add one more assumption: the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at the point \(P\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). What this means physically we said in section 1.16.5. Matter cannot be squeezed so that a fibre disappears, and CM concludes from this that the matrix \(\mat F\) is invertible (CM §3.3.1, PDF pp. 119-120). That a matrix which sends no nonzero vector to the zero vector really has an inverse matrix, we will show only in chapter 2. Until then the existence of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) is an assumption, which we check by calculation in the examples.

Let us start with the bar, where everything is a single number. A bar of length \(L_0\) gets longer, to the length \(L_1\). In section 1.1 we met the Green-Lagrange strain \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\). If we divide the change of the square of the length by the square of the new length, we get the quotient

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} .\]

Let us express it with the strain of the bar \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0\).

  1. From the definition of the strain, \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\). The square is a multiplied-out product, \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon) = L_0^2\,(1 + 2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), as in section 1.6.2.
  2. So the numerator is \(L_1^2 - L_0^2 = L_0^2\,(2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), and the denominator is \(2L_1^2 = 2L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2\).
  3. The factor \(L_0^2\) cancels:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} . \tag{1.56}\]
  4. The quotient differs from the strain \(\varepsilon\) by
    \[\varepsilon - \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{\varepsilon^2\,(3 + 2\varepsilon)}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} ,\]
    which for small \(\varepsilon\) is almost \(\tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). We got the numerator by multiplying out \((1 + \varepsilon)^2\) as in step 1 and collecting the terms: \(2\varepsilon + 4\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2 = 3\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3\). The Green-Lagrange strain \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), on the other hand, differs from \(\varepsilon\) by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\).

For a steel bar with \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) the new quotient is \(0{,}0009985\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}0010005\). The first differs from \(\varepsilon\) by one and a half per mille of its value, the second by half a per mille. For a rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm, \(\varepsilon = 0{,}5\), the new quotient is \((15^2 - 10^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = 125/450 = 0{,}278\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}625\) (figure 1.139). For large strains the two measures differ a lot.

Why is the new quotient always smaller than the Green-Lagrange one when the length changes? Both have the same numerator \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\). When the bar is stretched, \(L_1 > L_0\), so the new quotient divides a positive numerator by a larger number and is smaller. When the bar gets shorter, \(L_1 < L_0\), and the new quotient divides a negative numerator by a smaller number, so it is larger in size and again smaller. The strain \(\varepsilon\) always lies between the two. The Green-Lagrange strain is larger than it by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient is smaller by step 4, because a bar cannot disappear, so \(L_1 > 0\), \(\varepsilon > -1\) and \(3 + 2\varepsilon > 0\).

The new quotient has one more meaning. We let the stretched band of length 15 cm go back to 10 cm, and we take the length of the stretched band as the initial length. The Green-Lagrange strain of this unloading is \((10^2 - 15^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = -0{,}278\), the new quotient with the opposite sign. This is always so: when we swap the roles of the lengths \(L_0\) and \(L_1\), the Green-Lagrange quotient becomes \((L_0^2 - L_1^2)/(2L_1^2)\), which is the new quotient with the opposite sign. So the new quotient measures stretching with the length seen by someone who knows only the loaded body.

In space we proceed as in section 1.17.2 and first leave out the remainders, which we will justify in the theorem below. A fibre from the point \(P\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) with length \(h > 0\) has after loading, by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading and without the remainders, the vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat F\vek n\) (figure 1.140).

  1. Its length after loading is \(L_1 \approx h\,|\mat F\vek n|\). The vector \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, as we will show in the theorem below, so we may divide it by its length. We get the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\), the direction of the fibre after loading. The vector of the fibre after loading is thus \(h\,\mat F\vek n \approx L_1\,\vek m\).
  2. We express the vector of the fibre before loading with the vector after loading. By lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix, item 1 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, (1.43) and lemma 1.106, \(\mat F^{-1}(h\,\mat F\vek n) = h\,(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = h\,\vek n\). So \(h\,\vek n \approx L_1\,\mat F^{-1}\vek m\). The matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) takes the vector of the fibre after loading back to the vector before loading, just as for the sheared cube the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\) took back the edge \(AD\) (section 1.16.5).
  3. So the square of the length before loading is \(L_0^2 = h^2 \approx L_1^2\,|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2\). The same steps 2 to 5 as for \(|\mat F\vek n|^2\) in section 1.17.2, only with \(\mat F^{-1}\) instead of \(\mat F\) and \(\vek m\) instead of \(\vek n\), give
    \[|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2 = \vek m^\T\,(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\,\vek m .\]
  4. The vector \(\vek m\) is a unit vector, so \(1 = \vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\) as in step 6 there, and \(L_1^2 = L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\).
  5. We subtract the squares, divide by \(2L_1^2\) and subtract the two double sums term by term:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} \approx \frac{L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m - L_1^2\,\vek m^\T(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\vek m}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\,\tfrac12\big(\mat I - (\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\big)\,\vek m .\]

On the right there is again a single matrix, which depends only on the displacement field at the point \(P\), and the direction appears only in the vector \(\vek m\), this time in the direction of the fibre after loading. The matrix contains the transposed matrix of the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). Before we give the matrix a name, let us show that this is the same matrix as the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), so that we may denote both by one symbol.

Lemma 1.117 Inverse of the transposed matrix (inverzna matrika transponirane matrike)

Let a square matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\). Then the transposed matrix \(\mat A^\T\) also has an inverse matrix, and it is the transposed matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\):

\[(\mat A^\T)^{-1} = (\mat A^{-1})^\T .\]
Proof

We must show that the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T\) satisfies both equalities of definition 1.107 for the matrix \(\mat A^\T\).

  1. We write \(\mat B = \mat A^{-1}\). By (1.43), \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\) and \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\).
  2. We transpose the first equality. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat A\mat B)^\T = \mat B^\T\mat A^\T\), so \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I^\T\).
  3. The identity matrix equals its transposed matrix. The entry \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\) of the matrix \(\mat I^\T\) is \(I_{\mathrm{ji}}\) (definition 1.100), which is \(1\) for \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\) and \(0\) otherwise, the same as \(I_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.105). So \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I\).
  4. In the same way we transpose the second equality, \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\), and get \(\mat A^\T\mat B^\T = \mat I\).
  5. The matrices \(\mat A^\T\) and \(\mat B^\T\) are square matrices of order \(n\), and by steps 3 and 4 they satisfy both equalities (1.43) with \(\mat A^\T\) in the place of the matrix \(\mat A\). So \(\mat B^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\). By lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix there is no other, so \((\mat A^\T)^{-1} = \mat B^\T = (\mat A^{-1})^\T\).

Source: CM §2.3.6 (PDF p. 65) states the equality without proof, KREYSZIG §7.8, problems 13 and 14 (PDF p. 335), leaves its check and proof to the reader. The proof is not from the sources.

So we write the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T = (\mat A^\T)^{-1}\) more briefly as \(\mat A^{-\T}\), as CM does (CM §2.3.6, PDF p. 65). The proof used only the rule for transposing a product, the fact that the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, and the uniqueness of the inverse matrix. For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) (section 1.16.5), so by item 2 of lemma 1.101 and step 3 above, \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I^\T - \mat K^\T = \mat I - \mat K^\T\). This is the matrix that has a single nonzero entry off the main diagonal, \(-0{,}001\) in row \(z\) and column \(x\).

Definition 1.118 Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij)

Let \(\mat F\) be the deformation gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body, and let \(\mat F\) have an inverse matrix. The Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij) at the point \(P\) is the matrix

\[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat I - \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\big) , \tag{1.57}\]

where \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^{-1})^\T\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117). We denote its entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) by \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: CM (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133), BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49).

What kind of object is \(\mat E^*\)? Like \(\mat E\), it is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, calculated from the deformation gradient at one point. It is symmetric (definition 1.102). By items 3 and 1 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1})^\T = (\mat F^{-1})^\T(\mat F^{-\T})^\T = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\), and the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, so by item 2 of the same lemma \((\mat E^*)^\T = \mat E^*\). The matrix \(\mat E^*\) therefore has at most six different entries. We calculate it from the partial derivatives of the displacements at the point \(P\), but its numbers describe the fibres that pass through the point \(P_1\) after loading, in their directions after loading. The symbol \(\mat E^*\) is used by BOWER, while CM writes the same matrix with a small bold \(\mathbf e\).

CM calls this tensor the Almansi-Hamel or Euler strain tensor (Almansi-Hamelov ali Eulerjev tenzor deformacij), and in its examples the Almansi strain tensor (CM, PDF pp. 133-134). BOWER calls it the Eulerian strain tensor (Eulerjev tenzor deformacij) and denotes it by \(\mat E^*\) (BOWER §2.1.6, PDF p. 49). The name in this book joins the two names. CM also writes it with partial derivatives of the displacements with respect to the coordinates of the points after loading, and there the quadratic part has the opposite sign to that of the Green-Lagrange tensor (CM (3.4.25) and (3.4.27), PDF p. 133). We will not use such derivatives, because we name the points of a body by their position before loading.

Both matrices, \(\mat E\) and \(\mat E^*\), are calculated from the same matrix \(\mat F\). How do we get one from the other?

Lemma 1.119 Relation between the Euler-Almansi and the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (zveza med Euler-Almansijevim in Green-Lagrangeovim tenzorjem)

Let the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at an interior point \(P\) of a body have an inverse matrix, and let \(\mat E\) be the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\). Then

\[\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \mat E \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} . \tag{1.58}\]
Proof

We must show both equalities. We use the properties of the matrix product (lemma 1.99) and the fact that \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117).

The first equality.

  1. We substitute (1.57). By item 3 of lemma 1.99, used for multiplication from the left and from the right, \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F - \mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F\big)\).
  2. By lemma 1.106, \(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F = \mat F^\T\mat F\).
  3. By item 2 of lemma 1.99, \(\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F = (\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T})(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), the first because \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\). By lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\mat I = \mat I\).
  4. So \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I)\), which by (1.47) is the matrix \(\mat E\).

The second equality.

  1. We multiply the first equality from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\): \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\mat F^{-1}\).
  2. By item 2 of lemma 1.99 the right side equals \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T)\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\mat F^{-1})\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), and by lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\,\mat E^*\,\mat I = \mat E^*\).

Source: The definitions of the two tensors are CM (3.4.10) (PDF p. 129) and (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133). The proof is not from the sources.

So we get \(\mat E^*\) from \(\mat E\) by multiplying \(\mat E\) from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\), and \(\mat E\) from \(\mat E^*\) with the matrices \(\mat F^\T\) and \(\mat F\). When \(\mat E = \mat 0\), therefore also \(\mat E^* = \mat 0\), because every entry of a product with the zero matrix is a sum of products with zero, and the other way round. The proof used only the grouping of factors and the fact that the product of a matrix with its inverse matrix gives the identity matrix.

So far we have left out the remainders. As for the Green-Lagrange tensor, let us show that this is justified for ever shorter fibres. We will not need a new calculation with remainders, because the new quotient is expressed through the Green-Lagrange one.

Theorem 1.120 Strain of a short fibre relative to its length after loading (deformacija kratkega vlakna glede na dolžino po obremenitvi)

Let the displacement field of a body be continuously differentiable, \(P\) an interior point of the body, \(r > 0\) a number such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body (such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), \(\mat F\) the deformation gradient at \(P\), which has an inverse matrix, \(\mat E\) the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\), and \(\vek n\) a unit vector. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) let a fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). Its length before loading is \(L_0 = |h|\), and after loading \(L_1 = |\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}|\). Then \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, and for the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\):

  1. the quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined for all small enough \(|h|\) and approaches the number \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\),
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m , \tag{1.59}\]
  2. the two measures are related by the equality
    \[\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = \frac{\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} . \tag{1.60}\]
Proof

First we show that \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, then item 2, and from it item 1.

The vector \(\mat F\vek n\).

  1. Suppose that \(\mat F\vek n = \vek 0\).
  2. Then by item 1 of lemma 1.99, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat F^{-1}(\mat F\vek n) = \mat F^{-1}\vek 0\), and every entry of the product \(\mat F^{-1}\vek 0\) is a sum of products with zero, so it is zero.
  3. By (1.43) and lemma 1.106, however, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat I\vek n = \vek n\), which is not the zero vector, because its length is \(1\). This contradicts step 2.
  4. So \(\mat F\vek n \neq \vek 0\), and its length \(|\mat F\vek n|\) is positive. Every component of the vector \(\vek m\) is a component of the vector \(\mat F\vek n\) divided by \(|\mat F\vek n|\), so by (1.10) \(|\vek m|^2 = |\mat F\vek n|^2/|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1\), and \(\vek m\) is a unit vector.

2. The relation between the two measures.

  1. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). By step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n\) and \(G = \tfrac12\big(|\mat F\vek n|^2 - 1\big)\). So \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1 + 2G\), and by step 4 above this number is positive.
  2. By lemma 1.119, \(\mat E = \mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\), so \(G = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\,\vek n\).
  3. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \(\vek n^\T\mat F^\T = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.99 we may group the factors as we like. So \(G = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\vek n)\).
  4. We substitute \(\mat F\vek n = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m\). By item 2 of lemma 1.101, \((|\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m)^\T = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m^\T\), and by item 3 of lemma 1.99 we take the number out of each product. We get \(G = |\mat F\vek n|^2\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = (1 + 2G)\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).
  5. We divide by the positive number \(1 + 2G\) and get (1.60).

1. The limit.

  1. We write \(g(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) and \(c = 1 + 2G\), where \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) as above. By item 1 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = G\), and by step 1 of item 2, \(c = |\mat F\vek n|^2 > 0\).
  2. From the definition of the function \(g\) we get \(L_1^2/L_0^2 = 1 + 2g(h)\), when we multiply the equality \(g(h) = \tfrac12\big(L_1^2/L_0^2 - 1\big)\) by \(2\) and add \(1\).
  3. We use the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(c/4\): there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < c/4\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\). We may always narrow the band, as we said after the definition of the limit, so we take \(\delta_1 \le r\), and \(g(h)\) is defined for all these \(h\). For such \(h\), \(1 + 2g(h) = c + 2\big(g(h) - G\big) > c - c/2 = c/2\). So \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big) > 0\), hence \(L_1 > 0\), and the quotient \(a(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined. So we may apply the definition of the limit to the function \(a\), with \(\delta_1\) in the role of the number \(r\).
  4. For these \(h\) we divide the numerator and the denominator of the quotient \(a(h)\) by \(L_0^2\) and use step 2:
    \[a(h) = \frac{(L_1^2 - L_0^2)/L_0^2}{2L_1^2/L_0^2} = \frac{2g(h)}{2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)} = \frac{g(h)}{1 + 2g(h)} .\]
  5. By item 2, \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = G/(1 + 2G) = G/c\). We bring the two fractions to a common denominator:
    \[a(h) - \frac{G}{c} = \frac{g(h)\,(1 + 2G) - G\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} = \frac{g(h) - G}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} ,\]
    because the terms \(2\,g(h)\,G\) in the numerator cancel.
  6. By step 3 the denominator is larger than \((c/2) \cdot c = c^2/2\), so \(|a(h) - G/c| < 2\,|g(h) - G|/c^2\).
  7. We choose any error \(\eta > 0\). By the definition of the limit there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < \eta\,c^2/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_2\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), by step 6, \(|a(h) - G/c| < \eta\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so the limit of the quotient \(a(h)\) is \(G/c = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).

Source: BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49) writes item 1 for an infinitesimally short fibre, with the unit vector along the fibre after loading and without a limit, and leaves the proof to the reader. CM (3.4.23) (PDF p. 133) writes \((ds)^2 - (dS)^2 = 2\,d\vek x\cdot\mat E^*\cdot d\vek x\). The proof is not from the sources.

The theorem is the version in space of the quotient for the bar. The Euler-Almansi tensor gives, for every direction \(\vek m\) after loading, how much a short fibre has been stretched, measured with its length after loading. The vector \(\vek m\) is the direction of the fibre after loading up to the remainders, since by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading the vector of the fibre after loading is \(h\,\mat F\vek n\) plus the remainders. For negative \(h\) the fibre points in the direction \(-\vek m\), which does not change the double sum, because each of its terms is a product of two components of the direction. The proof showed why the theorem holds. The new quotient is exactly the Green-Lagrange quotient \(g\) divided by \(1 + 2g = L_1^2/L_0^2\), so we got its limit from theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, and item 2 is the same relation in the limit.

Item 2 relates the two measures of the same fibre. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) and \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\). From (1.60),

\[G - A = G - \frac{G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{G\,(1 + 2G) - G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{2G^2}{1 + 2G} = 2\,G\,A .\]

So the two measures of the same fibre differ by exactly twice their product. When \(|G| \le 0{,}001\), the difference is at most \(0{,}002\,|A|\) in size, two thousandths of the value \(A\). For small strains it therefore does not matter which of the two measures we use. With the strain of the fibre \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) of section 1.17.3 the relation is even simpler. By item 2 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(1 + 2G = \big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2\), so \(G = \varepsilon(\vek n) + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2\) and \(A = G/\big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2\), which is exactly the formula (1.56) with \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\vek n)\). So the curves of figure 1.139 hold for every short fibre, not only for the bar.

Let us test everything on the sheared cube, which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face we pushed sideways by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. The axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(z\) upward. The deformation gradient is \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat K\), where \(\mat K\) has the only nonzero entry \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\). Above we found \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) and \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I - \mat K^\T\).

  1. We multiply out the brackets term by term by item 3 of lemma 1.99 and lemma 1.106: \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat K^\T)(\mat I - \mat K) = \mat I - \mat K - \mat K^\T + \mat K^\T\mat K\).
  2. In the product \(\mat K^\T\mat K\) only the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\) is nonzero. Row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) is \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is also \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), and their product is \(0{,}001^2 = 10^{-6}\). The other rows of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) and the other columns of the matrix \(\mat K\) are zero.
  3. By (1.57), therefore,
    \[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat K + \mat K^\T - \mat K^\T\mat K\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & -0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us compare it with the Green-Lagrange tensor of the cube from section 1.17.2,

\[\mat E = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The matrices differ only in the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\), which has the opposite sign. How can \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) be positive and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) negative? By theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical before loading (\(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)), and by theorem 1.120 the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical after loading (\(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)). These are two different fibres (figure 1.141). The vertical edge \(AD\) leans and gets longer, from \(h\) to \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm. Vertical after loading, however, is the fibre \(BT\), which reaches from the corner \(B = (10\,000, 0, 0)\) to the point \(T = (9\,990, 0, 10\,000)\) on the top edge, 10 µm to the left of the corner \(C\). The point \(T\) moves 10 µm to the right, to the point \(T_1 = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\), where the corner \(C\) was before loading. So the fibre stands upright and gets shorter, from \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm to \(h = 10\,000\) µm. Its quotient is

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{h^2 - (h^2 + s^2)}{2h^2} = -\frac{s^2}{2h^2} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

exactly \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The shear that makes a vertical fibre lean and get longer makes a leaning fibre stand upright and get shorter.

The field of the cube is linear, so there are no remainders, and the equalities of theorem 1.120 hold for every fibre of the cube without a limit, as we saw for the Green-Lagrange tensor in section 1.17.2. Let us calculate both quotients for the fibres of the front face from section 1.6.2 and for the fibre \(BT\), from the lengths in micrometres.

fibre \(L_0\) \(L_1\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\)
bottom edge \(AB\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000\) \(0\) \(0\)
vertical edge \(AD\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,149{,}208\) \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,135{,}066\) \(-4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(-5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
fibre \(BT\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(10\,000\) \(-4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(-5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

The two columns differ by \(2GA\), as the relation above says. For the diagonals this is \(2 \cdot 5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which is exactly the difference \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} - 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\). For the edge \(AD\) and the fibre \(BT\) it is only \(2 \cdot (5 \cdot 10^{-7})^2 = 5 \cdot 10^{-13}\), so the columns differ only by a millionth of the value. We also get the last column from the matrix \(\mat E^*\) when we put in the direction of the fibre after loading. For the diagonal \(AC\) the vector after loading is \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\) with the length \(14\,149{,}208\) µm, so \(\vek m = (0{,}70746, 0, 0{,}70675)\). Only the terms with the indices \(x\) and \(z\) remain in the double sum:

\[\begin{aligned} \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m &= 2E^*_{\mathrm{xz}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{z}} + E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot 0{,}70746 \cdot 0{,}70675 - 5 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}70675^2 \\ &= 5{,}0000 \cdot 10^{-4} - 2{,}4975 \cdot 10^{-7} = 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} , \end{aligned}\]

as in the table.

For the plate that in section 1.17.6 we turned as a whole about the axis \(z\) with the numbers \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). Also \(\mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F\), \((0{,}6, -0{,}8, 0)\), multiplied by column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), which is the same triple, so \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}8 + (-0{,}8) \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and we get the others in the same way. So by definition 1.107 the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F\), and by lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^\T\). Transposing twice gives back the original matrix (lemma 1.101, item 1), so \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^\T)^\T = \mat F\). Then \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = \mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\) and \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\). Like the Green-Lagrange tensor, the Euler-Almansi tensor correctly says that no fibre gets longer, while the small strain tensor wrongly predicts a shortening by \(40\) %. The same follows from lemma 1.119, since \(\mat E = \mat 0\) gives \(\mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\,\mat 0\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat 0\).

For the hanging bar all partial derivatives are small. A steel bar 10 m long hangs under its own weight and is fixed only at the point \(O\), the centre of its upper end, the axis \(x\) points vertically down, and the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) lies 5 m below \(O\) and 4 mm from the axis of the bar. We calculate the inverse matrix of the deformation gradient at \(P\) with a computer, and how to calculate it by hand we will see in chapter 2. That it really is the inverse we check by multiplication, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\). By (1.57) we get

\[\mat E^* = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}951994 \cdot 10^{-6} & 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & 0 \\ 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

The Green-Lagrange tensor at \(P\) has \(1{,}952002 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7}\) on the diagonal, the small strain tensor \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\) (sections 1.17.2 and 1.17.3). Rounded to five significant digits, the diagonal entries of all three matrices are equal, and the entries off the diagonal differ by at most \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-15}\). The largest difference, between \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\), is \(7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\), about four millionths of the entry.

The differences on the diagonal have a simple pattern. For the entry \(xx\), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12} = \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12} = -\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), and for the entry \(yy\) likewise \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = 1{,}71 \cdot 10^{-13}\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = -5{,}14 \cdot 10^{-13}\). Why? A short fibre along the axis \(x\) leans only by the ratio \(4{,}7 \cdot 10^{-10}\), so it lies almost along the axis \(x\) both before and after loading, and the formulas for the bar hold for it. The Green-Lagrange strain is \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient, by step 4 of the derivation of the formula (1.56), almost \(\varepsilon - \tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). The entries \(E_{\mathrm{xy}} = -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) even have opposite signs. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), both consist only of products of partial derivatives of the size \(10^{-16}\) to \(10^{-15}\), and these products enter \(\mat E^*\) with other coefficients than \(\mat E\), as \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) do on the diagonal.

Let us also test theorem 1.120 on the bar. For the fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) of section 1.17.2, \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = -3{,}036443 \cdot 10^{-7}\), less than \(G = -3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7}\) by \(2GA = 1{,}84 \cdot 10^{-13}\). The quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\), calculated exactly from the field (1.18), comes within \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-12}\) of the value \(A\) for fibres of length 1 mm and 0,1 mm, as the theorem says.

So for small partial derivatives the matrices \(\mat E^*\), \(\mat E\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) differ only by terms with products of partial derivatives, and then we need not distinguish whether we give points and directions of fibres before loading or after it (CM §3.5.1, PDF p. 141, BOWER §2.1.7, PDF p. 50). For a single fibre we showed this exactly with the relation \(G - A = 2GA\). For all entries of the matrices at once we still need a bound for the entries of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\).

How close is \(\mat F^{-1}\) to the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\)? For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) exactly, because \(\mat K\mat K = \mat 0\) (section 1.16.5). For the hanging bar the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), which we computed with a computer, differs from the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\) by at most \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), in the entry \(xx\). This is the square of the largest partial derivative, \((1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 = 3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\). Why? We can express the difference \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) from the equation \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\), and we get \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). If \(\mat B\) is small, then \(\mat H\mat B\) is a product of two small matrices, and \(\mat B\) is almost \(\mat H\). That \(\mat B\) really is small, the same equation tells us when we read it as an inequality for the largest entry of \(\mat B\). As in section 1.17.3, let \(m\) be a number that no partial derivative of the displacement at the point exceeds in absolute value.

Lemma 1.121 Estimate of the inverse matrix (ocena inverzne matrike)

Let \(\mat H\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and \(m\) a number with \(0 < m \le \tfrac16\) such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all indices \(i\) and \(j\). Let the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), and let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\). Then

\[\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B , \tag{1.61}\]

and \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) and \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\) for all \(i\) and \(j\).

Proof

We must show both equalities and both estimates. The equalities come from the definition of the inverse matrix, the estimate for \(\mat B\) from the first equality read as an inequality, and the estimate for \(\mat H\mat B\) from the estimate for \(\mat B\).

  1. By definition 1.107 of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\). We insert \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) and \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\). By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and by lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \((\mat I + \mat H)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B + \mat H - \mat H\mat B\).
  2. This matrix is \(\mat I\), so by the rules of matrix arithmetic (lemma 1.95) \(\mat H - \mat B - \mat H\mat B = \mat 0\), that is, \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). This is the first equality.
  3. From \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\) and the first equality, \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B\), the second equality.
  4. Let \(\mu\) be the largest of the nine numbers \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}|\). Among finitely many numbers one is the largest.
  5. By the first equality, \(B_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ij}} - \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and the rule for the absolute value of a product (lemma 1.6), \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le |H_{\mathrm{ij}}| + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} |H_{\mathrm{ik}}|\,|B_{\mathrm{kj}}| \le m + 3m\mu\), since the sum has three terms and each is at most \(m\mu\).
  6. The inequality of step 5 holds for all entries, also for the entry with \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| = \mu\). So \(\mu \le m + 3m\mu\), that is, \((1 - 3m)\,\mu \le m\).
  7. Since \(m \le \tfrac16\), we have \(1 - 3m \ge \tfrac12\). Dividing the inequality by the positive number \(1 - 3m\) gives \(\mu \le m/(1 - 3m) \le 2m\). So \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\).
  8. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three terms, each at most \(m \cdot 2m\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers, therefore, \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\).

Source: LEBL2 prop. 8.2.6 (PDF pp. 23-24) proves the related statement that a matrix close enough to an invertible matrix is invertible too. The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

The lemma says that \(\mat F^{-1}\) equals \(\mat I - \mat H\) up to the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\), whose entries are at most \(6m^2\). The proof used the equation \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\) twice: first as an inequality that bounds the largest entry of \(\mat B\), then to estimate the correction \(\mat H\mat B\). We needed the condition \(m \le \tfrac16\) in step 7, so that the number \(1 - 3m\) is positive and not too small. The lemma does not prove that \(\mat F^{-1}\) exists but assumes it, like this whole section. For the cube \(m = 0{,}001\), \(\mat B = \mat K\) and \(\mat H\mat B = \mat K\mat K = \mat 0\). For the hanging bar \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the largest entry of \(\mat B\) is \(1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6}\), less than \(2m\), and the largest entry of \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), below the bound \(6m^2 = 2{,}29 \cdot 10^{-11}\). Now we can compare all three measures.

Corollary 1.122 Three strain measures for small partial derivatives (tri mere deformacije pri majhnih parcialnih odvodih)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point of a body and \(m\) a number with \(0 < m \le \tfrac16\) such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\), and let the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) have an inverse matrix. Let \(\mat E\), \(\mat E^*\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the Green-Lagrange strain tensor, the Euler-Almansi strain tensor and the small strain tensor at this point. Then for all \(i\) and \(j\)

\[\begin{aligned} |E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac32\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le 12\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{1.62}\]
Proof

We must show three estimates. We write each difference with products of matrices and bound it with lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix.

  1. By lemma 1.113 on the Green-Lagrange strain from the displacement gradient, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T + \mat H^\T\mat H)\), and by (1.51), \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\). So \(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\).
  2. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H^\T\mat H\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(m^2\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6), therefore, \(|E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\).
  3. Let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) as in lemma 1.121. By item 2 of lemma 1.101 on transposing a sum, a multiple and a product, and since the identity matrix equals its transpose, \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat I - \mat B)^\T = \mat I - \mat B^\T\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat B^\T)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B - \mat B^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\). By (1.57), therefore, \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat B + \mat B^\T - \mat B^\T\mat B)\).
  5. By lemma 1.121, \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.101, \(\mat B^\T = \mat H^\T - (\mat H\mat B)^\T\). Inserting this into step 4 and subtracting \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) gives
    \[\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon = -\tfrac12\big(\mat H\mat B + (\mat H\mat B)^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\big) .\]
  6. By lemma 1.121 every entry of the matrices \(\mat H\mat B\) and \((\mat H\mat B)^\T\) is at most \(6m^2\) in absolute value. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat B^\T\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} B_{\mathrm{ki}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(2m \cdot 2m = 4m^2\) by the same lemma, so it is at most \(12m^2\). By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12\,(6m^2 + 6m^2 + 12m^2) = 12m^2\).
  7. We write the difference as \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}} = (E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}) + (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}})\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and steps 6 and 2, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 12m^2 + \tfrac32\,m^2 = \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2\).

Source: CM §3.5.1 (PDF pp. 140-141) says that for small partial derivatives, when terms of the order of the square are dropped, the Green-Lagrange and the Eulerian strain tensor need not be distinguished. BOWER §2.1.7 (PDF p. 50) says that the infinitesimal strain approximates the Lagrange strain, and the Eulerian strain with the same accuracy, and leaves the latter to the reader. The estimates with fixed numbers and the proof are not from the sources.

The corollary says exactly what we saw on the numbers. For small partial derivatives the entries of all three matrices differ by at most a fixed number times the square of the largest partial derivative. For steel, where \(m\) is of the order \(0{,}001\), the differences are at most of the order \(10^{-5}\), a hundred times less than the partial derivatives themselves. The numbers \(\tfrac32\), \(12\) and \(\tfrac{27}{2}\) are the bounds that the proof gives, and with the same assumptions they cannot be made smaller. For the matrix \(\mat H\) with all nine entries equal to \(-\tfrac16\) and \(m = \tfrac16\) we computed with SymPy that all three bounds, and both bounds of lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix too, are attained exactly. The first bound is attained for every \(m\): if all nine entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) equal \(m\), every entry of the matrix \(\tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\) equals \(\tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\). In both examples below the actual differences are smaller than the bounds, about three times for the first estimate and at least six times for the other two.

  • Sheared cube, \(m = 0{,}001\): the bounds are \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(1{,}35 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(zz\), \(E_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - E_{\mathrm{zz}} = -10^{-6}\).
  • Hanging bar at the point \(P\), \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\): the bounds are \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(4{,}6 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(5{,}1 \cdot 10^{-11}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(xx\), \(1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(-5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12}\) and \(-7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\).

So in steel structures we use the small strain tensor, while for large strains, for example in rubber, we must say which measure we use and whether the direction of the fibre is given before loading or after it.

We can now calculate from the displacement field the strain at every interior point and in every direction. The Green-Lagrange tensor gives it exactly when we give the direction of the fibre before loading, and the Euler-Almansi tensor when we give it after loading, while for small partial derivatives the small strain tensor is enough. The path went from displacements to strains. Often we must go the other way: we know the six components of strain and look for the displacements. Is this always possible? We calculate six components from only three components of the displacement, so they cannot be arbitrary. Which conditions they must satisfy, we look at in the next section.

1.18 Do the strains fit together

In section 1.17 we computed from the displacement field of a body how the material is strained close to each point. When the partial derivatives of the displacements are small, this is described by six numbers, the components of the small strain tensor ((1.51)): three normal strains and three shear strains. Let us write them out once more:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.63}\]

On the right-hand sides only three functions appear, the displacement components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), while on the left there are six. In this section we ask the opposite question. If six functions are given, is there a displacement field from which we get them by (1.63)? We will see that there is not always one. Six functions that come from three cannot be arbitrary: they must satisfy six equations. First, on the example of a strip, we look at how strains can fail to fit together. Then we meet derivatives of partial derivatives and show that for them the order in which we differentiate does not matter. With this we derive the six equations and say what they mean. Then we show that the strains determine the displacements up to a shift and a small rotation of the body. Finally we look at when the equations are enough for a displacement field to exist, and why they are not enough for a body with a hole.

1.18.1 Six functions from three

Why would anyone know the strains but not the displacements? In this chapter we always went from displacements to strains. In chapter 3, though, we will learn how the strain of a piece of material depends on the forces acting on it, and on whether it is heated. Then we will often know the strains before the displacements. In a body that is heated unevenly, for instance, every piece wants to stretch in its own way, as much as it was heated. If these stretches do not fit together, the pieces cannot stretch as they would like to, and they push on each other or pull on each other. So we must be able to check whether prescribed strains fit together.

For the bar this question did not come up. There the strain was a single function \(\varepsilon(x)\), and we get the displacement of a point by adding up the elongations of all pieces from the fixed end to the point (we will write this precisely in section 3.5). In space, though, three functions give six, and this is the reason why the six functions cannot be arbitrary.

What it means that strains do not fit together is easiest to picture like this (CM §3.7.1, PDF p. 149). Before loading we cut the body into small cubes. We strain each cube separately as the given strains prescribe, and then try to put the cubes back together into a whole body. If the strains are arbitrary, the cubes do not fit together without gaps or overlaps. They fit only if the strain of every cube agrees with the strains of its neighbours.

Let us try this on an example. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in a plane in which we place the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.142). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the axis \(y\) across it, and the origin is at the middle of the left end. So the strip reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm and from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm. No force acts on it. This is a thought experiment: we prescribe a strain to every piece of the strip and ask whether the strip as a whole can take it. Let us prescribe

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \tag{1.64}\]

and let the other three components be zero. The number \(k\) is a constant. Since \(y^2\) has the unit m² and a strain has no unit, \(k\) has the unit m⁻². Let us take \(k = -10\) m⁻², so that the strains at the edges are a thousandth in size, which by section 1.1 is the upper limit for the strains of steel structures. The longitudinal fibre in the middle of the strip, where \(y = 0\), is to keep its length. The longitudinal fibres at the edges, where \(y = \pm 10\) mm, are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}01\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}001\), by a thousandth. The fibres at the height \(y = \pm 5\) mm are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}005\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00025\), four times less, because \(y\) is half as large there and so \(y^2\) is four times smaller. The transverse fibres are to keep their length, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), and the right angles between longitudinal and transverse fibres are to stay right, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\).

Do pieces strained like this fit together into a strip? Figure 1.143 on the right shows the strip cut into five horizontal bands of squares. We strained each band as (1.64) prescribes at its height and placed all bands on top of each other at the left end, so that they touch there. The band in the middle stays straight. The two bands above it curve upward, the two below it downward, and the farther a band lies from the middle, the more it curves. So gaps open between the bands, wider and wider toward the right end. The pieces do not fit together.

For comparison, figure 1.143 in the middle shows the same strip with the prescribed strain

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{y}{R} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \qquad R = 10\ \text{m} ,\]

and the other components zero. The longitudinal fibres above the middle get longer and those below it shorter, in proportion to the distance from the middle, at the edges by a thousandth, since \(0{,}01\ \text{m} / 10\ \text{m} = 0{,}001\). Here all bands curve in the same way, like parts of rings around the same centre, and they fit together without gaps. A bent horizontal bar, which we will treat in chapter 5, curves in a similar way.

For the second strip a displacement field exists. It is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{x\,y}{R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{x^2}{2R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

Let us check it with (1.63). We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives in which the other variables are treated as numbers, with the rules of lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation.

  1. In \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) the factor \(y/R\) is a constant, and the derivative of \(x\) with respect to \(x\) is \(1\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\).
  2. The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(y\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\).
  3. We have \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = x/R\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -2x/(2R) = -x/R\). The sum is zero, so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(x/R - x/R) = 0\).
  4. The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is zero, and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) do not depend on \(z\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero.

The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -x^2/(2R)\) does not depend on the height \(y\). So all longitudinal fibres curve into the same shape, and that is exactly why the bands fit together (figure 1.143, middle). The right end of the strip at \(x = 0{,}2\) m drops by \(0{,}2^2/(2 \cdot 10)\ \text{m} = 0{,}002\) m, by 2 mm.

For the first strip, though, we will not find such a field. Before we show this, let us write down precisely what we are looking for.

Definition 1.123 Compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije)

Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be functions of three variables defined at the interior points of a body. These functions are compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije) if there is a continuously differentiable displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 1.90), defined at the same points, such that the equations (1.63) hold at each of them.

Source: BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF p. 46), CM §3.7.1 (PDF p. 149).

The word compatibility means the ability to go together: strains are compatible if the strained pieces go together into a whole body. By definition 1.23 a displacement field assigns to every point a single displacement vector. This matters: pieces that do not fit together would mean that the same point had to get two different displacements, one as part of one piece and another as part of its neighbour. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) are compatible, since we found a displacement field for them. For the strains (1.64) we will show in section 1.18.3 that they are not.

Why do the bands of the first strip curve differently (figure 1.143, right)? The longitudinal fibres at different heights shorten differently, and we will see that this makes the strip curve, and the faster the strain changes with height, the more strongly it curves. To write this precisely we need the derivative of a partial derivative and the fact that it does not matter in which order we differentiate twice.

1.18.2 Second partial derivatives

Let us return to the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a diameter of 10 mm hangs and stretches under its own weight. It is held in an idealized way: only the point \(O\) at the centre of the top end is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie horizontally. By (1.18) the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of the displacement, along the axis \(y\), is

\[u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \qquad a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} ,\]

and by the table in section 1.7.2 its partial derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,y .\]

In section 1.7.3 we saw that the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) at the depth \(x + \Delta x\) is slightly different from that at the depth \(x\), because lower down the bar thins less (figure 1.48). So a partial derivative is again a function of the point, and we can ask how fast it changes as we move. This is a derivative of a derivative.

Let us compute how fast \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) changes with depth. We split the expression \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) into \(-0{,}6\,a\,L + 0{,}6\,a\,x\). The first term is a constant, with derivative zero, and by lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation the second has the derivative \(0{,}6\,a\). So

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big) = 0{,}6\,a = 1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

When we go down by 1 m, the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) grows by \(1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Since it is negative, its size decreases: lower down the bar thins less.

Definition 1.124 Second partial derivatives (drugi parcialni odvodi)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, and let its partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\) exist at all points whose distance from the point \(P\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Then \(\partial f / \partial x\) is again a function of three variables, defined at these points. Its partial derivative with respect to \(y\) at the point \(P\), if it exists, is the second partial derivative (drugi parcialni odvod) of the function \(f\), first with respect to \(x\) and then with respect to \(y\):

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big)(P) . \tag{1.65}\]

In the same way we define the second partial derivative for every pair of variables from \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), also for a pair of equal variables, which we write \(\partial^2 f / \partial x^2\). A second partial derivative with respect to two different variables is a mixed partial derivative (mešani odvod). Partial derivatives of third order are obtained in the same way from second partial derivatives, for example

\[\frac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\,\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}\Big)(P) .\]

Source: LEBL2 §8.6 (PDF p. 60), for functions of \(n\) variables and derivatives of any order.

A second partial derivative at a point is a number. As a function of the point it is again a function of three variables, which we can differentiate further. A function of three variables has nine second partial derivatives, one for each of the nine choices of the first and the second variable. The notation \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) is read from right to left: first we differentiate with respect to the variable standing closest to \(f\), that is \(x\), and then with respect to \(y\). Some books write a mixed derivative with subscripts, \(f_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and then the subscripts stand in the opposite order to our notation (LEBL2, PDF p. 60). As with partial derivatives, we do not use subscripts. The condition that \(\partial f / \partial x\) exists at all points near \(P\) is needed because the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 needs the function \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the points \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) for all small enough \(\Delta y\).

For the hanging bar we computed above the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\,\partial y = 0{,}6\,a\). Let us compute the other second partial derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) too. The derivative in a row is the first derivative, and the column says with respect to which variable we differentiate it the second time. Differentiating \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) with respect to \(y\) gives \(0{,}6\,a\), and with respect to \(x\) and to \(z\) zero, because \(x\) and \(z\) do not appear in the expression. The derivative of \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) with respect to \(x\) we computed above, and with respect to \(y\) and to \(z\) it is zero. The derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z\) is zero at every point, so all its derivatives are zero as well.

w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(0\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)

The two mixed derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) are equal (figure 1.144):

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\big(0{,}6\,a\,y\big) = 0{,}6\,a , \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big) = 0{,}6\,a .\]

The first says how fast \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) changes with the distance from the axis, that is, the rate at which the displacement toward the axis decreases as we go down. The second says how fast \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) changes with depth, that is, how strongly the bar thins. These two things sound different, yet they are equal. For the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), too, the two mixed derivatives are equal for every pair of variables. For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), for example, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\,\partial x = \partial / \partial y\,\big(2a\,(L - x)\big) = 0\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y = \partial / \partial x\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\).

Is the equality a coincidence? Let us look at four values of a function \(f\) at the corners of a small rectangle whose sides are parallel to the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.145). Let the coordinate \(z\) be \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) everywhere, so we leave it out of the notation and write \(f(x, y)\) instead of \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\). The corners are \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive numbers. We add the values with alternating signs:

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\quad - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) + f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.66}\]

We call the number \(g(s, t)\) the double difference. Its terms can be grouped in two ways.

  1. The first two and the last two: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change of \(f\) along the top side, in the direction of the axis \(x\), minus the change along the bottom side. Divided by \(s\), it gives approximately \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\) minus \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\). Divided further by \(t\), it gives approximately how fast \(\partial f / \partial x\) changes with \(y\), that is \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\).
  2. The first and the third, and the second and the fourth: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change along the right side, in the direction of the axis \(y\), minus the change along the left side. Divided by \(t\) and by \(s\), it is approximately \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\).

So the same number \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) approximates both mixed derivatives, and we expect them to be equal. For the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) of the hanging bar, which does not depend on \(z\), the double difference is

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= -0{,}6\,a\,\big[(L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\qquad - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)\,y_{\mathrm{P}} + (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\big] . \end{aligned}\]

In the square bracket the first two terms together give \(-s\,(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), and the last two give \(s\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\). The sum is \(-s\,t\), so \(g(s, t) = 0{,}6\,a\,s\,t\) and \(g(s, t)/(s\,t) = 0{,}6\,a\) for all \(s\) and \(t\), exactly the two mixed derivatives. For a general function, though, the quotient \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) need not equal either of the mixed derivatives at \(P\). With the mean value theorem 1.84, used twice, we show that it equals a mixed derivative at some point inside the rectangle. As the rectangle shrinks, this point approaches \(P\), and if the mixed derivative is continuous, its value approaches the value at \(P\).

Theorem 1.125 Symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (zamenljivost mešanih odvodov)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables defined at all points whose distance from the point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Let the partial derivatives \(\partial f / \partial x\) and \(\partial f / \partial y\) and the mixed derivatives \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) and \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) exist at all these points, and let the two mixed derivatives be continuous at the point \(P\) (definition 1.67). Then

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) . \tag{1.67}\]

The same holds for the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for the variables \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) are the same number. Throughout the proof the coordinate \(z\) equals \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\), so we leave it out of the notation: \(f(x, y)\) means \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), and likewise for the partial derivatives.

  1. We pick positive numbers \(s\) and \(t\) with \(s^2 + t^2 < r^2\). Every point \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + v, y_{\mathrm{P}} + w)\) with \(0 \le v \le s\) and \(0 \le w \le t\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{v^2 + w^2} \le \sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) from \(P\) ((1.10)). So the rectangle with the corners \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) lies entirely among the points at which, by assumption, we know all the derivatives used. Let \(g(s, t)\) be the double difference (1.66).
  2. For numbers \(v\) between \(0\) and \(t\) we define the function of one variable \(\varphi_1(v) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v)\). This is the change of \(f\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + v\). Putting in \(v = t\) and \(v = 0\) we get \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = g(s, t)\), since these are exactly the four terms of (1.66).
  3. Each of the two terms of \(\varphi_1\) is the function \(f\) along a line in the direction of the axis \(y\). Its derivative with respect to \(v\) is, by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, the partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial y\), which exists by assumption. The derivative of a difference is the difference of the derivatives (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation), so \(\varphi_1\) has a derivative at every point of the interval \([0, t]\), a one-sided one at the end points (definition 1.9). Since the inequality \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) is strict, the points just outside the rectangle are also closer to \(P\) than \(r\), so the partial derivative exists at the end points too as a limit on both sides, and this is also a limit from one side (section 1.3.3):
    \[\varphi_1'(v) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) .\]
    By lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, \(\varphi_1\) is continuous on the interval \([0, t]\).
  4. By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a number \(t_1\) between \(0\) and \(t\) such that \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = \varphi_1'(t_1)\,t\). By steps 2 and 3, therefore,
    \[g(s, t) = t\,\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\Big) .\]
  5. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) we define \(\psi_1(w) = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). The bracket of step 4 is \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0)\). The function \(\psi_1\) is the function \(\partial f / \partial y\) along the horizontal segment at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). Its derivative with respect to \(w\) is, by the definition of second partial derivatives 1.124, the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\), which exists by assumption, so \(\psi_1\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, s]\), one-sidedly at the end points, since the mixed derivative exists there as a limit on both sides, as in step 3. So by lemma 1.79 it is continuous on \([0, s]\).
  6. By the mean value theorem there is a number \(s_1\) between \(0\) and \(s\) such that \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0) = \psi_1'(s_1)\,s\). Let \(Q_1 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_1, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). With step 4 we get
    \[g(s, t) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) .\]
  7. We proceed in the same way with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swapped. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) let \(\varphi_2(w) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), the change in the direction of the axis \(y\) at the place \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w\). For it, too, \(\varphi_2(s) - \varphi_2(0) = g(s, t)\). Steps 3 to 6 with the variables swapped give a number \(s_2\) between \(0\) and \(s\), a number \(t_2\) between \(0\) and \(t\) and the point \(Q_2 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_2)\) such that
    \[g(s, t) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) .\]
  8. The right-hand sides of steps 6 and 7 are equal, because both equal \(g(s, t)\). We divide them by \(s\,t \neq 0\):
    \[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) .\]
  9. Now we use continuity. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). Since \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) is continuous at \(P\), for the error \(\eta/2\) there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that the value at every point whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(\delta_1\) differs from the value at \(P\) by less than \(\eta/2\). Likewise, for \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\).
  10. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) and \(r\), and take \(s = t = \rho/2\). Then \(s^2 + t^2 = \rho^2/2 < r^2\), so step 1 applies. The points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are at a distance less than \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} = \rho/\sqrt 2 < \rho\) from \(P\), since their coordinates lie strictly between the coordinates of the corners. Therefore
    \[\Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} , \qquad \Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} .\]
  11. By step 8 the difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is the sum of the differences of step 10:
    \[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big) + \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big) .\]
    By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1), and by step 10 the absolute value of the left-hand side is less than \(\eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).
  12. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely. The absolute value of the difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is not negative and is smaller than every positive number, so by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers it equals zero. The mixed derivatives at \(P\) are equal.
  13. For the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for \(y\) and \(z\) steps 1 to 12 are the same, only with the variables renamed.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.6.2 (PDF pp. 60-62). The source assumes that all partial derivatives up to second order are continuous at all points of an open set, and remarks that continuity of the two mixed derivatives is enough. The proof uses continuity only at the point \(P\). Steps 9 to 12 replace the limit of a function of two variables used by the source and are not from the source.

The proof wrote the double difference twice as the product of \(s\,t\) and a mixed derivative, once with one order of differentiation and once with the other, each time at some point inside the rectangle. As the rectangle shrinks, both points approach \(P\), and the continuity of the mixed derivatives makes their values approach the values at \(P\). The mean value theorem did the same job here, twice, as for the change of a field over a short step in section 1.15: it turned a difference of values into a derivative at a point in between.

Is the assumption of continuity needed? It is. In Exercise 8.6.2 (PDF p. 62), LEBL2 gives the function of two variables

\[f(x, y) = \frac{x\,y\,(x^2 - y^2)}{x^2 + y^2} \quad \text{for } (x, y) \neq (0, 0) , \qquad f(0, 0) = 0 ,\]

whose first order partial derivatives exist and are continuous, while the mixed derivatives exist but are not continuous at the origin and differ there. On the axis \(y\) the difference quotient with respect to \(x\) is \(\big(f(h, y) - f(0, y)\big)/h = y\,(h^2 - y^2)/(h^2 + y^2)\), and as \(h\) goes to zero with \(y \neq 0\), the numerator approaches \(-y^3\), the denominator \(y^2\), and the quotient \(-y\). So \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, y) = -y\), and this holds at \(y = 0\) too, since \(f\) is zero everywhere on the axis \(x\). In the same way we get the value \(\partial f / \partial y\,(x, 0) = x\) on the axis \(x\). Therefore \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(0, 0) = -1\), \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(0, 0) = 1\). For the hanging bar and for the strips of this section the displacement components are polynomials. Their partial derivatives of all orders are polynomials again, and these are continuous everywhere by corollary 1.69, that polynomials in \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are continuous.

In the equations we are looking for we will differentiate three times and swap the order in several places. So we extend the theorem to third derivatives.

Corollary 1.126 Independence of the order of differentiation (neodvisnost od vrstnega reda odvajanja)

Let \(D\) be a set of points in which every point is interior, that is, around every point \(P\) of \(D\) there is a number \(r > 0\) such that all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) are in \(D\). Let a function \(f\) have partial derivatives of first, second and third order at every point of \(D\), and let all these derivatives be continuous at every point of \(D\). Then at every point of \(D\) the second and third partial derivatives of \(f\) do not depend on the order in which we differentiate.

Proof
